records.jp: 『……そう……じっとしてて……いい子……』
records.en: Nurse Youko: 『...yes... stand firm like that... good boy...』
comments: Both him and his d***************k. Do notice how she's imitating Misato waaaay too close... -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese instructs the person to keep still; 'stand firm' gives a different posture and connotation.

highlights.text: stand firm

records.jp: 「しなかったら……太一にいじめられると思ったから……」
records.en: Youko: "If I hadn't... I thought Taichi would bully me..."
records.assessment: The Japanese gives the reason for acting: she thought Taichi would bully her if she did not do it. The English strands the conditional as an earlier unreal event and obscures that causal relation.

highlights.text: Youko: "If I hadn't... I thought Taichi would bully me..."

records.jp: 「してもいじめる」
records.en: Taichi: "Bullied regardless."
records.assessment: Taichi says that he will bully her even if she does help. The English removes the speaker and object and turns the threat into a bare past participle.

highlights.text: Bullied regardless.

records.jp: 端正な顔を、粘土のようにこねる。
records.en: Her noblewoman's face kneads like clay.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi kneads her well-formed face like clay. The English makes the face itself perform the kneading.

highlights.text: Her noblewoman's face kneads like clay.

records.jp: 基本が、排除するかスルーするかのどちらかだから。
records.en: Because at her foundation there are either removal or ignoring all the way through.
comments: See CCC3005 -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese explains that her basic responses are either eliminating something or ignoring it. The English produces an ungrammatical abstract construction and does not state those two alternatives clearly.

highlights.text: Because at her foundation there are either removal or ignoring all the way through.

records.jp: 「やわらかいほっぺだなぁ」
records.en: Taichi: "Soft cheeks yours, aren't they."
records.assessment: The Japanese is an ordinary observation that her cheeks are soft. The English inverts the possessive and attaches a mismatched question tag.

highlights.text: Soft cheeks yours, aren't they.

records.jp: 「ほっぺなんて持ってるから悪いんだ」
records.en: Taichi: "It's your having cheeks that's to blame."
records.assessment: The joke blames her for having cheeks; the English preserves the content in a markedly malformed possessive-gerund construction.

highlights.text: It's your having cheeks that's to blame.

records.jp: 見れば、軽い寝息。
records.en: On closer look, I see she has a light sleeper's breathing.
comments: PCP CCA0010
records.assessment: The Japanese describes the faint, gentle sound of her sleeping breath. The English instead classifies her as a light sleeper.

highlights.text: a light sleeper's breathing

records.jp: 額の髪をかきわける。
records.en: I draw through her hair to her forehead.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi parts or brushes aside the hair over her forehead. The highlighted phrase describes an unclear movement through the hair toward the forehead.

highlights.text: draw through her hair to her forehead

records.jp: 「……何するのさ」
records.en: Taichi: "...whass'at for."
records.assessment: The Japanese asks what Taichi is doing. The English asks for the purpose of a completed act and adds an unsupported dialect spelling.

highlights.text: whass'at for

records.jp: やはり世はすべからくメタゲーム。
records.en: Indeed society is metagame in every way.
comments: See CCB0005. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese generalizes that the world is entirely a metagame. The English substitutes society, omits the article or mass construction needed in English, and calques the predicate.

highlights.text: society is metagame in every way

records.jp: だが接近戦では勝ち目はない。
records.en: But close-quarters combat has no chance of success.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi has no chance of winning in close combat. The English assigns the lack of a chance to combat itself.

highlights.text: close-quarters combat has no chance of success

records.jp: 「こうなったら……キミの胸を揉んでやるさ！」
records.en: Taichi: "If this is how it's going to be... then your chest I shall be going over now!"
comments: 揉 Oh, it's not over by far. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi threatens to grope her breasts. The highlighted clause is ungrammatical and describes merely going over a chest rather than the explicit action.

highlights.text: your chest I shall be going over now

records.jp: 知ったことか！
records.en: What does she know!
records.assessment: 知ったことか is a dismissive declaration that he does not care. The English instead questions her knowledge.

highlights.text: What does she know!

records.jp: 「このまま揉み貫く！」
records.en: Taichi: "I shall be rubbing right through it!"
records.assessment: The Japanese means that Taichi will carry the groping through despite the risk. The English suggests rubbing physically through an object.

highlights.text: rubbing right through it

records.jp: 「そう……ノーブラ」
records.en: Youko: "Indeed... no-bra."
comments: See CCA0016. Someone was watching. See CCD1001 for more on this. -GHS
records.assessment: ノーブラ means that she is braless. The English copies the Japanese abbreviation as a nonstandard English noun.

highlights.text: no-bra

records.jp: 胸が肉質が高ければ高いほど、その分解速度は加速される。
records.en: The higher the voluminousness of the chest, the faster the velocity of that disassembly.
comments: And since the speed is high, the voluminousness of the chest is maximum. Therefore the chest is more likely to be Misato's than Youko's. And the trap was that "Youko" took Misato's bra off. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the better the quality of the flesh, the faster his intellect disintegrates. The English changes quality into volume and uses the malformed comparative 'higher the voluminousness.'

highlights.text: The higher the voluminousness of the chest, the faster the velocity of that disassembly.

records.jp: 気がつくと、両手で揉み込んでいた。
records.en: Before I knew it, I was sinking them into with both hands.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he found himself kneading with both hands. The English supplies the wrong action and leaves the preposition without an object.

highlights.text: sinking them into with both hands

records.jp: 耳に入って、理性を蒸発させる。
records.en: It enters the ear and make my rationality evaporate.
comments: Now THAT is dangerous. Mimi... -GHS
records.assessment: The grammatical subject is the singular voice, so the English verb must be 'makes.'

highlights.text: make my rationality evaporate

records.jp: まんまと誘惑されちゃってる。
records.en: Artfully been made prey of temptation.
records.assessment: まんまと means that he has been thoroughly or neatly taken in. 'Artfully' attributes artistic skill to the unstated process rather than describing his complete capitulation.

highlights.text: Artfully

records.jp: 先輩が起きてきた。
records.en: Senpai had awakened.
records.assessment: The Japanese reports that she woke up at this point. The past perfect incorrectly places the awakening before another past reference point.

highlights.text: had awakened

records.jp: 俺たちの痴態に目を留めた。
records.en: She took notice of our foolishness.
comments: And this is the absolutely first time ever in the whole of Cross Channel that anyone interacts with both Youko and Taichi... or do they? -GHS
records.assessment: 痴態 denotes the indecent or disgraceful spectacle before her. 'Foolishness' suppresses that specifically compromising quality.

highlights.text: foolishness

records.jp: 乳首と指先を切断してのける。
records.en: It severs the contact between fingertip and udder.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the chop severs contact between nipple and fingertip. 'Udder' replaces the human body part with an animal organ.

highlights.text: udder

records.jp: 「今のはイエロー停学ですから！」
records.en: Misato: "That now was a yellow suspension do you know!"
comments: RED SUSPENSION C'MON! -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese comic disciplinary declaration is intelligible, but the English word order and unpunctuated tag are ungrammatical.

highlights.text: That now was a yellow suspension do you know!

records.jp: 先輩は首を落とすような勇ましい仕草で、腕を薙いだ。
records.en: With a heroic gesture that reminds of the slaying of her enemy, Senpai scythed her arm sideways.
comments: It's a very chuuni gesture. And the very next line... -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese compares the bold arm motion to cutting off a head; it does not introduce an enemy whose slaying she recalls.

highlights.text: of her enemy

records.jp: 互いに同じ空間に居合わせることさえまれになった。
records.en: The mere mutual simultaneous presence of both in the same space became rarity.
records.assessment: The English count noun requires an article: their sharing the same space became a rarity.

highlights.text: became rarity

records.jp: 俺たちの不和は、誰の間にもあったのだ。
records.en: Our discord was something that existed between anyone.
comments: OK, Japan, you will now hand over the brilliant mind who decided fuwa is also friction, or it's 不和不和 time. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that discord existed among every one of them. 'Between anyone' is ungrammatical and fails to express the group-wide distribution.

highlights.text: existed between anyone

records.jp: 気がつくと曜子ちゃんは消えていた。
records.en: When I come to notice, Youko-chan had disappeared.
comments: As always, if she had never been there in the first place. Or, given Misato's refusal of noticing Taichi, maybe as if he was the one who left. -GHS
records.assessment: The surrounding narration is past-tense; the Japanese means 'when I noticed' or 'before I knew it,' not the malformed present-tense phrase.

highlights.text: When I come to notice

records.jp: 少しばかり物足りない。
records.en: A bit and no more of dissatisfaction.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that something feels a little lacking or unsatisfying. The English is an ungrammatical noun fragment and adds the unsupported limit 'and no more.'

highlights.text: A bit and no more of dissatisfaction.

records.jp: 少しばかり自分の席に座ってみる。
records.en: A while and no more I try to sit down in my seat.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he tries sitting in his own seat for a little while. The English uses inverted word order and again invents 'and no more.'

highlights.text: A while and no more I try to sit down in my seat.

records.jp: 少しばかり、物思いにふけってみる。
records.en: I will try to lose myself in reverie, a while and no more.
comments: He's just come to school, and he's going to sleep? This is narcolepsy. -GHS
records.assessment: 少しばかり means 'for a little while'; it does not insist 'and no more,' and the phrase is misplaced after the object.

highlights.text: a while and no more

records.jp: 目が覚める。
records.en: I was awake.
records.assessment: The Japanese narrates the transition of waking up. The English gives a past state of already being awake.

highlights.text: I was awake

records.jp: 机に突っ伏して寝ていたらしい。
records.en: Seems I had fallen prostrate on the desk and slept.
records.assessment: The Japanese says he apparently fell asleep slumped face-down over the desk. 'Fallen prostrate' suggests a full-body posture and coordinating it with 'slept' obscures the single event.

highlights.text: fallen prostrate on the desk and slept

records.jp: 人と触れあうことで生じる、様々な欲望の中で。
records.en: In the midst of so many desires produced by a meeting of touches with other people.
records.assessment: The Japanese refers to interacting or coming into contact with other people. The English calques the components into a physically incoherent 'meeting of touches.'

highlights.text: a meeting of touches with other people

records.jp: アンテナの根本には、機材やら工具やらが置かれている。
records.en: At the base of the antenna, machine parts and tools and the like lie scattered about.
records.assessment: 機材 means equipment or gear, not machine parts; 'lie scattered' also adds disorder to items merely said to be placed there.

highlights.text: machine parts

records.jp: アンテナを立ててＳＯＳ。これでバッチリ。
records.en: An SOS sent via the antenna. That fits right on the mark.
comments: The SOS is also hers, if it's yet not clear for some reason -GHS
records.assessment: これでバッチリ means that this makes the plan all set or perfect. The English invents fitting on a mark.

highlights.text: fits right on the mark

records.jp: みみ先輩らしい、素敵な計画である。
records.en: A wonderful plan this, so like Mimi-senpai.
records.assessment: The Japanese calls it a wonderful plan typical of her. The English uses an unlicensed inversion and a verbless comparison.

highlights.text: A wonderful plan this, so like Mimi-senpai.

records.jp: ははあ。確かに。
records.en: Hahaha! That's for sure.
comments: gurlz r short. Also see CCA0025C. SYMBOLISM!!! -GHS
records.assessment: ははあ is a sound of realization, like 'aha,' not laughter.

highlights.text: Hahaha!

records.jp: 脚立を立てて、その上にのぼる。
records.en: I erect the stepladder, and climb above.
comments: ... -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he climbs onto the stepladder. 'Climb above' describes a position higher than it rather than mounting it.

highlights.text: climb above

records.jp: 仕上げてやった。
records.en: And I was finished.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi finished the work for her. The English passive instead says that Taichi himself was finished.

highlights.text: I was finished.

records.jp: 『ワイヤー切れた、代用できるものを探さないと……（泣）』
records.en: 『A wire snapped, and I cannot look for something that could work as replacement (sob)』
records.assessment: 探さないと means that she must look for a substitute. The English reverses this into an inability to look.

highlights.text: I cannot look for something

records.jp: みんなで放送をするということが、妙に心を弾ませた。
records.en: the idea of broadcasting with everyone together was a strange encouragement for my heart.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the idea strangely excited or exhilarated him. The English turns the emotional response into an external encouragement directed at his heart.

highlights.text: a strange encouragement for my heart

records.jp: 健全さからは対角に位置する俺たちの、琴線に触れるのだ。
records.en: Wholesomeness harps on the heartstrings of us who exist on the opposite side from it.
comments: どうしてそんな琴！ -GHS
records.assessment: 琴線に触れる means 'strikes a chord.' 'Harps on' means to repeat something tiresomely and therefore reverses the intended attraction.

highlights.text: Wholesomeness harps on the heartstrings

records.jp: 「お元気ー？」
records.en: Nanaka: "In spirits?"
comments: I actually don't think there's a law that demands ghosts to always ask this question, but let's say it's totally gonna happen in the near future. It's forwards-compatible thinking, mine. -GHS
records.assessment: お元気 is the ordinary greeting 'How are you?' The bare prepositional fragment is not functional English dialogue here.

highlights.text: In spirits?

records.jp: 「そんなことより、あの祠って―――」
records.en: Taichi: "More importantly, that hokora---"
records.assessment: 祠 is a small shrine. The English leaves the common noun as an unexplained romanized Japanese word instead of translating it.

highlights.text: hokora

records.jp: 「楽しいって、言えるなら、いいじゃん」
records.en: Nanaka: "You said fun, and if you can say that, 's all right."
comments: CP CCA0023
records.assessment: The Japanese says that it is good if he can call the experience fun. The English first asserts that he already said the isolated word 'fun,' contradicting the following denial.

highlights.text: You said fun, and if you can say that

records.jp: つうか会話に脈絡ないんですけど。
records.en: There is no chain of logical connection going through this conversation, however,
comments: Oddly formal -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese colloquially says that the conversation has no logical continuity. The English expands this into an awkward literal chain running through it.

highlights.text: no chain of logical connection going through this conversation

records.jp: なんなんだこの唐突感動イベントは……。
records.en: what is even with this sudden Emotionally Moving Event...
comments: Technical term. It's got a CG and everything! -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese asks what this sudden touching scene is. The English question lacks a grammatical predicate and gratuitously capitalizes its descriptive phrase.

highlights.text: what is even with this sudden Emotionally Moving Event

records.jp: 不思議と、猥雑なものは感じない。
records.en: Inexplicably, I feel nothing out of order.
comments: CP CCA0023
records.assessment: 猥雑 specifically means something lewd, vulgar, or sexually sordid. The English erases that dimension and substitutes the vague idea of disorder.

highlights.text: nothing out of order

records.jp: 「強くならないと生きる資格がないわけじゃないから」
records.en: Nanaka: "Because never becoming strong is not a disqualification from living."
comments: CP CCA0023
records.assessment: The Japanese says that one need not become strong in order to deserve to live. 'Never becoming strong' adds permanent future failure and the nominal construction is an awkward calque.

highlights.text: never becoming strong is not a disqualification from living

records.jp: 「聞いちゃいねぇ」
records.en: Taichi: "Listen to what you're being told!"
records.assessment: 聞いちゃいねぇ means that Taichi was not listening or did not ask for the speech. The English instead orders Nanaka to listen.

highlights.text: Listen to what you're being told!

records.jp: 「ごめん、間違えたよ」
records.en: Nanaka: "Sorry, I mistook you, 's all."
records.assessment: Nanaka says that she was mistaken or got something wrong. 'Mistook you' specifically claims that she confused Taichi's identity with another person's.

highlights.text: I mistook you

records.jp: 「なにと？」
records.en: Taichi: "For what?"
records.assessment: Taichi asks what she mistook him for. 'For what?' instead asks the purpose or reason.

highlights.text: For what?

records.jp: 「理解できるように説明して」
records.en: Taichi: "Explain in ways I can understand."
records.assessment: The line asks for a single intelligible manner of explanation; the English plural produces a malformed collocation.

highlights.text: in ways I can understand

records.jp: 「キミってアンテナ設営の方、着手したみたいだけど、進捗はどう？」
records.en: Nanaka: "Say you, it looks like you're setting out on helping the construction on that antenna, but how's progress?"
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he seems to have begun the antenna installation and asks how it is progressing. The English adds 'helping,' uses a malformed 'setting out on ... construction,' and omits the article before 'progress.'

highlights.text: Nanaka: "Say you, it looks like you're setting out on helping the construction on that antenna, but how's progress?"

records.jp: 「そうだな、いろいろあるんだが」
records.en: Taichi: "Of course, there's a lots and a lots, but..."
records.assessment: The Japanese says simply that there are various things. The English invents repetition and twice combines the singular article with a plural noun.

highlights.text: there's a lots and a lots

records.jp: 「今日は白。でもちょっとかわいいの。ブラとおそろいのやつなんだ」
records.en: Nanaka: "Today they're white. But they're reeeally cute tho. They totally match the bra!"
comments: Buruma are worn OVER panties, so she's not lying. And since her talks with Taichi were all one-sided (Taichi couldn't speak as a baby), the question she's asking and the answer she's giving are all a thing of hers. That's some sexual pranking. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the underwear is somewhat cute and matches the bra. The English raises 'somewhat' to 'really' and adds emphatic slang to both clauses.

highlights.text: reeeally cute tho
totally match

records.jp: 少女の下着に思いを馳せた。
records.en: I reflect nostalgically on the girl's underwear.
comments: Do I even have to write a note here. -GHS
records.assessment: 思いを馳せる means letting one's thoughts dwell on something. The English adds nostalgia, which the Japanese does not state.

highlights.text: reflect nostalgically

records.jp: 「じゃ質問はこれで打ち切ります」
records.en: Nanaka: "Well, the questioning round is with this brought to a close."
records.assessment: The Japanese straightforwardly closes the questions. The English follows Japanese constituent order into an ungrammatical passive construction.

highlights.text: the questioning round is with this brought to a close

records.jp: 腕でバッテンを作る七香。
records.en: Nanaka crosses her arm into a X, making the Batten mark of denial and failure.
comments: See CCD1001, was a nickname proposal. It's also possibly a reference to the prescient diatribe Nyoro~n Churuya-san, which warned about the perils of consuming smoked cheese. Unfortunately they went unlistened, and that caused the great Smoked Collapse Event of 2007, which caused the daily intake of psychotropics in the average Japanese to effectively doubled, curiously to no apparent effect. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Nanaka makes an X with her arms. The English retains batten as an unexplained capitalized Japanese word and invents an explanatory doctrine of denial and failure.

highlights.text: the Batten mark of denial and failure

records.jp: 「次の機会だね」
records.en: Nanaka: "Next chance, 'K."
records.assessment: The Japanese says only that there will be another chance. The English appends an unsupported fragment.

highlights.text: 'K

records.jp: 小首を傾けて、可愛らしく問いかける。
records.en: Tilting my neck, I ask the question in an adorable way.
records.assessment: 小首を傾ける is a slight, often cute tilt of the head. The English substitutes the neck as the body part being tilted.

highlights.text: Tilting my neck

records.jp: 小首を傾けて、可愛らしく返された。
records.en: Tilting her neck, she answered the question in an adorable way.
records.assessment: 小首を傾ける describes a slight tilt of the head, not tilting the neck itself.

highlights.text: Tilting her neck

records.jp: 「まあ……こうなったとしか言えない」
records.en: Nanaka: "Well... besides that it did get like this I can't say."
comments: Well, it's not like anything more happened. Or that she physically *can* tell him anything. -GHS
records.assessment: Nanaka says that she can only say this is how things turned out. The English reverses the limiting construction into an ungrammatical 'besides' clause.

highlights.text: besides that it did get like this I can't say

records.jp: 「理由を考えようにも、ぜーんぜんわかりまっせーん」
records.en: Nanaka: "I think about the reason but still I don't understand aaaanything at aaall."
records.assessment: 理由を考えようにも means 'even if I try to think of the reason.' The English states an ongoing successful act of thinking and loses the concessive relation.

highlights.text: I think about the reason but still

records.jp: 「む、何が？」
records.en: Nanaka: "Mnuh, what is?"
records.assessment: The Japanese asks 'What is?' only because the preceding adjective is recoverable in Japanese. English requires that predicate to be supplied, such as 'What is weird?'

highlights.text: what is?

records.jp: 「普通、キミみたいな役割はもっと大人しい電波っぽい娘がやるものだろ！」
records.en: Taichi: "Normally, roles like yours would be assigned to a much more docile Denpa-emitter of a crazy girl, definitely."
comments: Nanaka's role as the Mysterious Phenomenon Explainer is indeed odd... until one notices the Mysterious Phenomenon is not scientific in nature, as it'd be in your normal anime or VN, but religious. Normally, the role would be Youko's, in fact, which means when SHE explains it it has to be troll. See CCZAS when Taichi (mis)"fixes" this discrepancy by making Youko the Club President. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says the role normally belongs to a quieter, denpa-like girl. The English invents an emitter, explicitly declares her crazy, and adds 'definitely.'

highlights.text: a much more docile Denpa-emitter of a crazy girl, definitely

records.jp: 「キミは勝ち気な幼なじみっぽいんだから、造形にふさわしく物語からの要請事項に従って俺の隣にでも住んで毎朝起こしに来いよ！」
records.en: Taichi: "You're the unyielding childhood friend type, therefore, obey the matters demanded from stories suitable to be molds and live next door to me and come wake me up every day!"
comments: "Be like an eroge character ripoff". Ironically, Youko (the real osananajimi) does come wake him, except... but even stranger, this same term 要請事項 returns in Youko's sendback route, see CCD5001 - this unfortunately demands a sort of odd translation so the term can be consistent. See CCZDXC for more molding. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese invokes story conventions appropriate to Nanaka's character design. The English turns the design into things suitable to be molds and produces an unintelligible demand phrase.

highlights.text: the matters demanded from stories suitable to be molds

records.jp: 「……アホかおまいは」
records.en: Nanaka: "...an idiot ya are."
records.assessment: The source uses a rough second-person form, but the English creates an ungrammatical inversion and a generic eye-dialect 'ya.'

highlights.text: an idiot ya are

records.jp: 「そーいうのを表層的な思考と言うんだ」
records.en: Taichi: "For that may certainly be said to be a surface-level reasoning!"
records.assessment: Nanaka says, 'That's what you call superficial thinking.' The English uses an ungoverned 'for,' an unnecessary passive, and a count noun where English requires 'reasoning' as a mass noun.

highlights.text: For that may certainly be said to be a surface-level reasoning!

records.jp: 「変わったことがしたければ、根底からやってみろ。今まで誰もしたことがないようなやつをだ！」
records.en: Taichi: "If you wanna make a change, try doing it from the grounds up. Do something that no one has ever done up until now!"
records.assessment: 根底から corresponds to the fixed English expression 'from the ground up,' with singular 'ground.'

highlights.text: from the grounds up

records.jp: 「俺は表層的なアンチテーゼにばかり目を奪われた低脳短絡ですーっ！！」
records.en: Taichi: "I am a short-cutting imbecile who is exclusively enthralled by superficial antithesiiiis!!!"
comments: See CCZDXC. Also, Tanaka just called anyone who thought this was about plot twists a moron. Condolences. -GHS
records.assessment: 低脳短絡 insults a stupid, simplistic thinker. 'Short-cutting' instead describes someone who takes practical shortcuts and is not an idiomatic personal epithet.

highlights.text: short-cutting imbecile

records.jp: 「泣くな泣くな、若者」
records.en: Nanaka: "Cry not, cry not little one."
comments: Mommy consoling her crying baby... as he, uhm, fails to design an eroge??? -GHS
records.assessment: 若者 addresses him as a young man or youth, not as a small child.

highlights.text: little one

records.jp: 「コレがまた意外と違うんだなぁ」
records.en: Nanaka: "This one's already unexpectedly different, yes."
records.assessment: Nanaka says, roughly, 'Surprisingly, that actually varies.' The English's 'already' and 'this one' do not identify the varying behavior and the sentence is not idiomatic.

highlights.text: This one's already unexpectedly different, yes.

records.jp: 「他の人たちは日曜夜の時点でもう気持ちが決まってるから、毎回似たような行動取るんだけどさ」
records.en: Nanaka: "The other guys, their emotions are already decided on that point on Sunday night, so they take similar actions every time."
comments: Now that's a complete load. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the others have made up their minds by Sunday night. The English literalizes feelings as decided objects and mistranslates the time boundary as a point on Sunday.

highlights.text: their emotions are already decided on that point on Sunday night

records.jp: 「うーん」
records.en: Taichi: "Naaah."
records.assessment: うーん marks hesitation or thought, like 'hmm.' 'Nah' communicates rejection or disagreement.

highlights.text: Naaah.

records.jp: だから今の状況は、そう悪くないと思ってる。
records.en: Therefore I don't think the way things are right now are all that bad.
records.assessment: The head of the subject is singular 'way,' so the English predicate must be 'is.'

highlights.text: the way things are right now are

records.jp: 「言ったことは守ろう」
records.en: Nanaka: "What I say I'll do."
records.assessment: Nanaka proposes that they keep what was said or honor the agreement. The English makes it a unilateral claim about whatever she says and does.

highlights.text: What I say I'll do.

records.jp: 快活だった表情が、危惧を形作る。
records.en: The expression on her face that was cheerful now takes the shape of apprehension.
records.assessment: The Japanese says her formerly cheerful expression becomes one of concern. The English literalizes the emotion as a shape taken by the face.

highlights.text: takes the shape of apprehension

records.en: Taichi: "...well."
records.assessment: そう acknowledges what she has said, like 'I see.' 'Well' instead signals hesitation or transition.

highlights.text: well

records.jp: 和ませることにした。
records.en: I decided to soften this down.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi decides to lighten the mood. 'Soften this down' is not the English idiom for that action.

highlights.text: soften this down

records.jp: 「ブラはフロントホックをつけて欲しいんですけど」
records.en: Taichi: "I would sure like for the bra to be front hook."
comments: Formal -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese requests a front-hook bra. English requires the compound adjective 'front-hooked' or the noun phrase 'a front-hook bra.'

highlights.text: the bra to be front hook

records.jp: 「自分で思っているほど、たいしたギャグじゃない」
records.en: Nanaka: "That's not as funny a joke as you think it is inside yourself."
comments: And she knows exactly. -GHS
records.assessment: 自分で思っているほど means 'as funny as you think it is.' The English adds a literal and redundant interior location.

highlights.text: inside yourself

records.jp: じきに我が家。
records.en: we ended up at my house.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that they soon reach his house. 'Ended up' implies an unintended destination not present in the source.

highlights.text: ended up at my house

records.jp: どこに帰っているんだろう、七香は。
records.en: where would Nanaka even go home to?
comments: In Heaven, DUH. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi wonders where she habitually goes home. The conditional 'would go' instead frames a hypothetical destination.

highlights.text: where would Nanaka even go home to?

records.jp: 頭だけ巡らせて、背後を視野におさめた。
records.en: I turned the head alone, laying the rear in my field of vision.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he turns only his head and brings the space behind him into view. The English uses 'rear' as an object and describes laying it somewhere.

highlights.text: laying the rear in my field of vision

records.jp: 離れているにもかかわらず、声は冴え冴えと耳に届いた。
records.en: Her voice carried clear and crisp in spite of being so distant, as if it had fangs that bit into my ears.
comments: See CCC0000. Sarcastic remark on how this has to be coincidental when, obviously, it is not. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says only that her voice reaches him with striking clarity despite the distance. The fangs and biting are invented imagery.

highlights.text: as if it had fangs that bit into my ears

records.jp: 俺も振り返した。
records.en: I also asserted back,
comments: Multiple meanings -GHS
records.assessment: 振り返した means that Taichi waves back. 'Asserted' is an unrelated speech-act verb.

highlights.text: asserted back

records.jp: 「お元気ー？」
records.en: Nanaka: "In spiriiits?"
comments: CP CCC0045A
records.assessment: お元気 is the greeting 'How are you?' Stretching the vowel does not make the bare prepositional fragment functional English.

highlights.text: In spiriiits?

records.jp: 「そんなことより、あの祠って―――」
records.en: Taichi: "More importantly, that hokora---"
comments: CP CCC0045A
records.assessment: 祠 is a small shrine. The English leaves the common noun as an unexplained romanized Japanese word instead of translating it.

highlights.text: hokora

records.jp: 「楽しいって、言えるなら、いいじゃん」
records.en: Nanaka: "You said fun, and if you can say that, 's all right."
comments: CP CCA0023
records.assessment: The Japanese says that it is good if he can call the experience fun. The English first asserts that he already said the isolated word 'fun,' contradicting the following denial.

highlights.text: You said fun, and if you can say that

records.jp: つうか会話に脈絡ないんですけど。
records.en: There is no chain of logical connection going through this conversation, however,
comments: CP CCC0045A
records.assessment: The Japanese colloquially says that the conversation has no logical continuity. The English expands this into an awkward literal chain running through it.

highlights.text: no chain of logical connection going through this conversation

records.jp: なんなんだこの唐突感動イベントは……。
records.en: what is even with this sudden Emotionally Moving Event...
comments: CP CCC0045A
records.assessment: The Japanese asks what this sudden touching scene is. The English question lacks a grammatical predicate and gratuitously capitalizes its descriptive phrase.

highlights.text: what is even with this sudden Emotionally Moving Event

records.jp: 不思議と、猥雑なものは感じない。
records.en: Inexplicably, I feel nothing out of order.
comments: CP CCA0023
records.assessment: 猥雑 specifically means something lewd, vulgar, or sexually sordid. The English erases that dimension and substitutes the vague idea of disorder.

highlights.text: nothing out of order

records.jp: 「強くならないと生きる資格がないわけじゃないから」
records.en: Nanaka: "Because never becoming strong is not a disqualification from living."
comments: CP CCA0023
records.assessment: The Japanese says that one need not become strong in order to deserve to live. 'Never becoming strong' adds permanent future failure and the nominal construction is an awkward calque.

highlights.text: never becoming strong is not a disqualification from living

records.jp: 「聞いちゃいねぇ」
records.en: Taichi: "Listen to what you're being told!"
comments: CP CCC0045A
records.assessment: 聞いちゃいねぇ means that Taichi was not listening or did not ask for the speech. The English instead orders Nanaka to listen.

highlights.text: Listen to what you're being told!

records.jp: 「ごめん、間違えたよ」
records.en: Nanaka: "Sorry, I mistook you, 's all."
comments: CP CCC0045A
records.assessment: Nanaka says that she was mistaken or got something wrong. 'Mistook you' specifically claims that she confused Taichi's identity with another person's.

highlights.text: I mistook you

records.jp: 「なにと？」
records.en: Taichi: "For what?"
comments: CP CCC0045A
records.assessment: Taichi asks what she mistook him for. 'For what?' instead asks the purpose or reason.

highlights.text: For what?

records.jp: 「理解できるように説明して」
records.en: Taichi: "Explain in ways I can understand."
comments: CP CCC0045A
records.assessment: The line asks for a single intelligible manner of explanation; the English plural produces a malformed collocation.

highlights.text: in ways I can understand

records.jp: 「キミってアンテナ設営の方、着手したみたいだけど、進捗はどう？」
records.en: Nanaka: "Say you, it looks like you're setting out on helping the construction on that antenna, but how's progress?"
comments: CP CCC0045A
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he seems to have begun the antenna installation and asks how it is progressing. The English adds 'helping,' uses a malformed 'setting out on ... construction,' and omits the article before 'progress.'

highlights.text: Nanaka: "Say you, it looks like you're setting out on helping the construction on that antenna, but how's progress?"

records.jp: 「そうだな、いろいろあるんだが」
records.en: Taichi: "Of course, there's a lots and a lots, but..."
comments: CP CCC0045A
records.assessment: The Japanese says simply that there are various things. The English invents repetition and twice combines the singular article with a plural noun.

highlights.text: there's a lots and a lots

records.jp: 「今日は白。でもちょっとかわいいの。ブラとおそろいのやつなんだ」
records.en: Nanaka: "Today they're white. But they're reeeally cute tho. They totally match the bra!"
comments: CP CCC0045A
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the underwear is somewhat cute and matches the bra. The English raises 'somewhat' to 'really' and adds emphatic slang to both clauses.

highlights.text: reeeally cute tho
totally match

records.jp: 少女の下着に思いを馳せた。
records.en: I reflect nostalgically on the girl's underwear.
comments: CP CCC0045A
records.assessment: 思いを馳せる means letting one's thoughts dwell on something. The English adds nostalgia, which the Japanese does not state.

highlights.text: reflect nostalgically

records.jp: 「じゃ質問はこれで打ち切ります」
records.en: Nanaka: "Well, the questioning round is with this brought to a close."
comments: CP CCC0045A
records.assessment: The Japanese straightforwardly closes the questions. The English follows Japanese constituent order into an ungrammatical passive construction.

highlights.text: the questioning round is with this brought to a close

records.jp: 腕でバッテンを作る七香。
records.en: Nanaka crosses her arm into a X, making the Batten mark of denial and failure.
comments: CP CCC0045A
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Nanaka makes an X with her arms. The English retains batten as an unexplained capitalized Japanese word and invents an explanatory doctrine of denial and failure.

highlights.text: the Batten mark of denial and failure

records.jp: 「次の機会だね」
records.en: Nanaka: "Next chance, 'K."
comments: CP CCC0045A
records.assessment: The Japanese says only that there will be another chance. The English appends an unsupported fragment.

highlights.text: 'K

records.jp: ここではたと考えた。
records.en: And there I suddenly had a sharp thought.
records.assessment: はたと考える means that he suddenly stops and thinks. The English instead characterizes the thought itself as sharp.

highlights.text: had a sharp thought

records.jp: あれ、こいつ……犯人なんじゃないか。
records.en: My my, this one... couldn't she be the culprit?
records.assessment: あれ marks sudden realization, like 'wait.' 'My my' is a coy or patronizing exclamation with a different voice.

highlights.text: My my

records.jp: 「もうダメだって言ったでしょ」
records.en: Nanaka: "I told you that any more are not happening!"
records.assessment: Nanaka says she already told him there would be no more questions. The English leaves the plural quantifier without a noun and uses a malformed event predicate.

highlights.text: any more are not happening

records.jp: 「ここに」
records.en: Nanaka: "This way."
comments: 個々に, here + individually -GHS
records.assessment: ここに answers 'where?' with 'here.' 'This way' instead points out a direction or method.

highlights.text: This way.

records.jp: どうも、キーパーソンだとは思うんだが……要領を得ないな。
records.en: Somehow, I was thinking of her as a Key Person, but... she doesn't seem to be relevant.
records.assessment: 要領を得ない means that Taichi cannot get a clear answer or make sense of her. It does not mean that she is irrelevant; the preceding clause explicitly calls her a key person.

highlights.text: she doesn't seem to be relevant

records.jp: 「祠行ったでしょ？」
records.en: Nanaka: "Did you go to the hokora then?
records.assessment: 祠 is a small shrine and should not remain as unexplained 'hokora'; the English dialogue also lacks its closing quotation mark.

highlights.text: Nanaka: "Did you go to the hokora then?

records.jp: 「いや、もうあの場所には行きたくないから」
records.en: Taichi: "Nah, I just don't really want to go that place anymore."
records.assessment: English requires the directional preposition: 'go to that place.'

highlights.text: go that place

records.jp: 「んー。あの子は、来て欲しがると思うよ」
records.en: Nanak: "Hmmm. But that girl, I think, would have wanted you to go there!"
records.assessment: The Japanese says she thinks the girl would want Taichi to come. The English changes present hypothetical desire to past desire, reverses 'come' to 'go there,' and misspells the speaker name.

highlights.text: Nanak: "Hmmm. But that girl, I think, would have wanted you to go there!"

records.jp: 曜子ちゃんの敵討ちをしてやれない俺だ。
records.en: Not when I am someone who isn't exacting revenge for you, Youko-chan.
records.assessment: Taichi describes himself as someone unable to avenge her, which is why he cannot face her. The English becomes a fragment, directly addresses her with 'you,' and fails to state the relation to the preceding shame.

highlights.text: Not when I am someone who isn't exacting revenge for you, Youko-chan.

records.jp: 「裏返せば、相手にも自分と対等になって欲しいってことだ」
records.en: Nanaka: "If you look it from the opposite side, it's wanting the other side to become equal to yourself, that's what."
comments: Well, no. If Taichi can't even look at Youko, then the implication is always inferiority, even when superiority is stated. No need to get in cultural polemics: since Taichi correctly believes Youko to be a wimp underneath it all, this may just be an implication of that reality. And, also, that Taichi can't look at Youko because he's the one who killed her, provided she ever existed at all. -GHS
records.assessment: 裏返せば means 'conversely' or 'looked at the other way.' The English construction lacks the required preposition after 'look' and literalizes a side.

highlights.text: If you look it from the opposite side

records.jp: 「ピーナッツ入り柿の種の尊厳を認めるんなら、弱い相手を弱いまま認めないとオカシイんじゃないかな」
records.en: Nanaka: "If you can accept that there's dignity in referring to peanuts as Seeds of Persimmon, then not accepting a weak companion that stays weak is kinda odd isn't it."
comments: Told you they were important. See above for the weakness part. If one can accept peanuts as seeds of persimmon, then one can accept as human what, by the standards of the world, isn't. This would mean Taichi has not forgiven Youko for what she did, not yet at least. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese invokes the dignity of the peanuts included in the snack called kaki no tane. The English instead claims that peanuts themselves are referred to as persimmon seeds.

highlights.text: dignity in referring to peanuts as Seeds of Persimmon

records.jp: 「だね。柿の種は桜庭だけど」
records.en: Taichi: "Ain't it. Kaki no Tane's Sakuraba thing tho."
comments: If Nanaka points to the hokora, and Sakuraba points to Nanaka... -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi agrees, then notes that 'kaki no tane' refers to Sakuraba in their analogy. 'Ain't it' reverses agreement, and the English leaves the snack name untranslated inside a malformed possessive fragment.

highlights.text: Taichi: "Ain't it. Kaki no Tane's Sakuraba thing tho."

records.jp: 「じゃ、気が向いたら行ってみようかな」
records.en: Taichi: "Well, if my mind changes I'll maybe give a try and go."
records.assessment: 気が向いたら means 'if I feel like it.' The English substitutes a change of mind and omits the object required by 'give a try.'

highlights.text: if my mind changes I'll maybe give a try and go

records.jp: 「うむ」
records.en: Nanaka: "'K!"
records.assessment: うむ is an affirmative 'yes' or 'mm-hm.' The clipped slang spelling and exclamation are unsupported.

records.jp: 「あたしもね、人間関係に資格なんてないと思ってる」
records.en: Nanaka: "Me too, yannow, I don't think I'm qualified for human relationships."
comments: It's about time this were revealed to mean nothing of what it sounds like it does. -GHS
records.assessment: Nanaka says that human relationships do not require qualifications. The English instead says that she personally lacks the qualifications for any relationship.

highlights.text: I don't think I'm qualified for human relationships

records.jp: 「太一も一緒の考えなら、嬉しい」
records.en: Nanaka: "The thought that Taichi is the same... it makes me happy."
comments: Think about this for a second: what mother would really be happy for her son to be an antisocial recluse? "Not qualified for human relationships" doesn't mean that; it means he's someone who seeks something higher than what's available in the world. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says she is happy if Taichi shares her view. The English says vaguely that Taichi himself is 'the same.'

highlights.text: The thought that Taichi is the same

records.jp: 「部活も頑張れ。仲間が死んでも頑張れ。大丈夫、来週には笑っていられっから」
records.en: Nanaka: "Give it all on club, too. True Companions may die, but still give it all. You'll be all right, because next week you'll be all laughs."
records.assessment: Nanaka urges him to persist with the club even if companions die and says he will be able to smile next week. The English turns the concessive event into a possibility, invents a capitalized class, and changes smiling into being an object of laughter.

highlights.text: True Companions may die
you'll be all laughs

records.jp: 「うわ、不謹慎なこと言うなっ」
records.en: Taichi: "Whoa, don't say imprudent stuff!"
comments: See CCA0030. Hum, if Kenneth Broadcast Channel would reveal that everyone's insane, this reveals... -GHS
records.assessment: 不謹慎 means insensitive or inappropriate toward a grave subject. 'Imprudent' means merely unwise or incautious.

highlights.text: imprudent

records.jp: 「二人死んでるんだぞー」
records.en: Taichi: "We got two dead dammiiit!"
records.assessment: The Japanese says that two people are dead. The English turns 'dead' into an unheaded count noun, uses a possession construction, and adds a curse.

highlights.text: We got two dead dammiiit!

records.jp: 「なんかさ、不思議な力持ってそうだし、アリバイとかトリックとか超越して自由に殺せるんじゃないの？　神殺人事件とか言ってさ。推理小説でも何でもないけど」
records.en: Taichi: Well, yannow, when it looks like you have inexplicable powers, couldn't you you transcend alibis and tricks and all that and be free to murder? It could be said to be a Murder by God. Not that it's a whodunit novel or anything though."
comments: Eight people, no one else - no one else at all... isn't this just the ultimate closed room mystery in a sense? But if the culprit is chance... then at the very least, it having been picked to be 'chance' is not, itself, random. This is Blessed Luck, meaning the culprit is, in that lateral and not-straightforwards sense, indeed God. This also hints at the motive: since no one dies, death alone can't be the point at all. This is subtly but pervasively anti-nihilistic. -GHS
records.assessment: The English dialogue is missing its opening quotation mark, duplicates 'you,' and renders 自由に殺せる as being 'free' or permitted to murder rather than able to kill without ordinary constraints.

highlights.text: Taichi: Well, yannow, when it looks like you have inexplicable powers, couldn't you you transcend alibis and tricks and all that and be free to murder? It could be said to be a Murder by God. Not that it's a whodunit novel or anything though."

records.jp: 「うーん、神ってのは近いかもね、けっこう」
records.en: Nanaka: "Huuum, God might be close I guess, and very much so."
comments: And she said it. -GHS
records.assessment: 神 is generic here and does not require capitalized 'God.' The appended coordination 'and very much so' is also ungrammatical for けっこう, which modifies how close the comparison is.

highlights.text: God might be close I guess, and very much so

records.jp: 「ひもパンいる？　あげようか？」
records.en: Taichi: "Want some jams? Shall I give you some?"
comments: Original is string bikini + intestine meat bread. This one you prolly gotta dic tho: http://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/jams -GHS
records.assessment: ひもパン means string panties, not jams.

highlights.text: jams

records.jp: 「ううん、いらない。もらってもソッコー捨てる」
records.en: Nanaka: "Nope, don'wann'em. Gimme that stuff and I'll just boom throw it away."
records.assessment: The Japanese says she does not want them and would throw them away immediately if given them. The English uses malformed contractions, changes a hypothetical receipt to an imperative, and invents 'boom.'

highlights.text: don'wann'em. Gimme that stuff and I'll just boom throw it away

records.jp: 「そーかい……」
records.en: Taichi: "Dooo you now..."
records.assessment: そーかい means 'Is that so' or 'I see.' The English asks an incomplete question about what she does.

highlights.text: Dooo you now...

records.jp: どこに帰っているんだろう、七香は。
records.en: where would Nanaka even go home to?
comments: CP CCC0045A
records.assessment: Taichi wonders where she habitually goes home. The conditional 'would go' instead frames a hypothetical destination.

highlights.text: where would Nanaka even go home to?

records.jp: 妙に会話が弾んで。
records.en: An odd conversation was stimulated.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that their conversation became strangely lively. The English makes the conversation itself odd and treats it as something externally stimulated.

highlights.text: An odd conversation was stimulated.

records.jp: ウマがあった。
records.en: We got along well, as if a rider and his horse.
comments: Expanded hyperliteral, given their relationship wasn't that far off. -GHS
records.assessment: ウマが合う is an idiom meaning that they hit it off. The English translates that meaning and then redundantly exposes the source idiom as a new literal comparison.

highlights.text: as if a rider and his horse

records.jp: 群青には完全に自分の世界で生きている者もいる。
records.en:
In Gunjou, there are people who live entirely
into their world,
comments: "I don't see live people." -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says some people at Gunjō live entirely in worlds of their own. The English uses non-Hepburn 'Gunjou' and the wrong preposition 'into.'

highlights.text: Gunjou

live entirely
into their world

records.jp: ある頃から、世界は狂人を生み出しはじめた。
records.en:
Ever since a time, the world had begun to give
birth to madmen.
records.assessment: ある頃から means 'from a certain point' or 'at some point.' The English phrase is not idiomatic and past perfect lacks a later past anchor.

highlights.text: Ever since a time, the world had begun

records.jp: 心の病は、ただ己だけの問題ではなくなっていた。
records.en:
The illness of the heart was no longer merely
a personal problem.
records.assessment: 心の病 here means mental illness, not a cardiac disease or a metaphorical illness of the heart.

highlights.text: illness of the heart

records.jp: 原因はわからない。
records.en: Origin is unknown.
records.assessment: The Japanese says the cause is unknown. The English chooses a different noun and omits the required article.

highlights.text: Origin is unknown.

records.jp: 水面下で動いている、と曜子ちゃんは言っていた。
records.en:
Motion beneath the water surface, said
Youko-chan. All behind closed doors.
comments: Keeping literal water surface, see CCC3012A. It's only maybe a very odd thing for Youko to say since she likely knows of this thing of his - may be why she immediately assumes an observer of worlds in CCD0021. While "beneath the water surface" would be all Youko says, because Youko, it's not clear enough in English so specified. -GHS
records.assessment: Youko says that measures are moving below the surface. The English produces a subjectless fragment from the literal water image and then adds the separate idiom 'behind closed doors.'

highlights.text:
Motion beneath the water surface, said
Youko-chan. All behind closed doors.

records.jp: だから群青学院は存在した。
records.en: That is why Gunjou Institute existed.
records.assessment: The place name 群青 is romanized Gunjō in standard Hepburn. 'Gunjou' uses an ad hoc ou sequence without recorded official Latin-script evidence.

highlights.text: Gunjou

records.jp: 独力で生きる力には欠けているが、当人の心は、もう人のそれを離れてしまっているのだ。
records.en:
Their power to live by their strength is lacking,
but their hearts are already distanced from
those of others.
records.assessment: The Japanese says they lack the ability to live independently and that their minds have departed from the human kind. 'Live by their strength' misstates independence, while 'distanced from those of others' weakens the categorical second clause.

highlights.text:
Their power to live by their strength is lacking,
but their hearts are already distanced from
those of others.

records.jp: 群青では友達を作るのは、少し難しい。
records.en: making friends in Gunjou is somewhat difficult.
records.assessment: The place name 群青 is Gunjō in standard Hepburn; the English uses the non-Hepburn spelling 'Gunjou.'

highlights.text: Gunjou

records.jp: 対話が成立しにくいからだ。
records.en:
Because it is difficult for dialogue to come
into existence.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that successful dialogue or communication is difficult. The English literalizes 成立 as a conversation coming into existence.

highlights.text:
for dialogue to come
into existence

records.jp: まともに会話が成り立つのは。
records.en: that can construct a normal conversation at all.
records.assessment: 会話が成り立つ means being able to hold or sustain a coherent conversation, not constructing one as an object.

highlights.text: construct a normal conversation

records.jp: 『ＯＫ、なんとかやっていけそうな気がしてきた』
records.en: Shinkawa: 『Okieh, I got the feeling I can work with this somehow.』
comments: PCP CCA0011C
records.assessment: The source begins with the English loan 'OK.' The invented eye-dialect spelling adds a voice not encoded by that form.

highlights.text: Okieh

records.jp: 結論は出ない。
records.en: Final words don't come.
records.assessment: 結論は出ない means that no conclusion presents itself. 'Final words' instead suggests a dying statement or the end of a speech.

highlights.text: Final words don't come.

records.jp: 「つぎはなんだよ」
records.en: Taichi: "What is even next now."
records.assessment: The Japanese asks roughly 'What next?' The English stacks incompatible focus adverbs into an ungrammatical question form.

highlights.text: What is even next now.

records.jp: 「わたしは下を脱ぎなさいと言いました」
records.en: Miki: "I have said to remove your belows."
comments: See CCC0026 -GHS
records.assessment: Miki says she told him to take off his lower clothing. The English lacks the object of 'said to' and invents the plural noun 'belows.'

highlights.text: I have said to remove your belows.

records.jp: シリアスに告げる。
records.en: So I proclaim with seriousness.
records.assessment: The Japanese says only that he tells her seriously. The English adds a connective and inflates speech into proclamation.

highlights.text: So I proclaim with seriousness.

records.jp: 「これを露出するということの意味、知ってのことか？」
records.en: Taichi: "That means to expose 'this' to the public, do you know that?"
records.assessment: Taichi asks whether she understands what exposing it means. The English adds 'to the public' and converts the embedded object into an ungrammatical assertion followed by a tag.

highlights.text: That means to expose 'this' to the public, do you know that?

records.jp: 「……世迷い言を」
records.en: Miki: "...meaningless whining."
records.assessment: 世迷い言 means nonsense or absurd talk. It does not characterize the speech as complaint or whining.

highlights.text: meaningless whining

records.jp: 「霧ちんは黙ってて」
records.en: Miki: "Kiri-chin will be silent."
records.assessment: Miki directly tells Kiri to be quiet. The English changes the imperative into a third-person future prediction and carries over the altered honorific as an unexplained form.

highlights.text: Kiri-chin will be silent.

records.en: Kiri: "...oh, 'K."
records.assessment: The Japanese is a hesitant assent. The clipped English slang spelling is unsupported.

highlights.text: 'K

records.jp: 「なっ、君は、君というヤツは……それでも科学者か！」
records.en: Taichi: "But! You... the person you are... you are still a scientist!"
comments: Doesn't seem so much a reference, as much as a masquerading of the simpler truth: Miki plays the "villain" by pushing her Dragon, Kiri, on Taichi because stories demand villains and their sidekicks. So Kiri is made to look like the villain, but she's just a manipulated puppet, and the true villain was the protagonist's pupil who turned to evil. This is all metagame within metagame. And then the true villain was coincidence, and coincidence was no villain but God. The End - Cross Channel. -GHS
records.assessment: それでも科学者か challenges whether she can still call herself a scientist. The English instead affirms that she remains one.

highlights.text: you are still a scientist!

records.jp: 「やむをえん……」
records.en: Taichi: "Can't avoid this..."
records.assessment: やむをえん means that the situation cannot be helped. The English leaves 'avoid' without an object and does not express reluctant acceptance.

highlights.text: Can't avoid this...

records.jp: 「この爆破スイッチを使うことになろうとは」
records.en: Taichi: "Then I will use this Self-Destruct Button!"
comments: See CCA0008, same term as his sexual molestation technique. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi says he never thought he would have to use the detonation switch. The English omits that surprise and necessity, changes the statement to a future decision, and invents capitalization.

highlights.text: Then I will use this Self-Destruct Button!

records.jp: 霧はクロスボウをおいて、トイレに入った。
records.en: Kiri put away the crossbow and went into the toilet.
comments: Since it fits into her pocket anyway. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese means that Kiri entered the restroom. In US English, going 'into the toilet' ordinarily means entering the fixture itself.

highlights.text: went into the toilet

records.jp: 「すべての淑女に安らぎあれ。妻よ子よ、すまん……愚かな父を許せ！」
records.en: Taichi: "Be all at peace, ladies. My wife, my son, sorry... forgive your stupid father!"
comments: They're probably still lost somewhere on the mountains he stupidly mistook for a hill. -GHS
records.assessment: 子 does not specify the child's sex. The English invents a son.

highlights.text: my son

records.jp: 「どうしたことだ、これは？　装置が作動せんとは？」
records.en: Taichi: "What is the meaning of this? Why doesn't the Device work?"
records.assessment: The Japanese uses the common noun 'device.' Capitalizing it as a proper or branded name is unsupported.

highlights.text: Device

records.jp: 「……ふふ、あなたの行動など、とうにお見通しだったのですよ、陛下！」
records.en: Miki: "...heheh, I have seen through all your actions and behaviors long ago, Your Highness!"
records.assessment: 陛下 is the address 'Your Majesty.' 'Your Highness' corresponds to a different rank and form of address.

highlights.text: Your Highness

records.jp: トイレから戻った霧が、のろのろとクロスボウを構え直した。
records.en: Returning from the toilet, Kiri sluggishly readjusted her crossbow posture.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Kiri sluggishly raises or takes aim with the crossbow again. The English makes the crossbow possess a posture that she readjusts.

highlights.text: readjusted her crossbow posture

records.jp: 「絶体絶命ですね」
records.en: Miki: "It is inescapable doom."
comments: On random and very much likely unrelated news, the Zettai Zetsumei Toshi series is 2002 at least... damn I really thought it was older. -GHS
records.assessment: 絶体絶命 identifies an inescapable predicament. The English supplies an empty pronoun and equates the situation with doom as a substance.

highlights.text: It is inescapable doom.

records.jp: 「科学に溺れ、人間工学を怠った……美希君、キミの負けだ！」
records.en: Taichi: "Wallowing in your science, ergonomics caught you off-guard... Miki-kun, this is how you are beat!"
comments: The subtext should be making your head spin right about here, especially considering she just goes and tries to kill him over this very comment. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi says Miki became lost in science and neglected ergonomics, so she has lost. The English makes ergonomics catch her off guard and ends with the ungrammatical passive 'how you are beat.'

highlights.text: Taichi: "Wallowing in your science, ergonomics caught you off-guard... Miki-kun, this is how you are beat!"

records.jp: 「させるか！」
records.en: Miki: "'Cause I'll let ya!"
comments: PCP CCC0006A
Hmmm. -GHS
records.assessment: させるか means 'Like hell I'll let you!' The English says the exact opposite—that she will allow it—and adds an unsupported causal fragment.

highlights.text: 'Cause I'll let ya!

records.jp: 咄嗟に霧が、切っ先をずらす。
records.en: At once Kiri shifts the point of attack.
records.assessment: 切っ先 is the physical tip or point of the weapon. 'Point of attack' is a tactical abstraction.

highlights.text: point of attack

records.jp: さすがに目視できても反応はできない。
records.en: As expectable, even if seeing it is possible, reacting is not.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that naturally he cannot react even though he can see it. 'As expectable' is nonidiomatic, and the gerund subjects are replaced by an abstract conditional construction.

highlights.text: As expectable, even if seeing it is possible, reacting is not.

records.jp: 振り返ると、廊下の壁に突き刺さっている。
records.en: I look behind and see it stuck on the wall of the corridor.
records.assessment: The Japanese says the projectile is embedded in the wall. 'Stuck on' places it against the surface rather than in it.

highlights.text: stuck on the wall

records.jp: うわ、遅れて冷や汗が出てきた。
records.en: Whoa, cold sweat came out behind schedule!
comments: see CCC4006 -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the cold sweat comes belatedly, after the danger has registered. 'Behind schedule' treats the bodily response like a delayed appointment or delivery.

highlights.text: came out behind schedule

records.jp: 「命なくしかけたんだけどなー、シャレじゃすまないよなー」
records.en: Taichi: "But I nearly lost my life didn't I, that just caaan't end with saying it was a joke can it!"
records.assessment: シャレじゃすまない is the idiom 'this is no laughing matter' or 'a joke won't make this right.' The English literalizes 'end with saying' into an ungrammatical tag construction.

highlights.text: that just caaan't end with saying it was a joke can it

records.jp: 葛藤が見て取れる。
records.en: I can understand her conflict.
records.assessment: 見て取れる means that the conflict is visibly perceptible. The English instead claims that Taichi intellectually understands it.

highlights.text: understand her conflict

records.assessment: The speaker label and dialogue are separated by two double quotation marks rather than a colon followed by one opening quotation mark.

highlights.text: Kiri" "

records.jp: 「やっぱいーや。勝手にお詫びの印をもらう」
records.en: Taichi: "Knew it, ain't happening. I'm getting a Seal of Apology on my own accord then."
records.assessment: やっぱいーや means that Taichi changes his mind and says 'Never mind.' The English instead claims prior knowledge and predicts that something will not happen.

highlights.text: Knew it, ain't happening.

records.jp: そんな擬態語が聞こえた。
records.en: That's the onomatopoeia that was audible.
comments: See CCB2007. Same issue. -GHS
records.assessment: The narrator specifically calls アケスケ a 擬態語, a mimetic word for a manner or state rather than a sound. Calling it onomatopoeia removes the deliberate joke that he supposedly hears a non-auditory mimetic expression.

highlights.text: onomatopoeia

records.jp: 「これぞスカートめくりの極み、パラシュート・デス・センテンス！」
records.en: Taichi: "This is Extreme of Skirt Flipping: the Parachute Death Sentence!"
records.assessment: The Japanese calls the move the pinnacle or ultimate form of skirt-flipping. 'Extreme of' is not a grammatical English superlative construction.

highlights.text: Extreme of Skirt Flipping

records.jp: 「スカートへアクセスする、指先が布をつまむその一瞬、全身の関節２４箇所を同時駆動させることによって、女子下半身における魅惑的閉鎖空間内に極小の乱気流を発生させる」
records.en: Taichi: "On access to the skirt, that 1 instant in which the fingertips clench the cloth, I make 24 joints simultaneously operate so that inside the ravishing sealed space of the lower portions of a girl's body outbreaks a turbulence most minute."
comments: Sealed space = recurring term. Not certain what is meant with that joints things, there's 28 joints total on the hand, so which 4 are missing? 2+4=6,+1 (the 1 instant the operation takes) =7. Forced... -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says the fingertips pinch the fabric and the coordinated movement generates a tiny turbulence. 'Clench' does not take cloth this way, while the English makes the turbulence itself 'outbreak' in an inverted, ungrammatical clause.

highlights.text: fingertips clench the cloth
outbreaks a turbulence most minute

records.jp: 「この作用により、めくりあげたスカートはパラシュート状に維持され、通常のスカートめくりの数倍の滞空時間をもって下着を衆目にさらしあげるのである！」
records.en: Taichi: "Via this act, the flipped skirt is maintained into the state of a parachute, and via an estimated flight duration many times that of an everyday skirt flip, most assuredly exposes the underwear to the public's attention!"
records.assessment: The Japanese says the lifted skirt is kept in a parachute shape. The English uses the wrong preposition and an unnecessarily literal state construction.

highlights.text: maintained into the state of a parachute

records.jp: 霧はばたばたとスカートを押さえつけている。
records.en: In a flap Kiri flaps her skirt down,
records.assessment: Kiri frantically holds or presses the skirt down. The English instead makes her flap it, conflating the idiom ばたばた with the physical motion of fabric.

highlights.text: flaps her skirt down

records.jp: が、押さえれば反対側が、より高くふわりとめくりあがる。
records.en: but the side opposite of her flapping flips fluffily higher.
comments: I have avoided "flips fluffily further up". Be glad. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that whenever she presses one side down, the opposite side floats even higher. The English invents a side opposite to an action called flapping and fails to bind the two sides.

highlights.text: the side opposite of her flapping

records.jp: まるで下方から風が吹き上げているかのように。
records.en: Exactly as if from the lower parts a wind were blowing upwards.
records.assessment: 下方 means 'from below.' 'The lower parts' can refer to a person's lower body and creates an unintended anatomical reading.

highlights.text: from the lower parts

records.jp: 「反間の計。今まで味方だったものが、これからも味方であるとは限らない」
records.en: Taichi: "Have counterintelligence measures. There is no certainty that those who have been allies thus far will be allies hereafter."
comments: Even though he's telling Kiri not to trust Miki, it doesn't really fit. -GHS
records.assessment: 反間の計 names a stratagem of turning an opponent's ally against them. The English changes this into an imperative to possess plural counterintelligence measures.

highlights.text: Have counterintelligence measures.

records.jp: 霧ちんはあたふたしていた。
records.en: Kiri-chin was in a feverish haste.
records.assessment: あたふた means that she is flustered and panicking. 'Feverish haste' describes speed or urgency rather than her confusion.

highlights.text: in a feverish haste

records.jp: もし公衆の面前でやったら悶死するやもしれぬ。
records.en: If there was real public presence, she could mayhap even experience death in agony.
records.assessment: The English stacks two modal expressions, 'could' and 'mayhap,' in one clause and nominalizes dying as experiencing death.

highlights.text: could mayhap even experience death

records.jp: さすが奥義。
records.en: So is expected from Esoterica.
records.assessment: The Japanese says, 'Just what you'd expect from a secret ultimate technique.' The English is missing a subject and uses 'esoterica,' a plural or mass noun for obscure knowledge, as the name of the move.

highlights.text: So is expected from Esoterica.

records.jp: 曜子ちゃんとか全然動じないからなぁ。
records.en: Youko-chan for example wouldn't be moved at all wouldn't she.
records.assessment: The English attaches an affirmative tag to a negative predicate and omits the punctuation that would separate it.

highlights.text: wouldn't be moved at all wouldn't she

records.jp: やっぱ慌てふためかれてこそのスカートめくり。
records.en: Indeed, a skirt flip needs to send in a flap.
comments: No, not planning to stop. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says skirt-flipping is worthwhile precisely because the target panics. The English leaves the person affected unstated and uses the malformed phrase 'send in a flap.'

highlights.text: a skirt flip needs to send in a flap

records.jp: 「パラシュート・デス・センテンスを成立させるための時間は、わずか０．０５秒に過ぎない。ではここで、そのプロセスをもう一度見てみることに―――」
records.en: Taichi: "To bring a Parachute Death Sentence into existence, the time taken is a mere 0.05" and no more. Therefore, let us now see the process for ourselves one more t---"
comments: See CCA0006 and CCB2015 - that's 2x faster than Taichi's intercranial Ph*tosh*p and as fast as the summoning of the Harakiri Blade! Hmmm, 5+2 (the times he tries to go and do them) =7? OK, too forced. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese gives 0.05 seconds. The English replaces the unit with a stray closing quotation mark and adds 'and no more.'

highlights.text: 0.05" and no more

records.jp: 霧ちんのスカートに手をかけた。
records.en: I had laid my hands on Kiri-chin's skirt and,
records.assessment: The Japanese gives the immediate action of reaching for or taking hold of the skirt. Past perfect incorrectly moves it earlier, and the appended conjunction leaves the sentence unfinished.

highlights.text: I had laid my hands on Kiri-chin's skirt and,

records.jp: 踵落としが、途中で縦横無尽に軌道を変化させる。
records.en: The dropped heel instills endlessly changing trajectories left and right as they please.
records.assessment: The Japanese says the descending heel changes its trajectory freely in every direction mid-kick. The English makes it instill multiple trajectories and assigns volition to those trajectories.

highlights.text: The dropped heel instills endlessly changing trajectories left and right as they please.

records.jp: まさに蹴りの乱気流だった。
records.en: It was definitely the turbulence of the kick.
comments: Same term as PDS -GHS
records.assessment: 蹴りの乱気流 is a turbulence or flurry of kicks. The singular English phrase describes a property of one kick.

highlights.text: turbulence of the kick

records.jp: 異常者扱いされた。
records.en: Treated as one abnormal.
records.assessment: 異常者 is a freak or abnormal person. The English uses the adjective 'abnormal' as an unheaded count noun.

highlights.text: Treated as one abnormal.

records.jp: 「先輩のチャレンジ精神は尊敬します」
records.en: Miki: "Your spirit of self-challenge is admirable, Senpai."
records.assessment: チャレンジ精神 is a willingness or drive to take on challenges. 'Self-challenge' is a literalized, nonstandard compound.

highlights.text: spirit of self-challenge

records.jp: 「しかし……仲悪いですねぇ、お二人は」
records.en: Miki: "Still... you get along bad, you two."
records.assessment: The standard English construction is 'you don't get along' or 'you get along badly'; the adjective cannot modify the verb.

highlights.text: you get along bad

records.jp: お互いに苦笑。
records.en: Reciprocal bitter smiles.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that they exchange wry smiles. The English is a verbless technical-sounding noun phrase, and 'bitter' overstates 苦笑.

highlights.text: Reciprocal bitter smiles.

records.jp: 「俺と霧とはミキミキを巡って恋のスキテキシュだからな」
records.en: Taichi: "Because me and Kiri are Worthy Rivals of Love over you, Miki-Miki."
comments: 好敵手 -GHS
records.assessment: The subject pronoun must be 'Kiri and I,' the standalone 'because' leaves a fragment, and the common descriptive phrase is needlessly capitalized.

highlights.text: Because me and Kiri are Worthy Rivals of Love

records.jp: 「ほーい。じゃせんぱい、またまたいつか」
records.en: Miki: "Yeeeesh. Well, Senpai, someday someday see you again!"
comments: いつか、わたし -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese gives a cheerful acknowledgment and 'see you again sometime.' The English changes it to an exasperated 'yeesh,' duplicates 'someday,' and uses ungrammatical word order.

highlights.text: Yeeeesh. Well, Senpai, someday someday see you again!

records.jp: 帰路を歩く。
records.en: Walking on the road home.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi walks home. The English is a subjectless participial fragment and literalizes the route as a road.

highlights.text: Walking on the road home.

records.jp: 結局、何もない一日を過ごしてしまった。
records.en: In the end, one whole day passed with nothing done.
comments: Will make more sense like this when it's 'pastad in CCC4005 -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says he ended up spending an uneventful day. The English says the day itself passed and changes absence of events into failure to do anything.

highlights.text: one whole day passed with nothing done

records.jp: それに……学校に行っても賑やかさは感じられない。
records.en: Besides... I might have gone to school, but I cannot feel its bustling liveliness.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that even when he goes to school, he cannot feel any liveliness. The English turns his actual attendance into an uncertain past possibility.

highlights.text: I might have gone to school

records.jp: 世界はガラスキになっている。
records.en: The world had become almost entirely uninhabited.
records.assessment: ガラスキ says the world is largely empty or sparsely populated. 'Almost entirely uninhabited' intensifies that state, and past perfect lacks a later past anchor.

highlights.text: had become almost entirely uninhabited

records.jp: 俺たちは、時の渦にとらわれた人類の残骸なんだろうか。
records.en: We might just be the wreckage of mankind caught in the swirl of an eddy of time.
records.assessment: 時の渦 is simply the vortex or eddy of time. The English redundantly places an eddy inside a separate swirl.

highlights.text: swirl of an eddy of time

records.jp: 坂の途中、立ち止まる。
records.en: Midway through a hill, I come to a halt.
records.assessment: 坂の途中 means partway up or down a slope. 'Through a hill' suggests passage inside or across the landform.

highlights.text: Midway through a hill

records.jp: 新川豊が雑木林を眺めていた。
records.en: Shinkawa Yutaka was gazing lost at a grove of trees.
records.assessment: The Japanese says only that he was gazing at the grove. 'Lost' invents a mental state and is not grammatically integrated as an adverb.

highlights.text: gazing lost

records.jp: 俺はそんな新川のもとに近寄り、声をかける。
records.en: As I was drawing nearer to Shinkawa as he was, I called out to him.
comments: "as I came closer to him" + "as I was beginning to understand who he was". Shinkawa's remembering, by the way, and see below for how Taichi also does. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi approaches Shinkawa and speaks to him. The English repeats 'as' and adds a meaningless trailing state clause.

highlights.text: As I was drawing nearer to Shinkawa as he was

records.jp: 見るからに夏の汗ではない。
records.en: On closer look, that's not the sweat of the heat of Summer.
records.assessment: The Japanese says it is clearly not ordinary summer sweat. The English stacks two possessive prepositional phrases and capitalizes the season.

highlights.text: the sweat of the heat of Summer

records.jp: ……などということはなく、
records.en: ...and all other things of that sort that didn't happen.
comments: ...except for Shinkawa actually dying. With this denial, not a single lie was expressed in these last two sentences, and removing them would only subtract information from the story. Even though said information is pretty much impossible to see without extreme care. Oh well. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese retracts the immediately preceding imagined event: nothing like that happened. The English invents multiple other events and attaches them to an ungoverned coordination.

highlights.text: and all other things of that sort that didn't happen

records.jp: 「あ、田崎商店のデコ軽トラだ」
records.en: Taichi: "Ah, it's the Tasaki Store's decorated company truck."
comments: Seems to mean it has a logo, but given below it's probably closer to some gaudy graffitied mess. As expectable of an ex-thug. -GHS
records.assessment: 軽トラ is a kei pickup truck. The English adds that it is a company vehicle rather than merely belonging to or advertising the store.

highlights.text: company truck

records.jp: 福顔のオヤジが、俺に向かって『いつもありがと～』と手を振った。
records.en: That smiling guy waved a 'thank you for everythi～ng' towards me and waved his hand.
comments: See CCA0004. Tanaka generally avoids having unvoiced characters have actual lines, although that'll become sorta awkward at times... like here. -GHS
records.assessment: The driver calls out the thanks while waving. The English makes the words themselves an object he waves, then redundantly says he waves his hand.

highlights.text: waved a 'thank you for everythi～ng' towards me and waved his hand

records.jp: 俺はお得意様だから。
records.en: Because I am quite the profitable customer.
comments: Should still have money now. -GHS
records.assessment: お得意様 means a valued regular customer. 'Profitable' introduces the store's economic assessment and need not follow from being a regular.

highlights.text: profitable customer

records.jp: 「昭和時代のマニアックな飲料水の入荷、いつもありがとー！」
records.en: Taichi: "Thank you for always stocking up on soft drinks for us Showa era fanatiiics!"
comments: I'm guessing he's using 飲料水 like this, because if they said there's a specific type of drinkable water aimed at Showa era fanatics I wouldn't bat an eye in disbelief. A pox on all your houses, Japan. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese thanks the shop for stocking obscure Showa-era beverages. The English instead describes the drinkers, including Taichi, as Showa fanatics.

highlights.text: soft drinks for us Showa era fanatiiics

records.jp: 伝説のソフトドリンクたち。
records.en: Legendary soft drink-tachi.
comments: Intentionally silly. This is Taichi sidetracking into weird to avoid dealing with Shinkawa, whom he long recognized even if he hasn't realized it yet at this point. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese plural suffix たち simply groups the legendary soft drinks. The English leaves it as an unexplained Japanese suffix on an English singular noun.

highlights.text: soft drink-tachi

records.jp: 元鉄オタだからビジネスもマニアックなのだろうか。
records.en: He's a former railway otaku, so that's likely why he's equally fanatical about his business.
records.assessment: The Japanese wonders whether his business is similarly niche because he used to be a train geek. It does not say he is fanatically devoted to commerce.

highlights.text: equally fanatical about his business

records.jp: とにかく新川は死ななかった。
records.en: Anyway, Shinkawa hadn't died.
comments: Still no lies. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese concludes the immediately imagined incident by saying Shinkawa did not die. Past perfect incorrectly places that non-event before a later past anchor.

highlights.text: hadn't died

records.jp: ピンピンしてる。
records.en: He was happy and lively.
comments: Focusing on happiness. That's what pisses him off about Shinkawa. -GHS
records.assessment: ピンピンしている means that he is alive and perfectly healthy or energetic. The English adds emotional happiness.

highlights.text: happy and lively

records.jp: 「今おまえは生死の境を彷徨った。俺がこうしてがっしと腕をキャッチしなかったら、その灰色の脳細胞はアスファルトの上でグロ画像になっていただろう」
records.en: Taichi: "You've wandered into the boundary between life and death right then. If I hadn't gone and caught your arm, those gray brain cells of yours would've become a Guro Scene over the asphalt."
comments: I decline responsibility to anyone who decides to GIS グロ画像 with safe search off without knowing what's gonna come up. -GHS
records.assessment: グロ画像 means a graphic or gore image. The English leaves guro unexplained and capitalizes the resulting phrase as a named scene.

highlights.text: a Guro Scene

records.jp: 「なんか……雑木林の奥とか見てたら……すげぇ気分悪くなってきて……昔から、そうなんだけどさ……わけ、わかんねぇんだけど……」
records.en: Shinkawa: "It's jus'... when I look like deep in the trees... I get this really bad feelin' and stuff... it's been like that since a long time ago... why, I totally dun'no tho..."
comments: See CCA0011C. That was 'zutto mae', this now is 昔 mukashi. It still means the same event, meaning that Taichi now is much further from those memories than he was back then. Time is passing whether he wants it or not. Maybe that's why these are sepia and those aren't... -GHS
records.assessment: The rough colloquial source supports informality, but these phrases misuse 'like,' pair 'since' with a duration, and invent a malformed contraction.

highlights.text: look like deep in the trees
since a long time ago
dun'no tho

records.jp: 青い空を見あげて、喘ぐように息を吐いた。
records.en: He then looked up at the blue sky, gasping as if pained.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he exhales as though gasping. The English adds pain and makes 'gasping' modify his looking up rather than the breath.

highlights.text: gasping as if pained

records.jp: 外障だと思っていた。
records.en: I had thought he was External Damage.
comments: His Ultramarine -GHS
records.assessment: 外障 abbreviates an external disability. 'Damage' describes injury to an object, not a person's disability, and the capitalization invents an official category name.

highlights.text: External Damage

records.jp: 群青にも少数ながら、外部障害保持者を受け入れる枠はあったから。
records.en: While in Gunjou they were a minority, there was a minimum quota of Persons Operating with External Impediments.
comments: Ugh, PC. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says Gunjō had a small admissions category for people with external disabilities. The English changes that to a minimum quota, uses a euphemistic invented title, and romanizes the place name nonstandardly.

highlights.text: While in Gunjou they were a minority, there was a minimum quota of Persons Operating with External Impediments.

records.jp: けど豊は内障……内部障害だったのかも知れない。今にして思えば。
records.en: But could Yutaka have been Internal Damage... Operating with Internal Impediment. Maybe. In retrospect,
comments: Nickname vs. PC term -GHS
records.assessment: 内障 and 内部障害 refer to an internal disability. The English first calls the person damage, then invents a capitalized euphemistic bureaucratic label.
