highlights.text: Internal Damage
Operating with Internal Impediment

records.jp: 俺も苦手だった。
records.en: I would also have felt ill at ease.
comments: Contrast the hokora. While Nanaka zubaaans him into the trees, she leads him to the hokora. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese states that Taichi was also uncomfortable in such spaces. The conditional perfect turns that fact into a hypothetical.

highlights.text: would also have felt

records.jp: 昔、心に傷を穿つ出来事があった。
records.en: A long time ago, there had been an event that had drilled a wound upon my heart.
records.assessment: The Japanese metaphor says an event once gouged a wound into his heart. The English doubles past perfect and uses the wrong preposition with the literal drilling image.

highlights.text: there had been an event that had drilled a wound upon my heart

records.jp: 『姪がさー、やっぱ群青行くんだけどさ、いろいろ教えてやらんと』
records.en: Shinkawa: 『Got a niece, ya know, 'course she goes to Gunjou, ya know, so she's telling me lots and lots of stuff.』
comments: PCP CCA0018B
records.assessment: Shinkawa says his niece will also attend Gunjō and that he needs to teach her various things. The English says she already attends and reverses the teaching direction so that she tells him things.

highlights.text: Shinkawa: 『Got a niece, ya know, 'course she goes to Gunjou, ya know, so she's telling me lots and lots of stuff.』

records.jp: しかも相当に可愛いとのこと。
records.en: How she was fairly cute, for starters.
records.assessment: The Japanese adds that she is reportedly quite cute. The English is an ungoverned 'how' fragment and makes the statement the first item in an unstated list.

highlights.text: How she was fairly cute, for starters.

records.jp: さらに揉めた。羨望と嫉妬だった。
records.en: And we furthermore discussed. It was envy with jealousy.
comments: See CCA0018B, it's just more remembering of how he didn't exactly look at girls with pure eyes... possibly ever. Not that Taichi isn't being a hypocrite here, but his fears that Yutaka would do bad stuff to Kiri are the source of his jealousy. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says the dispute or agitation intensified because of envy and jealousy. The English reduces it to further discussion and joins the two emotions with the wrong preposition.

highlights.text: we furthermore discussed. It was envy with jealousy.

records.jp: 俺は憎みはしなかった。
records.en: I did not have hatred.
comments: See CCC3026, CCC3030 -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says Taichi did not hate him. The English nominalizes the feeling and omits its object.

highlights.text: I did not have hatred.

records.jp: 『本気で、妹みたいなもんなんだよ。同居してるし』
records.en: Shinkawa: 『Seriously, she's kinda like a little sister, 's all. 's just cohabitation.』
comments: PCP CCA0018B
records.assessment: Shinkawa says the niece is like a little sister because they live together. The English adds a separate fragment dismissing the situation as 'just cohabitation.'

highlights.text: 's just cohabitation

records.jp: 可愛い血の繋がらない妹的存在と暮らしている。
records.en: He is living together with a Cute Non-Blood Related Imouto-like being.
comments: Fetishist term -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese describes living with a cute, unrelated, little-sister-like figure. The English leaves imouto untranslated, capitalizes the entire description, and dehumanizes her as a 'being.'

highlights.text: Cute Non-Blood Related Imouto-like being

records.jp: 二人とも群青に通うことになる。
records.en: The two of them ended up both going to Gunjou.
records.assessment: The place name 群青 is Gunjō in standard Hepburn, not 'Gunjou.'

highlights.text: Gunjou

records.jp: 『……たいしたもんじゃないんだけどな……あんま期待すんなよ？』
records.en: Shinkawa: 『...it ain't much of a big deal so... don't expect much, will ya?』
comments: PCP CCA0018B
records.assessment: Shinkawa says that his niece is nothing special. The English substitutes an impersonal 'it' and describes a situation as no big deal.

highlights.text: it ain't much of a big deal

records.jp: たいしたものじゃない。
records.en: Not much of a big deal.
comments: CP CCA0018B
records.assessment: The narration repeats that she is supposedly nothing special. The English again turns the person into an unspecified situation.

highlights.text: Not much of a big deal.

records.jp: 「どうした、二人とも黙っちゃって？　もしかして二人とも、照れちゃってるのか？　おいおい霧はともかく太一、こんな山猿に照れる必要ねーって」
records.en: Shinkawa: "What's it, you guys just shut up? Don'tcha tell me, you guys're all shy? C'mon, c'mon, I understand Kiri, but Taichi, no need to be all shy in front of this bumpkin, right!"
records.assessment: Shinkawa says that Kiri may be shy, but Taichi need not be shy around this mountain bumpkin. The English's 'I understand Kiri' changes the concession into comprehension and leaves the bumpkin's referent unclear.

highlights.text: Shinkawa: "What's it, you guys just shut up? Don'tcha tell me, you guys're all shy? C'mon, c'mon, I understand Kiri, but Taichi, no need to be all shy in front of this bumpkin, right!"

records.jp: 霧の目に、好意のかけらさえ、まったく見受けられない。
records.en: I could not catch a glint of favoritism in Kiri's eyes.
comments: That's the word generally used for Youko's feelings for Taichi. -GHS
records.assessment: 好意 means goodwill, affection, or favor toward Taichi. 'Favoritism' means unfair preferential treatment and changes the interpersonal judgment.

highlights.text: favoritism

records.jp: ことほどさようにツッコミとは、ある意味慈愛でもあるのだ。
records.en: The performance of a Straight-Man Retort is, in a certain sense, a representation of reciprocal kindness.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that tsukkomi is in one sense an act of benevolence. The English invents capitalization and 'reciprocal,' while its cumbersome gloss describes a performed representation rather than the retort itself.

highlights.text: a Straight-Man Retort is, in a certain sense, a representation of reciprocal kindness

records.jp: 「つうか、ナチュラルに砂糖じゃん、それ」
records.en: Shinkawa: "Right, naturally, ain't it sugar that."
comments: Seems he spotted him drinking a cup of sugar. Pun is "it's natural sugar" + "of course, moron, that's just sugar". -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says, 'That's literally just sugar.' The English forms neither a grammatical question nor declaration.

highlights.text: ain't it sugar that

records.jp: 身に染みた。
records.en: It's something that went all the way down to the heart.
comments: See CCC3027 - black sugar sediments in the heart... -GHS
records.assessment: 身に染みた means that the remark hit home or sank in. The English literalizes a physical path and uses 'to' rather than an idiomatic emotional construction.

highlights.text: went all the way down to the heart

records.jp: 「そーなんだよコイツ、やることすげーの。かなりびびるよ」
records.en: Shinkawa: "Doooes 'e now, this guy, that's some weeeird stuff he does. Pretty freaky!"
records.assessment: Shinkawa agrees that this is what Taichi does and says his behavior is extreme. The English turns the opening into a malformed question and leaves two competing subjects in one clause.

highlights.text: Doooes 'e now, this guy, that's some weeeird stuff he does.

records.jp: 「ああ、いや、それはね、セクハラといいますか……その……性的愛情表現って感じで決してやましい意図ではないという」
records.en: Taichi: "Ahhh, no, that would be well, calling it something like sexual harassment... it is... a sexual related expression of endearment that has no guilty intent whatsoever!"
comments: I think he meant "mean intent" there, but... cross conversation! -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese calls it a sexual expression of affection. The English uses the noun 'sexual' where the compound requires 'sexually related' or a direct adjective.

highlights.text: a sexual related expression of endearment

records.jp: 「あー、そうだったけかな！　ハハハ……」
records.en: Taichi: "Ahhh, that is what it seemed like! HA. HA. HA..."
comments: Mechanical laugh + continuing cross conversations. While the metasuggestions are that this his awkwarndness is real, from Kiri's side, Taichi is being a dangerous sociopath. That's why Kiri hates his guts. -GHS
records.assessment: そうだったっけ asks whether that was what the behavior was called. The English instead says the classification merely seemed that way.

highlights.text: that is what it seemed like

records.jp: 見えないナイフが、ざくざく突き刺さってくる。
records.en: A knife I could not see pierced me with slashes and thrusts.
comments: PCP CCC0014
Origins of the Knife (tune in tonight for part one, only on The History Channel). -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese imagines multiple invisible knives stabbing into him again and again. The English reduces them to one knife and adds slashing as a separate action.

highlights.text: A knife I could not see pierced me with slashes and thrusts.

records.jp: 「あー、嫌がる相手にはちゃんと慎んでるよ？　その、心の底から嫌がる相手は、わかるんで、ハイ」
records.en: Taichi: "Ahhh, I'm properly prudent with reluctant partners you know? That is, I can tell when a partner is disagreeing from the bottom of the heart, yesss!"
comments: Ambiguity continues -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi says he properly refrains with anyone who truly dislikes it. The English substitutes being 'prudent,' calls the girls partners, and weakens deep aversion to merely disagreeing.

highlights.text: Taichi: "Ahhh, I'm properly prudent with reluctant partners you know? That is, I can tell when a partner is disagreeing from the bottom of the heart, yesss!"

records.jp: 「あー、まあ嫌がってる、かな？　けどそれは表面的でしてな、お嬢さん。ホレ、口ではなんといっても体は正直みたいな」
records.en: Taichi: "Ahhh, was she reluctant, maybe I wonder? But that's just on the surface it is, ojou-san. Yes, because even if her mouth doesn't say it, her body has evidence."
comments: See CCA0012. Recurring ain't it. Right now, the reader should be thinking that he wasn't being funny when he wrote that, which is why it was repeated right at the start of this route. Kiri certainly doesn't. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi claims her reluctance is only superficial and invokes the cliche that whatever the mouth says, the body is honest. The English shifts to past tense and changes bodily honesty into unspecified 'evidence.'

highlights.text: Taichi: "Ahhh, was she reluctant, maybe I wonder? But that's just on the surface it is, ojou-san. Yes, because even if her mouth doesn't say it, her body has evidence."

records.jp: 吐き捨てるような小声。
records.en: In a low voice, as if spitting my way.
comments: See parts of Week 1... right around before meeting Kiri, actually. -GHS
records.assessment: Kiri speaks in a low voice as though spitting the words out. The English makes the narrator the object of spitting and uses 'way' without a meaningful role.

highlights.text: as if spitting my way

records.jp: バームクーヘンの縞模様を薄くはがすことに熱中している豊には、聞こえない。
records.en: Yutaka did not hear, lost as he is his enthusiastic tearing apart a Baumkuchen by thin stripes.
comments: great now I'm hungry again. This way of eating it seems to be the subject of at least one moe slice of life scene. I wouldn't know since I'm a teh litfags or something so I don't watch Animuhs unless they have like 300000 Hard Kanji's per scene or stuff. More on the topic: does Yutaka have ears that know how to hear? This is important, see Sakuraba below. -GHS
records.assessment: Yutaka is absorbed in peeling apart the cake's thin striped layers. The English omits 'in' after 'lost,' makes enthusiasm possess the action, and changes layers into a method 'by stripes.'

highlights.text: lost as he is his enthusiastic tearing apart a Baumkuchen by thin stripes

records.jp: このガキ、空気を読むということをしないのか。
records.en: Can't this ghoul of a brat just not read the mood?
comments: Another absolutely normal term that is also the name of a traditional Japanese monster, see CCA0018B. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi asks whether the brat cannot read the room. The English adds 'ghoul' and its double negative instead asks whether he can refrain from reading it.

highlights.text: Can't this ghoul of a brat just not read the mood?

records.jp: 俺は目で雄弁に語った。
records.en: I speak with eloquence via eyes.
comments: See CCA0027, CCB0022 -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says Taichi speaks eloquently with his eyes. English requires a determiner or possessive before the plural body part.

highlights.text: via eyes

records.jp: 「あ……やべ、生理はじまった。俺、ナプキン買ってくるから、その間二人で話しててくれよな？」
records.en: Shinkawa: "Ah... no way, my period's begun. I gotta put on a pad, so in the while you two get chatting will you?"
comments: As far as bad lies, this is Taichi level. Of course, they have the same backstory, likely the same teacher(s). However, what you're now wondering if whether Shinkawa, due to his backstory, has regular blood leaks from his being repeate-GHS
records.assessment: Shinkawa's excuse says he will go buy pads and asks them to talk in the meantime. The English changes buying to wearing one and uses the malformed temporal phrase 'in the while.'

highlights.text: I gotta put on a pad, so in the while

records.jp: 「わたしには、みゆきがスカートをめくられたがってる……とは思えないです」
records.en: Kiri: "Miyuki wanted her skirt flipped you say... that did not appear to be the case to me."
records.assessment: Kiri says she cannot believe Miyuki wants the treatment. The English changes the present desire under discussion into a completed past desire.

highlights.text: Miyuki wanted her skirt flipped

records.jp: 冷静に見ると、嫌いなタイプじゃない。
records.en: Looked at calmly, she is not the disliking type.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that, viewed calmly, Kiri is not a type Taichi dislikes. The English instead says that Kiri herself is not prone to disliking others.

highlights.text: she is not the disliking type

records.jp: むしろ好ましい……近づきたいと思わせる少女だった。
records.en: Rather, the likeable one... a girl that leaves me the sense of a desire to approach.
comments: Also be a measure of what she is (dere with a cover of tsun due to circumstances, like Touko), not just that she's his type... if only because his type is "attractive human females". ...well, "attractive aloof females", but... -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says she is actually likable, a girl who makes him want to get closer. The English lacks the subject for 'the likeable one' and converts desire into a sense she leaves him.

highlights.text: the likeable one... a girl that leaves me the sense of a desire to approach

records.jp: 「……佐倉さんは、正義漢だな」
records.en: Taichi: "...Sakura-san, you're a woman among women, a Woman of Justice."
comments: 漢. -GHS
records.assessment: 正義漢 calls her a person with a strong sense of justice. The English invents a gendered superlative and a capitalized title.

highlights.text: a woman among women, a Woman of Justice

records.jp: 「それがなにか？」
records.en: Kiri: "What would that even be?"
records.assessment: それがなにか means 'And what of it?' The English instead asks him to identify what the quality is.

highlights.text: What would that even be?

records.jp: 「いや、いいんだ。そういう人間は、どこにだって必要だと思うし」
records.en: Taichi: "Welll, it's a good thing. I think that's the kind of human that's necessary anywhere and everywhere."
records.assessment: The Japanese says people like that are needed everywhere. The English uses a categorical 'kind of human' and redundantly stacks two universal location phrases.

highlights.text: the kind of human that's necessary anywhere and everywhere

records.jp: 「今まで、キミみたいなタイプ、俺のそばにいなかったからさ」
records.en: Taichi: "Just, up until now, there's never been your kind of type around me."
comments: This only also refers to tsunderes. Only 'also'. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says he has never had her type around him. 'Kind of type' redundantly combines two classifiers.

highlights.text: your kind of type

records.jp: さすがマイフレン。大物である。
records.en: Just what I expected, my friend. A VIP you are.
records.assessment: 大物 calls Yutaka a formidable, unflappable character. 'VIP' instead assigns social importance, and the inversion adds an unsupported voice.

highlights.text: A VIP you are.

records.jp: 「群青はどう？」
records.en: Taichi: "How's Gunjou?"
records.assessment: The standard Hepburn romanization of 群青 is Gunjō, not 'Gunjou.'

highlights.text: Gunjou

records.jp: 「クラスに編入されてさ、いろんなタイプのヤツがいる。言葉の通じないヤツ、周囲が目に入らないヤツ、突発的に暴れるヤツ、まったく普通人みたいなヤツ」
records.en: Taichi: "There's all sorts of types that get put into classes. The type who can't understand your language, the type who doesn't see what's around them, the type that fires into rage suddenly, and the damnably normal-ish types."
comments: Misato and Miki are the first, Taichi is the second, Touko and Kiri are the third, Sakuraba and Tomoki are the fourth. Where Youko fits? Well, it should be obvious: the second. In other words, she's like Taichi. So very much that. -GHS
records.assessment: The list describes people one cannot communicate with, people oblivious to their surroundings, people with sudden violent outbursts, and apparently ordinary people. The English narrows communication to 'your language,' literalizes perception, and adds 'damnably.'

highlights.text: Taichi: "There's all sorts of types that get put into classes. The type who can't understand your language, the type who doesn't see what's around them, the type that fires into rage suddenly, and the damnably normal-ish types."

records.jp: 「けどみんな、世間に適応できなくて弾かれたのばっかりだ」
records.en: Taichi: "But all, to the last, have been repelled by society for being unable to conform to it."
records.assessment: The Japanese says they were rejected or excluded because they could not adapt to society. 'Repelled' depicts a physical force or mutual disgust rather than social exclusion.

highlights.text: repelled by society

records.jp: 「みんな、日本で屈指のどうかしてる人間なんだ。もちろん、俺もキミもだよ」
records.en: Taichi: "Everybody there's one of Japan's foremost damaged humans. Of course, me and you too."
records.assessment: Taichi calls everyone there one of Japan's most seriously messed-up people, himself and Kiri included. The English lacks a verb, dehumanizes them as 'damaged humans,' and uses object pronouns as subjects.

highlights.text: Taichi: "Everybody there's one of Japan's foremost damaged humans. Of course, me and you too."

records.jp: 「会話できる人間が何人いる？　友達と呼べる関係を築ける相手が何人いた？」
records.en: Taichi: "How many humans there that can manage a conversation? How many that can be party to building something that can be called friendship?"
comments: This "human" was censored in the PS2 version, furthering the idea that it should be left literal as often as possible. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese asks how many people can hold a conversation and with how many one can build a relationship called friendship. The first English question lacks 'are,' and the second turns a potential friend into a party to constructing an abstract thing.

highlights.text: Taichi: "How many humans there that can manage a conversation? How many that can be party to building something that can be called friendship?"

records.jp: 「たとえば……ガラスの割れる音を聞くと、異常に攻撃的になるヤツとかさ。うちのクラスにいるんだけど」
records.en: Taichi: "For example... someone who, when he hears the sound of glass being shattered, starts being abnormally aggressive. He's right in my class, you know."
comments: See CCC0011B, CCC0014. Glasswork gets cracked and he grows aggressive, hum, yes he's in Taichi's class indeed. Don't ask him whether Karade is a ripoff of Karate, either. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says the person becomes abnormally aggressive. 'Starts being' is a clumsy progressive calque for the change of state.

highlights.text: starts being abnormally aggressive

records.jp: 小ぶりの眉根が寄った。
records.en: The tiny gap between her eyebrows grew tighter.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that her small brows draw together. The English makes the gap between them the body part that tightens.

highlights.text: The tiny gap between her eyebrows grew tighter.

records.jp: 「そういう意味では……」
records.en: Kiri: "But I did not mean..."
records.assessment: そういう意味では begins a hesitant concession, 'In that sense...' The English instead explicitly denies that she meant it.

highlights.text: But I did not mean...

records.jp: 「俺の行動をどうかと思う。そう指摘して弾劾する。直してもらわなければならないと思う」
records.en: Taichi: "You have a problem with my conduct. You point it out and denounce it. It is absolutely unthinkable for you not to come and fix me."
records.assessment: Taichi says she believes he must correct his conduct. The English makes Kiri personally come fix him and frames failure to do so as unthinkable.

highlights.text: It is absolutely unthinkable for you not to come and fix me.

records.jp: 「群青でふりかざす考え方じゃないなぁ」
records.en: Taichi: "That ain't a way of thinking you can bandy around at Gunjou ya know."
comments: IOW this is her Ultramarine. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi says this is not a principle one should brandish at Gunjō. 'Bandy around' changes aggressive moral wielding into casual circulation, 'Gunjou' is non-Hepburn, and the eye dialect is unsupported.

highlights.text: Taichi: "That ain't a way of thinking you can bandy around at Gunjou ya know."

records.jp: 「キミがただの鈍い子なのか、それとも逆に、鋭く俺の性根を見抜いているのかはわからない」
records.en: Taichi: "Whether you're just dumb, or conversely, you very sharply saw through my character I can't tell."
comments: Choice of training spot, hypocrisy, being exploited by Miki, and being in love with Taichi and expressing it like this. Touko's nowhere near as dumb as her. In fact, the only one dumber than her are possibly Taichi and, by extension, Youko. -GHS
records.assessment: 鈍い means obtuse or insensitive here, not simply unintelligent. The English shifts the alternative insight into past tense and fails to close the embedded whether construction before the main clause.

highlights.text: Whether you're just dumb, or conversely, you very sharply saw through my character I can't tell.

records.jp: 「けど……久しぶりに、新しい出会いの中で人間扱いされた気がした」
records.en: Taichi: "But... it felt like a long time since I've been treated like a human by someone I just met."
comments: ...and yet, by implicitly believing he can improve, despite her Stereotypical Doomsaying Priest attitude, she still understands a little bit of him better than he does. To be able to understand this is the point of the the CS Lewis quote I open the book with. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says it felt like he had been treated as human for the first time in a long while. The English instead makes the elapsed time itself the feeling and mixes past and present perfect.

highlights.text: it felt like a long time since I've been treated

records.jp: 豊の目は節穴だな。
records.en: Yutaka's eyes are knotholes indeed.
records.assessment: 目は節穴 is an idiom meaning that Yutaka is a poor judge or effectively blind to her appeal. The English exposes the literal knotholes without conveying that function.

highlights.text: Yutaka's eyes are knotholes indeed.

records.jp: 「あれで結構、重いんだ」
records.en: Taichi: "She was quite serious... in that regard."
records.assessment: 重い here means that Miyuki's condition is fairly severe. 'Serious in that regard' is vague and can instead describe her attitude.

highlights.text: quite serious... in that regard

records.jp: 「詳しくは知らないけど、本人が孤独を感じすぎると、発症するみたい」
records.en: Taichi: "I don't know the details, but, it seems that when she starts feeling excessively lonely her symptoms come out."
records.assessment: 発症する means that the condition manifests or she has an episode. Symptoms do not idiomatically 'come out' in English.

highlights.text: her symptoms come out

records.jp: 「ちゃんとした病院施設に送られるってこと」
records.en: Taichi: "That she'll be sent to a proper hospitalization facility."
comments: This is the only indication that Class X isn't just another classroom. Then again, there's no certainty that Taichi knows, at this point, where she'll be transferred exactly, or even what Class X entails. It could even be "the" Research Building of CCA0013. This may be a plot hole, intentional deception, plot relevant or simply the character hazarding a guess with pretty much equal probability. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says she will be sent to a proper hospital facility. 'Hospitalization facility' is a nonstandard tautological compound.

highlights.text: proper hospitalization facility

records.jp: たとえば校庭。無人のトラック。
records.en: For example, the courtyard. The sports track left depopulated.
comments: See CCA0007. For example, the interior of the broadcast room. In which she was sealed despite Tomoki being right nearby for no apparent reason. Very likely, her condition is similar to present Taichi's: she just daydreams a lot. Later on, however... -GHS
records.assessment: 無人 means simply empty or unoccupied. 'Depopulated' implies an established population was removed.

highlights.text: depopulated

records.jp: たとえば教室。人がいても人同士の接続がない、断絶空間。
records.en: For example, the classroom. There are people, but no one to have a connection or a fellowship with; it is a space of disintegration.
comments: Do you feel it, beating over your head yet? How about now? -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese describes a room where people are present but disconnected from one another, a space of severance. The English instead says there is no available person to connect with and calls the space one of disintegration.

highlights.text: For example, the classroom. There are people, but no one to have a connection or a fellowship with; it is a space of disintegration.

records.jp: 「彼女が放送部に入ってるのは、ウチが自意識を保持している連中の集団だからだ」
records.en: Taichi: "She had joined the Broadcast Club because this in-group was an assembly of people maintaining a sense of self."
records.assessment: ウチ means their club, not a sociological in-group. The English also shifts the continuing reason for her membership into past tense and uses an abstract 'assembly.'

highlights.text: this in-group was an assembly

records.jp: 「そういう意図のもとで放送部は成立してる」
records.en: Taichi: "The Broadcast Club had been established with that intention as foundation."
comments: Now this is odd. Was this official? -GHS
records.assessment: The club exists on the basis of that intention. The English uses past perfect for an ongoing institution and omits the determiner before 'foundation.'

highlights.text: had been established with that intention as foundation

records.jp: 「他に部活なんていくつもないからね」
records.en: Taichi: "'Cause there's not much activity in the club besides that, you know."
records.assessment: The Japanese says there are not many other clubs. The English instead says this club contains little activity beyond the stated purpose.

highlights.text: there's not much activity in the club besides that

records.jp: 「友達を作るのは大変だ。でも作らずにはいられない。どうしてかわかる？」
records.en: Taichi: "Making friends is a hassle. But going without making some is unacceptable. Do you know why?"
records.assessment: 大変 means difficult, not merely bothersome. 作らずにはいられない says people cannot help making friends, whereas the English turns that compulsion into a normative prohibition.

highlights.text: a hassle
going without making some is unacceptable

records.jp: 「必要だからだ。心を育てるためには」
records.en: Taichi: "Because they're necessary. Necessary for the rearing of a heart."
records.assessment: 心を育てる means nurturing emotional or mental development. 'Rearing' ordinarily applies to children or animals and treats a heart as an independent creature.

highlights.text: the rearing of a heart

records.jp: 「みゆきともなりたいと思った。けど、ちょっとやり方がまずかったかもしれない」
records.en: Taichi: "I thought I would also have Miyuki become one. But the way I used wasn't quite the right one, maybe."
comments: Meaning she is NOT a friend. That's why she doesn't appear in the Cross World: they're not close enough. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi wanted to become friends with Miyuki. The English instead makes him cause Miyuki to become an unspecified object called 'one.'

highlights.text: I thought I would also have Miyuki become one.

records.jp: 「……じゃあ……セクハラしてたのって……わざとですか？」
records.en: Kiri: "...so... that sexual harassment... it is on purpose?"
records.assessment: Kiri asks whether the past harassment was deliberate. The English changes it to present tense and uses declarative question order.

highlights.text: it is on purpose?

records.jp: 「あの地味子ちゃんの、思い出の一つにでもなればなぁと」
records.en: Taichi: "I wanted to make that plain girl into one of my memories, that's it."
records.assessment: Taichi says he hoped the act might become one of the plain girl's memories. The English reverses possessor and object, making the girl into one of Taichi's memories.

highlights.text: make that plain girl into one of my memories

records.jp: 「携帯、ネット、手紙、友達」
records.en: Taichi: "Telephone, the 'net, letters, friendship."
comments: See CCA0017A, CCX0001 -GHS
records.assessment: 携帯 here means mobile phones or cellphones, not telephones in general.

highlights.text: Telephone

records.jp: 「そこに誰かいると期待して、言葉や情報や電波を発信するんじゃないか」
records.en: Taichi: "we dispatch language and information and radio waves because of that expectation that someone'll be there, isn't it?"
comments: We read to know we are not alone. See CCB0018: much more sensical now. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese asks whether people transmit those things expecting someone to be there. The English begins the sentence lowercase, uses 'dispatch' for communication, and attaches a singular tag to a plural subject.

highlights.text: we dispatch language and information and radio waves because of that expectation that someone'll be there, isn't it?

records.jp: 「……キミがどんなに止めてもやーめない」
records.en: Taichi: "...you can stop me however much you like but I'll neeever stop forever!"
records.assessment: The Japanese emphatically says he will not stop. The English redundantly adds 'forever' to 'never' and stretches the wrong lexical material.

highlights.text: neeever stop forever

records.jp: 「止めたかったら、止めれば。キックでも腕ひしぎでもシックスナインでも」
records.en: Taichi: "Try to stop me if you want me to stop. With kicks or face grabs or sixty-nine."
comments: I think it's the same "arm push" as in CCA0030, so tweaked to fit again -GHS
records.assessment: 腕ひしぎ is an arm lock, not a grab to the face.

highlights.text: face grabs

records.jp: 自分の吐いた言葉を反芻する。
records.en: Thinking over and over the words I lied out,
comments: Whoops, I toootally meant "laid". Yes, the term is compatible with 'lie'. -GHS
records.assessment: 吐いた言葉 means the words he uttered or spat out. 'Lied out' both invents deliberate falsehood at this point and is not an English phrasal verb.

highlights.text: words I lied out

records.jp: まるで自分が『不健全ながらも頑張ってる』みたいな。
records.en: it's just like there's something there that says, "he's hardworking, unwholesomeness notwithstanding".
records.assessment: Taichi reflects that he has made himself sound like someone trying hard despite being unhealthy. The English invents an external 'something' that says this and shifts self-reference into third person.

highlights.text: it's just like there's something there that says, "he's hardworking, unwholesomeness notwithstanding"

records.jp: やがて霧は決然と言った。
records.en: So said Kiri not long afterwards, resolute.
records.assessment: The Japanese says Kiri eventually speaks with resolve. The English uses an archaic inversion and leaves the adjective 'resolute' dangling after the clause.

highlights.text: So said Kiri not long afterwards, resolute.

records.jp: 「そう」
records.en: Taichi: "Well."
records.assessment: そう acknowledges her answer, like 'I see.' 'Well' signals hesitation or transition instead.

highlights.text: Well.

records.jp: 簡単に騙されてはダメだ。
records.en: Being easily deceived is unacceptable.
comments: Still ambiguous as to what she wasn't deceived about. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese directly says one must not be easily deceived. The English turns this into an impersonal judgment of acceptability.

highlights.text: Being easily deceived is unacceptable.

records.jp: 「すいません。よく、寝るんです」
records.en: Kiri: "Apologies. He is a... frequent sleeper."
comments: Narcolepsy. Taichi is very likely similar. -GHS
records.assessment: よく寝る means that he sleeps a lot. The English classifies him as a type of sleeper and inserts an unsupported hesitation.

highlights.text: a... frequent sleeper

records.jp: 「そうそう、もし潤いが欲しかったら、放送部に来るといい」
records.en: Taichi: "Right, right, so if want a little enrichment to your heart, do come to the Broadcast Club."
records.assessment: The Japanese invites Kiri to the club if she wants emotional enrichment. The English omits the subject 'you' and uses a cumbersome prepositional phrase.

highlights.text: so if want a little enrichment to your heart

records.jp: 「けど来たら、いじるぞ。覚悟の上、それなりに対策してから来るように」
records.en: Taichi: "But if you come, there'll be fiddling. Come only after having figured out countermeasures."
records.assessment: いじる means that Taichi will tease or mess with her. 'Fiddling' lacks an object and can describe irrelevant tinkering or sexual touching without identifying the promised treatment.

highlights.text: there'll be fiddling

records.jp: 俺が見た、はじめての笑顔がそれだった。
records.en: And that the first smile of hers that I had seen.
records.assessment: The English clause is missing the finite verb 'was.'

highlights.text: And that the first smile

records.jp: 後に美希と知り合った霧は、二人そろって放送部に入ることになった。
records.en: Having subsequently been acquainted with Miki, it became that her and Kiri came to the Broadcast Club together.
comments: They haven't joined yet, see CCZRooftop for when they do officially join. That sequence takes place after this scene. -GHS
records.assessment: Kiri later became acquainted with Miki, and the two joined the club together. The English's participial clause has no subject, then treats 'her' and Kiri as two separate people and uses an object pronoun as subject.

highlights.text: Having subsequently been acquainted with Miki, it became that her and Kiri came

records.jp: さらに意識は飛び、当時を克明に思い出す。
records.en: And further my awareness flies, remembering those days in detail.
comments: See CCX0001, this scene is very very very important. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says his consciousness leaps again and he recalls the time vividly. The English makes awareness itself remember while flying.

highlights.text: my awareness flies, remembering those days

records.jp: 二人は花壇に植えられた、二輪の花のようだった。
records.en: The two were like a pair of flowers as grown in a flowerbed.
records.assessment: The Japanese compares them to two flowers planted in a flowerbed. The English stacks 'like' and 'as' around a passive participle.

highlights.text: like a pair of flowers as grown

records.jp: なんとか嘘のあたりで殴り飛ばせた。
records.en: Halfway through saying lies he was struck down somehow.
comments: Lack of quotes seems significant. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi manages to punch Tomoki away just as he reaches the word 'lies.' The English removes Taichi as agent, makes the timing a generic act of lying, and says Tomoki is struck down by an unspecified cause.

highlights.text: Halfway through saying lies he was struck down somehow.

records.jp: 「いかにも！」
records.en: Taichi: "Extremely so!"
records.assessment: いかにも means 'Indeed' or 'Exactly,' affirming truth rather than degree.

highlights.text: Extremely so!

records.jp: 「ヘイ、インモラル、シスコン具合はどうなってるよ？　相変わらず愛変わらずって感じなんだろ？」
records.en: Taichi: "HEI, Immoral, how's that Siscon condition of yours been doing? Losing heart in having lost your heart to her, aren't you?"
comments: Ai kawarazu pun. 相変わらず as always, unchangingly / 愛変わらず love-unchanging -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese puns on 相変わらず by inserting 'love' while asking whether the degree of his sister complex is unchanged. The English invents two different heart idioms and a completed loss of love.

highlights.text: Losing heart in having lost your heart to her

records.jp: 首を締められた。
records.en: My neck was being wrung.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Tomoki strangles him. 'Wrung' is used for twisting liquid from cloth, and the progressive passive obscures the immediate attack.

highlights.text: My neck was being wrung.

records.jp: 本人がいるので、友貴も必死だ。
records.en: As the person being referred to was there, Tomoki also seems panicked on the brink of death.
records.assessment: 必死 says Tomoki is desperate because the person being discussed is present. The English literalizes the expression into being on the verge of death.

highlights.text: panicked on the brink of death

records.jp: 友貴の頭を、みみ先輩がチョップする。
records.en: Mimi-senpai implemented a chop on Tomoki's head.
comments: See CCC3030. Hmmm, this is the only mention of Taichi and Misato having nicknames, but they didn't have anything in the (later) CCA0027, may be an error. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says Misato chops Tomoki on the head. 'Implemented' treats the physical blow as a policy or procedure.

highlights.text: implemented a chop

records.jp: 「なんだなんだその虚弱っぷりは」
records.en: Taichi: "Whassit whassit with that weaknessism!"
records.assessment: The Japanese mocks her display of frailty. The English invents the nonword 'weaknessism' and doubles a malformed interrogative.

highlights.text: Whassit whassit with that weaknessism!

records.jp: 「三年生の方々がめでたくご卒業となり、その穴を埋めるかのように入ってきた君たち二人に、桜庭先生はたいへん期待しておられる」
records.en: Taichi: "The genteel third years will be happily moving on, therefore Sakuraba-sensei has worrisomely high expectations in regards to you both participating in the club for the purpose of filling that hole."
comments: See CCB0001. Still guessing he means that Misato is going towards third year, so she'll be moving on towards graduation... except club is flight for her, so she'll stick around until the Training Camp one year from this flashback. Taichi of this time can't know this, of course, so I guess he's assuming she'll relinquish the club within months. Or maybe he's just trolling. -GHS
records.assessment: The third-years are happily graduating, and the two newcomers seem to fill the gap, so Sakuraba has high expectations of them. The English changes 'happily' to 'genteel,' makes the expectations worryingly high, and assigns them a formal purpose of filling a hole.

highlights.text: Taichi: "The genteel third years will be happily moving on, therefore Sakuraba-sensei has worrisomely high expectations in regards to you both participating in the club for the purpose of filling that hole."

records.jp: 桜庭はクールな物事で立ち上がると、突っ込んだまま抜けなくなった指からビンをぶらさげたまま、語り出した。
records.en: Sakuraba stood like something cool, dangling an empty bottle stuck in his finger in ways seemingly unextractable, and begins to speak.
comments: Ohhh here it comes. -GHS
records.assessment: Sakuraba rises with cool composure and starts speaking while a bottle remains stuck on his finger. The English compares him to an unspecified cool object, tangles which object is stuck in which, and shifts 'began' to present tense.

highlights.text: Sakuraba stood like something cool, dangling an empty bottle stuck in his finger in ways seemingly unextractable, and begins to speak.

records.jp: 「今日はみんなに、柿の種の教訓を話したいと思う」
records.en: Sakuraba: "Today, I would like to hold a lesson with everyone regarding the Kaki, or Japanese persimmon."
comments: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaki_no_tane - the term can very nearly translate to 'parable' here, but let's not be TOO explicit... -GHS
records.assessment: 柿の種 is the named rice-cracker snack and the lesson concerns it. The English misreads it as a lesson about persimmons themselves.

highlights.text: a lesson with everyone regarding the Kaki, or Japanese persimmon

records.jp: 「柿の種にピーナッツ入っているものがある。知っているな」
records.en: Sakuraba: "There is a type of seed of persimmon, or Kaki no Tane, that is actually a peanut-based snack usually served with beer. Did you know?"
records.assessment: Sakuraba says some versions of the kaki no tane snack contain peanuts and asks whether they know that. The English describes a persimmon seed as a peanut-based snack and adds an unsolicited serving custom.

highlights.text: Sakuraba: "There is a type of seed of persimmon, or Kaki no Tane, that is actually a peanut-based snack usually served with beer. Did you know?"

records.jp: 美希はこくこくと頷く。
records.en: Bob bob steady nod goes Miki.
comments: PCP CCB0002
records.assessment: The Japanese says Miki nods repeatedly. The English turns the mimetic rhythm into two bare names and uses an inverted verb construction.

highlights.text: Bob bob steady nod goes Miki.

records.jp: 「そのピーナッツが許せないという奴は、意外と多い」
records.en: Sakuraba: "And people that won't accept these peanuts being referred to as Kaki no Tane are unexpectedly many."
records.assessment: The Japanese says many people surprisingly cannot stand the peanuts included in the snack. It does not say anyone calls the peanuts themselves kaki no tane.

highlights.text: won't accept these peanuts being referred to as Kaki no Tane

records.jp: 「は、ピーナッツが入ってこそ、ピーナッツ入り柿の種であるからですな？」
records.en: Taichi: "Ah, because certain peanuts are called Seeds of Persimmon, that would mean there are necessarily some peanuts that are of the genus of persimmon, and therefore persimmon trees that grow from these peanuts?"
comments: The logic is inescapable. The peanut snack are the humans, while the Seeds of Persimmon is the Blood of Christ. Can something that's not even remotely similar even become of Christ on the word of someone (hint, that's God)? That's the point of this parable. The most frustrating thing is that Taichi understands all this but just. won't. get. it. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi says peanut-containing kaki no tane is what it is precisely because it contains peanuts. The English invents a botanical genus of persimmon peanuts and trees grown from them.

highlights.text: Taichi: "Ah, because certain peanuts are called Seeds of Persimmon, that would mean there are necessarily some peanuts that are of the genus of persimmon, and therefore persimmon trees that grow from these peanuts?"

records.jp: 「そうだ。イヤなら純正の柿の種を食えばいい。ピーナッツ入り柿の種を手にピーナッツがイヤなどという弱音は、ピーナッツ入り柿の種の尊厳を損なうものだからだ」
records.en: Sakuraba: "Indeed. If you don't like that, then go eat actual persimmon seeds. Complaining that in peanut-based Kaki no Tane there should not be peanuts is to undermine the dignity of the persimmon-genus peanut."
comments: This might make a bit more sense after the cut scene of their drinking alcohol... but considering this has nothing to do with actual persimmon or peanuts, maybe not. -GHS
records.assessment: Sakuraba says peanut-haters should eat the plain snack and that complaining while holding the peanut-containing version insults that version's dignity. The English tells them to eat literal persimmon seeds and again invents a persimmon-genus peanut.

highlights.text: Sakuraba: "Indeed. If you don't like that, then go eat actual persimmon seeds. Complaining that in peanut-based Kaki no Tane there should not be peanuts is to undermine the dignity of the persimmon-genus peanut."

records.jp: 「だからオレは、あえて柿の種のピーナッツだけを食っている」
records.en: Sakuraba: "Therefore, I dare venture to only eat Kaki no Tane made of peanuts that grow from persimmon trees that have grown from persimmon-genus peanuts."
comments: And this all, somehow, ends up into curry. I used to end that with "because Cross Channel", but I since tried Kaki no Tane, and they're damn spicy - ergo the connection! -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says he deliberately eats only the peanuts from the snack. The English replaces this with an invented recursive botanical genealogy.

highlights.text: Kaki no Tane made of peanuts that grow from persimmon trees that have grown from persimmon-genus peanuts

records.jp: 醒めた。
records.en: I sober up.
records.assessment: 醒めた says Taichi's enthusiasm cools and he is disillusioned. The English specifically claims recovery from intoxication.

highlights.text: I sober up.

records.jp: 「オレを素に戻らせたおまえの引かせパワー、許し難い」
records.en: Taichi: "Your Pulling Power caused me to return to unembellishment, irremissible!"
comments: Hmmm, see CCA0006, CCA0015B, CCX0001. This may be referring to his admission above that he understands his argument perfectly, even metaphorically, perhaps even better than Sakuraba himself does... -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi condemns Sakuraba's power to make him recoil and snap out of his performance. The English misreads 引かせ as physical pulling, literalizes 素 as lack of embellishment, and ends with a dangling adjective.

highlights.text: Your Pulling Power caused me to return to unembellishment, irremissible!

records.jp: 「オレの話はこれで終わりだ」
records.en: Sakuraba: "My talk is with this concluded."
records.assessment: The Japanese simply says the talk is now over. The English calques Japanese constituent order into an unnatural passive.

highlights.text: My talk is with this concluded.

records.jp: まとめていた。
records.en: Collectively.
comments: Meaning she included them all. Same joke as the one Tomoki'll use, see CCA0007 -GHS
records.assessment: Misato's preceding line sums the men up as 'these are the people here.' The English supplies only an adverb and removes the act of summation.

highlights.text: Collectively.

records.jp: 「よくわかりました」
records.en: Miki: "I learned a lot."
records.assessment: よくわかりました says Miki now understands them well. It does not claim she acquired a large quantity of knowledge.

highlights.text: I learned a lot.

records.jp: 「なんとか、平気そうです。ね、さくちん？」
records.en: Miki: "For some reason, I feel alright here. Don't you, Saku-chin?"
comments: Still on sorta-last name basis. -GHS
records.assessment: なんとか means she thinks she can manage somehow, not that she feels all right for an unknown reason.

highlights.text: For some reason, I feel alright here.

records.jp: 「……やっていけと先生に言われましたんで」
records.en: Kiri: "...I was told by the teachers to work with this."
comments: "Make this work" seems better, but given her personality that'd be an intentionality that doesn't seem to be in the original. See CCC4009: there's difficulties in joining the club, even for them; seems more sensical that the teacher(s) would tell her to 'work with this' in general, not just to get in the club. -GHS
records.assessment: Kiri says a teacher told her to make it work or carry on there. The English changes the teacher to plural and leaves 'this' without a clear institutional referent.

highlights.text: by the teachers to work with this

records.jp: 「……だそうです」
records.en: Misato: "...so it seems to."
records.assessment: だそうです means 'that's what he says.' The English leaves 'to' without a complement and omits the report's speaker.

highlights.text: so it seems to

records.jp: 買収するか。見ればまだガキだし、もので釣るのがいいだろ。
records.en: Should we bribe them? Looking at them, they seem to be still brats, so we should be fine fishing with a lure.
comments: You insipid machiavellist. -GHS
records.assessment: もので釣る means bribing or enticing the girls with gifts. The English literalizes it into fishing and a lure rather than stating the human inducement.

highlights.text: fishing with a lure

records.jp: 「買収するか。見ればまだガキだし、もので釣るのがいいだろ。入部祝い作戦だ」
records.en: Taichi: "Should we bribe them? Looking at them, they seem to be still brats, so we should be fine fishing with a lure. The Congratulatory Gift for Club Joinance Strategy."
comments: PCP above, one suuubtle addition. -GHS
records.assessment: The English literalizes luring them with gifts as fishing and invents the nonword 'joinance' for a club-entry gift strategy.

highlights.text: fishing with a lure
Club Joinance

records.jp: 「また口に出してるから、太一」
records.en: Tomoki: "You passed thoughts through the mouth again, Taichi."
comments: See CCA0023. Wait, how does HE know?! Then again, right around here things get weird. It's very possible that he's not seeing things straight right now, and his memories are beginning to jumble. See CCX0001: a scene like this is right how it begins. -GHS
records.assessment: Tomoki says Taichi is speaking his thoughts aloud again. The English turns thought into an object mechanically passed through a mouth.

highlights.text: You passed thoughts through the mouth again

records.jp: 「んー、よしこれだ」
records.en: Taichi: "Hum, these would be right."
records.assessment: これだ is singular: Taichi chooses one thing as right. The English changes both demonstrative and verb to plural and conditional.

highlights.text: these would be right

records.jp: アイテムの一つは色紙。
records.en: One of the [ITEM]s is an elegant colored card.
records.assessment: 色紙 here is a square autograph board, not an elegant colored card.

highlights.text: an elegant colored card

records.jp: 「を心の師と仰ぐ愛貴族・黒須太一のサインをあげよう」
records.en: Taichi: "...most fervent admirer and heartfelt inspiree, the autograph of the 『Aristocrat of Love * Kurosu Taichi』."
comments: Full sentence is "From that Michael Jackson's inspiree, the autograph of Kurosu Taichi". Yeah, grammar's forced. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi says he reveres the referenced star as his mentor and will give Miki his own autograph. The English is a verbless possessive phrase that labels someone an 'inspiree' and never performs the offer.

highlights.text: Taichi: "...most fervent admirer and heartfelt inspiree, the autograph of the 『Aristocrat of Love * Kurosu Taichi』."

records.jp: 「君にはベースボールを今たらしめたビックマン、ベー○・ルース―――」
records.en: Taichi: "To you, from the Big Man who is right now baseball himself, Ba*e Luth's---
comments: See CCA0025B. Intentional mislomanization. AFAIK 'bikkuman' is just an alternate transliterating for big man (instead of bigguman), except... http://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%83%80%E3%82%A4%E3%83%A4%E3%83%A2%E3%83%B3%E3%83%89%E6%98%A0%E5%83%8F Look who's down there. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese calls Babe Ruth the big man who made baseball what it is today. The English says he literally is baseball now and misspells the censored proper surname as 'Luth.'

highlights.text: Taichi: "To you, from the Big Man who is right now baseball himself, Ba*e Luth's---

records.jp: 「太一人形を進呈しよう」
records.en: Taichi: "You are presented with a Taichi Doll."
comments: See CCC0000, CCC3025. Once more Taichi thinks he's the Popular Heroine. Want even more meta creepy? Compare a certain girl in Kana: Little Sister... -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi says he will present the doll to her. The English removes him as agent and turns the offer into a present passive declaration.

highlights.text: You are presented with a Taichi Doll.

records.jp: 先輩は眼鏡をつけていることからもわかる通り（？）規則の人。
records.en: Senpai, exactly as understandable from her vision magnified by glasses(?), is a person of rules.
comments: Glasses also literally means discernment, not exactly a small detail with her character given how clearly she sees through Taichi's act (and, by reflection, how Yusa does). I'd almost say "of course", but while I'm aware of the fetishism, I'm still reeling in shock that there isn't a directly sexual meaning in this Japanese word. How many does that make now? Five? -GHS
records.assessment: The joke says her rule-bound nature is evident merely from her wearing glasses. The English invents magnified vision as the evidence and makes the inference itself 'understandable.'

highlights.text: exactly as understandable from her vision magnified by glasses(?)

records.jp: 手も出さなかったので、ひもで首にかけた。
records.en: So as it will not slip from the hand, I had hung its neck with a cord.
comments: ...not even subtext... -GHS
records.assessment: Because Kiri did not even reach out to accept the doll, Taichi hangs it around her neck with a cord. The English invents preventing slippage, hangs the doll's own neck, and uses past perfect.

highlights.text: So as it will not slip from the hand, I had hung its neck with a cord.

records.jp: 「ご自分で作られたので？」
records.en: Miki: "Did you make this all by your own?"
records.assessment: The idiom is 'all on your own' or 'all by yourself.'

highlights.text: all by your own

records.jp: 「まめなやつだ」
records.en: Sakuraba: "Produceful guy him."
comments: まめ mamu = assiduous, legume -GHS
records.assessment: まめなやつ calls Taichi diligent or meticulous. The English invents 'produceful' and leaves the pronoun outside a grammatical clause.

highlights.text: Produceful guy him.

records.jp: 俺と桜庭と友貴は、顔を見合わせた。
records.en: Me and Sakuraba and Tomoki's gazing faces met.
records.assessment: Taichi, Sakuraba, and Tomoki look at one another. The English turns three people into possessors of a single compound subject, uses an object pronoun, and says faces meet.

highlights.text: Me and Sakuraba and Tomoki's gazing faces met.

records.jp: 「捨てようとしたのか？　捨てようとしたんだろう？」
records.en: Taichi: "Were you trying to throw it away? Did you believe you could throw it away?"
records.assessment: Taichi repeats his accusation—she tried to throw it away, did she not? The English instead asks whether she believed disposal was possible.

highlights.text: Did you believe you could throw it away?

records.jp: 「ちーす、霧って来てるかー？」
records.en: Shinkawa: "'ullo, Kiri came din't she?"
records.assessment: Shinkawa greets them and asks whether Kiri is there. The English changes presence to a past arrival, makes it a confirmation tag, and adds British eye dialect.

highlights.text: 'ullo, Kiri came din't she?

records.jp: 「ちょっと太一！　待っててって言ったじゃないの！　どうして一人で行っちゃうのよ！」
records.en: Touko: "Seriously, Taichi! Did I not tell you to wait did I not! Whyyy did you go on alone now!"
comments: She seems in the middle of her too-sticky period, likely not long before the format. -GHS
records.assessment: The English repeats the interrogative tail around the same clause, producing an ungrammatical double question.

highlights.text: Did I not tell you to wait did I not!

records.jp: 「今日の冷蔵庫はカラだぞ、部長先輩」
records.en: Sakuraba: "Today the fridge is emptiness, President-senpai."
records.assessment: The Japanese says the refrigerator is empty. The English substitutes an abstract noun for the required adjective.

highlights.text: the fridge is emptiness

records.jp: 「ちょっと買ってきますんで、ひきとめておいてください！」
records.en: Misato: "I will go buy a bit, please detain them!"
comments: Doesn't seem to actually have a positive meaning... -GHS
records.assessment: Misato asks the others to keep the visitors there while she shops. 'Detain' implies coercive or official confinement.

highlights.text: please detain them

records.jp: 「絶対ですよー！」
records.en: Misato: "There is absolute need!"
comments: Flight -GHS
records.assessment: Misato emphatically insists. The English nominalizes that insistence as an absolute need and omits the natural referent.

highlights.text: There is absolute need!

records.jp: 「いちおう挨拶に。その……身内が世話になるわけだしよ」
records.en: Shinkawa: "Just giving my greetings as far as it goes. Well... gotta be nice to the people who take care of your relatives."
records.assessment: Shinkawa is greeting the club because his relative will be in their care. The English turns this into generic advice that someone must be nice to caretakers of the listener's relatives.

highlights.text: gotta be nice to the people who take care of your relatives

records.jp: 「えっ、俺野球部だし」
records.en: Shinkawa: "Eh, I'm in the Baseball Club me."
records.assessment: The English adds a redundant object pronoun after the completed clause.

highlights.text: I'm in the Baseball Club me.

records.jp: 「野球部なんてありましたっけ？」
records.en: Miki: "We actually have have a Baseball Club?"
records.assessment: The auxiliary is duplicated.

highlights.text: have have

records.jp: 「ひたすら野球盤を遊ぶ、部員三人だけの組織だ」
records.en: Sakuraba: "They're playing Baseball Pinball with all they have, even if their entire club strength is three people."
comments: http://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%87%8E%E7%90%83%E7%9B%A4 -GHS
records.assessment: 野球盤 is a tabletop mechanical baseball board game, not pinball.

highlights.text: Baseball Pinball

records.jp: 「あー、太一！　あんたいったいどういうつもりで約束すっぽかして……」
records.en: Taichi: "Ahhh, Taichi! What the devil do you think you are doing, making arrangements and then standing people up..."
comments: Same as above. Curiously, she gets very possessive *before* she joins. Or maybe, since this part seems to be Taichi's hallucination, maybe she's tsundere here for the same reason Sakuraba was blonde in his dream: he just confuses future with past. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese line is Touko angrily addressing Taichi. The English assigns the line to Taichi, making him complain to himself.

highlights.text: Taichi:

records.jp: ぷんぷん振るが離れない。
records.en: Angry angry shaking, but there's no dropping it.
records.assessment: Touko shakes her hand vigorously or angrily but cannot release the object. The English repeats an adjective as a bare modifier and makes the lack of release an existential noun phrase.

highlights.text: Angry angry shaking, but there's no dropping it.

records.jp: 「じゃあアンタが責任取ってもらいなさいよ！」
records.en: Touko: "Than youuu go and take it as your responsibility!"
records.assessment: Touko tells Taichi to take responsibility by taking the object. The English misspells 'then' and turns the object into an abstract responsibility to be taken.

highlights.text: Than youuu go and take it as your responsibility!

records.jp: 「仲間でないと受け渡しはできないんだ」
records.en: Taichi: "If they're not part of your Nakama, then handing it over is impossible."
comments: TVTropes switched this to True Companions, I won't forgive this!! except at times because that's an adequate adaptation. Hum, this would mean that Miki and Touko are Nakama... or that Taichi makes rules up as he goes, yeah. -GHS
records.assessment: 仲間 means a companion, ally, or party member in the game joke. The English leaves the common noun as an unexplained romanized Japanese word.

highlights.text: Nakama

records.jp: 冬子はぱくぱくと口を開閉させた。金魚みたい。
records.en: Pak-pak, she makes her mouth open and close. Just like a goldfish.
comments: PCP CCA0016
Told you it had to do with arcade games. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese mimetic describes her mouth opening and closing like a goldfish. The English leaves the mimetic as an unexplained romanization and attaches it as a dangling phrase.

highlights.text: Pak-pak, she makes her mouth open and close.

records.jp: ぽつりと、桜庭が呟く。
records.en: Sakuraba muttered with a sigh.
comments: See CCC0041. Hum, maybe this is meant literally... -GHS
records.assessment: ぽつり means that Sakuraba mutters the line quietly or in isolation. It does not state that he sighs.

highlights.text: with a sigh

records.jp: 「石けん水の力でな」
records.en: Sakuraba: "With the power of soap water."
comments: He....... washed his hands of it? Of course I assume metaphorical meaning in his having a bottle stuck in his finger, why do you ask. -GHS
records.assessment: 石けん水 is 'soapy water,' not the nonidiomatic compound 'soap water.'

highlights.text: soap water

records.jp: ちょっとしたお祭り騒ぎ。
records.en: and quite a bit of a festival's revelry.
records.assessment: ちょっとした means a small, little festival-like commotion. 'Quite a bit' reverses that scale, and the possessive makes revelry belong to a literal festival.

highlights.text: quite a bit of a festival's revelry

records.jp: 視線が集まる。
records.en: The sights gather.
comments: PCP CCA0002
records.assessment: The Japanese says everyone's gazes converge on him. 'Sights' refers to views, attractions, or aiming devices, not the gathered attention of observers.

highlights.text: The sights gather.

records.jp: 「ちょっと薄いな。骨盤が当たる。もっと肉感的になれよ」
records.en: Taichi: "Sorta bony innit. I can touch the pelvis. Get more voluptuous you!"
comments: That's different from Miki's reaction in that script, though. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi says her backside lacks flesh and her pelvis presses against him. The English adds a British tag and changes involuntary contact into his ability to touch it.

highlights.text: bony innit
I can touch the pelvis

records.jp: ボールか俺は。
records.en: What am I a ball now?
records.assessment: The rhetorical question requires punctuation or a complementizer: 'What am I, a ball?'

highlights.text: What am I a ball now?

records.jp: 「あれは太一の特別サービスと見た」
records.en: Sakuraba: "I saw that as special service for Taichi."
records.assessment: The Japanese says Sakuraba judges that to have been special treatment for Taichi. The English literalizes 見た as visual perception.

highlights.text: I saw that as special service

records.jp: 「男っす！」
records.en: Miki: "Yamman!"
comments: Might be a reference, but she might just be copying Kiri here. -GHS
records.assessment: 男っす praises the display as manly or calls him a real man. 'Yamman' is an invented, opaque word.

highlights.text: Yamman!

records.jp: 良質の思い出。
records.en: A superior quality memory.
records.assessment: 良質 calls it a good or precious memory. 'Superior quality' is a product-ranking collocation.

highlights.text: A superior quality memory.

records.jp: 家の前、道路を誰かが歩いていた。
records.en: Someone is walking in front of the house, in the street.
records.assessment: The Japanese past narrative says someone was walking along the road.

highlights.text: Someone is walking

records.jp: 荷物を抱えている。
records.en: Holding a bag.
records.assessment: 荷物 says she is carrying luggage or a load. The English narrows it to one bag without source support.

highlights.text: a bag

records.jp: 階下に。
records.en: To the lower floor.
records.assessment: 階下 means downstairs. 'The lower floor' is a literal spatial description rather than the movement destination.

highlights.text: To the lower floor.

records.jp: 俺は見つからないよう気配を殺し、近づく。
records.en: I kill my presence as not to be seen, and close in.
records.assessment: 気配を殺す means suppressing all sign of one's presence. The English exposes the Japanese metaphor and uses 'as not to' instead of 'so as not to.'

highlights.text: I kill my presence as not to be seen

records.jp: この国で手に入る、強力無比な武器だ。
records.en: Coming into possession of that in this country means to have a weapon of power without compare.
records.assessment: The Japanese calls it an incomparably powerful weapon obtainable in the country. The English makes acquisition the subject, turns description into a definition, and uses an awkward noun phrase for power.

highlights.text: Coming into possession of that in this country means to have a weapon of power without compare.

records.jp: 静音性に優れ、破壊力に富む。
records.en: it has its edge in quietness, and is rich in destructive power.
comments: NOT abundant? That would've been... weird I suppose. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says it excels in quiet operation and packs great destructive power. The English uses abstract calques for both qualities.

highlights.text: has its edge in quietness, and is rich in destructive power

records.jp: 霧は引き金を引いた。
records.en: Kiri pulls the trigger.
comments: Squeeze it, idiot. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese past narrative says Kiri pulled the trigger.

highlights.text: pulls the trigger

records.jp: 風切り音が耳に残る。
records.en: The sound of slashed air remains in the ears.
records.assessment: 風切り音 is the whistle or rush of the projectile cutting through air, and the sound remains in Taichi's ears. The English turns the air into something already slashed and omits the possessor.

highlights.text: sound of slashed air remains in the ears

records.jp: ぎこちない。
records.en: Awkwardly.
records.assessment: The Japanese adjective says her handling is awkward. The English adverb has no verb or action to modify.

highlights.text: Awkwardly.

records.jp: では、誰と。
records.en: Well then, who with?
records.assessment: The training is for fighting, so 誰と asks against whom. 'With whom' can instead imply cooperation.

highlights.text: who with?

records.jp: 誰と……だろう……。
records.en: Who with... indeed...
records.assessment: The Japanese continues wondering whom she intends to fight. 'With' again obscures the adversarial role, while 'indeed' changes uncertainty into affirmation.

highlights.text: Who with... indeed...

records.jp: 動作が跳ね上がりかけた矢先、絶妙のタイミングで肩を押さえられた。
records.en: Just on the arrowtip of being about to leap into a rash motion, I was pushed down on the shoulder with a miraculous timing.
comments: See CCC3003. Was he about to charge at Kiri... perhaps in the path of a bolt? Leaving 'arrowtip' sort of literal, given it all. -GHS
records.assessment: Just as Taichi is about to jump, a hand presses his shoulder at exactly the right moment. The English literalizes 矢先 as an arrowtip, changes restraint to being pushed down, and makes the timing miraculous.

highlights.text: Just on the arrowtip of being about to leap into a rash motion, I was pushed down on the shoulder with a miraculous timing.

records.jp: 膝から力が抜けた。
records.en: Power was removed from the knees.
comments: He's literally swinging a pipe at readers' heads with this. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says the strength goes out of Taichi's knees. The English makes abstract power something passively removed from detached body parts.

highlights.text: Power was removed from the knees.

records.jp: 「毎日やっているみたい」
records.en: Youko: "Seems to do this every day."
records.assessment: The Japanese says Kiri apparently practices every day. The English omits the grammatical subject.

highlights.text: Seems to do this every day.

records.jp: 「……アレはどこから手に入れたの？」
records.en: Taichi: "...how did she even come into that thing?"
records.assessment: The Japanese asks where she obtained it. 'Come into that thing' is not the English acquisition construction.

highlights.text: how did she even come into that thing?

records.jp: 定期的な風切り音の合間、静寂に吸い取られる。
records.en: They are absorbed into the still quietness in the intervals between the periodic sound of slashed air.
records.assessment: The Japanese refers to the regular whistle or rush of bolts cutting the air. 'Slashed air' is a literalized result rather than the sound event.

highlights.text: the periodic sound of slashed air

records.jp: 心なしか肩を落とす。
records.en: She gives a somewhat discouraged drop of the shoulders.
records.assessment: The Japanese says her shoulders seem to droop slightly. The English nominalizes the motion as a drop that she gives.

highlights.text: gives a somewhat discouraged drop of the shoulders

records.jp: 「……婚約者だろ」
records.en: Taichi: "...like fiancees, right?"
records.assessment: Taichi says they are an engaged couple. 'Fiancees' denotes two women, and 'like' weakens the asserted relationship into comparison.

highlights.text: like fiancees

records.jp: 「そう、婚約者」
records.en: Youko: "Yes, fiancees."
records.assessment: The two-person mixed-gender engaged relationship cannot be denoted by the female plural 'fiancees.'

highlights.text: fiancees

records.jp: 悲嘆が心を塗りつぶす前に、霧が動いた。
records.en: Before grief could paint over the heart, Kiri had moved.
comments: See CCB0015B. He's probably referring to him recalling her betrayal... and possibly even rushing out to meet death. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese gives Kiri's movement as the next event before grief overwhelms him. Past perfect incorrectly places it before the established narrative point.

highlights.text: Kiri had moved

records.jp: 三巡して、霧は訓練を追えた。
records.en: Three rounds later, Kiri has finished with practice.
records.assessment: The surrounding past narration says Kiri finished her practice after three cycles. Present perfect shifts the temporal frame.

highlights.text: has finished with practice

records.jp: 「早計するための知恵じゃない」
records.en: Youko: "Wisdom is to not make rash conclusions."
records.assessment: The Japanese says wisdom is not meant for jumping to conclusions. The English splits the infinitive after a copula and turns the governing purpose into an awkward identity.

highlights.text: Wisdom is to not make rash conclusions.

records.jp: 「仮に世界が繰り返されているとするなら、今論じる必要はないと思う」
records.en: Youko: "Even if, provisionally, we take that the world is made to repeat itself, there is no need to discuss it now, I think."
records.assessment: The Japanese gives one hypothetical condition: if the world is repeating. The English redundantly stacks 'even if' and 'provisionally' and introduces an external agent making it repeat.

highlights.text: Even if, provisionally, we take that the world is made to repeat itself

records.jp: 押し黙る。
records.en: She keeps silent.
records.assessment: The Japanese says Taichi falls silent in response to Youko. The English assigns the silence to Youko.

highlights.text: She keeps silent.

records.jp: もう追跡する必要はなかった。
records.en: There is no need to pursue more.
records.assessment: The Japanese says there is no longer any need to follow her. 'Pursue' can imply hunting or attacking and 'more' does not express the temporal cessation.

highlights.text: no need to pursue more

records.jp: 平原に出て、的になっていた樹を調べる。
records.en: Coming out into the open space, I examine the timber that was turned target.
comments: 平原, odd term. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says he examines the tree used as a target. 'Timber' denotes wood as material, and the English omits 'into a' from its transformation construction.

highlights.text: the timber that was turned target

records.jp: 中身は……食い物だった。
records.en: Contents were... food.
records.assessment: The countable contents require a determiner here: 'The contents were food.'

highlights.text: Contents were

records.jp: 「……出来杉君だな、こりゃ」
records.en: Taichi: "...really giving it all like Dek**ugi-kun, aren't you.
comments: http://doraemon.wikia.com/wiki/Hidetoshi_Dekisugi There's no asterisk, but it's still censored, as it plays the pun straight: 'dekisugi' means "to do too much", but where in Doraemon it's written with other kanji, here it's written with the straightforwards kanji for "do/be able to". -GHS
records.assessment: The line's Dekisugi reference labels Tomoki an overachieving model child. The English paraphrase 'giving it all' does not preserve that function, adds a question tag, and fails to close the quotation mark.

highlights.text: Taichi: "...really giving it all like Dek**ugi-kun, aren't you.

records.jp: それほどまでに本気だということだ。
records.en: This is the level of seriousness this reaches,
records.assessment: The Japanese says this shows how serious Tomoki is. The English recursively makes seriousness reach a level and leaves the sentence open with a comma.

highlights.text: This is the level of seriousness this reaches,

records.jp: 霧の両親も教えてはくれなかったらしい。
records.en: Kiri's parents didn't seem to want to tell him.
records.assessment: The Japanese says Kiri's parents apparently did not tell him. The English changes the completed refusal or omission into an inferred lack of desire.

highlights.text: didn't seem to want to tell him

records.jp: そして新川豊に家族がいないこと。
records.en:
And then, Shinkawa Yutaka spoke of how he is
without family.
comments: This adaptation wouldn't be needed if the first sentence flowed with the rest... curse this NVL segment for5seconds! -GHS
records.assessment: This is another fact in the narrator's list: Yutaka has no family. The English invents a speech act by Shinkawa and shifts the past account into present tense.

highlights.text:
Shinkawa Yutaka spoke of how he is
without family

records.jp: そしてついには、霧とともに群青送り。
records.en:
And then, in the end, he was sent to Gunjou
together with Kiri.
comments: Awww, don't just use "soshite" twice in a row... -GHS
records.assessment: The place name 群青 is Gunjō in standard Hepburn, not 'Gunjou.'

highlights.text: Gunjou

records.jp: 基本的に心の治療という名目もあってか、群青での校則はあってなきに等しい。
records.en: Basically, with the pretext of healing the heart, Gunjou's school regulations are next to ignorable.
comments: PCP CCB0004C
records.assessment: The Japanese says the school rules at Gunjō are virtually nonexistent, partly under the pretext of mental treatment. The English says existing rules are merely ignorable, calls mental care 'healing the heart,' and uses non-Hepburn 'Gunjou.'

highlights.text: Basically, with the pretext of healing the heart, Gunjou's school regulations are next to ignorable.

records.jp: 治療という名目で人を隔離しているこの学校は、自意識さえあれば無法地帯だった。
records.en: The mere possession of self-awareness made a lawless space of this school designed to isolate people with the pretext of medical treatment.
comments: See CCA0021, CCA0007. Besides the meta (hi, trolled ones!), it's Gunjou that allows him to stay like this. I think the effect Tanaka's going with this concept of 'self-awareness' is that (sadly demonstrated) idea that the handlers of a nuthouse can't tell the insane ones from normal ones that were to be put in there by mistake. It's true because I'm totally sane and I was put in here by mistake so GET ME OUT OF HERE NOW DAMN GUAAAAAAARDJDSPGWE-GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says the school was a lawless zone for anyone still possessing a sense of self. The English makes possession of self-awareness the cause that transformed the school.

highlights.text: The mere possession of self-awareness made a lawless space of this school

records.jp: 「そうか……まあそういうと思ったがな……」
records.en: Shinkawa: "Right... well I thought, you know..."
records.assessment: Shinkawa says he figured Taichi would say that. The English omits the predicted speech and turns it into a vague act of thinking.

highlights.text: well I thought, you know

records.jp: 「俺は記憶ソーシツの新川を肯定するぞ。けど記憶喪失でない新川はご免被る」
records.en: Taichi: "I'll be positive on Shinkawa who has memories missing. But Shinkawa without memory loss is too unpleasant to accept."
comments: "I'll forgive you if you have memory loss, but if you don't, I won't". He may actually be consciously remembering at this point. He's lying to himself, however, see CCC3026, or rather, he's stating what he should do but won't, see CCC3030. Rules followed in the outwards, not in the depth, like Misato does, and as is his wont as a fallen human. Also, "I go well with Shinkawa with memory loss, but I don't with the one without memory loss". -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi says he accepts the amnesiac Shinkawa but wants no part of a version without amnesia. The English uses the nonidiomatic 'positive on' and invents unpleasantness as the reason for refusal.

highlights.text: be positive on Shinkawa
too unpleasant to accept

records.jp: 「また二人でつるんでる」
records.en: Kiri: "You two mate-ing again."
comments: So odd she'd use that term. -GHS
records.assessment: つるむ means the two are hanging out together again. 'Mate-ing' is a malformed coinage that suggests sex or animal breeding.

highlights.text: You two mate-ing again.

records.jp: 「どうしろと」
records.en: Taichi: "Make up your mind!"
records.assessment: Taichi asks what form of address she wants him to use. The English instead accuses her of indecision and orders her to resolve it.

highlights.text: Make up your mind!

records.jp: 寝ていた。
records.en: He fell asleep.
comments: So damn meta. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says they discover him already asleep. The English depicts the event of falling asleep at that moment.

highlights.text: He fell asleep.

records.jp: 「すぐ寝るな、コイツ」
records.en: Taichi: "Quick to sleep this guy."
comments: ONIIIIIIIIII-CHAAAAAAN WAKE UP -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese remarks that he falls asleep quickly. The English uses an adjective phrase before an unintegrated subject noun phrase.

highlights.text: Quick to sleep this guy.

records.jp: 「……昔からそうなんです」
records.en: Kiri: "...he has been like this since a long time ago."
comments: That "long time ago" again, see CCC3003. -GHS
records.assessment: English uses 'for' with a duration: 'for a long time.'

highlights.text: since a long time ago

records.jp: 「後遺症みたいなものらしくて……」
records.en: Kiri: "They seem to be something like after effects..."
comments: ITS YOUR FIRST DAY OF SCHOOL AT NEKO ACADEMY -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese calls the sleepiness something like a singular aftereffect. The English uses a plural pronoun without an antecedent and splits the compound 'aftereffects.'

highlights.text: They seem to be something like after effects

records.jp: 「前の学校で、友達なんていませんでしたから。兄にも私にも」
records.en: Kiri: "Because, at our previous school we did not have friends. Neither I nor Ani."
comments: Unclear if Kiri and Yutaka went to the same school, or if the two were simply in the same conditions.
records.assessment: 兄 means her older brother. The English leaves it as an unexplained Japanese kinship term instead of translating it.

highlights.text: Ani

records.jp: 「そして牙を剥くこともある」
records.en: Taichi: "And then you went and bared your fangs."
comments: Referring to CCC3004 -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese generalizes that victims may sometimes bare their fangs in response. The English assigns the action specifically to Kiri, shifts it into completed past, and adds reproachful 'went and.'

highlights.text: you went and bared your fangs

records.jp: 「……人間じゃないですか」
records.en: Kiri: "...are you not human?"
comments: Careful now: different from his usual taunt, "you are not a person". She wondering why he would even consider not defending himself from someone who'd shoot him to death. Interesting foreshadowing, on this. -GHS
records.assessment: Kiri protests that the supposedly wild beasts are human beings. The English instead asks whether Taichi himself is human.

highlights.text: are you not human?

records.jp: 低く、霧は吐いた。
records.en: So spat out Kiri, tone lowering.
records.assessment: The Japanese says Kiri spits the words out in a low voice. The English uses an archaic inversion and makes her tone an ungoverned progressive fragment.

highlights.text: So spat out Kiri, tone lowering.

records.jp: 「中にはね……本当に人じゃないのもいるんだ」
records.en: Taichi: "Inside here... truly, there's something not of the person."
comments: THIS is where her "you're not a person" will come from. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi says some among them truly are no longer human. The English substitutes a place called 'inside here,' changes people to one thing, and produces the non-English phrase 'not of the person.'

highlights.text: Inside here... truly, there's something not of the person.

records.jp: 「頑張って生きないとな。少しでも奴らに尻尾を振って、あの普通の人とかいう連中に、媚びをうってでもさ……生きんと」
records.en: Taichi: "I just do my best to live. I wag my tail a bit to those people that call themselves normal, launch myself into flattery a bit to them... I gotta live."
records.assessment: Taichi says he must work to survive even if that means wagging his tail and currying favor with so-called normal people. The English turns necessity into a current habit and says he 'launches' himself into flattery.

highlights.text: Taichi: "I just do my best to live. I wag my tail a bit to those people that call themselves normal, launch myself into flattery a bit to them... I gotta live."

records.jp: 「みんなの悪意が……」
records.en: Kiri: "Everybody's malicious..."
records.assessment: Kiri identifies everyone's malice as what frightens her. The English instead directly characterizes every person as malicious.

highlights.text: Everybody's malicious

records.jp: 彼女もまた、望んでここに来たわけでない。
records.en: She, herself, is not here because she has wished it.
records.assessment: The Japanese says she did not come there by choice. The English mixes present location with present perfect wishing in a nonidiomatic causal construction.

highlights.text: is not here because she has wished it

records.jp: 「……人間なんて、なくなる時にはあっさりなくなるって思ってます……だって、世界にはほとんど何もないから……」
records.en: Kiri: "...I think that humans, when they depart, will just vanish like that... because in this world there is nearly nothing."
comments: Their death, their total disappeareance... the end of the world. This is part of how Taichi's Settei will be constructed. -GHS
records.assessment: Kiri says humanity or human beings can disappear with shocking ease when the time comes. 'Depart' reframes this as individual death or leave-taking and the future tense makes it a prediction.

highlights.text: humans, when they depart, will just vanish like that

records.jp: 「きっと『何もない』方が多いんです。『なにかある』方は、ちょっとだけなんです！」
records.en: Kiri: "I am sure, there is Nothing in so much. In just so little is there Anything!"
comments: People, places, everything. -GHS
records.assessment: Kiri says the realm of nothingness is surely much larger and the realm where something exists only a little. The English uses two ungrammatical inversions and fails to make the comparative relation intelligible.

highlights.text: there is Nothing in so much. In just so little is there Anything!

records.jp: 「そういうのとは違って……そういう理由があるのとは違って……」
records.en: Kiri: "It is different from that... it is different in how there is a reason in that..."
comments: IOW, if this were sci-fi, there'd be some explanation. Troll 'em readers... -GHS
