records.assessment: The Japanese's joking stack of negatives resolves to an admission that he does feel some so-called gratitude toward his companions. The English's ungrammatical negative chain instead appears to deny ever giving or feeling gratitude.
records.remedy: I can't say I feel no so-called gratitude toward the friends who always put up with me.

highlights.text: I haven't but never given something that could be called gratitude

records.jp: 「いいんじゃないの。細かいことは」
records.en: Tomoki: "You sure it was right? All those details, I mean."
records.assessment: The Japanese reassures him that it is fine and dismisses the minor details. The English instead questions whether he was right and foregrounds those details, reversing the pragmatic force.
records.remedy: It's fine, isn't it? Don't sweat the details.

highlights.text: You sure it was right? All those details, I mean.

records.en: Sakuraba: "...don't they."
records.assessment: The Japanese is a brief agreement: 'Yeah' or 'Right.' The English is an incomplete negative tag question and does not express assent.
records.remedy: ...Yeah.

highlights.text: ...don't they.

records.en: Kiri: "Go."
records.assessment: The Japanese is only the initial syllable of the following formal acknowledgment, isolated as Kiri struggles to speak. Translating it as the imperative 'Go' invents lexical meaning and obscures the false start.

highlights.text: Go.

records.jp: お。
records.en: Go.
records.assessment: The narrator echoes Kiri's isolated opening syllable, not an imperative meaning 'go.' Assigning lexical meaning removes the mirrored hesitation.

highlights.text: Go.

records.jp: 「気が抜けたんじゃー！　慰めてくれー！」
records.en: Taichi: "I'm just exhausteeed! I'm being comforteeed!"
records.assessment: The Japanese is a request for Kiri to comfort him. The English turns it into a statement that the comforting is already happening.
records.remedy: I'm exhausted! Comfort meee!

highlights.text: I'm being comforteeed!

records.jp: 「あ、でも……やっていただくようなことは……」
records.en: Misato: "Ah, but... letting you do this, that would be..."
records.assessment: The Japanese trails off while explaining that there is not really anything for them to do. The English instead frames the problem as permission to let them do an unspecified 'this,' omitting the absence of available work.
records.remedy: Ah, but... there isn't really anything for you to do...

highlights.text: letting you do this, that would be

records.jp: 「あの、その、でも今までずっとサボって……」
records.en: Miki: "Uhm, well, but you have been cutting up until now..."
records.assessment: The Japanese says they have been skipping or slacking off from club activities. 'Cutting up' means behaving noisily or mischievously, not being absent.
records.remedy: Um, but you've both been skipping club all this time...

highlights.text: you have been cutting up until now

records.jp: 「……決まりだね」
records.en: Taichi: "...determined innshe."
records.assessment: The Japanese means that the matter is settled. The English is malformed and appears to describe a woman as determined, which is a different proposition.
records.remedy: ...Then it's settled.

highlights.text: ...determined innshe.

records.jp: 敬礼して告げた。
records.en: So I proclaimed with a bow.
records.assessment: The Japanese says he announces this while giving a military salute, matching the surrounding soldier routine. A bow is a different gesture and removes that visual continuation.
records.remedy: I announced it with a salute.

highlights.text: with a bow

records.jp: 「しょーですよー、ごじゆーにー」
records.en: Taichi: "Shoo we are, feel free twhoo."
comments: Cutesy -GHS
records.assessment: The slurred Japanese means roughly 'That's right, be my guest.' The English changes the first clause to a first-person plural statement and is not coherently recoverable as the response.
records.remedy: Thaaat's right, be my gueeest.

highlights.text: Shoo we are, feel free twhoo.

records.jp: 「……ま、ここまでつきあったし。好きにすれば」
records.en: Taichi: "...bah, I went together with this so far. I'll do as you like."
records.assessment: The Japanese tells Miki that, since he has gone along this far, she may do as she likes. The English instead promises that he will act according to her wishes.
records.remedy: ...Well, I've gone along with it this far. Do what you like.

highlights.text: I'll do as you like.

records.jp: 人類の意地をかけて、平常でいてやるのもいいだろう。
records.en: It's probably in the disposition of mankind this preference to do what is usual.
records.assessment: The Japanese proposes defiantly maintaining ordinary life for the sake of humanity's pride. The English recasts that deliberate stance as a probable innate human disposition and loses the wager of pride.
records.remedy: For the sake of humanity's pride, it might be good to insist on carrying on as normal.

highlights.text: It's probably in the disposition of mankind this preference to do what is usual.

records.jp: 「返すなよ。絶対に返すなよ？　やるんだからな」
records.en: Taichi: "Do not give this back! Absolutely do not give this back get it? I'll do you in if you do!"
records.assessment: The Japanese explains that he is giving Sakuraba the handkerchief outright, which is why it must not be returned. The English instead threatens to kill or attack him if he returns it.
records.remedy: Don't return it. Absolutely don't return it, okay? I'm giving it to you.

highlights.text: I'll do you in if you do!

records.jp: そろって人を責め立てる。
records.en: Gathering together, torturing people!
comments: This isn't as funny, considering he probably saw the cruelty of the women of the Hasekura firsthand. See CCD0022A now. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says the two girls join together in berating or blaming him. 'Torturing' materially escalates their verbal reproach into inflicted torment.
records.remedy: They gang up on me and lay into me.

highlights.text: torturing people

records.jp: 「何もわかってない……」
records.en: Kiri: "I don't get this at all..."
comments: As I always do, I suspect more dick puns. -GHS
records.assessment: Kiri tells the narrator that he understands nothing. The English instead has Kiri say that she herself does not understand, reversing the subject.
records.remedy: You don't understand anything...

highlights.text: I don't get this at all

records.jp: 「わかった……だがたかが風呂に一日入らなかったくらいでこの仕打ち……」
records.en: Taichi: "I get it... but this poor treatment just because I didn't take a bath every day, really..."
records.assessment: The Japanese protests that he skipped bathing for only one day. The English instead says he failed to bathe every day, which can describe a recurring habit and loses the one-day limitation.
records.remedy: all this just because I went one day without a bath

highlights.text: just because I didn't take a bath every day

records.jp: 異常者扱い。
records.en: The treatment for one abnormal.
comments: PCP CCC3002
records.assessment: The Japanese says he is being treated as a freak or abnormal person. The English can only mean treatment intended for an abnormal person and does not express how the girls are labeling him.
records.remedy: They're treating me like a freak.

highlights.text: The treatment for one abnormal.

records.jp: 「……え、なにされるの俺？」
records.en: Taichi: "...eh, what are you making me do?"
records.assessment: The Japanese asks what the girls are going to do to him. The English asks what they are making him do, reversing who performs the unknown action.
records.remedy: ...uh, what are you going to do to me?

highlights.text: what are you making me do?

records.jp: 「じゃー！」
records.en: Miki: "And now...!
records.assessment: The Japanese is the prolonged sound of water gushing from the opened hose, not a transitional phrase meaning 'and now.' The English removes the sound effect that motivates the next line.
records.remedy: Whoooosh!

highlights.text: And now...!

records.jp: 二人はデッキブラシを持って……デッキブラシっ！
records.en: Shipdeck scrub in hand, the two... SHIPDECK SCRUB?!
comments: Likely just a long-handled floor brush -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese names a deck brush, the physical tool the two are holding. 'Shipdeck scrub' describes an action or cleaning session rather than the brush.
records.remedy: deck brush

highlights.text: Shipdeck scrub

records.jp: くそう、これも朝からカンパンなんて食べたせいか！
records.en: Dammit, did they confuse me with a deck oven? Is it because I've eaten Kanpan from a house decked with them this morning? It's because I have a mess inside, don't I!
comments: See CCC4002. Mess Hall. No one got it? No one? Well, huff! *stomps away* -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese only curses and wonders whether this treatment is another consequence of eating hardtack that morning, activating the homophone with 'deck.' The English invents a deck oven, a house decked with food, and an internal mess, none of which occurs in the source wordplay.
records.remedy: Damn it, is this another consequence of eating hardtack first thing this morning?!

highlights.text: Dammit, did they confuse me with a deck oven? Is it because I've eaten Kanpan from a house decked with them this morning? It's because I have a mess inside, don't I!

records.jp: あの店主（女性・美人・２５歳）、自身も変態だから見境無く売るな。
records.en: That shopkeeper (female - hot - 25) is a pervert herself, so she sells everything indiscriminately.
comments: And THIS is why Taichi is always there. See CCB0008. Curiously, the implication there is that Miki could *not* buy her panties normally, here it seems the opposite, that it was the owner of the shop who sold them to Miki. More interesting it's that Taichi immediately runs to thinking that the owner would've sold her this stuff, not that she's no more and therefore Miki would've had no problem pilfering the stuff! 2+5=7, as typical, and perhaps also a hint of sorts. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese is the narrator's admonition that the shopkeeper should not sell things indiscriminately just because she is a pervert herself. The English changes that command into a descriptive causal claim that she does sell everything.
records.remedy: That shopkeeper is a pervert herself, but she shouldn't sell things indiscriminately.

highlights.text: so she sells everything indiscriminately

records.jp: 俺が苦労して実施した、合宿はなんだったのだろう。
records.en: What even went wrong with that training camp that I went to so much trouble to establish by force?
comments: Remember what's about to happen. Miki's fake club cannot stand anymore than Taichi's training camp could. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese asks what the training camp he worked so hard to carry out had amounted to. It does not state that the camp went wrong or that he established it by force; those possibilities are raised only in the following self-questioning line.
records.remedy: What, then, was that training camp I went to so much trouble to organize?

highlights.text: What even went wrong with that training camp
to establish by force

records.jp: 人はどうやって触れあえばいいのか。
records.en: What is the right way for people to touch each other?
records.assessment: The Japanese asks how people should connect or interact with one another, a thematic social question. 'Touch each other' narrows that reciprocal contact to physical touching and loses the broader relational sense.
records.remedy: How are people supposed to connect with one another?

highlights.text: touch each other

records.jp: それに……学校に行っても賑やかさは感じられない。
records.en: Besides... I might have gone to school, but I cannot feel its bustling liveliness.
comments: CP CCC3003
records.assessment: The Japanese says that even when he goes to school, he cannot feel any liveliness. The English turns his actual attendance into an uncertain past possibility.
records.remedy: Besides... even when I go to school, I can't feel any liveliness there.

highlights.text: I might have gone to school

records.jp: 「…………そ、そうでした」
records.en: Misato: "......w-, well, is it indeed."
records.assessment: The Japanese is Misato remembering and conceding: 'Oh, that's right.' The English instead sounds like a doubtful question about whether the claim is true.
records.remedy: ...O-oh, that's right.

highlights.text: well, is it indeed

records.jp: 「ベトナムコンプレックスどもめが！」
records.en: Taichi: "Damn you Vietnam Complex!"
comments: See below. PS2: "you damn war-guzzling losers!" The word he uses for 'losers' also means "unmarried woman over 30 with child". Ouch. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese insult addresses the group as people with a 'Vietnam complex.' The English instead appears to address the abstract complex itself and loses the plural human target of the joke.
records.remedy: Damn you Vietnam-complex freaks!

highlights.text: Damn you Vietnam Complex!

records.jp: くそ、なんか半分本気だな、こっちは。
records.en: Crap, am I half-serious or what.
comments: Meaning not giving his full...? -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese observes that the opponent on this side is half serious about killing or hurting him. The English makes the narrator question whether he himself is half serious.
records.remedy: Damn, this one's half serious, isn't she?

highlights.text: am I half-serious or what

records.jp: 「お前がな！」
records.en: Taichi: "And you ain't!"
records.assessment: The Japanese retort means 'You're one to talk' or 'You're the impudent one.' The English negative instead denies an unspecified predicate and does not return the accusation.
records.remedy: You're one to talk!

highlights.text: And you ain't!

records.jp: これも外れたが、霧はさらに体勢を崩した。
records.en: That also successful, Kiri's posture collapses even more.
records.assessment: The Japanese explicitly says the second shot also missed, although Kiri lost her balance further. The English calls the shot successful, reversing the result.
records.remedy: That one missed too, but Kiri lost her balance even further.

highlights.text: That also successful

records.jp: 洗面器の水で、血を洗い流す。
records.en: I was away the blood with the water in the rinse basin.
comments: Which was there. Somehow. Left behind despite humanity being gone. Like it was in the toilets, and home, and more. More and more credible, isn't it. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says he washes the blood away with water from the basin. The English's 'was away' is not a grammatical rendering of that action and leaves the procedure unclear.
records.remedy: I wash the blood away with water from the basin.

highlights.text: I was away the blood

records.jp: 染みたらしい。
records.en: Looks like it permeated.
records.assessment: The Japanese says the disinfectant apparently stung the wound. 'Permeated' describes soaking or penetration and does not convey the painful sensation demonstrated by her cry.
records.remedy: Looks like that stung.

highlights.text: Looks like it permeated.

records.jp: 包帯どめ。
records.en: Dressing's crap.
comments: See CCA0017A -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese names a bandage fastener or clip as the next medical item. The English instead makes a derogatory statement that the dressing is bad.
records.remedy: Bandage clip.

highlights.text: Dressing's crap.

records.jp: 「なに。医者もいないし、怪我は一大事だ。自愛してくれ」
records.en: Taichi: "What for. There's no doctors anymore, injuries are a very big deal. We gotta take care of ourselves."
records.assessment: The Japanese directly tells Miki to take care of herself because injuries are serious without a doctor. The English generalizes the instruction into a mutual 'we,' weakening the personal concern that prompts her reply.
records.remedy: Take good care of yourself.

highlights.text: We gotta take care of ourselves.

records.jp: 「思い出にせよ」
records.en: Taichi: "Though you got memories!"
records.assessment: The Japanese tells Miki to make the kiss a memory or remember it fondly. The English instead asserts that she possesses unspecified memories and introduces an unsupported adversative.
records.remedy: Make it a memory.

highlights.text: Though you got memories!

records.jp: 「で、俺のことをふたりじめしてくれ」
records.en: Taichi: "Well, please count me as two."
comments: 二人締め? Seems to be Osakan. And of course she can count him as two, though his other is still another "girl". I know Youko is Taichisexual, and also Taichi in drag, but can we have those Kiri/Youko fanfics already? -GHStillHereToHelp
records.assessment: The Japanese asks the two girls to keep him all to themselves, continuing the joke that only the girls are doubled. The English instead asks to count the narrator numerically as two people.
records.remedy: Then the two of you can have me all to yourselves.

highlights.text: please count me as two

records.jp: 「警戒されているらしい」
records.en: Taichi: "You seem to be vigilant."
records.assessment: The Japanese has the narrator observe that he is apparently being guarded against. The English instead tells Miki that she seems vigilant, changing the passive target into the active subject.
records.remedy: Looks like you're on your guard against me.

highlights.text: You seem to be vigilant.

records.jp: 「性欲をもてあます」
records.en: Miki: "Sexual desire incontrollable."
comments: PCP CCC4001
records.assessment: The Japanese is a complete statement that the speaker cannot control or has more sexual desire than she knows what to do with. The English uses the nonstandard adjective 'incontrollable' in an ungrammatical fragment.
records.remedy: I can't control my sexual desire.

highlights.text: Sexual desire incontrollable.

records.jp: 霧はどんな秘密を握られているんだろう。
records.en: What secret could Kiri possibly be hiding?
records.assessment: The Japanese passive says that someone has a secret of Kiri's in hand and is using it as leverage over her. The English instead makes Kiri the person concealing a secret and loses the leverage relationship.
records.remedy: What kind of secret does she have on Kiri, I wonder?

highlights.text: What secret could Kiri possibly be hiding?

records.jp: 「暗くなる前につけたのはいいけど、暗くなる前に帰らないとな」
records.en: Taichi: "It's good we got here before it got dark, but we can't get home before it's dark, so..."
comments: Repeating Taichi repeats stuff? Maybe he's just tired. Or Tanaka's sloppy on editing, as he's been throughout this route. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that they must return before it gets dark. The English says that returning before dark is impossible, reversing obligation into inability.
records.remedy: we need to get home before it gets dark

highlights.text: we can't get home before it's dark

records.jp: 「夕日だよ？」
records.en: Miki: "Twilight, was else?"
comments: "I heard the last movie was awesome (with the reminder that good and awesome are unrelated)!" -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese reply identifies the sunset and means 'what else?' The English substitutes twilight and contains the grammatical error 'was else.'
records.remedy: The sunset, what else?

highlights.text: Twilight, was else?

records.jp: 「これって夕日でしょ？」
records.en: Kiri: "Isn't this the twilight?"
comments: No, seriously, she means it in the (echo) SYMBOLISM! (echo) way. IT IS THE TWILIGHT OF THE ROUTE, AND ALSO OF THE STORY OFMGFMVLSADZDSRP -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese asks whether the visible phenomenon is the setting sun. The English calls it twilight, obscuring the following distinction between sunset and afterglow.
records.remedy: the sunset

highlights.text: the twilight

records.jp: デートというか、多感なオトモダチ同士って感じだな。
records.en: More than a date, this feels more like bonding between emotionally sensitive friends.
records.assessment: The Japanese says this feels less like a date and more like an outing among sensitive friends. 'More than a date' reverses the comparison by suggesting something beyond or more significant than a date.
records.remedy: Rather than a date

highlights.text: More than a date

records.jp: ま、楽しそうだからいいか。
records.en: Well, we're having fun so it's good.
records.assessment: The Japanese observes that the girl appears to be enjoying herself. The English changes this external observation into a claim that the whole group is having fun.
records.remedy: she looks like she's having fun

highlights.text: we're having fun

records.jp: 希望は通るが。
records.en: Wishes are conveyed, but...
records.assessment: The Japanese says that students' preferences or requests are honored. The English only says that wishes are communicated, changing whether they are acted upon.
records.remedy: They do honor our preferences, though.

highlights.text: Wishes are conveyed

records.jp: 二人とも一個下の三年生として編入された。
records.en: The two of them were admitted as third years one school level below.
comments: Middle school. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says the two entered as third-years one year below the narrator. 'One school level below' suggests a different division of schooling rather than the adjacent year or grade.
records.remedy: third-years, one year below me

highlights.text: one school level below

records.jp: 「あとさ、桜庭の柿の種の説法とか覚えてる？」
records.en: Taichi: "And then, do you remember that sermon Sakuraba did on seeds of persimmon?"
comments: Oh yes. Word used has explicit religious undertone. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese names Kaki no Tane, the established rice-cracker snack, in recalling Sakuraba's lecture. The English parses the compound literally as actual persimmon seeds and changes the object being discussed.
records.remedy: Kaki no Tane rice crackers

highlights.text: seeds of persimmon

records.jp: 「シャレになりません」
records.en: Kiri: "Do not make this a joke."
records.assessment: The Japanese evaluates the situation as too serious to be a joke. The English turns that reaction into an instruction not to make a joke, changing the utterance's function.
records.remedy: That's no joke.

highlights.text: Do not make this a joke.

records.jp: 「うむ。もはやベティだった」
records.en: Taichi: "Yep. It was exceedingly Neya."
records.assessment: The Japanese extends the preceding beta or hackneyed joke by personifying it as the name Betty. 'Neya' has no support in the source and breaks both the wordplay and the explanation that follows.
records.remedy: It was practically Betty by then.

highlights.text: It was exceedingly Neya.

records.jp: 「ま、とにかくシェイクスピアだ。日本名にしたら……フッ、振槍さんってとこか」
records.en: Taichi: "Well, anyway, Shakespeare. If I'd have to make the name in Japanese, let's see, kanji for shake read 'furu' and kanji for spear read 'yari', so..."
comments: Little point without kanji, so replacing with a really lame overexplaining. That's the entirety joke anyway. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese completes the literalized name joke with 'Furuyari-san.' The English explains the component readings but omits the resulting name that the next reaction answers.
records.remedy: Well, anyway, Shakespeare. In Japanese that would make him... Mr. Furuyari, I suppose.

highlights.text: Well, anyway, Shakespeare. If I'd have to make the name in Japanese, let's see, kanji for shake read 'furu' and kanji for spear read 'yari', so...

records.jp: 「さあ？」
records.en: Miki: "Who cares?"
comments: Usually it'd be a "dunno", but voice is obviously annoyed. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese means 'Who knows?' and answers uncertainty about the spelling. 'Who cares?' instead dismisses the question as unimportant.
records.remedy: Who knows?

highlights.text: Who cares?

records.en: Miki: "...a play with major twists?"
comments: Term also refers to a performance with lots of twists, so it ties to the above. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese jokes that the casting is a reversal because the two expected roles were swapped. The English interprets the expression as plot twists and loses the gender-role reversal being discussed.
records.remedy: ...a role-reversal play?

highlights.text: a play with major twists?

records.assessment: The clipped Japanese reaction expresses aversion or 'no way.' 'Come on' instead urges continuation or objects in a different register and does not preserve the recoil.

records.jp: 「そのハモりなんかムカつく」
records.en: Taichi: "Those harmonics kinda piss me off."
comments: see CCA0015, CCA0027, CCC0031B... it may be crap but it's a running gag. And having the PS2 and PC version running parallel means I just heard a quartet. Yay. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese refers to the two girls saying the same line in harmony or unison. 'Harmonics' denotes acoustic overtones and does not identify their synchronized speech.
records.remedy: That harmony

highlights.text: Those harmonics

records.jp: 「で、我が貞操を守るため、俺は平手を繰り出した。それがヤツの耳に当たって……まあちょっと怪我をさせてしまったのだ」
records.en: Taichi: "Then, to protect Our Chastity, I lunged at him with the palm of the hand. And I struck right on the ears... leaving him, well, with a bit of an injury it seems."
comments: ...and Taichi retaliates violently, leaving him with the above (psychological) wound. And then Sakuraba pretty much relents and acts nicely, if pushily, around him. Very odd that the injury does seem to be caused by something a liiittle worse than the palm of his hand; like a large knife he *needs* to protect himself (see CCC4010). The comparison with Yutaka, here, is very interesting. How did Taichi genuinely expect Yutaka to die by just falling off the stairs? -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the narrator delivered an open-handed slap to protect his own chastity. The English changes 'my' to 'our' and describes a vague lunge with a palm instead of the slap whose impact injured the ear.
records.remedy: to protect my chastity, I slapped him.

highlights.text: to protect Our Chastity, I lunged at him with the palm of the hand.

records.jp: 「そんなのは一人でたくさん……というか、俺が求めてるのは普通の人間関係なんだー、と夕日に叫びたいお年頃なわけだ。はい、おしまい。おもしろかったか？」
records.en: Taichi: "And then, on my own, there's so much I... well, better should I say, what I pursue are normal human relatiooons!, that's what I want to scream to the sunset at the time of my life I currently am at. There, all done. Was it interesting?"
records.assessment: The Japanese idiom says that even one person like that is already more than enough. The English turns it into a broken statement about the narrator being alone and loses the limit on troublesome relationships.
records.remedy: One person like that is already more than enough...

highlights.text: And then, on my own, there's so much I...

records.jp: 二人はこくこくと頷いた。
records.en: Bob bob steady nod in duo.
comments: PCP CCB0002
records.assessment: The Japanese simply says that both girls nodded repeatedly. The English is an ungrammatical string of nouns and modifiers rather than an intelligible narrative sentence.
records.remedy: The two of them nodded eagerly.

highlights.text: Bob bob steady nod in duo.

records.jp: 沈んだ日。その光だけが、空をよじのぼって。
records.en: The sun had sank. Only its light, now, clambers up in the sky.
records.assessment: The Japanese presents the sun as already set and its light climbing the sky in one past-tense image. The English uses the ungrammatical past participle 'sank' after 'had' and abruptly shifts the light into present tense.
records.remedy: The sun had sunk. Only its light climbed up the sky.

highlights.text: The sun had sank. Only its light, now, clambers up in the sky.

records.jp: 俺たちは、美希が泣いている理由さえわからず。
records.en: We had no understanding even the reason why Miki was crying,
records.assessment: The Japanese says they did not even understand why Miki was crying. The English omits the preposition required by 'understanding' and leaves the sentence grammatically malformed.
records.remedy: We didn't even understand why Miki was crying

highlights.text: We had no understanding even the reason why Miki was crying

records.jp: 「やっと来れた」
records.en: Taichi: "I finally larrived."
comments: The literal one is wrong due to ranuki kotoba which is uhmmm you either know or you could likely not care less, so look it up if you really want to. Let's just say it's about removing 'ra' from verbal forms, which, Research (AKA a little googlin') indicates that it's more typical of typo or misuse for affectation than a proper form. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese uses a colloquial ra-dropping form of 'could come.' The English creates the nonexistent word 'larrived,' which is not intelligible on its own and reverses omission into an added initial sound.
records.remedy: I finally managed to come.

highlights.text: I finally larrived.

records.jp: ら抜き言葉で、俺は感慨を示した。
records.en: I expressed my strong feelings by unnecessarily making a word start with "la".
comments: The difficulty with adapting 'ranuki kotoba'? See CCZAS, where all the "ra" that Taichi removes end up. ...I sort of wish I was kidding, but no, that's exactly it. This won't be the first reference to the cut scenario, by the way. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese explicitly comments on ra-nuki, a form made by dropping a ra syllable. The English says a sound was added to the start of a word, reversing the linguistic mechanism it purports to explain.
records.remedy: with a colloquial ra-dropping form

highlights.text: by unnecessarily making a word start with "la"

records.jp: 何十往復すればこんなことになるのだろう。
records.en: This is what would happen when you go around and around many times.
comments: This one's just rubbing it in reader's faces. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese asks how many dozens of round trips would be needed to produce so many overlapping tracks. The English turns the question into a generic assertion and omits both the round trips and the scale.
records.remedy: How many dozens of round trips would it take to leave tracks like this?

highlights.text: This is what would happen when you go around and around many times.

records.en: I tried to immerse myself in thought---
comments: HACK Cornholio must've been here. -GHS
records.assessment: The authoritative Japanese is only a silent exclamation of sudden alarm. The English invents a full narration about trying to think and replaces the reaction entirely.

highlights.text: I tried to immerse myself in thought---

records.jp: 探すのは違和感だけだ。
records.en: The only thing I can search for is the sense of physical discomfort.
comments: There's that term again. -GHS
records.assessment: In this search, iwakan means an anomaly or something out of place that might reveal a hidden threat. 'Physical discomfort' turns the external irregularity into a bodily sensation and misstates what the narrator is scanning for.
records.remedy: anything that feels out of place

highlights.text: sense of physical discomfort

records.jp: 俺の目は違和感を逃がさない。
records.en: That sense of physical discomfort will never escape from my eyes.
comments: If the sense of physical discomfort is something that doesn't exist, then what IS he finding? -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says the narrator's eyes do not miss anomalies. The English again makes the anomaly a bodily discomfort and then makes that sensation the subject escaping from his eyes, producing an incoherent relation.
records.remedy: My eyes never miss anything out of place.

highlights.text: That sense of physical discomfort will never escape from my eyes.

records.jp: 慎重に迂回して、根本に近づく。
records.en: I prudently walk around it, to near the tree roots.
records.assessment: The Japanese says he circles carefully and approaches the base of the suspicious setup. It does not identify tree roots; the English introduces a tree-specific target and obscures that he is inspecting the trap.
records.remedy: and approach its base.

highlights.text: to near the tree roots.

records.jp: 段差に注意をはらっていると、死ぬことになるわけだ。
records.en: If I gone to the step without paying attention, I would have been dead.
records.assessment: The Japanese says the victim dies if attention is directed to the visible step, because that distraction hides the trap. The English says death follows from not paying attention to the step, reversing the trap's design as well as using an ungrammatical verb form.
records.remedy: If you focus on the step, the trap kills you.

highlights.text: If I gone to the step without paying attention, I would have been dead.

records.jp: 胸を中心に血が広がっている。
records.en: Blood spread into the center of her chest.
comments: Well, she gave love a bad name, so there. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says blood has spread outward with the chest as its center, describing the visible extent around the wound. The English reverses that direction and says the blood moved into the chest's center.
records.remedy: Blood had spread out from the center of her chest.

highlights.text: Blood spread into the center of her chest.

records.jp: ……本当は、獅子にも狼にもなれた彼女だ。
records.en: ...truth is, she had become more like a lion or a big bad wolf.
records.assessment: The Japanese says she was in truth capable of becoming a lion or a wolf, contrasting that potential with the rabbit image. The English says she had already become like them and adds the fairy-tale register 'big bad.'
records.remedy: she was capable of becoming a lion or a wolf.

highlights.text: she had become more like a lion or a big bad wolf.

records.jp: 俺の半身が死んだ。
records.en: Half of my body had died.
comments: I guess this is the death of Taichi Of This World. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese uses 'half of me' for a person experienced as part of oneself. 'Half of my body' literalizes it as physical anatomy and loses the relational meaning.
records.remedy: Half of me had died.

highlights.text: Half of my body had died.

records.jp: 「茂みに入るから、持ってただけだ」
records.en: Taichi: "I had to get through the ticket, that's why I do, no other reason."
records.assessment: The Japanese says he was only holding the knife because he was entering the thicket. The English mistranslates 'thicket' as 'ticket' and leaves the explanation grammatically incoherent.
records.remedy: I only had it out because I was going into the thicket.

highlights.text: I had to get through the ticket, that's why I do, no other reason.

records.jp: 存外、俺は衝撃を受けていたらしい。
records.en: Unexpectedly, I too seem to have struck with a big impact.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that, contrary to expectation, the narrator seems to have been deeply shocked. The English makes him the ungrammatical agent of 'have struck' rather than the person affected by the shock.
records.remedy: Apparently, I was more deeply shocked than I'd expected.

highlights.text: I too seem to have struck with a big impact.

records.jp: 曜子ちゃんを火葬にした。
records.en: I decided to cremate Youko-chan.
comments: Cremating people without proper equipment is really hard. Trust me, I totally watched it on CSI and stuff and didn't try it myself. Certainly not while the stupid bas--- the "alleged victim" was alive. Plus, given Week 2, where Touko smells Taichi's roasted potatoes from the fricking other side of town, there wouldn't be one person in there who wouldn't be complaining about the really striking smell of burning flesh. (Or at least, I assume it's striking, as I don't have first-hand experience that I'd explicitly discuss without the presence of my attorney.) -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese reports the cremation as a completed action. The English reports only a decision to cremate, leaving whether it happened unresolved despite the following burial.
records.remedy: I cremated Youko-chan.

highlights.text: I decided to cremate Youko-chan.

records.jp: 犯人を捜し出して、殺害するに決まっていた。
records.en: Search and locate the culprit, then murder, that was obvious.
records.assessment: The Japanese says she would certainly find the culprit and kill them. The English leaves 'murder' without its required object and does not form a grammatical prediction about her action.
records.remedy: She would obviously hunt down the culprit and kill them.

highlights.text: Search and locate the culprit, then murder, that was obvious.

records.jp: 書面に。
records.en: While writing,
records.assessment: The Japanese fragment continues the decision to write a diary with the idea of putting the feelings down in writing. 'While writing' instead introduces a simultaneous action that is not present.
records.remedy: Put it down in writing.

highlights.text: While writing,

records.en: Miki: "...eh?'
records.assessment: The translated reaction has mismatched quotation marks, opening with a double quote and closing with a single quote. This corrupts the bounded dialogue presentation.
records.remedy: Miki: "...eh?"

highlights.text: Miki: "...eh?'

records.jp: 「彼女、可愛いね。どうしちゃったの？　困ってるみたいだけど？」
records.en: Taichi: "A girl, and cute. What are you doing? You look troubled. Are you?"
records.assessment: The Japanese directly addresses the girl, calls her cute, and asks what happened because she seems troubled. The English turns the address into a fragment about 'a girl,' asks what she is doing instead of what is wrong, and appends an unsupported second question.
records.remedy: Hey, miss. You're cute. What's wrong? You look like you're in trouble.

highlights.text: A girl, and cute. What are you doing? You look troubled. Are you?

records.jp: 「まあ待ちたまえ」
records.en: Taichi: "Oh, but gladden me with waiting!"
records.assessment: The Japanese is a mildly affected but straightforward instruction to wait a moment. The English invents a request to 'gladden' the speaker and is not an intelligible equivalent.
records.remedy: Now, wait just a moment.

highlights.text: Oh, but gladden me with waiting!

records.jp: どうやって逃げようか、思案している風に見える。
records.en: The face I'm looked at with screams, "I'm thinking about how to get away from this".
records.assessment: The Japanese says she looks as though she is considering how to escape. The English makes the narrator the object of an ungrammatical passive construction and personifies the face as screaming a sentence.
records.remedy: She looked as if she were working out how to get away.

highlights.text: The face I'm looked at with screams, "I'm thinking about how to get away from this".

records.jp: 「じゃあ何だったらもらってもいい？」
records.en: Taichi: "Then what would you like to give me?"
records.assessment: The Japanese asks what item it would be acceptable for him to receive instead. The English asks what she positively wants to give him, changing permission into preference.
records.remedy: Then what would you be willing to give me?

highlights.text: Then what would you like to give me?

records.jp: 「わたしの一生つかいっぱしりになってくれ、とか」
records.en: Miki: "Say I wanted to concede you to become my gopher for life."
comments: Twisting the words straight off the gate. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese proposes demanding that the narrator serve as her errand boy for life. 'Concede you to become' is ungrammatical and uses a verb meaning grant or admit rather than demand service.
records.remedy: What if I demanded that you be my errand boy for life?

highlights.text: Say I wanted to concede you to become my gopher for life.

records.jp: 「やっぱ今のナシ。かわりによつんばいになって犬の……きゃっ！？」
records.en: Miki: "Indeed I can do without for now. Instead, I'll give you the order to get on all fours, then, like a dog... KYAH?!"
comments: This form will return in CCC4022, keeping it a bit unique-ish. See CCC0026 for the replay. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese retracts the previous demand: 'Forget that one.' The English instead sounds as though she can temporarily manage without an unspecified object.
records.remedy: Actually, forget that one.

highlights.text: Indeed I can do without for now.

records.jp: 「……ちょ、これもナシ！　ええと、ええと……」
records.en: Miki: "...wa-, this I can also do without! Uhm, uhmmm..."
records.assessment: The Japanese again cancels a proposed demand, saying that one does not count either. The English repeats the unrelated idea of managing without something.
records.remedy: Forget this one too!

highlights.text: this I can also do without!

records.jp: 「地毛なんですね、その白髪」
records.en: Miki: "That bleached-white hair is your real hair, isn't it."
records.assessment: The Japanese realizes that the white hair is the narrator's natural, undyed hair. Calling it 'bleached-white' directly implies chemical coloring and contradicts that realization.
records.remedy: That white hair is your natural color

highlights.text: That bleached-white hair is your real hair

records.jp: 人と違えば、不気味に見える。
records.en: Being different from people's means they look eerie.
comments: Still wishing the artwork would actually show this. "People" meant, given it's him, specifically as non-human and not just as in 'other people'. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says eyes look eerie when they differ from other people's eyes. The English uses the incomplete possessive 'people's' without the compared noun and leaves the causal statement malformed.
records.remedy: When eyes differ from everyone else's, they look eerie.

highlights.text: Being different from people's means they look eerie.

records.jp: 「このせいで、いろいろつらい目に遭ってきた」
records.en: Taichi: "Because of these, I have had to see so many heart-rending hardships in my life."
comments: 目に遭って be met with hardships, but literally reads "meet with my eyes" -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese idiom means that he has suffered many painful experiences because of his eyes. The English literalizes the visual component as 'see hardships' and produces an unnatural relation.
records.remedy: I've suffered through a lot because of them.

highlights.text: I have had to see so many heart-rending hardships in my life.

records.jp: 「はじめてですよ、そんなの」
records.en: Miki: "First time I've been, you know."
records.assessment: The Japanese says this is the first time she has ever been picked up or hit on. The English omits the complement after 'been,' leaving both the event and the sentence incomplete.
records.remedy: This is the first time anyone's ever hit on me.

highlights.text: First time I've been, you know.

records.jp: 「君ならそうだな……五歳から俺の射程距離内だと言える」
records.en: Taichi: "You do look like it is... it could be said that you've been within my striking range from the age of five."
comments: This sounds more pedophilic than it probably is... maybe. See CCA0020 and CCA0006. It's not actually clear whether it was HIS being five or hers, given his early days with Nanaka. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese begins 'As for you, let's see' and then makes the age-five joke. The English invents the incoherent clause 'You do look like it is' before the otherwise recognizable claim.
records.remedy: For you, let's see... I'd say you've been in my strike zone since age five.

highlights.text: You do look like it is... it could be said that you've been within my striking range from the age of five.

records.jp: が、俺が門を越える方がはやい。着地。
records.en: but I'm faster in going beyond the gate. And land.
records.assessment: The Japanese says he clears the gate before the guards can react, then lands. The English uses an awkward gerund construction and leaves 'And land' without a finite verb or narrative-fragment form that reads coherently.
records.remedy: but I get over the gate first. I land.

highlights.text: but I'm faster in going beyond the gate. And land.

records.jp: そいつらを尻目に、美希を捜す。
records.en: Keeping them in the corner of my eyes, I search for Miki.
comments: Note he never seems to pay for this, or even be caught. It's very possible the guards ignored him as he's harmless. It's possible that in the coming years, his comings and goings become so routine that they don't even bother running after him. Just like Combat the dog. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese idiom says the narrator disregards the guards or looks on contemptuously as he searches. 'Keeping them in the corner of my eyes' instead says he continues monitoring them.
records.remedy: Ignoring them

highlights.text: Keeping them in the corner of my eyes

records.jp: 霧が美希を背後にかばう。
records.en: Kiri guards Miki's rear.
comments: Seems more metaphorical than literal... since they're sitting and everything. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says Kiri moves in front of Miki and shields her behind herself. The English instead says Kiri guards Miki's backside, losing both the protective positioning and the action's intent.
records.remedy: Kiri moves protectively in front of Miki.

highlights.text: Kiri guards Miki's rear.

records.jp: 「わたしがちゃんと面倒見ます。先輩には関係ありません」
records.en: Kiri: "I will be watching out for her and well. There is nothing here of concern to you, Senpai."
records.assessment: The Japanese says Kiri will take proper care of Miki. The English appends 'and well' to 'watching out for her,' producing an ungrammatical phrase that does not clearly express caretaking.
records.remedy: I'll take proper care of her.

highlights.text: I will be watching out for her and well.

records.jp: 「じゃーこのパンはどうするの？」
records.en: Taichi: "Welll what do I do with this bread?'
records.assessment: The translated line opens with a double quotation mark and closes with a single quotation mark, corrupting the bounded dialogue presentation.
records.remedy: Taichi: "Welll, what do I do with this bread?"

highlights.text: Taichi: "Welll what do I do with this bread?'

records.jp: 「……買い取りましょうか？」
records.en: Miki: "...should we just buy it?"
records.assessment: The Japanese has Miki offer to buy the bread from the narrator herself. The English changes the singular buyer to an unspecified 'we,' weakening the direct offer and changing who would pay.
records.remedy: shall I buy it from you?

highlights.text: should we just buy it?

records.jp: 昼を挟む。
records.en: Noon interrupts me.
records.assessment: The Japanese marks the work being interrupted by or spanning the lunch break. The English personifies noon as directly interrupting the narrator and does not convey the break in activity.
records.remedy: I break for lunch.

highlights.text: Noon interrupts me.

records.jp: 人類がもうとうになくなっていることに。
records.en: how long ago mankind had gone.
comments: Yeah, how many years has it been now? -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says the narrator had forgotten the fact that humanity vanished long ago. The English says he forgot how long ago it happened, preserving awareness of the event but losing track only of its timing.
records.remedy: that humanity had vanished long ago.

highlights.text: how long ago mankind had gone.

records.jp: 風前の灯火なんだ。
records.en: We are as a candle in front of the wind.
records.assessment: The Japanese idiom depicts a flame about to be blown out, meaning their continued existence is in imminent peril. The literal English image is not an established equivalent and leaves that implication opaque.
records.remedy: We're a candle flame about to be snuffed out.

highlights.text: We are as a candle in front of the wind.

records.jp: 「友貴と、喧嘩してしまいました」
records.en: Misato: "I have been... fighting with Tomoki."
comments: Her getting injured would've meant a pretty big fight with him, as it's not the first time he's rescued her from something like that. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese reports that she got into a fight with Tomoki, a completed incident that explains her present mood. The English progressive presents an ongoing series or action instead.
records.remedy: I... had a fight with Tomoki.

highlights.text: I have been... fighting with Tomoki.

records.jp: 「わたし、口うるさいですから」
records.en: Misato: "Because I... am a shrew."
records.assessment: The Japanese self-criticism is that she nags or fusses too much. 'Shrew' is a much harsher gendered character judgment and changes the restrained self-reproach into an insult.
records.remedy: Because I... nag him too much.

highlights.text: Because I... am a shrew.

records.jp: 「……そうなんですか？」
records.en: Misato: "...is that how I am?"
records.assessment: After the narrator says he is like her, the Japanese asks whether that is really true about him. The English instead has her ask for confirmation about her own nature.
records.remedy: ...are you really?

highlights.text: ...is that how I am?

records.jp: 先輩は童女のようにほころぶ。
records.en: Senpai's smile frays around the edges like little girl's.
comments: Just a little bit... wrong -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says her expression blossoms into a smile like a little girl's. 'Frays around the edges' suggests deterioration or strain, reversing the image, and the comparison is grammatically incomplete.
records.remedy: Senpai's face blossoms into a little girl's smile.

highlights.text: Senpai's smile frays around the edges like little girl's.

records.jp: 「またテンパっちゃって、どうしたんだ？」
records.en: Taichi: "You're about to blow up again, what even happened?"
records.assessment: The Japanese says she has panicked or lost her composure again. 'About to blow up' suggests imminent anger or explosion rather than her already flustered state.
records.remedy: You're panicking again

highlights.text: You're about to blow up again

records.jp: 「桐原先輩の家ですよ。ご自分の部屋で」
records.en: Kiri: "At Hasekura-senpai's house. In her own private room."
records.assessment: The Japanese identifies Kirihara-senpai's house. The English substitutes Hasekura, changing the named location and person associated with it.
records.remedy: At Kirihara-senpai's house.

highlights.text: At Hasekura-senpai's house.

records.jp: 霧を取り押さえるのは簡単だが。
records.en: Subduing Kiri would simple, but,
comments: But he's King of Smarts, too. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says subduing Kiri would be easy. The English omits the required copular verb and leaves the clause ungrammatical.
records.remedy: Subduing Kiri would be simple

highlights.text: Subduing Kiri would simple

records.jp: 「……殴り飛ばしてやりたいけどな」
records.en: Taichi: "...though I'd like to toss you off somewhere, you know."
comments: He totally could. Right where Yutaka fell, for example. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says he would like to punch her hard enough to send her flying. The English replaces the blow with an unspecified act of tossing her away.
records.remedy: I'd like to punch you flying

highlights.text: I'd like to toss you off somewhere

records.jp: 「死ね、死んでしまえ！　そんなに殺したかったら自分を殺せ！　狂人！　地獄に落ちろ！　たった八人しかいない……この世界で……どうかしてる！！」
records.en: Kiri: "Die! Just make the world happy and die! If you love killing so much then kill yourself! Lunatic! Go to hell! There's just eight people... in this world... you are insane!!!"
comments: Yup, totally Taichi that's lost his mind. But this is possibly the fruit of all the lies from last route. And this route the lies are only increasing. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese only repeats an angry command to die. The English adds the assertion that his death would make the world happy, introducing a distinct accusation not present in the source.
records.remedy: Just die already!

highlights.text: Just make the world happy and die!

records.jp: 削除してやろうか？―――
records.en: Should I just delete this?---
comments: He intends on stopping to consider her as existing. Not that he'd be unjustified in wanting to really hurt her, given she's groundlessly accused him of being a murderer, threatened him with a weapon, AND she went and pressed his berserk buttons by being serious in her hatred AND talking about his looks (the thing about his eyes). Plus he's an unadmitted emotional wreck since he just can't bring himself to state it out loud how much Youko's death hurts him (same as with previous route and Touko). Nasty? perhaps; the overreaction of a psychotic murderer? Not even close. His reaction is borderline saintly compared to what most people'd have at this point. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese contemplates eliminating Kiri herself. The English points to an unspecified object as 'this,' obscuring that the thought targets the person in front of him.
records.remedy: Should I delete her?

highlights.text: Should I just delete this?

records.jp: 「は、俺もう行くわ。ちょっと調べてみるよ。その冬子の死んだ現場ってやつ」
records.en: Taichi: "Hah, I shall go too, yes. I wanna investigate things out a bit... the Touko crime scene, I mean."
records.assessment: The Japanese says the narrator is leaving now. 'Too' incorrectly makes the departure parallel to someone else's action and blurs the immediate exit.
records.remedy: I'm leaving now

highlights.text: I shall go too

records.jp: 胸元からシーツまでを濡らして、赤黒く変色させていた。
records.en: Soaking her from the pit of the stomach down to the sheets, it had become a discolored dark red.
comments: This much bleeding hints that she was alive when she was stabbed. The answer then becomes simple: if Kiri never saw the body, and just listened to what Miki told her (I mean, why even go to the Kirihara mansion in the first place?), then the Knife is only in Taichi's mind. The bleeding doesn't exist; it just tells us that Touko is still alive, and likely sleeping in the infirmary after a collapse. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says the blood soaked from the chest area down to the sheets. The English relocates the wound and staining to the pit of the stomach.
records.remedy: from her chest

highlights.text: from the pit of the stomach

records.jp: 冬子らしい、気高い死体だと思った。
records.en: I though this noble corpse was so Touko-like.
records.assessment: The English uses 'though' where the past-tense verb 'thought' is required, leaving the narration ungrammatical.
records.remedy: I thought this noble corpse

highlights.text: I though this noble corpse

records.jp: ……誰が殺したのだろう。
records.en: ...someone must have killed her.
records.assessment: The Japanese asks who killed her. The English replaces the open question with the tautological assertion that someone must have done it.
records.remedy: ...who killed her, I wonder.

highlights.text: ...someone must have killed her.

records.jp: 「思春期です」
records.en: Tomoki: "I am adolescent."
records.assessment: The Japanese answer is the life stage 'adolescence.' The English uses the count noun 'adolescent' without an article.
records.remedy: I'm an adolescent.

highlights.text: I am adolescent.

records.jp: とても人を殺す余裕があるとは思えなかった。
records.en: I didn't think there was much space in there to kill someone.
records.assessment: The Japanese says the two seemed to have no emotional leeway or capacity to commit a murder. The English turns that figurative leeway into physical space 'in there.'
records.remedy: they had the composure to kill anyone

highlights.text: there was much space in there to kill someone

records.jp: 「最後に教えてくれ。君は高校生で女子高生と女子校生で生徒手帳なのではないのかね？」
records.en: Taichi: "Tell me one last thing then. Are you not the student identification of a female hi-school student and a high female school student that's a high school student, aren't you?"
comments: And now, a line that was pure comedic FAIL in the original is actually good. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese deliberately piles together her status as a high-school girl, the two earlier compound-word labels, and her student ID. The English makes her the identification document itself and forms a syntactically incoherent double question.
records.remedy: So you're a high-school girl, a girls'-school student, and you do have a student ID, right?

highlights.text: Are you not the student identification of a female hi-school student and a high female school student that's a high school student, aren't you?

records.jp: たちまち目が吊り上がる。
records.en: All at once she stares at me from the top of her eyes.
records.assessment: The Japanese says her eyes turn sharply upward in anger. The English invents an impossible viewing position 'from the top of her eyes.'
records.remedy: her eyes immediately narrow in anger.

highlights.text: she stares at me from the top of her eyes.

records.jp: ……俺が言う台詞じゃないけどな。
records.en: ...but isn't that the line I should be saying.
comments: Because he "doesn't" feel anguish at all, though that's delusional. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese admits that the narrator is hardly in a position to say this. The English instead asks whether it is precisely the line he should be saying, reversing his self-qualification.
records.remedy: though I'm hardly one to talk.

highlights.text: isn't that the line I should be saying.

records.jp: 「わたしは美希といます！　あなたは一人で勝手にいればいい。どうせ……あなたが犯人なんだから」
records.en: Kiri: "I will be staying with Kiri! You'd best stay alone on your own as you like! Because... you are the culprit after all."
records.assessment: The Japanese has Kiri say that she will stay with Miki. The English says she will stay with herself, substituting Kiri for Miki and breaking the protective declaration.
records.remedy: I will be staying with Miki!

highlights.text: I will be staying with Kiri!

records.jp: 「俺は話したい相手に話しかけるよ。相手がどう反応するかは、そいつの自由」
records.en: Taichi: "I will talking with anyone I want to talk with. How and whether that person responds will be left to that person's free will."
records.assessment: The English combines the auxiliary 'will' with the participle 'talking' instead of the required base verb.
records.remedy: I will talk with anyone

highlights.text: I will talking with anyone

records.jp: 「それ俺のせいちゃうで……」
records.en: Taichi: "Is that my fault too now..."
comments: She does pin the blame of everything bad in her life on anyone she can find. It's her way of Escape. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese dialectal line denies responsibility: 'That isn't my fault.' The English turns it into a question about whether it is also his fault.
records.remedy: That's not my fault...

highlights.text: Is that my fault too now...

records.jp: もう霧はダメだ。
records.en: Kiri has now spoiled,
records.assessment: The Japanese says Kiri is beyond help or no good now. 'Spoiled' primarily suggests food going bad or a child being indulged and does not convey the judgment.
records.remedy: Kiri is beyond help now

highlights.text: Kiri has now spoiled

records.jp: 「ねえ？」
records.en: Taichi: "Nay?"
records.assessment: The Japanese tag seeks agreement: 'Right?' The archaic negative 'nay' instead expresses or solicits disagreement.
records.remedy: Right?

highlights.text: Nay?

records.jp: 「ねー？」
records.en: Miki: "Naaay?"
records.assessment: The Japanese playfully echoes the request for agreement. The stretched English 'nay' retains the opposite negative meaning.
records.remedy: Riiight?

highlights.text: Naaay?

records.jp: 「君も気をつけたまえ。もし犯人だったら……そーとーエロいことになりますよ」
records.en: Taichi: "You also gladden me with some wariness. If you were the culprit... sooo maaany perverted things shall happen!"
comments: Seems to be talking just to Miki. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese warns the listener to be careful too. The English invents a request to please the speaker with wariness and is not an intelligible warning.
records.remedy: You'd better be careful too.

highlights.text: You also gladden me with some wariness.

records.jp: 「わかるもんか」
records.en: Kiri: "And I'll believe that!"
records.assessment: The Japanese rejects the narrator's confidence with 'How would you know?' The English instead predicts that she will believe him, reversing the skeptical response.
records.remedy: How would you know?

highlights.text: And I'll believe that!

records.jp: あ、今のは効いたぞ。
records.en: Ah, that one struck and bad.
records.assessment: The Japanese says the remark hit hard. The English coordinates the adjective 'bad' with the verb and leaves the idiom ungrammatical.
records.remedy: that one hit hard.

highlights.text: that one struck and bad.

records.jp: 霧は踵を切り返し、走り去った。
records.en: Twisting her knee backwards on her heel, Kiri runs away.
comments: HACK SFX -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese idiom says Kiri turns on her heel and runs away. The English describes her knee twisting backward, suggesting an injury rather than a pivot.
records.remedy: Turning on her heel

highlights.text: Twisting her knee backwards on her heel

records.jp: 「美希ぽんです。何でしょう？」
records.en: Miki: "This is Miki-pon. What do we do?"
records.assessment: The Japanese asks the narrator what he wants after acknowledging the nickname. The English asks for a joint course of action instead.
records.remedy: What is it?

highlights.text: What do we do?

records.jp: 蝋燭に火を。
records.en: Fire in the candle.
comments: CP CCC3011
records.assessment: The Japanese says the narrator lights the candle. 'Fire in the candle' is a static, unidiomatic noun phrase and does not express the action.
records.remedy: I light the candle.

highlights.text: Fire in the candle.

records.jp: ……犯人はどういう目的で、二人を殺害したのだろう。
records.en: ...the culprit has murdered two people for whatever motive.
comments: BTW: even knowing who the killer is, the motive remains something worth thinking about. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese asks what objective led the culprit to kill the two victims. 'For whatever motive' dismisses the motive as unspecified instead of posing the question under investigation.
records.remedy: what objective did the culprit have in killing them?

highlights.text: for whatever motive.

records.jp: 平原に出て、的になっていた樹のあたりを調べる。
records.en: Coming out into the open space, I examine around the timber that was turned target.
comments: PCP CCC3012A
Hmmm, odd change. Might just be an older revision. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says he examines the area around the tree that served as the target. The English uses 'timber' for the standing tree and omits the article and preposition required by 'turned into a target.'
records.remedy: the tree that had been used as a target.

highlights.text: the timber that was turned target.

records.jp: 考えてないわけじゃないのか。
records.en: That just means he hasn't thought through this at all, doesn't it.
records.assessment: The Japanese says it is not as though he has failed to think about the trip, meaning he has considered it to some degree. The English states the opposite: that he has not thought it through at all.
records.remedy: so he has given it some thought after all

highlights.text: he hasn't thought through this at all

records.jp: 「ハンディ（無線機）は持って行けよ。電波、どこからも出てないみたいだし、たぶん通じるだろ」
records.en: Taichi: "Bring hAndy (not just the Capp, the radio as well) with you. It doesn't look like there's radio waves anywhere, but maybe you'll catch some."
comments: ハンディ is also short for handicap. Anthropomorphized because Sakuraba is as Yutaka. And also Taichi thinks him retarded. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says no one else appears to be transmitting, so their own radios will probably connect without interference. The English instead suggests he may catch unspecified outside radio waves.
records.remedy: No one else seems to be transmitting, so it should probably get through.

highlights.text: It doesn't look like there's radio waves anywhere, but maybe you'll catch some.

records.jp: 「Could you pay me back the shipping charge.（お願いします、返品の送料を払ってください）」
records.en: Sakuraba: "(...)"
comments: The only better way to translate this would be to find some way to add furigana. ...oddly he sounds sorta-french-ish here, and so does the new actor. -GHS
records.assessment: The authoritative line contains a complete English sentence followed by its Japanese gloss. The GHS line replaces the entire spoken sentence with an ellipsis placeholder.
records.remedy: Sakuraba: "Could you pay me back the shipping charge?"

highlights.text: Sakuraba: "(...)"

records.jp: 「What a fiasco it is!（それはなんとひどい事件なのでしょう）」
records.en: Sakuraba: "(...)"
comments: He's also obviously reading from some phrasebook. The new actor isn't even trying on this, he sounds "what! fiasco! it is." -GHS
records.assessment: The authoritative line contains a complete English exclamation followed by its Japanese gloss. The GHS line replaces all of it with an ellipsis placeholder.
records.remedy: Sakuraba: "What a fiasco it is!"

highlights.text: Sakuraba: "(...)"

records.jp: 十万円金貨が十五枚入っていた。
records.en: Inside there were fifteen gold coins, ten thousand yen each.
comments: CP CCC3012B
records.assessment: The Japanese specifies fifteen gold coins worth 100,000 yen each. The English renders them as 10,000 yen each, reducing the denomination by a factor of ten.
records.remedy: one hundred thousand yen each

highlights.text: ten thousand yen each

records.jp: 「はっ？」
records.en: Taichi: "But?"
comments: CP CCC3012B
records.assessment: The Japanese is a startled 'Huh?' The English supplies an adversative conjunction and implies a contrast that is not present.
records.remedy: Huh?

highlights.text: But?

records.jp: 人類滅亡前、まだ金が意味のある時代に一度でもせびっていたら。
records.en: If, before the Fall of Mankind, in the times when money still had significance, I had only just once extorted him some money...
comments: CP CCC3012B
records.assessment: The Japanese says the narrator regrets not wheedling or begging some money from him earlier. 'Extorted' implies coercive criminal extraction and substantially changes the imagined act.
records.remedy: wheedled some money out of him

highlights.text: extorted him some money

records.jp: 「作者は……ええと……鑑定書があるな。伝周文筆さんか」
records.en: Taichi: "Author... uhmmm... there's an expert certification. A certain Assumed Tensho Shubun-san?"
comments: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensh%C5%8D_Sh%C5%ABbun this one I had to cross-reference Wikipedia in English and Japanese to figure out; 伝 intermediary for "assumed XXX" is not really a common meaning. And there's the kanji 筆 for 'brush' after the actual name (周文 shubun) that's confusing. It simply means "attributed to the brush of". -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese attribution formula says the work is attributed to the painter Shūbun. The English invents 'Tensho' as part of a personal name and treats the attribution marker as a title.
records.remedy: It says it's attributed to Shūbun.

highlights.text: A certain Assumed Tensho Shubun-san?

records.jp: 震えていると、桜庭は唐突に言った。
records.en: And while shaking, all of a sudden Sakuraba said,
records.assessment: The Japanese says Sakuraba speaks while the narrator is still trembling. The English's introductory participle makes Sakuraba the one who is shaking.
records.remedy: While I was still shaking, Sakuraba suddenly said

highlights.text: And while shaking, all of a sudden Sakuraba said

records.jp: 「そういう意味じゃない。俺は精神的には不能だから、そっちの欲望はほとんどない」
records.en: Sakuraba: "That's not what I mean. I have a mental incompetency, so I don't have desires of that kind."
comments: Vs. want. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says he is psychologically impotent, explaining his lack of sexual desire. 'Mental incompetency' instead suggests impaired intelligence or legal capacity.
records.remedy: I'm psychologically impotent

highlights.text: I have a mental incompetency

records.jp: 「俺の性欲は、あの日、あの時のおまえに奪われたままさ」
records.en: Sakuraba: "You stole my sexual desire, that day, that time, and that's how it's still is."
records.assessment: The English combines the contraction 'it's' with a second finite 'is,' producing an ungrammatical predicate.
records.remedy: that's how it still is.

highlights.text: that's how it's still is.

records.jp: 「必要な機材も運んだし」
records.en: Taichi: "She's even carrying up the machine parts she needs."
records.assessment: The Japanese says the necessary equipment has already been carried up. The English presents an ongoing action and narrows equipment to machine parts.
records.remedy: We already carried up the necessary equipment.

highlights.text: She's even carrying up the machine parts she needs.

records.jp: 「みたいだね」
records.en: Tomoki: "So like him."
records.assessment: The Japanese means 'It looks that way' in response to the report that he left. The English instead comments that the behavior is characteristic of him.
records.remedy: Looks like it.

highlights.text: So like him.

records.jp: 「やるかー！」
records.en: Taichi: "Will you let me off easilyyy!"
records.assessment: The Japanese is the narrator's challenge to fight: 'You wanna go?' The English asks whether Tomoki will let him off easily, reversing agency and changing the challenge into a plea.
records.remedy: You wanna go?!

highlights.text: Will you let me off easilyyy!

records.jp: 「寝坊してしまいました～」
records.en: Misato: "I am so much a sleepyheaaa～d."
records.assessment: The Japanese says she overslept, a completed event explaining her late arrival. The English labels her generally sleepy instead.
records.remedy: I overslept～.

highlights.text: I am so much a sleepyheaaa～d.

records.jp: 「そう……でも……手伝ってくれたんですね、あの子……」
records.en: Misato: "Yes... but... he is still helping us, he is..."
records.assessment: The Japanese expresses relief that Tomoki did help them despite the conflict. The English present progressive says he is still helping at that moment, although the work was completed earlier.
records.remedy: he helped us after all

highlights.text: he is still helping us

records.jp: 「良かったですね」
records.en: Taichi: "So glad he is."
records.assessment: The Japanese tells Senpai that this is good news for her. The English makes the absent Tomoki the person who is glad and uses an inverted fragment.
records.remedy: That's good, isn't it?

highlights.text: So glad he is.

records.jp: 訓練の成果を見せてもらおうじゃないか。
records.en: you want to show me the results of all your practice, don't you?
records.assessment: The Japanese says the narrator will have Kiri show him the results of her practice. The English instead attributes a desire to show him to Kiri and turns the resolve into a tag question.
records.remedy: let's see the results of all your practice.

highlights.text: you want to show me the results of all your practice, don't you?

records.jp: 確実な場面で。
records.en: someplace safe, I'm certain.
records.assessment: The Japanese says she will attack at a moment when success is certain. The English changes this to a safe place and makes the narrator's certainty the point, losing the attack criterion.
records.remedy: when she is certain of the shot.

highlights.text: someplace safe, I'm certain.

records.jp: やはり慣れた空間でないと、困難なのかもな。
records.en: As I thought, without someplace she's comfortable with, she's just distressed.
records.assessment: The Japanese speculates that attacking may be difficult unless Kiri is in familiar surroundings. The English instead says unfamiliar surroundings emotionally distress her and omits the practical difficulty.
records.remedy: it may be difficult unless she's somewhere familiar.

highlights.text: she's just distressed.

records.jp: 冬子がいたら、そう言ってやろうと思っていたのだ。
records.en: If Youko had been among us, that's what I thought I would be telling her.
comments: CP CCC3017
records.assessment: The Japanese says what he intended to tell Touko. The English substitutes Youko, changing the referenced person in the reflection.
records.remedy: If Touko had been among us

highlights.text: If Youko had been among us

records.jp: 来るな。
records.en: Don't come here...
comments: Seems to be sort of begging. -GHS
records.assessment: In context the Japanese is the narrator's prediction 'Here she comes,' as the presence approaches and the door opens. The English reads it as an imperative telling her not to come.
records.remedy: Here she comes.

highlights.text: Don't come here...

records.jp: 走り去る霧の背中。
records.en: There's Kiri's runaway behind.
records.assessment: The Japanese presents the sight of Kiri's back as she runs away. 'Runaway behind' is not an intelligible noun phrase and uses 'behind' for a person's back.
records.remedy: Kiri's back as she runs away.

highlights.text: There's Kiri's runaway behind.

records.en: Taichi: Hahah..."
records.assessment: The translated dialogue has a closing quotation mark but no opening quotation mark, corrupting the bounded presentation.
records.remedy: Taichi: "Hahah..."

highlights.text: Taichi: Hahah..."

records.jp: 後づけの理性だ。
records.en: The postscript of rationality.
records.assessment: The Japanese calls reason an after-the-fact layer applied on top of instinct. 'Postscript of rationality' suggests written text and leaves the psychological relation opaque.
records.remedy: Reason only gets added after the fact.

highlights.text: The postscript of rationality.

records.jp: 少し不安定になると役に立たなくなる。
records.en: If one becomes somewhat freaked out, all their abilities disappear.
comments: Sukoshi Fuantei - heh, SF. "Fuantei" is what's used for Taichi's unstable intellect in CCA0003. Maybe that's what it was all along... -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that reason becomes useless when the narrator grows even slightly unstable. The English generalizes this to all of any person's abilities disappearing.
records.remedy: reason stops being useful.

highlights.text: all their abilities disappear.

records.jp: 身体のバネを全部使って、上体をそらした。
records.en: Using the entirety of the springiness of my body, I twisted my upper half.
comments: ...unrivaled springiness... -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says the narrator uses his whole body's spring to arch or throw his upper body backward. Twisting is a rotational motion and does not describe the evasion.
records.remedy: I arched my upper body backward.

highlights.text: I twisted my upper half.

records.jp: 胸に手を当てて確認した。
records.en: I confirmed by putting a hand on the dead of the chest.
records.assessment: The Japanese says he puts a hand to his chest to check his heartbeat. 'Dead of the chest' is a mistaken substitution for 'center of the chest' and creates an unrelated death image.
records.remedy: the center of my chest.

highlights.text: the dead of the chest.

records.jp: 罠があるかも知れないし、無茶はしないか。
records.en: Not unreasonable to think there'd be traps or the sort.
records.assessment: The Japanese reasons that Kiri probably will not attempt anything reckless because this is his home ground and there may be traps. The English preserves only the possibility of traps and omits the conclusion about her behavior.
records.remedy: There may be traps, so she probably won't try anything reckless.

highlights.text: Not unreasonable to think there'd be traps or the sort.

records.jp: 人為的なものだ、これは。
records.en: This thing here is... unnatural.
comments: That leaves the SUPERnatural. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese concludes that the death is caused by human action or deliberately engineered. 'Unnatural' can mean merely unusual and does not clearly establish human agency.
records.remedy: This was done deliberately by someone.

highlights.text: This thing here is... unnatural.

records.jp: 理解などしなくていいと思った。
records.en:
I thought it'd be good even without
understand of any sort.
records.assessment: The Japanese says he decided he no longer needed to understand others. The English uses the verb 'understand' where the noun 'understanding' is required and leaves the thought malformed.
records.remedy: without any understanding at all.

highlights.text:
without
understand of any sort.

records.jp: よくわからなくなってきた。
records.en: I just never understand that very well.
records.assessment: The Japanese says the narrator is becoming confused or is starting not to understand what is happening. The English turns it into a stable, habitual inability to understand a particular 'that.'
records.remedy: I'm starting not to understand anything anymore.

highlights.text: I just never understand that very well.

records.jp: 自分をおさえて。
records.en: Restrain yourself now.
records.assessment: The Japanese fragment continues the narrator's retrospective question about having restrained himself until now. The English converts it into a present imperative addressed to someone else.
records.remedy: Holding myself back.

highlights.text: Restrain yourself now.

records.en: Kiri: "...murderer!
records.assessment: The translated dialogue opens a quotation but never closes it, corrupting the bounded line presentation.
records.remedy: Kiri: "...murderer!"

highlights.text: Kiri: "...murderer!

records.jp: 飛びかかってきた。
records.en: I leaped at it,
records.assessment: The Japanese says Kiri lunges at the narrator through the obscured view. The English makes the narrator leap at an unspecified object, reversing attacker and target.
records.remedy: She lunged at me

highlights.text: I leaped at it

records.jp: 刃物が握られている。
records.en: it's clasping something bladed.
records.assessment: The Japanese says a blade is gripped in Kiri's hand. The English makes the wrist or an unspecified 'it' the agent clasping something and uses an unnatural indefinite description.
records.remedy: she is gripping a blade.

highlights.text: it's clasping something bladed.

records.jp: 俺がやったんじゃないのに。
records.en: Even if I wasn't the one who did him in.
records.assessment: The Japanese asserts the fact that the narrator did not do it and laments the accusation despite that fact. 'Even if' makes his innocence hypothetical or concessive rather than asserted.
records.remedy: Even though I wasn't the one who did it.

highlights.text: Even if I wasn't the one who did him in.

records.jp: 霧の感情は、もう壊れかけている。
records.en: Kiri's feelings are now completely wrecked.
comments: And that "+ tears" was toootally sane. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says Kiri's emotions are on the verge of breaking down. The English says they are already completely destroyed, overstating both completion and degree.
records.remedy: Kiri's emotions are close to breaking.

highlights.text: Kiri's feelings are now completely wrecked.

records.jp: 身を起こそうとして……失敗する。
records.en: She tries to sit up... failure.
records.assessment: The Japanese says she tries to raise herself and fails. The English substitutes an unintegrated noun for the required finite result.
records.remedy: She tries to sit up... and fails.

highlights.text: failure

records.jp: 感情は一切、読み取れない。
records.en: All sentiments, without exceptions, impossible to read.
records.assessment: The Japanese states that no emotion can be read from her. The English omits the finite verb and produces a malformed fragment.
records.remedy: Not a trace of emotion can be read from her.

highlights.text: All sentiments, without exceptions, impossible to read.

records.jp: 「でもないけど。俺は誰も殺してないよ。殺したくない」
records.en: Taichi: "Not exactly. But I didn't kill anyone. I didn't want to kill!"
records.assessment: The Japanese expresses his present refusal or desire not to kill, not a past lack of desire.
records.remedy: I don't want to kill anyone.

highlights.text: I didn't want to kill!

records.jp: 謝罪の言葉も成り立たず。
records.en: Without letting her finish her words of apology,
comments: This is important considering how difficult it is for Kiri to apologize. He doesn't really want to even hear it; but whether he doesn't accept it, or is satisfied with unexpressed repentance, is at this point intentionally unclear. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says her attempted apology never forms into words. The English instead makes the narrator actively prevent her from finishing it.
records.remedy: Her words of apology never fully formed.

highlights.text: Without letting her finish her words of apology,

records.jp: 骸を矢ごと引き抜く。
records.en: I yank the bolt out of her shell as well.
records.assessment: The Japanese says he pulls the corpse off him with the arrow still in it. The English instead says he extracts the bolt from her body and mistranslates the corpse as a shell.
records.remedy: I pull the corpse off me, bolt and all.

highlights.text: I yank the bolt out of her shell as well.

records.jp: 「話が繋がらない」
records.en: Taichi: "The two sentences don't flow together."
records.assessment: The idiom means that her explanation does not add up or connect logically. The English recasts it as prose-editing commentary about two sentences.
records.remedy: That doesn't add up.

highlights.text: The two sentences don't flow together.

records.jp: 「ノートには、土曜日までの毎日が克明に記されていて、筆記者は先輩でした」
records.en: Miki: "In the notebooks, a daily life was diarized in detail up to Saturday, and the writer was you, Senpai."
comments: HE doesn't notice his own handwriting, remember CCC0007, only his style. How did she recognize it? By the same, perhaps... -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says each day's events were recorded in detail. The English's singular 'a daily life' is malformed and changes what was recorded.
records.remedy: every day was recorded in detail

highlights.text: a daily life was diarized

records.jp: 「毎回死んでるってことじゃないですか」
records.en: Miki: "Isn't it just dying, ever single time?"
records.assessment: The phrase contains a clear typographical error that makes the adverbial expression ungrammatical.
records.remedy: every single time

highlights.text: ever single time

records.jp: 「世界がもうこれっぽっちも進まないとしても……わたしは、自覚のない繰り返しにはいたくない」
records.en: Miki: "The world might be advancing just this little but... I don't want to repeat myself without being aware."
