records.assessment: The Japanese says that Miki has remained dark and gloomy throughout this period. The English turns that continuing state into the beginning of an awkwardly phrased habit.
records.remedy: had been gloomy the whole time

highlights.text: began to always be in a dark mood

records.jp: 霧はずっと困っている。
records.en: Kiri began to be always stumped.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Kiri has remained troubled throughout. The English changes the continuing state into its onset and uses 'stumped,' which suggests inability to solve a problem.
records.remedy: had been troubled the whole time

highlights.text: began to be always stumped

records.jp: そしてとうとう、最後の通学日となった。
records.en: And then it came to a head here, the last day of her going to this school.
comments: In other words it's not Sunday. Although Kiri could just up and change schools mid-year, it being the last day of school before vacation better fits. In fact, see CCA0022: maybe they have their CC test 'round the last week before Summer break or so, which is how they know she's recovered. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says only that Kiri's final day of attending school finally arrived. The English adds the claim that a conflict or crisis came to a head.
records.remedy: at last, her final day at the school arrived

highlights.text: it came to a head here

records.jp: 「ずっとうまくつきあっていくしかないんだよー」
records.en: Miki: "I just gotta be with someone all the time you know!"
comments: This is closer to her ultramarine. And the one she was with wasn't Kiri; it was Taichi. Kiri was her Dragon. -GHS
records.assessment: Miki says that because her condition is innate, she has no choice but to learn to live with it successfully. The English instead says that she must continually be with another person.
records.remedy: I just have to learn to live with it

highlights.text: I just gotta be with someone all the time

records.jp: 霧は怯える。最後なのに。
records.en: Kiri is terrified. Even if it's their last.
records.assessment: The Japanese means that Kiri is frightened even though this is their last day together. The English changes the concessive fact into a conditional possibility.
records.remedy: Even though this is their last day together.

highlights.text: Even if it's their last.

records.jp: 美希の本音。
records.en: and Miki's the true feelings,
records.assessment: The possessive phrase contains an extraneous definite article and is ungrammatical.
records.remedy: Miki's true feelings

highlights.text: Miki's the true feelings

records.jp: おろおろとしてしまう。
records.en: Nervously flustered as she is,
records.assessment: The Japanese is a complete past-narrative statement that Kiri became flustered. The English is a dangling present-tense subordinate fragment.
records.remedy: Kiri became flustered.

highlights.text: Nervously flustered as she is,

records.jp: いろいろな言い訳が渦巻く。
records.en: all sorts of and all kinds of excuses swirl into an eddy.
comments: Symbols! Dunno of what. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that all sorts of explanations whirl through her mind. The English needlessly duplicates 'all sorts' with 'all kinds' and adds a separate eddy image.
records.remedy: all sorts of explanations swirled through her mind

highlights.text: all sorts of and all kinds of excuses swirl into an eddy

records.jp: と、脂汗を流しつつ、アイス・バーで地面に疑似蝋燭プレイをしてしまう霧。
records.en: And with those thoughts, Kiri's melting vanilla bar went riding her sweaty fingers and did a mock candle torture sex play onto the ground surface.
comments: Incredibly inappropriate sex reference + in particular a type of torture you'd expect in the Hasekura Mansion post-Shinkawas + candles (see CCA0012) = strong hints that Taichi is the narrator. And how does he know all this if he's not hanging around there? ...and if the explanation of why he loves candles isn't that they're bright and flicker (and he's near-blind and has low sensitivity to anything that isn't in motion), that may even be it. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese jokes that, while breaking into an oily sweat, Kiri lets the melting bar perform a mock candle-wax routine on the ground. The English invents travel along her fingers, explicitly labels the gag torture and sex, and adds the redundant 'ground surface.'
records.remedy: Sweating nervously, Kiri let her ice-cream bar perform a mock candle-wax routine on the ground.

highlights.text: went riding her sweaty fingers
torture sex play onto the ground surface

records.jp: 美希の愛想が良くなって、霧は狼狽えた。
records.en: As Miki's civility improved, Kiri became flustered.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Miki suddenly became more amiable or friendly. 'Civility improved' reduces a visible change in manner to an abstract increase in politeness.
records.remedy: Miki suddenly grew more amiable

highlights.text: Miki's civility improved

records.jp: ドラマっぽく決められない。
records.en: Irresoluteness worthy of a soap opera.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Kiri cannot bring the moment to a dramatic conclusion. The English instead describes irresolution itself as soap-opera-worthy.
records.remedy: She could not pull off a dramatic finish.

highlights.text: Irresoluteness worthy of a soap opera.

records.jp: やっとの思いで絞り出した。
records.en: And after great consideration, what she managed to squeeze out was,
records.assessment: やっとの思いで means that Kiri barely managed after great effort, not that she arrived at the words through prolonged consideration.
records.remedy: with enormous effort

highlights.text: after great consideration

records.jp: 精一杯の言葉だ。
records.en: Words with the whole might of her spirit.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that these words are the best Kiri can manage. The English converts that idiom into a nonidiomatic noun phrase about spiritual might.
records.remedy: It was the best she could manage.

highlights.text: Words with the whole might of her spirit.

records.jp: 「離れていても」
records.en: Kiri: "Even if we separate."
comments: Because of quantum entanglement. I'm only sort-of kidding. I think. -GHS
records.assessment: Kiri means that their bond persists while they are physically apart. 'If we separate' instead frames separation itself as an uncertain future event and can suggest ending the relationship.
records.remedy: Even when we're apart.

highlights.text: Even if we separate.

records.jp: と顎で、霧のアイスを指した。
records.en: With the chin, she points to Kiri's ice cream.
records.assessment: The English omits the possessive determiner for Miki's chin and shifts the surrounding past narration into present tense.
records.remedy: She pointed with her chin

highlights.text: With the chin, she points

records.jp: 美希はイヤホンをつけて、片方を霧に渡す。
records.en: Miki plugged in the earphones, and handed over one to Kiri.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Miki put on the earphones before handing one side to Kiri. The English substitutes the distinct technical act of plugging them into a device.
records.remedy: put on the earphones

highlights.text: plugged in the earphones

records.en: Kiri: "Is it...?"
records.assessment: Kiri asks whether this is the rumored broadcast. The English omits the deictic complement and leaves the question incomplete.
records.remedy: Is this it...?

highlights.text: Is it...?

records.jp: ネットで話題になりはじめ、今やいろいろな都市伝説を生み出しながら日本中を駆けめぐっている。
records.en: I started as a topic of discussion on the 'net, and it has now run throughout Japan, giving birth to all kinds of urban legends.
comments: "It also ended up overseas, but even in the late '10s most people in America still thought there was nothing there beyond tentacle rape due to the first-wave spread of the '90s, and so current trends like imouto and imouto and imouto went mostly ignored." -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the mysterious broadcast became a topic online. The English replaces that subject with the first-person pronoun.
records.remedy: It became a topic of discussion online

highlights.text: I started as a topic of discussion

records.jp: 「今日は昔話をしたいと思います」
records.en: Taichi: "Today I think I will want to reminisce, and talk about the past."
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the speaker intends to tell an old story. The English adds a future desire to reminisce and then duplicates that activity as talking about the past.
records.remedy: I'd like to tell an old story today

highlights.text: I think I will want to reminisce, and talk about the past

records.jp: 放送部員たちの心に、奇妙な思い出だけを残していなくなった。
records.en: Nothing of him was left but odd memories inside the hearts of the Broadcast Club members.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the person disappeared after leaving only strange memories in the members' hearts. The English omits the disappearance as an event and instead asserts that nothing else of him remained.
records.remedy: He disappeared, leaving only strange memories

highlights.text: Nothing of him was left but odd memories

records.jp: 「でもきっと、俺はこのことを話したことがあったはずです」
records.en: Taichi: "But I'm sure I have had to speak of this once."
records.assessment: The Japanese expresses the speaker's certainty that he must have told this story before. The English changes epistemic inference into an obligation to speak and reduces an unspecified prior occasion to exactly once.
records.remedy: I must have talked about this before

highlights.text: I have had to speak of this once

records.jp: 失踪でも消失でもない。
records.en: He has neither run away nor has he ceased to exist.
records.assessment: The Japanese contrasts disappearance in the senses of going missing and vanishing. 'Run away' imputes a voluntary act, while 'ceased to exist' escalates disappearance into nonexistence.
records.remedy: It was neither going missing nor vanishing.

highlights.text: run away
ceased to exist

records.jp: 実際に聞くのは、二人ともはじめてだ。
records.en: Hearing this in the flesh was the first time for both of them.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that this is the first time either has actually heard the broadcast. 'In the flesh' requires physical personal presence and is inapplicable to a radio transmission.
records.remedy: It was the first time either of them had actually heard it.

highlights.text: Hearing this in the flesh

records.jp: やがてノイズが、少年の声をかき消して。
records.en: Before long, the interference of white noise erased the boy's voice.
comments: The specific word for what he interposes between him and the world. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that radio noise drowns out or obliterates the audible voice. 'Erased' instead depicts removal of a recorded or written object.
records.remedy: drowned out the boy's voice

highlights.text: erased the boy's voice

records.jp: 「うん……間違いないよ。例の……部活だと思う」
records.en: Miki: "Yup... no mistake! It's... those club activities, I think."
comments: Wonder if Tanaka was in the eroge club. Wait, they have those in Japan, right? Anime can't lie. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese refers to the particular club that has been discussed. The English turns it into plural activities and loses the identifying force of 例の.
records.remedy: that club we've heard about

highlights.text: those club activities

records.jp: 向こうの世界と、こっちの世界。
records.en: There is world on the other side, and a world on this side.
comments: See CCA0002. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese juxtaposes the world over there and the world here. The English omits the article required before singular count noun 'world.'
records.remedy: The world on the other side

highlights.text: There is world on the other side

records.jp: そして一人で、部活動をしている。
records.en: And then he was having club activities, alone.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he is continuing the club's activities alone. The English uses the nonidiomatic collocation 'have club activities' and shifts the ongoing present into past progressive.
records.remedy: he is carrying on with the club alone

highlights.text: he was having club activities

records.jp: 「会いたいね」
records.en: Miki: "I wanna meet him."
records.assessment: 会いたい means wanting to see an already-known person, not meet him for the first time.
records.remedy: I want to see him.

highlights.text: I wanna meet him.

records.jp: 「会いたい……」
records.en: Kiri: "I wanna meet him..."
comments: Still the same, meet vs. cross. -GHS
records.assessment: 会いたい means wanting to see an already-known person, not meet him for the first time.
records.remedy: I want to see him...

highlights.text: I wanna meet him...

records.jp: だとしても桜庭は口にする。
records.en: yet Sakuraba put them to his mouth.
records.assessment: 口にする means that Sakuraba nevertheless speaks the words aloud. The English literalizes the expression as physically placing words at his mouth.
records.remedy: said them aloud

highlights.text: put them to his mouth

records.jp: 迷惑にならない限りやりたいことをするし、気に入ったヤツとつるむ。
records.en: He does all he wants within the limits of becoming a nuisance, Mate-ing with anyone who catches his fancy.
comments: That could be either... -GHS
records.assessment: Sakuraba does what he wants so long as it does not inconvenience others and associates with people he likes. The English reverses the limiting condition so that nuisance becomes permitted and mistranslates casual association as the malformed sexual term 'Mate-ing.'
records.remedy: He does what he wants as long as it bothers no one, and hangs around with people he likes.

highlights.text: within the limits of becoming a nuisance
Mate-ing

records.jp: どこかで生きているんだな、と桜庭は思った。
records.en: You're living off somewhere aren't ya, thought Sakuraba.
records.assessment: Sakuraba thinks that the person is alive somewhere. 'Living off' normally means subsisting on a resource or depending financially on someone, and the direct thought also lacks its required comma.
records.remedy: So you're alive somewhere, Sakuraba thought.

highlights.text: You're living off somewhere aren't ya

records.jp: 彼の心はそれで満ちて、幸せになった。
records.en: His heart was with that satisfied, and he felt happy.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that this knowledge filled Sakuraba's heart and made him happy. The English follows Japanese constituent order into an ungrammatical passive construction.
records.remedy: That knowledge filled his heart

highlights.text: His heart was with that satisfied

records.jp: 妙な気配を感じたが。
records.en: I had felt a strange presence.
records.assessment: The Japanese uses が to leave a contrastive thought hanging: he sensed something strange, but finds no confirming presence. The English closes the thought and changes simple perception to past perfect.
records.remedy: I sensed something strange, but...

highlights.text: I had felt a strange presence.

records.jp: 「みんなの……声が……したような……」
records.en: Taichi: "As if... the voices of everybody... were there..."
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he thought he heard everyone's voices. The English instead says that the voices were physically present.
records.remedy: I thought... I heard everyone's voices...

highlights.text: the voices of everybody... were there

records.jp: 屋上にはなんの気配もない。
records.en: On the rooftop there's no presence of no sort.
comments: Part meta, part religious... part literally real. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that there is no sign of anyone on the rooftop. The English double negative reverses that proposition and is ungrammatical in the surrounding register.
records.remedy: there was no sign of anyone

highlights.text: there's no presence of no sort

records.jp: 静まりかえっている。
records.en: It had all quietened down.
comments: Of course; they all left before he woke up. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese describes the rooftop as utterly silent. The English past perfect implies that prior activity there has now subsided and adds the vague totalizer 'all.'
records.remedy: It was utterly silent.

highlights.text: It had all quietened down.

records.jp: 「なんだよ……みんなして……」
records.en: Taichi: "The hell... you guys doing..."
records.assessment: The Japanese is a complete colloquial question. The English omits the auxiliary verb needed after the interrogative phrase.
records.remedy: What the hell... are you guys doing...?

highlights.text: The hell... you guys doing...

records.jp: 「あとでな……」
records.en: Taichi: "Do it later..."
records.assessment: あとでな is a sleepy postponement or farewell meaning 'later.' The English invents an imperative telling the others to perform an unspecified action later.
records.remedy: Later...

highlights.text: Do it later...

records.jp: 「おい、太一」
records.en: Sakuraba: "Hoy, Taichi."
comments: This beginning part is, besides the troll and the first warning that Taichi isn't "right" yet (and will never be, for that), a very good test of reading comprehension. Being able to spot all the parts of the story and flashback this is made up from, and most importantly how Taichi has modified them, gives an excellent reading key for exactly the kind of similarities, overlaps, and connections that need to be made throughout. If you 'get' how this is just a riff on the same verse, you might 'get' the harder parts of this. -GHS
records.assessment: The ordinary attention-getter おい is 'hey' here. 'Hoy' is an uncommon nautical or archaic-sounding interjection unsupported by the source voice.
records.remedy: Hey

highlights.text: Hoy

records.jp: あれ、桜庭？
records.en: Oh my, Sakuraba?
comments: Setting is CCC3004. -GHS
records.assessment: あれ marks mild surprise or recognition, equivalent here to 'huh?' The English gives Taichi the markedly genteel exclamation 'oh my.'
records.remedy: Huh, Sakuraba?

highlights.text: Oh my

records.jp: 「……ＤＪなんだろう？」
records.en: Sakuraba: "...you're the DJ aren't you?'
records.assessment: The dialogue begins with a double quotation mark but closes with an apostrophe, leaving mismatched quotation marks.
records.remedy: aren't you?"

highlights.text: aren't you?'

records.jp: 「先輩のＤＪ、ちょっと楽しみー」
records.en: Miki: "I'm sorta looking forward to your DJ, Senpai!"
records.assessment: DJ is the role or activity Taichi will perform, not a possessed person or object. The English therefore requires a gerund or role construction.
records.remedy: looking forward to hearing you DJ

highlights.text: looking forward to your DJ

records.jp: 「わたしは、先輩が恥かくところが楽しみです」
records.en: Kiri: "Me, I am looking forwards to Senpai shaming himself."
comments: See CCC3030. -GHS
records.assessment: In the phrasal verb 'look forward to,' 'forward' is not pluralized.
records.remedy: looking forward to

highlights.text: looking forwards to

records.jp: 「原稿、どうだ」
records.en: Sakuraba: "Howsit, that script."
records.assessment: Sakuraba asks how the script is. The English uses the unrelated colloquial greeting 'howsit' and leaves 'that script' as a detached afterthought.
records.remedy: How's the script?

highlights.text: Howsit, that script.

records.jp: 内容は……よくわからない。読めてはいるのに、理解できない。
records.en: Contents... I don't really get this. Read I can read, but I can't understand.
comments: And now he as the storyteller realizes that he's on the same level as the reader. But Taichi doesn't need to understand the script; that's the job for others, if they want to. See CCC3028, as well as the challenge near the end of this route. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese contrast means that Taichi can read the words but cannot understand them. The English reproduces the Japanese topic-focus order in an unnatural inversion.
records.remedy: I can read it

highlights.text: Read I can read

records.jp: 「ちょっと、何ぼんやりしてんの？　しゃんとしなさいよ」
records.en: Touko: "Come on now, what're you being all slack-jawed for? Be dignified already!"
comments: See CCD2002, exact words he uses at her. -GHS
records.assessment: Touko asks why Taichi is spacing out and tells him to pull himself together. 'Slack-jawed' adds an open-mouthed appearance, while 'be dignified' changes alertness and composure into social dignity.
records.remedy: Why are you spacing out? Pull yourself together.

highlights.text: being all slack-jawed
Be dignified already

records.jp: 「何なのその顔。気合い足りないんじゃない？」
records.en: Touko: "What's that face for. Don't you got enough fighting spirit now?"
comments: Irony, given she lacks the fire to live for most of the story. -GHS
records.assessment: After auxiliary 'do,' the verb must appear in its base form: 'have,' not 'got.'
records.remedy: Don't you have

highlights.text: Don't you got

records.jp: 「今なにか言ったかしら一年生～」
records.en: Touko: "I wonder if you just said something, you first ye～ars!"
comments: Revenge for dumping the autograph on her? -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese addresses the first-year students collectively. The English requires the compound noun 'first-years'; inserting the prolonged-sound mark inside 'years' does not supply the missing construction.
records.remedy: you first-yeaars

highlights.text: you first ye～ars

records.jp: 「ラブラブなんて、言ってません」
records.en: Kiri: "Have said nothing like 'lovey-love'."
records.assessment: The English finite clause omits its subject.
records.remedy: I said nothing

highlights.text: Have said nothing

records.jp: 「斬っちゃおうかしら？」
records.en: Touko: "Should I just slay them, I wonder?"
records.assessment: Touko directly threatens the first-years she is addressing. The English switches the targets into third-person 'them,' as if she were discussing absent people.
records.remedy: Maybe I should cut you two down?

highlights.text: slay them

records.jp: 「先輩なら助けてくださいよ」
records.en: Kiri: "You can help us, Senpai so get on it!"
comments: Lit. "please", but tone is this -GHS
records.assessment: Kiri appeals to the obligation attached to Taichi's senior status: if he is their senpai, he should help. The English instead states mere ability.
records.remedy: If you're our senpai, then help us

highlights.text: You can help us

records.jp: おいおい……都合良いな。
records.en: My my... I'm so convenient, am I.
records.assessment: 都合が良い here means that the others are opportunistically treating Taichi as useful when it suits them. The English instead calls Taichi himself convenient.
records.remedy: How convenient for you...

highlights.text: I'm so convenient, am I.

records.jp: 「よっし、あった！　はぁ、あぶなかった……」
records.en: Tomoki: "The-ere, done! Sigh, that was close..."
comments: See CCA0007 -GHS
records.assessment: Tomoki exclaims that he found the fault or connection he was seeking. 'Done' skips the discovery and presents the repair as already completed.
records.remedy: There, found it!

highlights.text: The-ere, done!

records.jp: 「いや、断線。だからケーブル類、買い直せって言ったんだけど」
records.en: Tomoki: "Nope, severance. And that's why I toldja to go buy a better type of cable."
comments: Taichi is disconnected from the world like an antenna with a snapped cable. SY[snip] -GHS
records.assessment: Tomoki says that a wire is broken and that he had told them to replace the cables. 'Severance' is not the normal term for this electrical fault, and the English invents a recommendation to buy a superior cable type.
records.remedy: No, a broken wire. That's why I told you to replace the cables.

highlights.text: severance
go buy a better type of cable

records.jp: 「うるさいなぁ、自立の時なんだよ、ぼかぁ」
records.en: Tomoki: "Shaddap you, I'm at the time of self reliance, ah' am!"
comments: He's not talking but he's talking, and that's obvious since he's hallucinating... but how often has this happened so far? Like with the further weeks showing sepia during flashbacks while the first week doesn't, it could very well be the same here. See CCA0011A, it's unfortunately not visible here but it's the same as his "pwease" back there. -GHS
records.assessment: Tomoki says that he has reached the age or stage of becoming independent. The English uses the calque 'at the time of,' omits the hyphen in 'self-reliance,' and invents a malformed eye-dialect tag.
records.remedy: I'm at the age when I need some independence!

highlights.text: I'm at the time of self reliance, ah' am!

records.jp: 「無性に旅に出たくなった。行くか」
records.en: Sakuraba: "I want to asexcessively go on a journey. Wanna go?"
comments: 無性 is also 'asexual', and given Sakuraba... -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Sakuraba has been seized by an urge to travel. The English fuses an adverb into the nonexistent word 'asexcessively' and places it inside an ungrammatical infinitive construction.
records.remedy: I've got an irresistible urge to travel.

highlights.text: I want to asexcessively go on a journey.

records.jp: 「いつも思うんですけど、旅行の資金とかどうしてるんですか？」
records.en: Miki: "I'm always thinking of doing that, but what do I do about the travel expenses?"
records.assessment: Miki says that she has always wondered how Sakuraba finances his trips. The English instead says that Miki continually considers traveling and asks how she herself should handle the expense.
records.remedy: I've always wondered: how do you pay for your trips?

highlights.text: I'm always thinking of doing that, but what do I do about the travel expenses?

records.jp: 「あるだけでやりくりするのが敏腕トラベラー」
records.en: Sakuraba: "Managing with just what you have somehow is what makes a competent Traveler."
records.assessment: The Japanese uses an ordinary descriptive compound for a capable traveler. The English arbitrarily capitalizes the common noun as though it were a formal title.
records.remedy: capable traveler

highlights.text: competent Traveler

records.jp: 「月給３０００円の自分には想像がつかないですねー」
records.en: Miki: "With a monthly allowance of 3,000 yen that's just sooo beyond even imagination."
comments: See CCD4003 -GHS
records.assessment: 月給 means monthly pay or salary. The English changes Miki's earnings into money given to her as an allowance.
records.remedy: monthly salary

highlights.text: monthly allowance

records.jp: 「だまされちゃ駄目よ。桜庭の家って甘々なんだから。あるだけってのでたぶん何十万とかよ」
records.en: Touko: "Don't you let yourself be fooled now! Sakuraba's family's made of naive spoiling. His 'just what you have somehow' must run in the hundreds of thousands!"
comments: See the coins scene - it does. -GHS
records.assessment: Touko says that Sakuraba's family is extremely indulgent toward him. The English depicts the family as physically made of an abstract and oddly qualified substance called 'naive spoiling.'
records.remedy: Sakuraba's family spoils him rotten.

highlights.text: Sakuraba's family's made of naive spoiling.

records.jp: 「さー、初めてのＤＪ、鬼が出るか」
records.en: Miki: "Who knows, it's his first DJ, maybe some demon will appear."
comments: Symbo -GHS
records.assessment: 鬼が出るか蛇が出るか is a paired idiom for not knowing what may emerge or happen. The English treats its first half as a literal prediction of a demon and does not communicate the idiom.
records.remedy: Who knows how his first time as DJ will turn out

highlights.text: maybe some demon will appear

records.jp: 「蛇が出るか」
records.en: Kiri: "Maybe a snake will appear."
comments: lism! -GHS
records.assessment: This is the answering half of 鬼が出るか蛇が出るか, a paired idiom meaning that the outcome is unknown. The English presents the snake as a literal possible event.
records.remedy: Could be anything.

highlights.text: Maybe a snake will appear.

records.jp: 「悪い方しか想定されてないって」
records.en: Tomoki: "Don't just assume something bad'll happen just because you never know what'll happen."
comments: The above two are halves of 鬼が出るか蛇が出るか, "you never know what'll happen", but since there's SYMBOLISM!!! in the literal meaning, the non-literal one goes in the tsukkomi. -GHS
records.assessment: Tomoki objects that they are considering only bad outcomes. The English adds a causal explanation about general uncertainty that is not present in his retort.
records.remedy: You're only imagining bad outcomes.

highlights.text: just because you never know what'll happen

records.jp: 「楽しみですっ」
records.en: Yusa: "I look forwards to this!"
records.assessment: In the phrasal verb 'look forward to,' 'forward' is not pluralized.
records.remedy: look forward to

highlights.text: look forwards to

records.jp: 「肩の力を抜いていきなさい」
records.en: Youko: "Take the tension out of your shoulders now."
records.assessment: 肩の力を抜く is an idiom telling Taichi to relax and not try too hard. The English translates it as a literal physical extraction of tension from his shoulders.
records.remedy: Just relax and take it easy.

highlights.text: Take the tension out of your shoulders

records.jp: 都合の良さに、不安がよぎる。だけど。
records.en: In the convenience of this all, anxiety flashes by. However,
comments: First sign. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the suspicious convenience or perfection of the situation gives him a passing anxiety. The English uses a malformed prepositional phrase that does not identify what troubles him.
records.remedy: A flicker of anxiety passed through me at how convenient it all was.

highlights.text: In the convenience of this all

records.jp: また学校に泊まってしまった。
records.en: I slept over at school again, dammit.
comments: Misato again. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he ended up sleeping at school again but contains no curse or explicit burst of anger.
records.remedy: I ended up sleeping at school again.

highlights.text: dammit

records.jp: 人らしい日々のため、自宅に戻りたいところなのにな。
records.en: When I have to go back to my house in order to live my days like a decent person...
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he wants to return home in order to live something resembling ordinary human days. 'Decent person' introduces a moral judgment about his character.
records.remedy: to live something resembling a normal human life

highlights.text: like a decent person

records.jp: でも一人で準備をするのは、なかなか大変だ。
records.en: But getting this thing ready on my own is really really difficult.
records.assessment: なかなか means considerably or rather difficult. The English invents emphatic repetition unsupported by the source cadence.
records.remedy: really difficult

highlights.text: really really difficult

records.jp: 意識的に声を出す。
records.en: I deliberately vocalize.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi consciously speaks aloud. 'Vocalize' is a technical and intransitive description that obscures the simple act of using his voice.
records.remedy: I deliberately speak aloud.

highlights.text: I deliberately vocalize.

records.jp: 曜子ちゃんが作ってくれた弁当も、もはやない。
records.en: The lunch that Youko-chan used to prepare was now also no more.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the lunches once prepared for him are gone. The English reproduces the Japanese adverbial sequence in a nonidiomatic predicate.
records.remedy: was gone now too

highlights.text: was now also no more

records.jp: 周囲を見渡す。
records.en: I pass my gaze on the surroundings.
records.assessment: The Japanese simply says that Taichi looks around. The English calques the movement of a gaze into a malformed action performed 'on' the surroundings.
records.remedy: I look around.

highlights.text: I pass my gaze on the surroundings.

records.jp: うまいはずのコロッケパンも、口にする気にはならない。
records.en: I can't bring myself to even taste the croquette bread, however delicious it should be.
comments: See CCB2010, CCC0025. Symbolism. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that even the croquette bread, which ought to taste good, fails to appeal to him. The English turns expected tastiness into an open-ended concessive degree and disconnects it from the speaker's prior knowledge.
records.remedy: even though it was supposed to be good

highlights.text: however delicious it should be

records.jp: 望んで得たもの。
records.en: The obtainment of what I desired.
records.assessment: The Japanese noun phrase means 'what I wanted and obtained.' The English uses the awkward nominalization 'obtainment' and an unnecessary prepositional construction.
records.remedy: What I wanted and obtained.

highlights.text: The obtainment of what I desired.

records.jp: 心は、楽。
records.en: The heart is at ease.
records.assessment: The Japanese refers to Taichi's own emotional state. The English turns his heart into a generic definite object detached from him.
records.remedy: My heart is at ease.

highlights.text: The heart is at ease.

records.jp: 改善しようのない素直な自分でいられる世界。
records.en: A world where I can live honestly about the impossibility of my ever improving.
comments: Hints that this is far from over start here. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he can remain his unchangeably straightforward or unvarnished self. The English instead says that he honestly acknowledges a proposition about being unable to improve.
records.remedy: remain my unvarnished self, beyond any hope of improvement

highlights.text: live honestly about the impossibility of my ever improving

records.jp: この二つはよくセットで用いられる概念なのに、俺の場合は破綻している。
records.en: Though these two concept are often used as a set, in my case that fell completely apart.
records.assessment: The demonstrative and numeral require the plural noun 'concepts.'
records.remedy: these two concepts

highlights.text: these two concept

records.jp: 他は１。
records.en: Rest was at 1.
records.assessment: The English omits the definite article required by 'the rest.'
records.remedy: The rest were at 1.

highlights.text: Rest was at 1.

records.jp: バランスは暗に否定されていて、何が正しいのかわからなくなる。
records.en: Once balance is indirectly rejected, what is correct becomes unknowable.
records.assessment: The Japanese states an ongoing condition in which balance is tacitly rejected. The English converts it into a temporal or conditional event introduced by 'once.'
records.remedy: With balance tacitly rejected

highlights.text: Once balance is indirectly rejected

records.jp: 心穏やかに、生きていけている。
records.en: I can live with gentleness in my heart.
records.assessment: 心穏やかに means living calmly or peacefully. 'Gentleness' instead describes kindness or mildness of character.
records.remedy: live in peace

highlights.text: with gentleness in my heart

records.jp: 「……思い出は、たくさんあるしな」
records.en: Taichi: "...there's lots of memories, aren't there."
records.assessment: The plural noun requires 'there are,' and the tag question must agree with that verb.
records.remedy: there are lots of memories, aren't there

highlights.text: there's lots of memories, aren't there

records.jp: 常に共にいながら、共依存にはなかった二人。
records.en:
These two were living together all day
while never becoming co-dependent.
comments: That's not quite what co-dependence non-means (either English or Japanese). I suspect he's using it as synonym for Alter Egos, which are impossible. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the two were always together without becoming codependent. The English adds cohabitation and restricts their constancy to the span of each day.
records.remedy: always together

highlights.text: living together all day

records.jp: 片方はかつてあったものの代理を求めた。
records.en:
One side sought replacement for something that
was there before,
comments: Kiri -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that one of them sought a substitute for something once possessed. The singular count noun 'replacement' requires a determiner.
records.remedy: sought a replacement

highlights.text: sought replacement

records.jp: 片方は頼ってきた少女を道具立てた。
records.en: one side arranged that reliant girl into a tool.
comments: Miki -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that one person made an instrument or prop of the girl who relied on her. The English uses 'arranged into' as a transformation verb and obscures the exploitation.
records.remedy: made a tool of the girl who depended on her

highlights.text: arranged that reliant girl into a tool

records.jp: 幸福なる接点の発見。
records.en:
The discovery of that tangent point is a
blessed happiness.
records.assessment: 接点 is a point of contact here, not specifically a mathematical tangent point. The source is a noun fragment about discovering a blessed point of contact; the English adds a finite equation to an abstract 'happiness.'
records.remedy: The discovery of a blessed point of contact.

highlights.text: that tangent point

is a
blessed happiness

records.jp: 美希が霧を切に想うには、莫大な経験が必要で。
records.en:
For Miki to regard Kiri with honesty, a large
amount of experience will be necessary.
records.assessment: 切に想う means to care or feel deeply and earnestly for someone. The English replaces emotional intensity with honesty.
records.remedy: care deeply for Kiri

highlights.text: regard Kiri with honesty

records.jp: 霧が罪悪の呪縛から解き放されるには、時間がかかりそうで。
records.en:
For Kiri to be released from the curse of her
guilt it should take time.
records.assessment: The Japanese makes an observational prediction that the process seems likely to take time. 'Should' can instead sound normative, and the subordinate clause requires a comma.
records.remedy: it looked as though she would need time

highlights.text: it should take time

records.jp: 二人がこっちに駆けてきた。
records.en: the two have run over here.
comments: They're there, they just can't get through to him. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese narrates the two running toward him in the simple past. The English shifts to present perfect and 'run over' can also mean strike with a vehicle.
records.remedy: the two came running toward me

highlights.text: the two have run over here

records.jp: 鼻先を少女の微風が、そっと撫でた。残り香のように。
records.en: The tip of the nose is gently caressed by soft breeze of girl. As if a lingering scent.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that a breeze made by the girls gently brushed the tip of Taichi's nose. The English omits possession of the nose and both articles from the phrase 'soft breeze of girl,' reducing the pair to a generic singular.
records.remedy: A soft breeze from the girls gently brushed the tip of my nose.

highlights.text: The tip of the nose
by soft breeze of girl

records.jp: 錯覚だけど。
records.en: But it is just illusion.
records.assessment: The singular count noun 'illusion' requires an article.
records.remedy: just an illusion

highlights.text: just illusion

records.jp: 閉じこめる必要はもうない。
records.en: There is no more need for it to imprison,
comments: But it could never imprison him, see CCC4012 -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that there is no longer any need to shut people inside. The English invents an impersonal subject 'it,' omits the person confined, and leaves the sentence hanging on a comma.
records.remedy: There is no longer any need to keep anyone shut inside.

highlights.text: There is no more need for it to imprison,

records.jp: 傷つく者のない世界だからだ。
records.en: because this is a world where no one exists who can hurt.
records.assessment: The Japanese describes a world in which no one can be hurt. The English reverses patient and agent, describing a world without anyone capable of hurting others.
records.remedy: no one can be hurt

highlights.text: no one exists who can hurt

records.jp: 無論、授業時間中に脱走しても咎められることはない。
records.en: I will not be reproached should I desert during school hours, of course.
comments: Like he never was, because he can escape the guards easily. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese casually refers to slipping away or escaping during class. 'Desert' invokes permanent abandonment of a duty, especially a military post.
records.remedy: slip away during class

highlights.text: desert during school hours

records.jp: 適当に食物と飲み物をあさる。
records.en: I scrounge food and drink as appropriate.
comments: The curry bread was probably the day before. -GHS
records.assessment: 適当に here means casually or indiscriminately rummaging for whatever food and drink he can take. 'As appropriate' instead implies considered adherence to a standard.
records.remedy: I rummage around for whatever food and drink I can find.

highlights.text: as appropriate

records.jp: なぜだかこちらでは、腐食という現象は起こらない。
records.en: For whatever reason, here the phenomenon of saprophagy does not occur.
comments: Because fresh food is still brought in. -GHS
records.assessment: 腐食 here denotes food rotting or decaying. Saprophagy is the act of an organism feeding on decaying matter, an entirely different phenomenon.
records.remedy: decay

highlights.text: saprophagy

records.jp: 毎週そうしているように。
records.en: as I end up doing every week.
records.assessment: The Japanese says neutrally that this is his weekly practice. 'End up doing' adds inadvertence or an unintended outcome.
records.remedy: as I do every week

highlights.text: as I end up doing every week

records.jp: 『×月○日　菓子パン１１０円＋カップ麺１８０円＋緑茶王１１０円』
records.en:
X/O
Sweetened bun
Cup Noodles
Green King Tea
110￥+180￥+110￥
comments: Not signed. Same "date" as Sakakibara diary. Day of Cross, Month of Loop. See CCZAS. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese is a single dated itemized memo that keeps each price beside its product. The English separates all prices from their items, omits the day marker, pluralizes the single cup noodle, and reverses the product name 緑茶王.
records.remedy: Month X, Day O: sweet bun ¥110 + cup noodle ¥180 + Green Tea King ¥110

highlights.text:
X/O
Sweetened bun
Cup Noodles
Green King Tea
110￥+180￥+110￥

records.jp: それさえも放棄するなら、緩慢な死に身を置くようなものだからだ。
records.en: Because abandoning even that is to arrange for a slow death.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that abandoning even this effort would amount to placing oneself in a state of gradual death. 'Arrange for' instead implies deliberately organizing that death as an intended outcome.
records.remedy: would be like consigning myself to a slow death

highlights.text: to arrange for a slow death

records.jp: 背筋を伸ばし、顎を引き。
records.en: Head held high, chin jutting out,
records.assessment: 顎を引く means drawing or tucking the chin in. The English depicts the opposite physical movement, projecting it outward.
records.remedy: chin tucked in

highlights.text: chin jutting out

records.jp: 凛と、歩いたものだった。
records.en: so cold and dignifed she was when she walked.
comments: She's probably doing so right now. -GHS
records.assessment: 凛と describes Touko's dignified or commanding bearing as she walked. The English adds emotional coldness, uses marked inversion, and misspells 'dignified.'
records.remedy: She used to walk with such dignity.

highlights.text: so cold and dignifed she was

records.jp: ひとたび手を差し伸べられると、慣れていないのか、すぐに堕落した。
records.en: She was not accustomed to it, perhaps, so that if a hand was extended in help just once she immediately grew corrupt.
records.assessment: Once someone reached out to her, Touko quickly went soft or let herself go because she was unused to kindness. 'Corrupt' adds moral depravity.
records.remedy: quickly went soft

highlights.text: grew corrupt

records.jp: 溶けた冬子は危なっかしかった。
records.en: The Winter Child, Touko, grew dangerous when melted.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that a softened or emotionally melted Touko seemed precarious. The English inserts a literal gloss of the characters in her name and changes 'precarious' into actively dangerous.
records.remedy: Once Touko melted, she seemed terribly vulnerable.

highlights.text: The Winter Child, Touko
grew dangerous when melted

records.jp: 優しくされただけで、壁を取りはらってしまった。
records.en: If merely treated kindly, her wall would end up torn down.
records.assessment: The Japanese narrates an actual past result: mere kindness made Touko remove her barriers. The English recasts it as a hypothetical or habitual conditional and makes the wall passively torn down.
records.remedy: The slightest kindness made her tear down her walls.

highlights.text: If merely treated kindly, her wall would end up torn down.

records.jp: 不器用さが、人付き合いの苦手さを示している。
records.en: Her clumsy tactlessness expressed her lack of skill at socializing.
records.assessment: 不器用さ means awkwardness or clumsiness, which demonstrates difficulty dealing with people. The English redundantly adds 'tactlessness,' a harsher claim about social insensitivity.
records.remedy: awkwardness

highlights.text: clumsy tactlessness

records.jp: どんなに信頼できても、適切な距離は置くべきだ。
records.en: However much reliance there might be, an appropriate distance ought be kept.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that an appropriate distance should be kept even with someone completely trustworthy. The English replaces trustworthiness with the degree of reliance already placed on the person.
records.remedy: No matter how trustworthy someone is

highlights.text: However much reliance there might be

records.jp: してもいい人は、依存しあえばいい。
records.en: Those who don't mind can go and be dependent.
comments: I truly cannot tell if Tanaka's still sorta half-assed in the end, or if he's just trolling that hard. In the end, for some things, there's nothing but conjecture. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that people willing to accept the risk may depend on each other. The English omits the mutual relation and leaves a one-way dependence without an object.
records.remedy: depend on each other if they want

highlights.text: go and be dependent

records.jp: 曜子ちゃんのこともあるけれど。
records.en: There's that about Youko-chan, however.
records.assessment: The Japanese elliptical aside means that Youko is also a reason for his aversion. The English literalizes the deictic construction into an opaque phrase.
records.remedy: There's also what happened with Youko.

highlights.text: There's that about Youko-chan

records.jp: どうも俺は、美しく佇むものが好きのようだ。
records.en: It seems that I like beautiful and still things, very much so.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he seems drawn to things or people that stand beautifully. The English turns 佇む into motionless stillness and adds emphatic 'very much so.'
records.remedy: things that stand beautifully

highlights.text: beautiful and still things, very much so

records.jp: ……耐えられているのかな？
records.en: ...will enduring that be possible?
comments: Both her and Taichi. Taichi's sins are not gone simply because he changes so as to effectively vow not to commit more. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi wonders whether Touko is managing to endure the situation now. The English omits Touko as subject and turns the question into an abstract future possibility of 'enduring.'
records.remedy: I wonder if she's holding up.

highlights.text: will enduring that be possible?

records.jp: そんな俺を侮辱する、舌足らずで居丈高な言葉が、聞こえた。
records.en: And so I heard those contemptuous, lisping, high-handed words she had for what I did.
records.assessment: He imagines the childish or inarticulate, imperious words that would insult him as he is. The English diagnoses a lisp and redirects the imagined contempt from him to a past action.
records.remedy: I heard her childish, imperious voice insulting the person I was.

highlights.text: lisping
words she had for what I did

records.jp: たまり場だった場所。
records.en: The place was a gathering area.
comments: See CCA0007 -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese noun fragment identifies the clubroom as the place that used to be their hangout. The English makes this an ordinary past statement about a generic designated gathering area.
records.remedy: The place that had been our hangout.

highlights.text: The place was a gathering area.

records.jp: あいつらの姿は、当然ない。
records.en: Their profiles, naturally, are nowhere.
comments: Class is still in session. That, or it's 4 AM. -GHS
records.assessment: 姿 means their figures, presence, or sight of them. 'Profiles' instead suggests side views or personal records.
records.remedy: There was no sign of them

highlights.text: Their profiles

records.jp: どこにでもある関係。に近い。
records.en: A relationship that could exist anywhere, anytime. Something near that.
records.assessment: The Japanese calls it close to an ordinary relationship found anywhere. The English adds 'anytime' and separates the qualifier into an abrupt afterthought.
records.remedy: Close to the kind of relationship found anywhere.

highlights.text: anywhere, anytime. Something near that.

records.jp: ただ手放したものの尊さまばゆさ、想うほどにおこる胸の軋みが、喉を詰まらせて。
records.en: Just the dazzling holiness of things released from grasp, that the more my thoughts went over imagining them, the more my throat grew tightened by the creaking discord of my what's in my breast.
comments: Regret for having let that get away from him. Though it would've happened anyway; and perhaps it has. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the dazzling preciousness of what he relinquished and the ache in his chest whenever he thinks of it choke off his voice. The English substitutes religious holiness, loses the parallel subjects, duplicates the thought process, and collapses into the nonsensical phrase 'my what's in my breast.'
records.remedy: The dazzling preciousness of what I had let go, and the ache in my chest whenever I thought of it, choked off my voice.

highlights.text: Just the dazzling holiness of things released from grasp, that the more my thoughts went over imagining them, the more my throat grew tightened by the creaking discord of my what's in my breast.

records.jp: ぼんやりと突っ立っていた。
records.en: I stood up absent-mindedly.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi remained standing there blankly. The English changes a continuing posture into the event of rising to his feet.
records.remedy: I stood there blankly.

highlights.text: I stood up absent-mindedly.

records.jp: 再び部活。
records.en: Once again to club.
records.assessment: The Japanese elliptical transition means returning to club work. The English uses 'club' without the noun or activity required after 'to.'
records.remedy: Back to club work.

highlights.text: Once again to club.

records.jp: どの程度頑張れば、一人でも準備が整うのか。
records.en: To what extent must I persist to get everything in order even if alone?
records.assessment: Taichi asks how hard he must work to complete the preparations by himself. The English makes being alone a hypothetical concession rather than his actual working condition.
records.remedy: to get everything ready by myself

highlights.text: even if alone

records.jp: 何度も繰り返したことだ。
records.en: This is something I've done all over again so many times.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he has performed the task many times. 'All over again' adds the notion that each repetition restarts after an interruption or unwanted result.
records.remedy: many times

highlights.text: all over again

records.jp: 知識もついた。
records.en: I had the knowledge.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi acquired knowledge through repetition. The English describes simple possession and omits that acquisition.
records.remedy: I had gained the knowledge.

highlights.text: I had the knowledge.

records.jp: 手順も極められた。
records.en: I had resolved on a procedure as well.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he mastered the procedure. 'Resolved on' means that he decided to adopt one, not that he perfected his command of it.
records.remedy: mastered the procedure

highlights.text: resolved on a procedure

records.jp: 回り道をしながら。
records.en: while detouring on diversions.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he will take detours. The English redundantly expresses the same idea twice and uses the nonidiomatic preposition 'on.'
records.remedy: taking detours

highlights.text: detouring on diversions

records.jp: ある意味彼女のしていたことも、回り道だ。
records.en: In a certain sense, in what she did there were also detours.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that what she was doing was itself a kind of detour. The English instead says that her work contained multiple detours among other elements.
records.remedy: what she did was also a kind of detour

highlights.text: in what she did there were also detours

records.jp: 「元気にちんたら部活しよう」
records.en: Taichi: "Let's put some pep into our slow-handed tardy club."
records.assessment: Taichi cheerfully proposes taking their sweet time over club work. The English turns the adverbial joke into two incompatible adjectives modifying the club itself.
records.remedy: Let's cheerfully take our sweet time with club work.

highlights.text: Let's put some pep into our slow-handed tardy club.

records.jp: と声を出し。
records.en: I vocalize.
records.assessment: The Japanese simply says that he speaks the words aloud. 'Vocalize' is a technical and intransitive description that obscures the act.
records.remedy: I say aloud.

highlights.text: I vocalize.

records.jp: なのに空は未だ、律儀な営みを繰り返していた。
records.en: nevertheless the sky still did its job over and over again, with integrity.
records.assessment: The Japanese personifies the sky as faithfully continuing its regular cycle. The English reduces the cycle to a job, adds an iterative phrase, and uses 'integrity' as a personal moral quality.
records.remedy: faithfully continued its regular cycle

highlights.text: did its job over and over again, with integrity

records.jp: 鏡の中に忘れ去られた、虚像の夏であるかのように。
records.en: As if a hologram of Summer, left behind inside a mirror,
comments: The Melty Blood term for Hologram Summer is actually 幻影の夏, but this is so similar it works just too well. Also 1 Cor 13:12, all but explicit here. -GHS
records.assessment: 虚像 is the virtual or reflected image left in a mirror, not a hologram. The English also arbitrarily capitalizes the season.
records.remedy: the virtual image of summer

highlights.text: a hologram of Summer

records.jp: 実像に遅れて光のはやさで消える。
records.en: it disappears at the speed of light, late behind the real image.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the virtual image lags behind the real one before vanishing at light speed. The English uses the ungrammatical phrase 'late behind' and does not clearly express the lagging relation.
records.remedy: lagging behind the real image

highlights.text: late behind the real image

records.jp: 宇宙史の一刹那、人にとってのＸ週間。
records.en: An instant in the history of the universe is for a person just one week, week 'X'.
comments: But is it parallel? Though in (distant) retrospect, this might justify trying to connect the week, mathematically, to a day. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese equates an instant of cosmic history with an unspecified X weeks in human terms. The English fixes that interval at one week and then adds 'week X' as though X labeled the week.
records.remedy: an instant in cosmic history; X weeks to a person

highlights.text: is for a person just one week, week 'X'

records.jp: 簡単に調理し、生ゴミはポリ袋にまとめてしまう。
records.en: Simple cooking, with trash collected in a plastic bag.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he cooks something simple and gathers the food waste into a plastic bag. The English is a verbless fragment and generalizes the specified raw food waste to all trash.
records.remedy: I make a simple meal and gather the food waste into a plastic bag.

highlights.text: Simple cooking, with trash collected in a plastic bag.

records.jp: 夕風が焦げ臭い。
records.en: The evening breeze tastes burnt.
records.assessment: 焦げ臭い describes the smell of something scorched carried on the evening breeze. The English assigns the sensation to taste.
records.remedy: The evening breeze smells scorched.

highlights.text: The evening breeze tastes burnt.

records.jp: 「いけね！」
records.en: Taichi: "Dammit!"
records.assessment: いけね is an alarmed realization equivalent to 'uh-oh' or 'crap.' The English makes it a direct curse of anger.
records.remedy: Uh-oh!

highlights.text: Dammit!

records.jp: さすがに食べられない。
records.en: As expectable, inedible.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that, unsurprisingly, the ruined food cannot be eaten. 'As expectable' is not idiomatic in this adverbial use, and the English is an overly compressed fragment.
records.remedy: Unsurprisingly, it was inedible.

highlights.text: As expectable, inedible.

records.jp: 食べ終わる頃には、すっかり夜。
records.en: By the time I had finished eating, is was fully night.
records.assessment: The English contains a simple 'is/it' typographical substitution and uses the nonidiomatic predicate 'fully night.'
records.remedy: it was fully dark

highlights.text: is was fully night

records.jp: 今夜あたり、来るかな。
records.en: Has it come just this night, I wonder.
records.assessment: Taichi wonders whether something will come around tonight. The English changes the anticipated event into a present-perfect question about whether it has already arrived, while 'just this night' is nonidiomatic.
records.remedy: I wonder if it'll come tonight.

highlights.text: Has it come just this night

records.jp: 何も起こらない。
records.en: Nothing has happened.
comments: That hasn't stopped him from diarizing before, see Week 1, especially see CCA0015C. Three quarters of that stuff was made up! -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese describes the continuing condition that nothing happens in this world. The English limits the claim to events completed up to the present moment.
records.remedy: Nothing happens.

highlights.text: Nothing has happened.

records.jp: 可能性さえない。
records.en: Not even the possibility anything would.
records.assessment: The Japanese complete noun phrase says that not even possibility exists. The English omits both the preposition after 'possibility' and the verb completing what anything would do.
records.remedy: There isn't even any possibility.

highlights.text: Not even the possibility anything would.

records.jp: なぜ日記なんてつけたんだ、俺は。
records.en: The hell you've been keeping the diary for, you.
records.assessment: Taichi asks himself why he started keeping a diary. The English switches to second person, omits the interrogative auxiliary, and adds a final accusatory 'you.'
records.remedy: Why the hell did I start keeping a diary?

highlights.text: The hell you've been keeping the diary for, you.

records.jp: 閉じる。イヤになった。
records.en: I closed it up. This began to taste bad.
records.assessment: イヤになった means that he became fed up or disgusted with the diary. The English invents a gustatory change in how an unspecified object tastes.
records.remedy: I was sick of it.

highlights.text: This began to taste bad.

records.jp: すぐに気が散ってしまう。
records.en: Soon my focus scatters.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he quickly becomes distracted. The English literalizes attention as a physical collection that scatters.
records.remedy: I quickly get distracted.

highlights.text: my focus scatters

records.jp: このコミックも、続きを読む機会はない。
records.en: I will never have the chance to ever read the continuation of this comic, either.
comments: He's not reading a manga? *badum-tish* -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he will have no chance to continue reading this comic. The English redundantly marks the same absolute temporal negation with both 'never' and 'ever.'
records.remedy: never have the chance to read

highlights.text: never have the chance to ever read

records.jp: 明日は本屋に行って、完結したコミックセットを漁ってこよう。
records.en: Tomorrow I will go to a bookstore and hunt down the complete comic book set.
comments: And that's why he could never read the conclusion ever: he didn't own it, as the implication is that the comic has ended its run and is available complete. Pure troll. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi plans to browse or rummage for manga series that are already complete. The English instead presupposes one particular complete set that he will track down.
records.remedy: browse for some completed manga series

highlights.text: hunt down the complete comic book set

records.jp: 「寝るぜー！」
records.en: Taichi: "Get sleeping!"
records.assessment: Taichi declares that he is going to sleep. The English changes the first-person declaration into an imperative addressed to someone else.
records.remedy: I'm gonna sleep!

highlights.text: Get sleeping!

records.jp: 暴れてみる。
records.en: I try raging.
comments: To exhaust himself? -GHS
records.assessment: 暴れる describes Taichi physically thrashing around on the bed. 'Raging' instead describes intense anger or an uncontrolled event.
records.remedy: I try thrashing around.

highlights.text: I try raging.

records.jp: 「ぎゃーす！　ぎゃーす！」
records.en: Taichi: "Noooise! Noooise!"
comments: Seems to be a variant on "gyaasuka", see CCC3018 -GHS
records.assessment: ぎゃーす is a repeated nonsensical yell. The English assigns the cries the lexical meaning 'noise,' turning sound into a shouted metacommentary.
records.remedy: Gyaaah! Gyaaah!

highlights.text: Noooise! Noooise!

records.jp: 涼しい夏。
records.en: A cool Summer.
comments: It's probably early Spring by now. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese uses the common noun for the season. The English arbitrarily capitalizes it as a proper name.
records.remedy: summer

highlights.text: Summer

records.jp: 「この疲労を利用して、一気に眠りに就く」
records.en: Taichi: "Making use of this tiredness, I shall fall asleep in a single beat!"
records.assessment: 一気に means going to sleep all at once or in one quick push. 'In a single beat' introduces an unsupported rhythmic unit and is nonidiomatic for falling asleep.
records.remedy: fall asleep in one go

highlights.text: fall asleep in a single beat

records.jp: 声をかける者はなく、届けられるささやかな好意もない。
records.en: With no one to call out to, there are no little pleasantries to deliver.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that nobody will speak to Taichi or deliver any small kindness to him. The English makes Taichi the person lacking someone to address and turns kindness received into pleasantries he would deliver.
records.remedy: No one would speak to me, and no small kindness would arrive.

highlights.text: no one to call out to
no little pleasantries to deliver

records.jp: むしのいい話だ。
records.en: But that would only be self-convenience.
records.assessment: むしのいい話 means a selfishly convenient expectation. The English creates the nonidiomatic abstraction 'self-convenience.'
records.remedy: a selfishly convenient fantasy

highlights.text: self-convenience

records.jp: 未練を振り切る勢いで、元気よく歩き出す。
records.en: Shaking off regrets by force, I set up to walk with energy.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he sets off walking briskly, with enough force to shake off his lingering attachment. 'Set up to walk' normally means prepare an arrangement rather than begin walking.
records.remedy: I set off at a brisk walk.

highlights.text: I set up to walk with energy.

records.jp: 口笛も、今朝は幾度となく掠れた。
records.en: And my whistling, as well, this morning just kept growing husky.
comments: This seems oddly ambiguous. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that his whistle repeatedly cracked or came out hoarse that morning. The English depicts a single continuing process in which the whistle grows progressively huskier.
records.remedy: kept coming out hoarse

highlights.text: just kept growing husky

records.jp: プレハブにしまった工具を引っ張り出し、所定の位置に並べる。
records.en: Take out the tools stored in the prefab, and line them up in the pre-decided order.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi takes out the stored tools and arranges them in their designated positions. The English omits the first-person subject and changes spatial positions into a predetermined sequence.
records.remedy: I take out the tools stored in the prefab and arrange them in their designated places.

highlights.text: Take out the tools
pre-decided order

records.jp: ただ少し横になるだけ。
records.en: I just lay down a bit, that's all.
records.assessment: In the surrounding present-tense narration, the intransitive verb requires 'lie,' not past-tense 'lay.'
records.remedy: I just lie down

highlights.text: I just lay down

records.jp: さすがに丸一日何もしないのは、どうだろう。
records.en: And if in the end I spend a whole day doing nothing, what will I do?
records.assessment: Taichi rhetorically questions whether spending an entire day doing nothing is really acceptable. The English instead asks what action he will take afterward.
records.remedy: is it really okay to spend an entire day doing nothing?

highlights.text: what will I do?

records.jp: 懊悩の五回転。
records.en: Five revolutions of anguish (oh no).
comments: Not a figure of speech that I can find. See CCB2002, going with the same joke. Maybe he just tumbles around the floor. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese compressed comic phrase describes five turns or revolutions of anguish. The English adds an explanatory reaction in parentheses that is not part of the source.
records.remedy: Five revolutions of anguish.

highlights.text: (oh no)

records.jp: 急ぎ、作業に取りかかる。
records.en: I set out to work, in a haste.
records.assessment: The fixed expression is 'in haste' or 'in a hurry,' without an indefinite article before 'haste.'
records.remedy: in haste

highlights.text: in a haste

records.jp: 束ねられた水流はたちまち風に散らされ、水煙と化す。
records.en: The collected water jet is promptly scattered by the wind, morphing into a mist.
records.assessment: The Japanese describes a focused stream of water instantly scattered into spray by the wind. 'Collected' suggests accumulated water, while 'morphing' imports conspicuously technical slang into plain narration.
records.remedy: The focused stream was instantly scattered by the wind and turned to spray.

highlights.text: The collected water jet
morphing into a mist

records.jp: 薄暮を雅に飾った。
records.en: It adorns the dusk with refinement.
records.assessment: The Japanese narrates the rainbow adorning the dusk in the past. The English shifts to present tense.
records.remedy: It adorned

highlights.text: It adorns

records.jp: 少し気がまぎれた。
records.en: It set my mind astray a little.
comments: True mind screw starts about here. But it's peanuts compared to what came before - provided you understood it. -GHS
records.assessment: 気がまぎれる means that the sight distracted Taichi from his distress or took his mind off it. 'Set my mind astray' instead suggests leading his judgment into error.
records.remedy: It took my mind off things for a moment.

highlights.text: It set my mind astray

records.jp: 通学坂。
records.en: The Hills to School.
records.assessment: 通学坂 is the school-commute slope or hill, not a plural proper name. The English invents capitalization and changes one slope into multiple hills.
records.remedy: The hill to school.

highlights.text: The Hills to School.

records.jp: 思い出すもの
records.en: A thing of memories,
records.assessment: The Japanese fragment introduces the people or things that the place makes him remember. The English turns memory into a substance possessed by one generic thing.
records.remedy: What it brings to mind:

highlights.text: A thing of memories

records.jp: 口にすると、心臓が握りしめられてしまう。
records.en: On her name passing my mouth, my physical heart feels like it's being seized.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that speaking her name makes his heart feel squeezed. The English literalizes 口にする as a name physically passing through his mouth and adds 'physical' as a needless anatomical gloss.
records.remedy: Saying her name made my heart clench.

highlights.text: On her name passing my mouth
my physical heart

records.jp: ただ……姿を見せなくなっただけじゃないか。
records.en: It's just... she merely doesn't want to show herself to me, doesn't she.
records.assessment: The Japanese says only that Nanaka stopped appearing. The English invents a continuing desire to hide specifically from Taichi.
records.remedy: she merely stopped showing up

highlights.text: she merely doesn't want to show herself to me

records.jp: ……というのは作りすぎか。
records.en: ...but I might be making too much of this.
records.assessment: Taichi wonders whether he has embellished or invented the imagined characterization too freely. 'Making too much of this' instead normally means overreacting to a real fact.
records.remedy: maybe I'm embellishing too much

highlights.text: making too much of this

records.jp: そんな気もするのだ。
records.en: That is what it felt like she would.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he has the feeling she might appear. The English leaves 'would' without the verb phrase it substitutes and uses an opaque deictic frame.
records.remedy: I couldn't shake the feeling that she might.

highlights.text: That is what it felt like she would.

records.jp: 俺もまた、悠長に生きていかねばならない。
records.en: And I myself must absolutely live deliberately.
records.assessment: 悠長 means that he must live unhurriedly or take his time. 'Deliberately' instead means intentionally or carefully.
records.remedy: live at an unhurried pace

highlights.text: live deliberately

records.jp: 急げば、すぐに弾けてしまう。
records.en: If hurried, I would just explode.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that if Taichi rushes through life, he will quickly burst or break. The English passivizes him as though someone else hurries him.
records.remedy: If I rush, I'll burst in no time.

highlights.text: If hurried, I would just explode.

records.jp: 漫画は面白い。
records.en: The manga is funny.
records.assessment: 面白い says that the manga is interesting or entertaining. 'Funny' narrows that evaluation to humor.
records.remedy: entertaining

highlights.text: funny

records.jp: 今はそれが少々こたえる。
records.en: Right now, that takes just a minute amount of toll.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that seeing so many people is somewhat hard on him right now. The English uses an ungrammatical partitive construction and minimizes the burden to a nearly nonexistent quantity.
records.remedy: is somewhat hard on me

highlights.text: takes just a minute amount of toll

records.jp: 「そうなん～♪」
records.en: Taichi: "Strand~ing♪"
comments: It can mean "that's right" with a Kansai ~nan, but see CCA0002: same word as what can happen on these hills/mountains, and we know what that represents I hope. Also, that's the province where the doll town Kounosu is, see CCA0018B. As usual, the truth comes out of his mouth without him being openly aware that it is. -GHS
records.assessment: そうなん is the improvised answering phrase 'that's right' or 'is that so,' sustaining the loose song. The English replaces it with the unrelated lexical item 'stranding.'
records.remedy: That's riiight~♪

highlights.text: Strand~ing

records.jp: ほどよく時間が潰れる。
records.en: Time is wasted with moderation.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the activity kills just the right amount of time. The English moralizes the passing time as waste and uses 'moderation' as an awkward manner adverbial.
records.remedy: It passes just the right amount of time.

highlights.text: Time is wasted with moderation.

records.jp: 部室や図書室から持ってきた本で、たちまち屋上はいっぱいになる。
records.en: Books brought from the club room and the library one by one fill the rooftop to the brim.
comments: See CCC0044, he's beginning to Youko it up it seems. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the books fill the rooftop in no time. The English adds a gradual one-by-one process, contradicting たちまち.
records.remedy: fill the rooftop in no time

highlights.text: one by one fill the rooftop

records.jp: 「……しかし、本当にＳＯＳだったら、もっと効率良い方法っていくらでもあったよなぁ」
records.en: Taichi: "...still, if I were to really send an SOS, there'd lots of more efficient ways to do it."
records.assessment: The existential construction omits 'be,' and the comparative phrase requires 'many' rather than 'lots of.'
records.remedy: there'd be many more efficient ways

highlights.text: there'd lots of more efficient ways

records.jp: 電波がないなら、ハンディ機で場所選んだ方が確実ではやかったろう。
records.en: As there's no EM waves, picking a location for the wireless transceivers would be a safer and faster bet.
comments: See CCD0022A, Misato claims the mountains are a problem. Credibility unknown. Yeah, he COULD just write a book or something, but truth is, few have heard of Romeo Tanaka as it is; if he were an LN writer, that'd be even less so. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that without radio reception, it would have been more reliable and faster to choose a suitable place with a handheld radio. The English claims that electromagnetic waves do not exist, pluralizes the device, and makes its location itself the object being selected.
records.remedy: With no reception, using a handheld radio to find a suitable location would have been faster and more reliable.

highlights.text: As there's no EM waves
picking a location for the wireless transceivers

records.jp: 人など生存していないことに。
records.en: how neither people nor anything has survived.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that no people have survived. The English expands this into the extinction of everything whatsoever.
records.remedy: that no people had survived

highlights.text: neither people nor anything has survived

records.jp: だから結果的には部活は正解で、部活である以上ある程度の無駄を含んでしかるべきなのだった。
records.en: Therefore, as far as results are concerned, club activities are the right choice, and it is appropriate for the club to include a degree of waste higher than the intrinsic.
comments: The problem is, this applies to before the loop exactly as well as it does afterwards. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that, as a club activity, it was only natural for the work to contain some inefficiency. The English invents a comparison to an undefined intrinsic level and leaves 'the intrinsic' without a noun.
records.remedy: some degree of inefficiency was only natural

highlights.text: a degree of waste higher than the intrinsic

records.jp: 気がついたら商店街まで来ていた。
records.en: And when I noticed, I have come all the way to the shopping street.
records.assessment: The Japanese narrates a completed realization in the past. The English combines a past subordinate clause with present perfect in the main clause.
records.remedy: when I noticed, I had come

highlights.text: when I noticed, I have come

records.jp: 夜の散歩者になってしまった。
records.en: I ended up as a night walker.
records.assessment: The Japanese calls Taichi someone out wandering at night. 'Night walker' is not the ordinary expression for this and can carry unrelated occupational or supernatural associations.
records.remedy: a nighttime wanderer

highlights.text: a night walker

records.jp: 「帰ろう」
records.en: Taichi: "Wanna go home."
records.assessment: Taichi resolves or proposes to go home. The English turns that volition into a statement of desire or a question addressed to another person.
records.remedy: Time to go home.

highlights.text: Wanna go home.

records.jp: かけ回って疲れた。
records.en: I was tired of running around.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that running around made him physically tired. 'Tired of' instead means bored, annoyed, or unwilling to continue.
records.remedy: tired from running around

highlights.text: tired of running around

records.jp: 自分に挨拶。
records.en: A salute to myself.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi directs the ordinary bedtime greeting to himself. 'Salute' adds a formal or military gesture.
records.remedy: A greeting to myself.

highlights.text: A salute to myself.

records.jp: 色とりどりの屋根に押しつぶされた無数の日常。
records.en: on countless daily existences squished down under an infinite variety of roofs.
records.assessment: The Japanese evokes countless ordinary lives crushed beneath roofs of many colors. The English converts 'countless' into an infinite variety of roofs and calques 日常 as the unnatural 'daily existences.'
records.remedy: countless ordinary lives crushed beneath multicolored roofs

highlights.text: daily existences squished down under an infinite variety of roofs

records.jp: そして山々。あるいは海。
records.en: And then at the mountains. At times at the sea.
records.assessment: The Japanese appends the mountains, or perhaps the sea, to the visible world. The English inserts prepositions without governing verbs and mistranslates あるいは 'or' as the temporal phrase 'at times.'
records.remedy: And the mountains. Or perhaps the sea.

highlights.text: And then at the mountains. At times at the sea.

records.jp: その先にどんな光景が続くのか、想像できなくなっている。
records.en: What scenes could be perduring beyond those I could not even imagine.
comments: It's heaven out there. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he has lost the ability to imagine what scenery continues beyond them. The English uses the obscure and ill-fitting verb 'perduring' and fails to form a grammatical embedded question.
records.remedy: I could no longer imagine what scenery lay beyond them.

highlights.text: What scenes could be perduring beyond those I could not even imagine.

records.jp: たまにくりだした『都会』の息吹。
records.en: On occasion, the City would dispatch its feeling, its very breath.
comments: Heaven, occasionally, farts in his general direction. Hmmm, I'm not sure if that's the best way of putting it. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese refers to the feel or breath of the city into which Taichi occasionally ventured. The English makes the city the agent that dispatches an abstract feeling outward.
records.remedy: The breath of the 'city' I occasionally ventured into.

highlights.text: the City would dispatch its feeling, its very breath

records.jp: 忘れかけて、薄らいで。
records.en: I had begun to forget it, so faint it was.
records.assessment: The Japanese coordinates the city memory being half forgotten and fading. The English changes the fading into the cause of his forgetting and presents it as a completed state.
records.remedy: I was beginning to forget it as it faded.

highlights.text: so faint it was

records.jp: きっと、芯となる思いがないからで。
records.en: Because it had no desire to become the core of this, definitely.
comments: Seems to mean 'to expand into a big city' (AKA "to become a fallen world for humans to live in") -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi infers that the memory fades because he himself lacks a central sustaining feeling. The English assigns desire to the memory and says that it does not wish to become the core of an unspecified thing.
records.remedy: Probably because I had no feeling at my core to sustain it.

highlights.text: it had no desire to become the core of this

records.jp: 俺の目は、いつだって人に据えられていたのだと、わかる。
records.en: And with these eyes I have, stared at by people at any time, anywhere, I knew.
comments: Hair??? -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi realizes that his own eyes have always been fixed on people. The English reverses viewer and viewed so that people stare at his eyes, adds 'anywhere,' and leaves the realization without a grammatical object.
records.remedy: I realized that my eyes had always been fixed on people.

highlights.text: with these eyes I have, stared at by people at any time, anywhere

records.jp: どんな生き物だってそうだ。
records.en: Any living creature could be said to be that,
records.assessment: The Japanese states directly that every living creature is essentially alone. The English weakens the claim into a tentative possibility of saying so.
records.remedy: Every living creature is the same.

highlights.text: could be said to be that

records.jp: けど、それを自覚するのは人だけで。
records.en: but to be aware of it is only for people.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that only humans are aware of that isolation. The English calques the exclusivity construction into an unnatural predicate.
records.remedy: only humans are aware of it

highlights.text: to be aware of it is only for people

records.jp: それでも学校には行かないと。
records.en: And yet, if I don't go to school...
records.assessment: The Japanese says that despite his sleep deprivation, he still has to go to school. The English turns the obligation into an incomplete negative conditional.
records.remedy: Even so, I have to go to school.

highlights.text: if I don't go to school...

records.jp: ここで自堕落になってしまうと、あとがつらい。
records.en: If I end up dissolute here, later on it will be painful.
records.assessment: 自堕落になる means letting oneself go or becoming idle and undisciplined. 'Dissolute' adds strong moral implications of vice or sexual excess.
records.remedy: let myself go

highlights.text: end up dissolute

records.jp: 孤独について付け加えるなら。
records.en: It will become an additional burden on solitude.
records.assessment: The Japanese is a transition meaning 'to add something about loneliness.' The English instead predicts that an unspecified thing will burden solitude itself.
records.remedy: To add something about loneliness:

highlights.text: It will become an additional burden on solitude.

records.jp: 人はいつだって周囲に、他者の圧力を感じている。
records.en: At any time, at any moment, people feel the pressure of those others around them.
records.assessment: The Japanese uses one ordinary adverb meaning 'always.' The English duplicates the same temporal meaning in two adjacent phrases.
records.remedy: People always

highlights.text: At any time, at any moment

records.jp: 抑圧が過ぎれば心が歪む。
records.en: If that restraint is excessive, the heart distorts.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that excessive repression makes the heart become warped. The English uses 'distort' intransitively as though the heart performs the distortion.
