records.remedy: the heart becomes warped

highlights.text: the heart distorts

records.jp: けどそんな濃度を持った自分などいない。
records.en: But no self can exist that has that kind of density.
records.assessment: Taichi says that he does not possess a self concentrated enough to remain coherent under infinite diffusion. The English turns this personal limitation into a universal claim that no such self can exist.
records.remedy: But I don't have a self with that kind of density.

highlights.text: no self can exist that has that kind of density

records.jp: 世界と同化した自分。
records.en: a self that has assimilated with the world.
comments: I can imagine at least a couple of variants, and so could Tanaka. This is naturally troll. -GHS
records.assessment: 同化する here means merging into or becoming one with the world. 'Assimilate with' is nonidiomatic and can imply cultural adaptation rather than dissolution into the world.
records.remedy: merged into the world

highlights.text: assimilated with the world

records.jp: 世界と等しくなった自分は、己が中心に置いてきたちっぽけな肉体を、忘れてしまわないか？
records.en: Wouldn't it end up forgotten, that tiny little physical body that is deposited in the very center of a self that has become equal with the world?
comments: This explains the Cross World psychologically. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese asks whether the self, expanded to equal the world, would forget the tiny body it had placed at its own center. The English makes the body passively forgotten, describes it as deposited inside the self, and obscures who performs both actions.
records.remedy: Wouldn't a self as vast as the world forget the tiny body it once placed at its center?

highlights.text: Wouldn't it end up forgotten
that is deposited in the very center of a self

records.jp: そもそも、どうして心なんてものが、人に宿ったのだろう―――
records.en: But to begin with, why is this thing, this heart, even dwelling inside of people---
comments: Dun dun DUNNN -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese wonders why hearts ever came to dwell in people. The English changes the question of origin into a present-progressive state and uses an intrusive apposition.
records.remedy: why did anything like a heart ever come to dwell in people

highlights.text: why is this thing, this heart, even dwelling inside of people

records.jp: こころがいたい。
records.en: Heart hurts.
records.assessment: The Japanese refers to Taichi's own heart. The English omits the possessive determiner required by the singular count noun.
records.remedy: My heart hurts.

highlights.text: Heart hurts.

records.jp: かつてはびっくり箱だったのに。
records.en: When it was once a jack-in-the-box.
comments: Something you wind up and wind up, and then out comes, perhaps surprising you, perhaps looking creepy, but otherwise completely harmless. Another metaphor for the truth about Taichi. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese contrasts the empty box now with what had once been a jack-in-the-box. The English begins a subordinate 'when' clause but provides no governing main clause.
records.remedy: Even though it used to be a jack-in-the-box.

highlights.text: When it was once a jack-in-the-box.

records.jp: むしろ恐い。
records.en: Or rather of fear.
comments: These are both heart and school (was that necessary to add yes it was yes it was). -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the emptiness is, if anything, frightening. The English attaches 'of fear' to the preceding box as an incomplete noun phrase.
records.remedy: If anything, it was frightening.

highlights.text: Or rather of fear.

records.jp: そんな感じだ。
records.en: That's what it felt.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that this is how it feels to Taichi. The English omits the complement 'like' and shifts the present reflection into past tense.
records.remedy: That's how it feels.

highlights.text: That's what it felt.

records.jp: だって以前は、触れれば手応えのある、近しい誰かがいたのだから。
records.en: When before there was someone close, someone close who would respond when touched.
records.assessment: The Japanese explains that there used to be someone close whose presence gave a tangible response whenever he reached out. The English starts an ungoverned 'when' clause and needlessly repeats 'someone close.'
records.remedy: After all, there used to be someone close who responded whenever I reached out.

highlights.text: When before there was someone close, someone close who would respond when touched.

records.jp: 無理して入った。
records.en: I discarded reason and went inside.
records.assessment: 無理して means that Taichi forced or pushed himself to enter. The English invents the stronger philosophical act of abandoning reason.
records.remedy: I forced myself to go inside.

highlights.text: I discarded reason

records.jp: 声が出にくい。
records.en: Vocalizing is hard.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that his voice is difficult to get out. 'Vocalizing' is an abstract technical activity and loses the immediate bodily difficulty.
records.remedy: It's hard to get my voice out.

highlights.text: Vocalizing is hard.

records.jp: 言葉を構築しにくい。
records.en: Construction of language is hard.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that forming words is difficult for him. 'Construction of language' instead suggests creating an entire linguistic system.
records.remedy: It's hard to form words.

highlights.text: Construction of language is hard.

records.jp: だめだ、掠れる。
records.en: That's bad, I got hoarse.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that his attempted voice is coming out hoarse or cracking now. The English makes Taichi as a person become hoarse in a completed past event.
records.remedy: My voice keeps coming out hoarse.

highlights.text: I got hoarse.

records.jp: だから主観記述によってどこまでも喜怒哀楽。
records.en: Therefore, there's always emotion to be found in subjective descriptors.
comments: Here Umineko enters in its Core arcs. -GHSoHelpful
records.assessment: The Japanese says that subjective description permits the full range of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure to any extent. The English reduces that range and freedom to a generic observation that some emotion is always present in descriptive labels.
records.remedy: With subjective narration, I can express joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure without limit.

highlights.text: there's always emotion to be found in subjective descriptors

records.en: (lol)
comments: I wanted smileys but GUESS WHAT. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese uses the parenthetical stage direction or emotion tag '(laugh).' The English converts it into internet-chat slang.
records.remedy: (laugh)

highlights.text: (lol)

records.jp: あー、よくわかる、それ。
records.en: Ahhh, I get it well that one.
records.assessment: The Japanese colloquial phrase means that he understands that feeling well. The English follows Japanese adverb order into an ungrammatical construction.
records.remedy: I understand that one perfectly.

highlights.text: I get it well that one.

records.jp: 微妙にチュートン騎士みたいだな。
records.en: Subtly like the Teutonic Knights, innit.
comments: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teutonic_Knights -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese casual tag is an ordinary reflective だな. The English assigns Taichi a conspicuously British dialect marker unsupported by his source voice.
records.remedy: in a way

highlights.text: innit

records.jp: 気合いで髪の色素も抜けたし。
records.en: The pigment in my hair was lost via yelling.
comments: See CCA0013, CCC0011C. Further evidence. -GHS
records.assessment: 気合い means force of will, fighting spirit, or sheer intensity. The English changes that force into the physical act of yelling.
records.remedy: through sheer force of will

highlights.text: via yelling

records.jp: 俺の内部にある殺人技術も一週間ほどで完成したしね。
records.en: The skills of a killer that exist inside of me were also constructed in the span of a week.
comments: This is likely how long it passed from the contract to the deed. Then again, if it was enough for God... -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the murder techniques within him were perfected in about a week. The English changes techniques for killing into abilities possessed by a generic killer, uses the awkward location 'inside of me,' and says skills were constructed rather than completed.
records.remedy: The murder techniques within me were perfected in about a week.

highlights.text: The skills of a killer that exist inside of me were also constructed

records.jp: オークニーの新石器時代の中心地に至ってはオークニーノシンセッキジダイノチュウシンチっていうリュウグウノツカイ的な。
records.en: And as for the Heart of Neolithic Orkney, that sounds very much like a giant oarfish saying he art of Neoli the Corkney.
comments: Really weird line. Adapted the joke to another erroneous kana splitting, should at least sound equally bizarre and the point doesn't seem to be in the letter anyway. If there's any, it's how the oarfish is the King of Herrings; I strongly suspect Tanaka is implying this is a very big, and very red one. http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_of_Neolithic_Orkney - no relation between it and oarfishes that I can find.

Except! One of the most famous ruins of neolithic orkney is Skara Brae, which featured in both The Bard's Tale and Ultima, both classic RPGs. One of the developers of both also worked on Wizardry, which was so popular in Japan it had Japan-only sequels and inspired the author of Dragon Quest. Reaching, but only so much given how much Taichi seems to be into this. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese joke treats the uninterrupted Japanese title 'Heart of Neolithic Orkney' as though it were the long species name of an oarfish-like creature. The English instead makes a giant oarfish speak a garbled phrase and introduces unrelated word fragments.
records.remedy: Render the title as a comically uninterrupted creature name, in parallel with 'oarfish.'

highlights.text: sounds very much like a giant oarfish saying he art of Neoli the Corkney

records.jp: 行って、今日も圧倒的な全能感に包まれてやるぞ。
records.en: I'll go, and just watch me getting enveloped by an overwhelming feeling of omnipotence even today!
records.assessment: The Japanese expresses Taichi's forceful intention to go and bask in the feeling again. The English combines imperative 'watch' with a gerund where a finite future construction is required.
records.remedy: I'll go bask in that overwhelming sense of omnipotence again today.

highlights.text: just watch me getting enveloped

records.jp: 友貴との記憶はいくらでもある。
records.en: I still have a number of memories with Tomoki.
records.assessment: いくらでも emphasizes that he has endlessly many or as many memories as he could want. 'A number of' merely means an unspecified quantity and loses the abundance.
records.remedy: countless memories

highlights.text: a number of memories

records.jp: ふたりは、桜庭を入れた三人は、いつだって楽しかったシステムを備えていたのでしたよ（†）
records.en: The two of us, and with Sakuraba that'd be the three of us, we had readied a SIStem to have fun wherever and whenever! (†)
comments: Even closer to Tower of Friends now. Given it's Tomoki, it's likely that the "system" refers to the System Component/Siscon joke. I put it in with the same gusto as some bizarrely giant vaguely dildo-shaped household item goes into the pussy of a loli in a dark nukige. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the pair, or trio with Sakuraba, had a system that always made things fun. The English changes possession into deliberate preparation, adds 'wherever,' and inserts unexplained internal capitalization into 'system.'
records.remedy: we had a system that made things fun whenever we were together

highlights.text: readied a SIStem to have fun wherever and whenever

records.jp: 『それ』が爆発しそうになった。
records.en: Seemed "it" was close to exploding.
records.assessment: The English finite clause omits the dummy subject required before 'seemed.'
records.remedy: It seemed "it" was close to exploding.

highlights.text: Seemed "it" was close to exploding.

records.jp: ごちそうさま。
records.en: A most delicious meal.
records.assessment: ごちそうさま is the conventional expression spoken after finishing a meal, here used metaphorically after swallowing. The English replaces the speech act with a formal evaluation that the meal was delicious.
records.remedy: Thanks for the meal.

highlights.text: A most delicious meal.

records.jp: 俺の内部にあるものは、底にずっしり横たわって出てこない。
records.en: What exists on my inside lays heavily on the bottom and doesn't come out.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that what is inside him lies heavily at the bottom. The English uses the nonidiomatic location 'on my inside' and the transitive verb 'lays' without an object.
records.remedy: What is inside me lies heavily at the bottom

highlights.text: What exists on my inside lays heavily on the bottom

records.jp: 舐・め・す・ぎ。
records.en: Taken! Too! Light! Ly!
comments: I'm so lucky with syllabification. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese emphatically syllabifies the accusation that he has taken the work far too lightly. The English shifts into a passive past participle, splits 'lightly' at a false morphological boundary, and never identifies what was underestimated.
records.remedy: Way! Too! Com! Pla! Cent!

highlights.text: Taken! Too! Light! Ly!

records.jp: 新人キャンペーンの一環として。
records.en: First part of our Newman Movement.
comments: Sounds oddly Nietzscheian, but that's it. -GHS
records.assessment: 新人キャンペーン is a campaign or initiative for a newcomer. The English invents the proper name 'Newman Movement,' introducing both an unrelated surname and a larger organized movement.
records.remedy: newcomer campaign

highlights.text: Newman Movement

records.jp: 五分後、細々としたことを考えるのがイヤになってやめた。
records.en: Five minutes later, I was thinking about all and sundry and it started leaving a bad taste in my mouth so I stopped.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that after five minutes he became sick of thinking through all the little details and stopped working. The English changes details into miscellaneous people or things and invents a gustatory bad-taste reaction.
records.remedy: Five minutes later, I got sick of thinking through all the little details and quit.

highlights.text: I was thinking about all and sundry and it started leaving a bad taste in my mouth

records.jp: 大丈夫。二巻がある。
records.en: It's alright. There are two acts.
records.assessment: The joke pivots from 一環, one component, to the homophonically patterned 二巻, volume two. 'Two acts' is neither volume two nor a useful sound-based partner for the preceding 'first part.'
records.remedy: There's always volume two.

highlights.text: There are two acts.

records.jp: 一環が終わっても、二巻がある。
records.en: Once the first part ends, there's the second act.
records.assessment: The source deliberately jumps from 'one component' to 'volume two' on the shared sound of the counters. The English makes a normal, semantically connected progression from a first part to a second act, erasing the mistake that prompts the next line.
records.remedy: Even when one part ends, there's volume two.

highlights.text: Once the first part ends, there's the second act.

records.jp: おや？
records.en: Mother of---?
comments: As random as it has always been. -GHS
records.assessment: おや is a mild realization equivalent to 'huh?' or 'wait.' The English invents the beginning of an English curse.
records.remedy: Wait...?

highlights.text: Mother of---?

records.jp: 一環と二巻って繋がってないじゃないか。
records.en: "First part" and "second act" aren't connected are they not.
comments: PCP CCC3004
records.assessment: The Japanese notices that 'one component' and 'volume two' only sound connected while denoting unrelated things. The chosen English terms are in fact semantically connected, and the negative tag is ungrammatical.
records.remedy: Wait, 'one part' and 'volume two' have nothing to do with each other.

highlights.text: "First part" and "second act" aren't connected are they not.

records.jp: 動くもののない世界きつい。なんか出ろ。
records.en: A world without nothing moving kills my heart. Happen, something!
records.assessment: The Japanese complains that a world with nothing moving is unbearable and demands that something appear. The English double negative implies that something is moving and forms the demand with reversed, ungrammatical word order.
records.remedy: A world with nothing moving is unbearable. Come on, something appear!

highlights.text: A world without nothing moving
Happen, something!

records.jp: ゲットできないからな。
records.en: Because I can't perform a GET on it.
comments: "Sure. WALK to the sun." -GHS
records.assessment: ゲットできない uses casual loanword language for being unable to obtain or catch it. The English invents the execution of an uppercase technical operation.
records.remedy: get hold of it

highlights.text: perform a GET on it

records.jp: もっとガーンと行って欲しい。
records.en: I wish something'd happen that was much more like 'dun-dun-dunnn'.
records.assessment: ガーンと asks for a much more forceful, explosive impact. The English converts that impact into a musical dramatic-sting sound effect.
records.remedy: go out with a much bigger bang

highlights.text: like 'dun-dun-dunnn'

records.jp: 確か桜庭が。
records.en: I'm sure Sakuraba has.
comments: Pun with 白色矮性, "white dwarfism"? Taichi's the White/Silver one of the duo. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese fragment means 'if I remember right, Sakuraba...' as Taichi recalls the source of the next verbal chain. The English supplies an unsupported perfect auxiliary with no recoverable verb phrase.
records.remedy: If I remember right, Sakuraba once...

highlights.text: I'm sure Sakuraba has.

records.jp: 役不足を感じた確信犯が的を得たのだろうか。
records.en: Would the premeditated crime of feeling above the role hit the target?
comments: Laterally 'fit the bill', but it connects to below. It also refers to the sun, see CCC3022 where he uses the same word. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese deliberately chains conventionally misused expressions, with a 'conviction offender' as the person who feels a role is beneath him and hits a target. The English makes a crime itself the agent and substitutes 'premeditated crime' for the person denoted by 確信犯.
records.remedy: Did the conviction offender who felt the role was beneath him hit the mark?

highlights.text: the premeditated crime of feeling above the role

records.jp: 与えられたフィールドに不満がある思想犯がアーチェリーに使われる的を手に入れた。
records.en: Those white-collar criminals guilty of being unsatisfied with their given fields merely acquire targets for archery use.
comments: See CCC3022 - mess with Kiri, get crossbow'd. More interesting is that this is a definition of 違和感 which I've kept as "sense of physical discomfort". If SPD is all but a chuuni warning signal, then it would come from a dissatisfaction of this sort. -GHS
records.assessment: 思想犯 means an ideological or thought criminal. The English changes the offense to financially motivated white-collar crime, pluralizes the person, and thereby breaks the continuing verbal chain.
records.remedy: The thought criminal dissatisfied with his assigned field obtained an archery target.

highlights.text: Those white-collar criminals

records.jp: 俺を見てくれ。
records.en: Look at me please.
comments: PCP CCA0002
And there we go again. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese imperative asks to be looked at without a politeness marker. The English adds 'please,' softening the abrupt demand.
records.remedy: Look at me.

highlights.text: please

records.jp: 架空の枝を地面に引き寄せる力……引く力だ！
records.en: The power that draws the Air branch towards the ground... it's Pulling Power!
comments: 引く力 was only ever used in CCA0002 -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese calls the branch imaginary and then identifies the force drawing it toward the ground as an attractive force. The English changes 'imaginary' into 'Air' and invents a capitalized superhero-like name.
records.remedy: The force drawing the imaginary branch toward the ground... attraction!

highlights.text: Air branch
it's Pulling Power!

records.jp: フェンスは工業用の巨大ペンチみたいので破壊した。
records.en: The fence was wrecked as if by a pair of gigantic industrial-use pliers.
comments: That's what he just did as he goes to try to kill himself of course. Odd he wouldn't use the weak spot - but does it even exist? The pliers are what Tomoki uses to wreck the antenna so there's a pair in the prefab, see CCD1001 (they're just 'large' but here = chuunidenpa). -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi actually broke the fence with something like enormous industrial pliers. 'As if by' instead makes the pliers merely a visual comparison and removes the tool used.
records.remedy: with something like a gigantic pair of industrial pliers

highlights.text: as if by a pair of gigantic industrial-use pliers

records.jp: 引力と名付けた！
records.en: I shall name you Attractive Force... no, because this matter is most grave, Gravity!
comments: Pun seems a little more obvious in Japanese, though perhaps not to this extent. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says only that he named the force 引力, attraction or gravity. The English invents a revision from one English name to another and adds an extended grave/gravity pun.
records.remedy: I named it gravity!

highlights.text: Attractive Force... no, because this matter is most grave, Gravity!

records.jp: シナプス跳躍をして。
records.en: taking the synaptic jump.
comments: A real thing? http://wiki.answers.com/Q/How_does_a_message_jump_across_the_synaptic_gap_and_passes_to_the_next_neuron though this still seems to be about how he's about to jump down. And he's likely still there when he starts hallucinating all the next stuff! -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese depicts words leaping across synapses. The English turns the action into taking one definite object called 'the synaptic jump.'
records.remedy: leaping from synapse to synapse

highlights.text: taking the synaptic jump

records.jp: 出会い別れそして再会という感動を挟む余地無し。
records.en: leaving no space for the interposing the deep emotions of meeting and parting and then reuniting.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that there is no room to insert the moving sequence of meeting, separation, and reunion. The English combines 'for' with the gerund's object in an ungrammatical construction.
records.remedy: no room to interpose the moving sequence

highlights.text: no space for the interposing the deep emotions

records.jp: 俺がしろしめしたいのは＊＊＊＊＊＊＊＊＊。
records.en: What I wanna know is how to ru*********.
comments: "To know" + "to rule", splitting the difference because Take Over The World -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese completely censors the object after 'what I want to rule.' The English exposes an uncensored semantic lead-in inside the asterisks and therefore weakens the source's total redaction.
records.remedy: Censor the entire redacted expression after 'what I want.'

highlights.text: how to ru

records.jp: そして倒した。
records.en: And then she's defeated.
comments: Killed? See CCA0019 - same term, and as Tomoki says, not that kind of 'fainted'. This reminds me sooo much of the true best VN ever written, Atashinoriri. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi then defeated her. The English removes him as agent and shifts the completed action into a present-state passive.
records.remedy: And then I defeated her.

highlights.text: she's defeated

records.jp: じくり、と心が疼く。
records.en: Squeak, and my heart aches like a living thing left out in the freezing winter.
comments: PCP CCB2012 for the same reason of 冬子 vs 疼. Jikuri doesn't seem to be a known SFX, or anything at all, except... 軸力/axial tension? -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese describes a slow, focused throb of pain in his heart. The English invents a squeaking sound and an elaborate image of a living creature abandoned in winter.
records.remedy: My heart throbbed with a slow ache.

highlights.text: Squeak
like a living thing left out in the freezing winter

records.jp: 口説き抜く。
records.en: Woo continuously.
records.assessment: 口説き抜く means carrying the attempt through to the end and winning the person over, not merely wooing for an unspecified continuous duration.
records.remedy: I woo her to the bitter end.

highlights.text: Woo continuously.

records.jp: 高らかに口説きあげる。
records.en: Raising the loudness of the wooing.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi loudly or triumphantly talks Kiri up. The English turns the action into an abstract increase in the volume level of 'the wooing.'
records.remedy: I woo her at the top of my lungs.

highlights.text: Raising the loudness of the wooing.

records.jp: 申し分のないナンパ。
records.en: Uncriticizable Nanpa.
comments: Let's go with the tech term. See CCA0008. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese calls it flawless pickup or flirting. 'Uncriticizable' is unnatural evaluative English, and leaving nanpa as a capitalized unexplained loanword obscures the action.
records.remedy: Flawless pickup artistry.

highlights.text: Uncriticizable Nanpa.

records.jp: しかし色よい返事はもらえない。
records.en: But a favorable response in good color I don't get.
comments: Just means favorable response, but also literal because she went white and, most importantly, bled. Interesting he considers this just him hitting on her; that's very likely not incorrect, given what The Great Pattern means to him. -GHS
records.assessment: 色よい返事 is an idiom for a favorable answer. The English translates the color component literally and follows Japanese word order into an ungrammatical inversion.
records.remedy: But I get no favorable answer.

highlights.text: a favorable response in good color I don't get

records.jp: 悔いる。
records.en: Regret.
records.assessment: The Japanese is a finite action: Taichi regrets it. The English turns it into a bare abstract noun.
records.remedy: I regret it.

highlights.text: Regret.

records.jp: 畜生、畜生！
records.en: Fuck, fuck!
records.assessment: 畜生 is a frustrated 'damn it' here. The English escalates the exclamation to the strongest ordinary English profanity without additional source support.
records.remedy: Damn it, damn it!

highlights.text: Fuck, fuck!

records.jp: やらずに後悔するより、やって後悔すべきなのに！
records.en: When it ought be better to regret doing than to regret not doing!
records.assessment: The Japanese says that one should regret acting rather than regret never acting. The English begins with an ungoverned 'when' clause and omits 'to' after 'ought.'
records.remedy: I ought to regret doing it rather than regret not doing it!

highlights.text: When it ought be better

records.jp: 一人じゃ調整できないよ。
records.en: I just can't get adjusted to being alone, you know.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the required adjustment or coordination cannot be performed by one person alone. The English instead says that Taichi cannot psychologically acclimate to solitude.
records.remedy: I can't make the adjustment by myself.

highlights.text: get adjusted to being alone

records.jp: さあ霧、オラの気持ちに応えてくれ！
records.en: Well, Kiri, have a response to me's feelings!
comments: See CCA0030, Sakuraba, same "ora". -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese asks Kiri to respond to Taichi's feelings. The English uses 'me's' as an impossible possessive and the nonidiomatic collocation 'have a response to.'
records.remedy: answer my feelings

highlights.text: have a response to me's feelings

records.jp: モノローグを駆使して俺は告った。
records.en: So I proclaimed while freely making use of monologue.
records.assessment: 告る is colloquial slang for confessing romantic feelings. 'Proclaimed' omits the romantic object and loses the slang distinction discussed immediately afterward.
records.remedy: I confessed my feelings

highlights.text: I proclaimed

records.jp: 実は告るって言葉嫌いだった。
records.en: Truth is, I hated the word 'proclaim'.
comments: Hence why I had to translate it so specifically alll the way through. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi says that he dislikes the slang verb kokuru, 'confess one's love.' The English names a different ordinary English verb, breaking the metalinguistic link to the preceding line.
records.remedy: the word 'confess'

highlights.text: the word 'proclaim'

records.jp: ギャランドゥがいい。
records.en:
>   happy trail
Gyarandou is nice.
comments: http://oshiete.goo.ne.jp/qa/1788928.html Not to be confused with Gal Undo, which is a fighting game Cancel Move where you travel back in time and kill the parents of the guy you're fighting, so you automatically win the match. -GHS
records.assessment: The English supplies a gloss but romanizes ギャランドゥ with an ad hoc ou ending. Standard Hepburn gives Gyarandū; if a documented Latin-script brand form is intended, that evidence must be recorded separately.
records.remedy: Gyarandū

highlights.text: Gyarandou

records.jp: モノローグを駆使して俺はギャランドゥ。
records.en: So I gyarandou'd while freely making use of monologue.
comments: Reflects above. -GHS
records.assessment: The improvised verb is built from a non-Hepburn romanization and then given an English apostrophe-d suffix. Standard Hepburn would retain the long vowel as Gyarandū before any functional wordplay solution.
records.remedy: Gyarandū'd

highlights.text: gyarandou'd

records.jp: イカしてる。
records.en: Daaaymn I'm so awesome.
comments: Seems to be just an old-fashioned term. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the newly coined expression is cool. The English makes Taichi praise himself personally, adds a curse, and greatly expands the line.
records.remedy: That's cool.

highlights.text: Daaaymn I'm so awesome.

records.jp: ギャラクシーって銀河っぽい単語と語感が似てるのもいい。
records.en: I like how it resembles the impact of the galaxy-like word Gyarak'shi too.
comments: TRANSLINGUALISM IS ABOUT TO E-X-P-L-O-D-E. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Gyarandū has a pleasant phonetic resemblance to gyarakushī, 'galaxy.' The English changes sound into impact and supplies a malformed pseudo-romanization rather than standard Hepburn.
records.remedy: I also like how Gyarandū sounds a little like gyarakushī, 'galaxy.'

highlights.text: resembles the impact
Gyarak'shi

records.jp: で、霧、どうなの？
records.en: So, Kiri, how about, 'K?
comments: TL NOTE: K means の means no wait what the FUUUUU-GHS
records.assessment: Taichi simply asks Kiri what she thinks. The English appends an unexplained apostrophe-K fragment that is absent from the Japanese wordplay sequence.
records.remedy: So, Kiri, what do you think?

highlights.text: 'K

records.jp: 霧は真剣に言った。
records.en: Kiri said with an edge that wasn't of a wooden sword:
comments: Kiri's about sharp knives, and see CCC4014 where she's a wooden log (due to :reasons:). More contrast this way. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says only that Kiri spoke seriously. The English invents an elaborate sword-edge contrast unrelated to the line.
records.remedy: Kiri answered seriously:

highlights.text: with an edge that wasn't of a wooden sword

records.jp: 手榴弾が爆発しました。
records.en: The flashbang had exploded.
comments: That's likely the SFX it actually had. -GHS
records.assessment: 手榴弾 is a hand grenade. A flashbang is a distinct non-fragmentation stun device.
records.remedy: hand grenade

highlights.text: flashbang

records.jp: 俺たちは死んだ。
records.en: We had died.
records.assessment: The Japanese simple past states that the two died as the immediate result. The English past perfect incorrectly places that death before another past reference point.
records.remedy: We died.

highlights.text: We had died.

records.jp: ウォーロック・モーロックの邪悪な計画を阻止するには、パラグラフの１に戻って冒険をやり直さなければならない。あなたの次なる冒険に、女神のじゅうぶんな加護があらんことを―――
records.en: To foil the evil plan of the Warlock Morlock, you must return to Paragraph 1 and redo your adventure from the beginning.
records.assessment: The Japanese continues with a full conventional benediction wishing the reader ample protection from the goddess on the next adventure. The English omits that entire closing sentence.
records.remedy: Add the omitted closing wish for the next adventure.

highlights.text: To foil the evil plan of the Warlock Morlock, you must return to Paragraph 1 and redo your adventure from the beginning.

records.jp: おおっと、いました！
records.en: Ohmmmy, she was here!
comments: These few sorta-formal. Very odd. -GHS
records.assessment: おおっと marks a mock-presenter's sudden discovery: 'whoa, there she is.' The English invents a stretched 'oh my' and changes immediate sight into a past statement.
records.remedy: Whoa, there she is!

highlights.text: Ohmmmy, she was here!

records.jp: さすが正式な訓練を受けた市原です。
records.en: Naught else may be expected from one who received formal Ichihara training.
comments: See CCC3019A. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese attributes the feat to formally trained Ichihara herself. The English turns her family name into a type or school of training that some unnamed person received.
records.remedy: Just what you'd expect from the formally trained Ichihara.

highlights.text: one who received formal Ichihara training

records.jp: 異質です。
records.en: It is heterogeneous.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that she is qualitatively alien or different from ordinary people. 'Heterogeneous' is a technical property of a mixture and is not an idiomatic description of a person.
records.remedy: She's fundamentally different.

highlights.text: It is heterogeneous.

records.jp: えーと、ごっつ優秀すぎるって感じで異質です。
records.en: Uhmmm, it is heterogeneous due to feeling like extra-super competent.
comments: Osaka-ben, going with slight off-tone -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese explains that her difference lies in being far too extraordinarily capable. The English retains the inapplicable technical adjective and uses a malformed causal phrase ending in 'competent.'
records.remedy: She's different because she is simply far too capable.

highlights.text: heterogeneous due to feeling like extra-super competent

records.jp: 失敗がない人間って、どうなんでしょう？
records.en: What does one do about humans that have no failings?
records.assessment: Taichi wonders what one should make of a person who never fails. The English instead asks what action should be taken regarding multiple humans without character flaws.
records.remedy: What are we supposed to make of someone who never fails?

highlights.text: What does one do about humans that have no failings?

records.jp: そりゃほとんどアータ！　ホーリーウッドの一時間四十五分時点の主人公の性能ですよ。
records.en: That is almost like an ah'tress! That is the performance of a Holywood protagonist at the one hour, forty-five minutes mark!
comments: Now this is odd. The terms should be "actor" and "hollywood", but the transliteratearearezddfweasdings are off - in the case of "aata", which should be 'akuta', waaay off. And Hollywood written like that gives me just http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Holywood which is... hmmm. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese mock address アータ is not 'actress,' while the following reference is to a Hollywood protagonist. The English invents an eye-dialect occupation and misspells Hollywood.
records.remedy: Why, that's practically the performance of a Hollywood protagonist

highlights.text: ah'tress
Holywood

records.jp: ラスト十分前が一番性能が高いわけですな。
records.en: Before the last ten minutes, their performances are at the absolute highest, indeed.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that a protagonist's abilities peak during the ten minutes before the ending. The English says they peak before that final ten-minute interval begins.
records.remedy: In the final ten minutes

highlights.text: Before the last ten minutes

records.jp: ラスト十分まで昼寝しまくって、最後に超人モードになって敵を倒すストーリー。
records.en: A story where until the last ten minutes he does nothing but take naps, then at the end he goes into Hyperman Mode and defeats the bad guy.
comments: That's your average poorly-written bottom-loaded piece of crap, lots of stuff like it. Guessing troll. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the hero enters a generic superhuman mode. The English invents and capitalizes the proper transformation name 'Hyperman Mode.'
records.remedy: superhuman mode

highlights.text: Hyperman Mode

records.jp: あとまったく脈絡なくもう一つ考えた。
records.en: And then without a damn trace of logical connection I had one more idea:
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the next idea has absolutely no logical connection, without adding a curse.
records.remedy: without any logical connection whatsoever

highlights.text: damn

records.jp: 人類滅亡からはじまるストーリー。
records.en: a story that has its beginning with the Fall of Mankind.
comments: Cross Channel is pre-apocalyptical in the strictest of terms, therefore what's at the start can't be the destruction of mankind. OTOH, this is him chuunin'. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese plainly says that the story begins with humanity's extinction. The English substitutes a capitalized, euphemistic phrase that can mean moral decline rather than annihilation.
records.remedy: the extinction of humanity

highlights.text: the Fall of Mankind

records.jp: これやん。
records.en: That, yah.
records.assessment: The Japanese colloquial exclamation means 'This is it' or 'that's the one.' The English produces an incomplete deictic fragment with an unsupported dialect spelling.
records.remedy: This is it.

highlights.text: That, yah.

records.jp: まさに俺って感じだ。
records.en: Really feels me-ish.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the idea feels exactly like Taichi. The English omits the subject and creates the awkward adjective 'me-ish.'
records.remedy: That feels exactly like me.

highlights.text: Really feels me-ish.

records.jp: そこいらどうなんだろう？
records.en: Well, what do we do about that?
records.assessment: Taichi wonders how that moral comparison should be judged. The English asks what practical action should be taken.
records.remedy: I wonder how that balance works out.

highlights.text: what do we do about that?

records.jp: 俺は問いかけた。
records.en: I asked out.
records.assessment: 問いかける means that Taichi posed the question. 'Asked out' means inviting someone on a date and lacks an object here.
records.remedy: I posed the question.

highlights.text: I asked out.

records.jp: すっげ哲学的。まいった。勝てない。
records.en: Waaay philosophical. Bummer. I can't beat this.
comments: See CCA0015B -GHS
records.assessment: まいった here means that the answer has defeated or outdone him. 'Bummer' instead labels the situation disappointing.
records.remedy: You got me.

highlights.text: Bummer.

records.jp: 大きく出たな。
records.en: A big one came out!
records.assessment: 大きく出た means that Misato made an audacious or grand claim. The English literalizes size and emergence as a large object coming out.
records.remedy: That's a bold claim!

highlights.text: A big one came out!

records.jp: さすがみみみ先輩。
records.en: What else from Mimimi-senpai.
records.assessment: The Japanese means 'just what you'd expect from Mimimi-senpai.' The English omits the verb and uses an opaque rhetorical fragment.
records.remedy: Just what you'd expect from Mimimi-senpai.

highlights.text: What else from Mimimi-senpai.

records.jp: だから大好きというのが本音だ。
records.en: Therefore great love is the true intent here.
comments: Given she was in love with him and very very much from the start, I'd say it's hers, but leaving it ambiguous, as it could be the reading key for CCA0010 - his true intent was getting consoled, not diving into her boobs. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi says frankly that this is why he loves her. The English turns his feeling into the abstract subject 'great love' and his candid admission into an unspecified intent.
records.remedy: That's why I love her, honestly.

highlights.text: Therefore great love is the true intent here.

records.jp: 実は好きでも何でもない。
records.en: Truth is, love's sorta whatever.
records.assessment: The Japanese bluntly retracts the claim: in truth, he does not like her at all. The English instead expresses vague indifference toward love as a concept.
records.remedy: Actually, I don't like her at all.

highlights.text: love's sorta whatever

records.jp: 好きになるって設定上で定めただけだ。
records.en: That we'd fall in love is just something established by the scenario's Settei.
comments: Meta VN/(pre)chuuni. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi says only that the setting defines him as liking her. The English makes the love mutual, invents a scenario as possessor, and leaves 設定 as an unexplained capitalized loanword.
records.remedy: The setting merely says that I'm supposed to like her.

highlights.text: That we'd fall in love
scenario's Settei

records.jp: やさぐれちゃったよ！！
records.en: She's sulking now!!!
records.assessment: The Japanese first-person comic outburst says that Taichi himself has become sullen or cynical. The English assigns the state to a woman.
records.remedy: Now I'm getting bitter!

highlights.text: She's sulking now

records.jp: 超可愛いのになぁ。
records.en: C'mon, but it's Hyper Kawaii...
records.assessment: The Japanese says in colloquial Japanese that the nickname is extremely cute. The English mixes an English intensifier with an unexplained Japanese adjective and capitalizes both.
records.remedy: super cute

highlights.text: Hyper Kawaii

records.jp: 慰めてもらうしか。
records.en: I get nothing but consolation.
comments: And now it's as close to the term constantly used for masturbation as the original is. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi decides that he has no choice but to seek comfort from Miki. The English states that consolation is already the only thing he receives.
records.remedy: I'll have to get Miki to comfort me.

highlights.text: I get nothing but consolation.

records.jp: 多重放送になった俺だ。
records.en: I ended up as a multiplex broadcast.
comments: Indeed, as mentioned above, it's why he carried a remote in CCB2015. This is like leaving the damn chainsaw fuel on Mars... -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese jokes that Taichi's repeated internal voices have become a layered or multiple broadcast. The English says that Taichi himself literally became the broadcast medium.
records.remedy: My voice turned into a multiplex broadcast.

highlights.text: I ended up as a multiplex broadcast.

records.jp: しっかし、すげえサービス精神旺盛な成果物だな。
records.en: Annnd yet, that's one finished delivered product that's chock full of that waaay amazing Service spirit!
comments: Supposing 'fanservice' (see, uhm, panties). This is going double meta. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese calls the work a product overflowing with eagerness to entertain or please. The English stacks redundant production adjectives and capitalizes an awkward calque as though it were a named doctrine.
records.remedy: That's one work packed with an incredible eagerness to please.

highlights.text: finished delivered product
Service spirit

records.jp: アダルト・カテゴリに入れるのか？
records.en: Will it be put in the Adults category?
comments: *checks age rating* 18+. ...WAIT THIS HAS PORN? NOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO I'M TRANSLATING A PORN GAME FROM JAPAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA-GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese refers to the singular adult category. The English uses the plural personal noun 'Adults' as an attributive category name.
records.remedy: adult category

highlights.text: Adults category

records.jp: ただ下着を見るだけの俺になってしまいそうだ。
records.en: It seems I ended up as someone who just looks at panties.
comments: See CCB0007 -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that at this rate Taichi is liable to become such a person. The English says that the transformation already happened and only now appears evident.
records.remedy: It looks as though I'll become

highlights.text: It seems I ended up

records.jp: よしなろう。
records.en: That'd be good thing to be.
records.assessment: The Japanese is Taichi's immediate resolution: 'All right, I'll become one.' The English turns it into a hypothetical evaluation and omits the article before 'good thing.'
records.remedy: All right, I'll become one.

highlights.text: That'd be good thing to be.

records.jp: 俺はおよそ十四時間、下着を凝視した。
records.en: And I, for roughly fourteen hours, fixed a stare on the underwear.
comments: Damn, that's around two hours. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he stared fixedly at the underwear. The English calques the act into the nonidiomatic collocation 'fix a stare on.'
records.remedy: stared fixedly at the underwear

highlights.text: fixed a stare on the underwear

records.jp: グンナイ。
records.en: GUNAI (good night).
records.assessment: The source gives only the stylized phonetic form グンナイ. The English appends an explanatory parenthesis rather than allowing the stylization to function directly.
records.remedy: G'night.

highlights.text: (good night)

records.jp: 部活に精を出す。
records.en: I spurt forth my spirit in the club.
comments: 精を出す (I put my spirit into it)　-> 精液を出す (I ejaculate) -GHS
records.assessment: 精を出す is an idiom meaning to apply oneself diligently. The English turns effort into a bodily emission of spirit and adds sexualized physical imagery.
records.remedy: I throw myself into club work.

highlights.text: I spurt forth my spirit in the club.

records.jp: エッチラオッチラ。
records.en: Laboriously with a lot of sexfort.
comments: ECCHI-raocchira -GHS
records.assessment: エッチラオッチラ is a fixed comic description of laborious effort. The English invents a sex pun and the nonexistent blend 'sexfort.'
records.remedy: Heave-ho, heave-ho.

highlights.text: with a lot of sexfort

records.jp: だめって、何が？
records.en: Can't, what exactly?
records.assessment: Taichi asks what exactly is forbidden. The English copies Japanese ellipsis and word order into an unnatural question.
records.remedy: What exactly can't I do?

highlights.text: Can't, what exactly?

records.jp: 語句の連結が外れてできた言葉の海から、俺は手を伸ばす。
records.en: I stretch my hand out from the ocean of words that had managed to undo the connection with sentences.
comments: See CCC3007. That's what Taichi is lost in contemplation of, except for a radius of about 6-7 people. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese describes a sea of words formed when the connections among phrases came apart. The English makes words intentionally succeed at severing a connection they had 'with sentences' and does not identify the relations among the words themselves.
records.remedy: the sea of words left when the links between phrases came apart

highlights.text: words that had managed to undo the connection with sentences

records.jp: くるりと意識を反転して（たこ焼きのように）現世に戻る。
records.en: Suddenly spinning and covering myself in consciousness (like a takoyaki) I return to the present world.
comments: Seems to refer to how they're cooked. Since we're on the subject, legend has it that the reason the Japanese roast and eat octopus was in memory of the Great Fetish Fire of 2067, which ended the great majority of tentacle porn (and tentacle porn writers, though some historians deny this ever happened because it's yet controversial whether any ever existed). -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi flips his consciousness around like turning a takoyaki and returns to the present world. The English instead makes him spin bodily and wrap himself in consciousness.
records.remedy: I flip my consciousness over (like a takoyaki) and return to the present world.

highlights.text: spinning and covering myself in consciousness

records.jp: 意識が現世を観測してのけた。
records.en: Consciousness wrung to observing the present world.
comments: See CCA0016. Welcome back to Foggy Kamisaka. It still ain't the real world. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that his consciousness successfully managed to observe the present world. The English uses 'wrung' without a coherent object or construction.
records.remedy: My consciousness managed to observe the present world.

highlights.text: Consciousness wrung to observing the present world.

records.jp: 俺は、自ら破壊したフェンスから身を乗り出そうとしていた。
records.en: I had just about begun to lean myself out of the fence that I had wrecked by myself.
comments: Now go back through the VN and find how many imaginary 'branches' there are. Let's start with Mutsumi telling Taichi to sweep Youko's ex-room in CCC3012B. And did he really do all that stuff above after breaking the fence, or was he always here? And did he break the fence or just use the available hole? -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he was about to lean his body out through the opening in the fence. The English uses the transitive reflexive 'lean myself' and treats the fence as a container he is emerging from.
records.remedy: lean out through the opening in the fence

highlights.text: lean myself out of the fence

records.jp: フェンスは扉大にくりぬかれていた。
records.en: The fence had been excavated into door size.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that a door-sized opening had been cut out of the fence. 'Excavated' refers to digging earth or removing buried material, and 'into door size' is ungrammatical.
records.remedy: A door-sized opening had been cut out of the fence.

highlights.text: excavated into door size

records.jp: 俺がやった。その記憶がある。
records.en: My doing. I have the recollections of that.
records.assessment: The Japanese gives two direct assertions: he did it, and he remembers doing it. The English creates a possessive noun fragment and pluralizes memory into formal 'recollections.'
records.remedy: I did it. I remember.

highlights.text: My doing. I have the recollections of that.

records.jp: 記憶するはしからズタズタに分断され、他の言語に混じって判断できなくなっていたんだ。
records.en: No sooner than they had been memorized they had been torn up into tiny pieces and mixed with other languages, that I could no longer decipher them.
comments: See the top, that's why he can't understand the script Sakuraba wrote. And therefore, the real difficulty in understanding all the VN. It's actually easier to do so as a foreigner, paradoxically enough: the less you're bound to the conventions of read Japanese, the easier it is to notice how much Tanaka hides in plain sight. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that memories were shredded even as he formed them and mixed with other language until he could no longer judge them. The English changes remembering into deliberate memorization, pluralizes 'language,' and joins the result with an ungrammatical 'that.'
records.remedy: As soon as I formed a memory, it was torn apart and mixed with other language until I could no longer make sense of it.

highlights.text: No sooner than they had been memorized
mixed with other languages, that

records.jp: ずっと力んでいたせいか。
records.en: Perhaps because they have been gripping all along.
records.assessment: The Japanese attributes the pallor to prolonged straining or tension. The English narrows that cause to the fingertips themselves continuously performing the act of gripping.
records.remedy: Maybe because I had been straining so hard.

highlights.text: because they have been gripping all along

records.jp: 重心を背後に引き戻した。
records.en: I restore my center of gravity to my back.
comments: He was leaning forwards. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi shifts his center of gravity backward to regain safety. The English treats his back as a location to which the center of gravity belongs or returns.
records.remedy: I shift my center of gravity backward.

highlights.text: restore my center of gravity to my back

records.jp: なおフェンスに食い込んでいる指。苦労してはがす。
records.en: Still the fingertips eat down into the fence. I peel off with difficulty.
comments: Because his recovery was automatic. Given everything, this would normally require a memory reset. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that his fingers are still digging into the fence and that he painfully peels them away. The English personifies the fingertips as eating downward and omits the object of 'peel off.'
records.remedy: My fingers are still dug into the fence. I struggle to peel them away.

highlights.text: the fingertips eat down into the fence. I peel off

records.jp: 裏返すと、うっすらと網目状に血が浮いていた。
records.en: When I turn them upside down, blood was surfacing in a reticulate.
records.assessment: When he turns his hands over, faint blood rises in a mesh pattern. The English shifts tense, uses the adjective 'reticulate' as an incomplete count noun, and omits the pattern's visible form.
records.remedy: faint blood had risen in a mesh pattern

highlights.text: blood was surfacing in a reticulate

records.en: Taichi: "I...
records.assessment: The English dialogue opens a quotation mark but never closes it.
records.remedy: Taichi: "I..."

highlights.text: Taichi: "I...

records.jp: 自殺しようとしたことが、信じられない。
records.en: I can't believe it, I was trying to commit suicide.
records.assessment: The English joins two independent clauses with a comma and makes 'it' an unexplained object before restating the actual fact.
records.remedy: I can't believe I was trying

highlights.text: I can't believe it, I was trying

records.jp: たくさん殺して、生きたのだから。
records.en: Because you made a living by killing so much.
comments: The 14(?) at the mansion and possibly all of humanity in the same sense, not the rest. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi tells himself that he killed many and nevertheless lived, which is why he must not die now. The English shifts to second person and turns survival after killing into earning a livelihood through killing.
records.remedy: Because I've killed so many and survived.

highlights.text: you made a living by killing so much

records.jp: 呼んでも、彼女はあらわれない。
records.en: I call her, but the girl does not turn up.
comments: I don't think it was her who yanked him up. This was him on his own power, and nothing else but the memories to help him. This is the great big change, the rest is just him... kinda realizing it or something. The simplest message is against suicide. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese uses the established pronoun 'she.' Calling her 'the girl' introduces detached narrator language at an intimate moment.
records.remedy: she

highlights.text: the girl

records.jp: どっかに人！
records.en: Anywhere, people!
records.assessment: Taichi desperately calls for any person to be somewhere. The English reverses the order into an ungrammatical location-plus-plural fragment.
records.remedy: Someone! Anywhere!

highlights.text: Anywhere, people!

records.jp: 机を倒していく。
records.en: I throw around the desks.
comments: This desk. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he knocks desks over as he proceeds. 'Throw around' suggests lifting and hurling them in multiple directions.
records.remedy: knock over the desks

highlights.text: throw around the desks

records.jp: どんどん倒していく。
records.en: Knock them down one after the other.
comments: This desk. -GHS
records.assessment: The surrounding first-person narration requires an explicit subject in this English sentence.
records.remedy: I knock them down

highlights.text: Knock them down

records.jp: 教科書が床に滑り落ちる。
records.en: Textbooks slip down to the ground.
comments: This desk. -GHS
records.assessment: The textbooks slide onto the interior floor. 'Ground' normally denotes outdoor earth or terrain.
records.remedy: to the floor

highlights.text: to the ground

records.jp: 二人はいない。
records.en: The two are not among us.
comments: This desk. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says simply that neither of the two is present. 'Not among us' can imply that they are dead or excluded from a group.
records.remedy: Neither of them is here.

highlights.text: The two are not among us.

records.jp: この空間には誰もいない。
records.en: In this room there is no one.
comments: Is an eyesore! ...seriously, they translated it like that? I know it's about the eyes like it is here, but... -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese expands the realization to this entire space, not merely the current room. The English narrows the absence to one room.
records.remedy: In this whole space

highlights.text: In this room

records.jp: 長細い空間。
records.en: A thin and narrow space.
records.assessment: 長細い describes a long, narrow space. The English replaces length with thinness and then redundantly adds narrowness.
records.remedy: A long, narrow space.

highlights.text: A thin and narrow space.

records.jp: 挟み撃ちにされたら助からないという危機感。
records.en: A sense of impeding danger that says I would never survive should I be subjected to a pincer attack.
records.assessment: The intended word is 'impending,' not 'impeding,' and the internal warning does not literally speak a proposition.
records.remedy: impending danger: I would never survive

highlights.text: impeding danger that says

records.jp: 敵は虚無だ。
records.en: The enemy are the Nihil.
comments: FINALLY getting out of that Nietzscheian bullcrap. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese personifies a single abstract enemy: the void or nothingness. The English pluralizes it, uses plural agreement, and invents the proper collective name 'the Nihil.'
records.remedy: The enemy is the void.

highlights.text: The enemy are the Nihil.

records.jp: このままでは俺は拡散して、希薄になってしまう。
records.en: If I keep this up I will spread, and end up diluted.
comments: See above, the Endless Self thing. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that if the surrounding condition continues, Taichi will diffuse. The English implies that his own continuing behavior causes the danger.
records.remedy: If this keeps up

highlights.text: If I keep this up

records.jp: 階段を通過し、二年教室。
records.en: I pass through the staircase to the Second Years' classroom.
records.assessment: Taichi goes via the stairs to a second-year classroom. A staircase is traversed along, not passed through, and the English invents a capitalized plural possessive name.
records.remedy: I take the stairs to a second-year classroom.

highlights.text: pass through the staircase
Second Years' classroom

records.jp: けど主がいない。
records.en: But its master is not here.
records.assessment: The fortress metaphor's 主 is its occupant or mistress, Touko. 'Master' introduces a masculine or owner-servant nuance.
records.remedy: its mistress

highlights.text: its master

records.jp: でも少しくらいいてくれてもいいじゃないか。
records.en: But wouldn't it have been nice if she had stayed here for just a little more?
records.assessment: The Japanese wishes that she could have remained for at least a little while. 'A little more' presupposes an earlier additional stay that is not stated.
records.remedy: for at least a little while

highlights.text: for just a little more

records.jp: こけつまろびつ、門をまたぐ。
records.en: Running and falling and stumbling I fly across the gate.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi crosses the gate while stumbling and tumbling. The English invents flight and uses 'across' for passing a gate boundary.
records.remedy: I stumble and tumble through the gate.

highlights.text: I fly across the gate

records.jp: 俺は街中を彷徨う。
records.en: I roam downtown,
records.assessment: 街中 means throughout the town or city. 'Downtown' restricts the search to a central commercial district.
records.remedy: through the town

highlights.text: downtown

records.jp: そもそも交差世界の残滓でしかないここに、もともと生者がいたのかどうか。
records.en: Whether or not these dregs of a crossed world that these are, and nothing more, ever held the living in the first place.
comments: DUN DUN DUNNN no wait wait wait I mean SYMBOLISM!!! -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese wonders whether living people ever existed in this place, which is only the residue of intersecting worlds. The English duplicates 'these,' leaves a relative clause without a predicate, and turns the local place into plural dregs as the container.
records.remedy: Did living people ever exist here in the first place, in a place that is only the residue of intersecting worlds?

highlights.text: Whether or not these dregs of a crossed world that these are, and nothing more, ever held the living in the first place.

records.jp: 一軒一軒、家を確かめていく。
records.en: Building by building I examine the houses.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he checks the houses one by one. The English adds a broader building-by-building count before narrowing the same objects back to houses.
records.remedy: I check the houses one by one.

highlights.text: Building by building I examine the houses.

records.jp: 「……ったくなぁ……一人もいねー」
records.en: Taichi: "...'mmit now... there's nobodyyy!"
records.assessment: The Japanese frustrated filler is roughly 'honestly' or 'damn.' The English creates the malformed clipped string ''mmit.'
records.remedy: damn it

highlights.text: 'mmit now

records.jp: どんだけ捜しても。
records.en: Howevermuch whateverway I search,
records.assessment: The Japanese means 'no matter how hard I looked.' The English fuses 'however much' into one word and adds the nonexistent compound 'whateverway.'
records.remedy: No matter how hard I looked

highlights.text: Howevermuch whateverway I search

records.jp: もう誰もいないのだった。
records.en: there was no one anymore anywhere.
comments: Notice how he never ever goes out that trail into the outside world? Or search for anyone but Kiri, Miki and Touko, who would be in the classrooms? -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that nobody was left. The English stacks three negative scope expressions without idiomatic ordering.
records.remedy: there was no one left anywhere

highlights.text: no one anymore anywhere

records.jp: 激しい運動をするため、脳が用いられたためだろうか？
records.en: It's because to make strenuous movements I needed to make use of the brain, right?
comments: Uhmmm... but it does connect to CCD5001, something that is a purely physical activity due to bodily want is a necessary "waste" that allows the margin for higher, spiritual, mental functions. The mind can work when the body shuts up, to say. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi wonders whether he calmed down because strenuous exercise occupied or used his brain. The English says he deliberately needed his brain in order to produce movement and uses the count noun 'movements.'
records.remedy: Maybe because strenuous exercise occupied my brain?

highlights.text: to make strenuous movements I needed to make use of the brain

records.jp: 突き動かされて、山に。
records.en: Stimulated, I head to the mountains.
records.assessment: 突き動かされて means driven or compelled by an inner impulse. 'Stimulated' suggests mere arousal or increased activity.
records.remedy: Driven by an impulse

highlights.text: Stimulated

records.jp: あのぼやけた不確定な理解不能空間は、きれいさっぱり消失していた。
records.en: That blurry, indeterminably incomprehensible space had vanished without a trace.
records.assessment: The Japanese coordinates the space as blurry, indeterminate, and incomprehensible. The English turns 'indeterminate' into an adverb modifying incomprehensibility.
records.remedy: blurry, indeterminate, incomprehensible

highlights.text: indeterminably incomprehensible

records.jp: いや、万かも知れない。
records.en: Nah, it might even be tens of thousand.
records.assessment: The quantified count noun requires the plural 'thousands.'
records.remedy: tens of thousands

highlights.text: tens of thousand

records.jp: 憤り。
records.en: Resentment.
records.assessment: 憤り is immediate anger or indignation. 'Resentment' more often denotes a lingering grievance toward an agent.
records.remedy: Anger.

highlights.text: Resentment.

records.jp: 絶望。
records.en: Desperation.
records.assessment: 絶望 is despair or hopelessness. 'Desperation' is an urgent drive to act under extreme pressure and does not preserve the loss of hope.
records.remedy: Despair.

highlights.text: Desperation.

records.jp: 心からもたらされるものに束縛され、俺は立ちすくんだ。
records.en: Shackled by what is brought out from the bottom of my heart I stood, petrified.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that things produced by his heart bind him in place. The English adds 'the bottom of' and omits the comma required before the main clause.
records.remedy: Shackled by what my heart produced, I stood

highlights.text: from the bottom of my heart I stood

records.jp: あたりまえの感情。
records.en: An everyday emotion.
records.assessment: あたりまえ describes the wish to flee as a natural or entirely understandable emotion. 'Everyday' instead suggests frequency or ordinariness in daily life.
records.remedy: A natural emotion.

highlights.text: An everyday emotion.

records.jp: 必死で養った、俺のちっぽけな心にもそれはあった。
records.en: It existed in this frantically cultivated, worthlessly tiny heart of mine as well.
records.assessment: The Japanese calls the heart tiny but says Taichi nurtured it desperately. The English changes desperate effort to frantic cultivation and adds the judgment that the heart is worthless.
records.remedy: the tiny heart I had desperately nurtured

highlights.text: frantically cultivated, worthlessly tiny heart

records.jp: 補正する『ずれ』はなくなったんだ。
records.en: Correction: the 'shift' was no more.
comments: Indeed, as said above the gate wasn't there before Sunday in CCD0023, though on Monday there was a "phase shit", see CCD0101. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the discrepancy which might have been corrected no longer exists. The English turns 'correction' into an editorial label and merely says the shift is gone, obscuring its role as the object of correction.
records.remedy: There was no longer any 'discrepancy' left to correct.

highlights.text: Correction: the 'shift' was no more.

records.jp: 『Ｘ』の字を想定してみればわかる。
records.en: Understandable if looking at the very character "X".
comments: This is his rationalization, which is of course nonsense. If he's thousands of week past the point of crossing, how does everyone hear his message? The delusion comes in simple examination of what he's saying: the world that exists at the center of the X would no longer be at the center of the X because it's moved on. So just where is it? This sounds so much like a deep statement that is yet ultimately nonsensical. Now see the end of CCD4003: Miki said it, yet once again. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the idea becomes clear if one imagines the shape of the letter X. The English supplies neither the person who understands nor an idiomatic conditional construction.
records.remedy: You can see it if you picture the letter X.

highlights.text: Understandable if looking at the very character "X".

records.jp: 俺はもう一本の流れに乗ったのか？
records.en: Did I ride a third flow here?
comments: See CCZAS - of course, he rode the flow of Denpa to this place. But if there's a third flow, then it's an asterisk, specifically what's referred to as a 'full-width' asterisk, "*" instead of ※. And that's an euphemism for asshole, as uhmmm "illustrated via Sakuraba". IOW, this explanation is literally full of shit. -GHS
records.assessment: The passage has established two intersecting flows. もう一本 asks whether Taichi moved onto the other or another one, not a third flow.
records.remedy: Did I move onto the other flow?

highlights.text: a third flow

records.jp: 流れゆく二本の残像の交差点。
records.en: The afterimage of the Cross Point of two continuing flows.
records.assessment: The Japanese describes the present town as the point where two flowing afterimages intersect. The English instead makes the Cross Point itself an afterimage and leaves an isolated noun phrase whose relations are unclear.
records.remedy: The intersection of two afterimages flowing onward.

highlights.text: The afterimage of the Cross Point of two continuing flows.

records.jp: 『実』が過ぎ去り『虚』になったクロスポイント。
records.en: A Cross Point where Real has passed by and became Imaginary.
comments: COUGH COUGH. -GHS
records.assessment: The coordinated perfect construction requires 'has become,' while the source describes the completed transition from real to unreal.
records.remedy: has passed by and become

highlights.text: has passed by and became

records.jp: ゲートが消えるまで、どれだけの時間がかかったのか知れない。
records.en: How much time it had passed before the gate had disappeared, I have no idea.
comments: Has he never even looked at the gate before here in any week he was here after CCD5001? I tend to doubt it. Another explanation: he hasn't been living at the hokora at all; since there's no reset, and he's meta-aware now that he's finished his religious awakening, so he simply doesn't reset. But that means he hasn't been going to church every Sunday; hence, he's forgetting. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says he does not know how much time elapsed before the gate disappeared. The English gives impersonal 'time' an expletive 'it' and uses an unnecessary past perfect for the elapsed time.
records.remedy: How much time passed before the gate disappeared

highlights.text: How much time it had passed before the gate had disappeared

records.jp: どっちにしても、俺は堪え忍んだ。
records.en: Whichever it is, I will have to patiently endure this.
records.assessment: The Japanese states that, whichever duration was true, Taichi endured it. The English changes the completed endurance into a future obligation.
records.remedy: Either way, I endured it.

highlights.text: I will have to patiently endure this.

records.jp: 逃げ場が遠のくほどの時を、闘い抜いた。
records.en: In times when the place of refuge grows farther, the struggle is to the bitter end.
comments: Which is why he removed it. Then again, the other side is death, metaphorically even if the literal is troll, although it's not troll and yeah I'm going cross-eyed. At least there aren't allegorical layers being added every five minutes to no payoff like in Forest because the author can't hack it, let's go with that. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi says that he fought his way through a span of time so long that escape receded into the distance. The English makes this a general present-tense maxim, removes him as subject, and turns duration into plural occasions.
records.remedy: I fought through a stretch of time long enough for escape itself to recede into the distance.

highlights.text: In times when the place of refuge grows farther, the struggle is to the bitter end.

records.jp: 「逃げ場がないなら……生きるしか……ないもんな……」
records.en: Taichi: "If I have no place of refuge... outside of living on... I've nothing... nothing..."
comments: No places to escape from living life, no ways to go 'home' manually: ergo, no suicide. NOW he's rejected death! After all, there's two forms of suicide: wanting not to live, and wanting to live in this dreg of a 'real' world. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese means that if there is nowhere to run, he has no choice but to live. The English substitutes 'outside of living on,' leaves the construction without a coherent complement, and repeats an unsupported 'nothing.'
records.remedy: If there's nowhere to run... then I've got no choice... but to live...

highlights.text: If I have no place of refuge... outside of living on... I've nothing... nothing...

records.jp: 「ざまあみろ、だ」
records.en: Taichi: "Just dessert, yes."
records.assessment: ざまあみろ is the taunt 'serves you right,' not the food-related phrase 'just deserts'; the English additionally misspells that separate idiom as 'dessert.'
records.remedy: Serves you right.

highlights.text: Just dessert, yes.

records.jp: トゥルー俺、ざまあみろ。
records.en: Just dessert, oh true self.
records.assessment: The repeated ざまあみろ is again a taunt addressed to the 'true me.' The English replaces it with a misspelled and contextually different idiom.
records.remedy: Serves you right, true me.

highlights.text: Just dessert, oh true self.

records.jp: 編み上げられる、架空のタペストリー。
records.en: An Air tapestry is being knit.
records.assessment: 架空 means imaginary or fictitious here. The English turns it into the capitalized noun 'Air,' and the progressive passive reads as a new action rather than the appositive image in the source.
records.remedy: An imaginary tapestry, woven together.

highlights.text: An Air tapestry is being knit.

records.jp: それは彩なす情意のきらめき。
records.en: That is the glittering sparkle of the varipatterned varicolor of emotions.
comments: Assuming 2001: A Space Odyssey reference at this point. Well, we had David Bowie. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese describes a variegated shimmer of feeling. The English piles a redundant 'glittering sparkle' onto the malformed inventions 'varipatterned' and 'varicolor,' leaving no coherent English image.
records.remedy: the variegated shimmer of emotion

highlights.text: the glittering sparkle of the varipatterned varicolor of emotions

records.jp: 声のかぎりに。
records.en: Up to the boundaries of voice.
records.assessment: 声のかぎり means with all the voice one has, conventionally 'at the top of one's lungs.' The English treats voice as a spatial territory with boundaries.
records.remedy: At the top of my lungs.

highlights.text: Up to the boundaries of voice.

records.jp: それはもう声ではなかった。
records.en: That's no longer voice.
records.assessment: The English lacks the article required for the count noun 'voice' and shifts the surrounding past narration into a contracted present.
records.remedy: It was no longer a voice.

highlights.text: That's no longer voice.

records.jp: 視野がエフェクトで埋まる。
records.en: My field of vision covers with special effects.
comments: 109 is a common one, though 10 is my favorite. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that visual effects fill his field of vision. The English makes the field of vision perform the transitive action 'covers' but supplies no object.
records.remedy: Visual effects fill my field of vision.

highlights.text: My field of vision covers with special effects.

records.jp: レースのように美しいが、おどろおどろしい情念で編み上げられている。
records.en: Beautiful as if lace it was, yet, it was being knit out of hair-raisingly eerie emotions.
records.assessment: The Japanese compares the vision to beautiful lace while saying that disturbing passions compose it. The English inverts the comparison into ungrammatical word order and stacks incompatible adverbial forms.
records.remedy: Beautiful as lace, yet woven from disturbing passions.

highlights.text: Beautiful as if lace it was, yet, it was being knit out of hair-raisingly eerie emotions.

records.jp: 揺れれば、垣間見える不浄の荒野。
records.en: Shake it, and you can get a peephole's glimpse on a wasteland of impurities.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that when the lace-like vision sways, an unclean wilderness can be glimpsed through it. The English commands an unspecified 'you' to shake it, invents a peephole, and uses the wrong preposition after 'glimpse.'
records.remedy: When it sways, an unclean wilderness shows through in glimpses.

highlights.text: Shake it, and you can get a peephole's glimpse on a wasteland of impurities.

records.jp: 幻だと思う反面、真実だとも把握していた。
records.en: It's an illusion, I think, but on the other hand I also get that it is truth.
records.assessment: In this construction the count noun requires an article: he also understands that it is the truth.
records.remedy: it is the truth

highlights.text: it is truth

records.jp: 極まった精神が、その表層をして潜在意識と接続する現象。
records.en: The Phenomenon where a soul reaches the extreme of an impasse, and that layer becomes connected to the subconscious.
comments: Psychological Explanation at the very least. Though since all science is troll, that's only an explanation for those who'll settle for it. Taichi himself does. -GHS
records.assessment: The source describes a mind pushed to an extreme, whose surface connects with the subconscious. The English changes mind to soul, invents an impasse, and makes an unspecified layer the subject of the connection.
records.remedy: a mind pushed to its limit connects its surface layer to the subconscious

highlights.text: a soul reaches the extreme of an impasse, and that layer becomes connected

records.jp: 側面にあるもの。
records.en: There is something on its side.
comments: See Week 1, where he keeps striking the side of his head. That's why smacking his head works, like in Another Story when Miki batons him. Is it a tumor? Well, not necessarily, but since Youko has been described as something that can be read as 'tumor'... -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese fragment points to what exists as a facet or side of consciousness. The English instead locates an unspecified object beside another unspecified thing.
records.remedy: What lay along that facet.

highlights.text: There is something on its side.

records.jp: それは錯綜する感情と距離を置く、沈着な知識の層。
records.en: That is the layer of the precipitated knowledge laid to keep the complicated emotions at a distance.
comments: It's all the bullshit we've read so far, IOW. And it's about to talk. So how reliable is it going to be? -GHS
records.assessment: 沈着 describes the layer as calm or composed; it does not mean chemically precipitated. The source says this calm layer of knowledge stands apart from tangled emotions, not that someone laid it down in order to keep them away.
records.remedy: a calm layer of knowledge that stands apart from the tangled emotions

highlights.text: the layer of the precipitated knowledge laid to keep the complicated emotions at a distance

records.jp: 俺は変性意識状態に陥ったのではない。
records.en: I have not been trapped in a condition of Altered State.
comments: He hasn't gotten trapped into a Cross World with a time loop; he's always lived there, the condition just worsened. -GHS
records.assessment: The established term 変性意識状態 is 'an altered state of consciousness.' The English treats 'Altered State' as a capitalized entity governed by the malformed phrase 'a condition of.'
records.remedy: an altered state of consciousness

highlights.text: a condition of Altered State

records.jp: 最初から、変性したままだったんだ。
records.en: from the very beginning it had been, denatured.
records.assessment: Together with the preceding fragment, the Japanese resolves into one declaration that his consciousness had been altered from the start. The English repeats the subject and finite verb after 'My awareness had been,' and uses 'denatured,' which normally describes proteins or alcohol, for consciousness.
records.remedy: altered from the very beginning.

highlights.text: from the very beginning it had been, denatured.

records.jp: 俺は変質してしまった。
records.en: I completely degenerated.
records.assessment: 変質した says that he underwent a qualitative change or became altered. 'Degenerated' adds moral or biological deterioration not present in the word itself.
records.remedy: I was altered completely.

highlights.text: I completely degenerated.

records.jp: 心の振幅が制御できない。
records.en: I cannot control the amplitude of the vibration of my heart.
records.assessment: 心の振幅 is a metaphor for the range or swings of emotion. The English literalizes it as a physical heart vibrating at an uncontrolled amplitude.
records.remedy: the swings of my emotions

highlights.text: the amplitude of the vibration of my heart

records.jp: 虚無的な対話と思考は、理性にかわって意識を保持した。
records.en: nihilistic conversations and thoughts working to protect the consciousness in the stead of rationality.
comments: All the weird stuff, again. But this also hints that it should be examined seriously: it's merely the *protection* of consciousness, not its complete removal. Which is how this is a stream of bull that yet makes sense. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says nihilistic dialogue and thought maintained consciousness in place of reason. 'Protect' changes maintenance into defense, and the idiom is 'in place of' or 'instead of,' not 'in the stead of.'
records.remedy: maintaining my consciousness in place of reason

highlights.text: working to protect the consciousness in the stead of rationality

records.jp: 吹き出る汚水を、泥水が覆うように。
records.en: So as to cover with muddy water the sewage being blown out.
comments: And serious examination reveals Taichi's error: there's no sewage down there at all! The problem is the muddy water, not what's below it. Or rather: there's sewage covering up the muddy water; and muddy it may be, but as Taichi says, in the desert even that is precious. -GHS
records.assessment: The source compares the mechanism to muddy water covering gushing sewage. The English front-loads purpose syntax without a governing clause and places the object after a heavy modifier in nonidiomatic order.
records.remedy: Like muddy water covering the sewage that gushes out.

highlights.text: So as to cover with muddy water the sewage being blown out.

records.jp: 最古の記憶が、タールめいた深層に漂っていた。
records.en: the recollections of that which is so far gone floated up from that tar-like substance that was the deepest layer.
comments: This is the true payoff of keeping the oldest/psychopath pun, see CCA0001. This is his problem: not memorizing or having memories, but recall. It's all in a stream of tar and mud, but it's what the layers LOOK like, not what they actually are. -GHS
