records.assessment: 最古の記憶 means his oldest memory. The English replaces that precise superlative with a vague description of something distant in time and pluralizes the memory.
records.remedy: my oldest memory

highlights.text: the recollections of that which is so far gone

records.jp: それは意識変性の起こる、さらなる以前の物語だ。
records.en: This is a story even older story than when that of the denaturing of my consciousness.
comments: He's kidding himself if he thinks the denaturing happened there. It crystallized, perhaps. Nothing else. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese calls it a story from still earlier than the alteration of his consciousness. The English repeats 'story,' strands 'that of,' and never forms a grammatical comparison.
records.remedy: It was a story from even before my consciousness was altered.

highlights.text: This is a story even older story than when that of the denaturing of my consciousness.

records.jp: だって俺は記憶を失ってなどいな爆発―――
records.en: But I said I'm not suffering from memory loEXPLOSION---
comments: Just cut off right there -GHS
records.assessment: The source has his thought that he had not lost his memory break apart at the word 'explosion.' The English adds that he 'said' something, reframes loss as suffering from a condition, and collapses the designed interruption into the malformed token 'loEXPLOSION.'
records.remedy: But I hadn't lost my memo—EXPLOSION—

highlights.text: But I said I'm not suffering from memory loEXPLOSION---

records.jp: 「必死に生きてたからさ、パパ」
records.en: Nanaka: "He lived on so desperately, that Papa."
records.assessment: The speaker affectionately explains that Papa was fighting desperately to live. The English produces a dislocated 'that Papa' after a comma and makes 'desperately' modify the bare fact of living rather than his determined effort.
records.remedy: Because your papa was fighting so hard to live.

highlights.text: He lived on so desperately, that Papa.

records.jp: 「太一はこれから、いっぱい苦労すると思う」
records.en: Nanaka: "Taichi will have lots of hardships from now on, I think."
comments: This is nearly identical to the way Youko normally speaks, ergo leaving it third person. -GHS
records.assessment: The speaker is addressing Taichi directly and says she thinks he will face many hardships. The English switches the address to a detached third-person statement using his name.
records.remedy: I think you're going to face a lot of hardship from now on, Taichi.

highlights.text: Taichi will have lots of hardships from now on, I think.

records.jp: 「あたしも、もういないパパも、味方になってあげられないんだ」
records.en: Nanaka: "Neither me, nor papa who's no more... can be your allies now."
records.assessment: The coordinated subject requires 'neither I nor,' and 味方になってあげられない means they cannot be there for or support him. 'Allies' introduces formal factional language into intimate speech.
records.remedy: Neither I nor your papa can be there to support you.

highlights.text: Neither me, nor papa who's no more... can be your allies now.

records.jp: 「すごく、すごく愛してる。生んで良かったって、思う」
records.en: Nanaka: "Really, really love you. I think it's so good I had you."
records.assessment: 生んで良かった means that she is glad she gave birth to him. The English's 'it's so good I had you' is unidiomatic and can suggest possession or an unspecified event rather than childbirth.
records.remedy: I'm so glad I gave birth to you.

highlights.text: I think it's so good I had you.

records.jp: 「もし生まれ変われたら、もう一度生んであげたいってくらいだよ」
records.en: Nanaka: "So much that if I were born again, I would want to have you one more time!"
records.assessment: The Japanese explicitly says that if reborn, she would want to give birth to Taichi again. 'Have you' leaves the central act ambiguous and 'one more time' sounds transactional rather than intimate.
records.remedy: I'd want to give birth to you all over again

highlights.text: I would want to have you one more time

records.jp: 記憶していた。
records.en: It was in my memories.
records.assessment: The Japanese directly says that Taichi remembered it. The English makes the event an impersonal object located among plural memories rather than his act or retained recollection.
records.remedy: I remembered it.

highlights.text: It was in my memories.

records.jp: 人は、そんなことまで覚えていることができる。
records.en: People can recall things as far as that.
comments: Actually up to several months further. -GHS
records.assessment: そんなことまで means that human memory can retain even something like this. The English calques the particle as a spatial extent attached to 'things.'
records.remedy: remember even something like that

highlights.text: recall things as far as that

records.jp: 覚えていたんだ。
records.en: I recalled it.
records.assessment: The Japanese emphasizes that the memory had been retained all along, not that he performed a new act of recollection at this moment.
records.remedy: I had remembered it.

highlights.text: I recalled it.

records.jp: 喜怒哀楽、いずれにも属さない激情。
records.en: Violent emotions that are not covered by the basic descriptors of happiness, fear, sorrow, pleasure.
records.assessment: 喜怒哀楽 conventionally enumerates joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure. The English replaces anger with fear, changing one of the four emotions explicitly named by the source.
records.remedy: joy, anger, sorrow, or pleasure

highlights.text: happiness, fear, sorrow, pleasure

records.jp: 「俺、おぼえてた……母さんのこと……」
records.en: Taichi: "I... remembered... about mother..."
records.assessment: Taichi says that he remembered his mother. English 'remembered about' is nonidiomatic here, while lower-case 'mother' after no determiner reads as neither a proper form of address nor a normal noun phrase.
records.remedy: I... remembered you... Mom...

highlights.text: I... remembered... about mother...

records.jp: ちっぽけだと思っていた自分の心に、なんてものが秘められていたのだろう。
records.en: This heart of mine I thought so tiny, yet what a thing was kept hidden within.
records.assessment: The Japanese marvels at what had lain hidden in the heart he thought insignificant. The English front-loads the object without a relative marker and joins an exclamation to it with a coordination that never forms a complete sentence.
records.remedy: What could have been hidden in this heart of mine that I had thought so small?

highlights.text: This heart of mine I thought so tiny, yet what a thing was kept hidden within.

records.jp: 人捜しの長い旅に疲れ果て死ぬとき、はじめて振り返ると捜し人が無言でついてきていて、にっこりとほほえみかけてきたような。
records.en: It's as if you're dead exhausted after a long voyage in search of someone, and then the very first time you turn around there the person you were looking for was, wordlessly following you, grinning into a smile.
comments: How I wish that is what it felt to analyze this. Ugh. -GHS
records.assessment: The source likens the feeling to reaching death exhausted by a long search, only then looking back and finding the sought person silently following and smiling. 'Dead exhausted' turns actual dying into an intensifier, the tense shifts from present 'you turn' to past 'was,' and 'grinning into a smile' distorts the gentle smile.
records.remedy: As if, when I finally died exhausted from a long journey searching for someone, I looked back for the first time and found them following silently behind me, smiling.

highlights.text: It's as if you're dead exhausted after a long voyage in search of someone, and then the very first time you turn around there the person you were looking for was, wordlessly following you, grinning into a smile.

records.jp: すべてが無条件に肯定されてしまいそうな。
records.en: It felt as if everything could unconditionally become positive.
comments: The love of a parent. ...and all sins will be made nothing but the stumbling of babies as they learn to walk... -GHS
records.assessment: 肯定される means that everything feels accepted or affirmed without condition. The English instead says events or things undergo a change into the abstract property 'positive.'
records.remedy: everything might be accepted unconditionally

highlights.text: everything could unconditionally become positive

records.jp: 記憶はもう一つあった。
records.en: There is one more recollection.
records.assessment: The Japanese narration states that there was another memory, matching the surrounding past discovery. The English shifts it into an existential present.
records.remedy: There was one more memory.

highlights.text: There is one more recollection.

records.jp: もう一つの、思い出をすくい取る。
records.en: One more memory that I can scoop out.
records.assessment: The Japanese narrates Taichi actively scooping up another memory. The English turns the action into a relative-clause possibility modifying the memory and leaves it as a fragment without the intended finite action.
records.remedy: I scoop up one more memory.

highlights.text: One more memory that I can scoop out.

records.jp: 俺の幼児期は、闇とともにあった。
records.en:
The time of my babyhood was an existence together
with darkness.
comments: See CCB0018. And it's explained! -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that his early childhood was spent with or accompanied by darkness. The English makes a span of time itself 'an existence' and uses the nonidiomatic term 'babyhood.'
records.remedy: My infancy was spent in darkness.

highlights.text:
The time of my babyhood was an existence together
with darkness.

records.jp: 七香は……母さんは、俺を抱いて暗闇に身を置いていた。
records.en:
Nanaka... mother was hugging me as she laid
down in pitch-black darkness.
comments: Given all the things about Taichi's eyes, this darkness may merely be her being near dead. -GHS
records.assessment: 身を置いていた says that she remained or kept herself in the darkness while holding him. The English invents the physical action of lying down and intensifies darkness to 'pitch-black.'
records.remedy: held me while keeping herself in the darkness

highlights.text:
laid
down in pitch-black darkness

records.jp: 母と子は闇に沈められていた。
records.en: A mother and a child sinking into the darkness.
records.assessment: The Japanese gives a completed passive condition: mother and child had been submerged in darkness. The English changes it into an active progressive fragment.
records.remedy: Mother and child were submerged in darkness.

highlights.text: A mother and a child sinking into the darkness.

records.jp: どんな理由があったのか知らない。
records.en: What was the reason for that I have no idea.
comments: This is nothing but pure conjecture, I admit, but could he be the son of that tortured and killed servant couple? Slightly more probable that his backstory is actually Youko's, which he pushed on another persona to keep himself sane - provided Youko never existed, however, rather than just after the Mansion events. -GHS
records.assessment: The English copies Japanese topic order without the punctuation or clause structure needed in English.
records.remedy: I have no idea why.

highlights.text: What was the reason for that I have no idea.

records.jp: 長い時間。
records.en: For long long hours,
records.assessment: The Japanese says only 'a long time.' The English narrows the unknown duration to hours and adds colloquial repetition not present in the source.
records.remedy: For a long time

highlights.text: For long long hours

records.jp: 俺はそれを感じ取った。
records.en: That's the feeling I took from that.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that even as an infant he sensed her sadness and fear. The English recasts this as a later interpretive takeaway from an event.
records.remedy: I could sense it.

highlights.text: That's the feeling I took from that.

records.jp: 俺はそれをなんとなく理解している。
records.en: That, one way or another, I had understood,
comments: When he was literally weeks old? Yeah, keep projecting your current knowledge on your memories, buddy. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says he somehow understands that fact together with his inability to console her. The English changes the continuing realization to past perfect and leaves an inverted subordinate fragment.
records.remedy: Somehow, I understood that,

highlights.text: That, one way or another, I had understood,

records.jp: 二人とも、泣くこともできずにいた。
records.en: There we laid, both of us, incapable of crying.
records.assessment: The intransitive past tense of 'lie' is 'lay'; 'laid' requires an object. The source simply says that neither of them could cry.
records.remedy: There we lay

highlights.text: There we laid

records.jp: 気がつくと、俺は闇の中でも母を見ることができるようになっていた。
records.en:
When I came to notice, I seemed to have
become capable of seeing mom in the darkness.
comments: He just finished using the very word 'darkness', kanji and all, to describe his mother's fear. That's what his eyes actually allow him to see, the truth of people below what they seem to be - just what he says Kiri can do. And this explains his night vision: he sees, even if he doesn't necessarily understand. Like the script all the way above, though examples of Taichi telling the truth without telling it are nearly everywhere. Note that "and then I noticed". -GHS
records.assessment: 気がつくと means 'before I knew it' or 'when I realized it,' and the source states that the ability had developed. The English calques the noticing construction and adds 'seemed,' weakening the fact.
records.remedy: Before I knew it, I had become capable

highlights.text:
When I came to notice, I seemed to have
become capable

records.jp: 生後数ヶ月、中脳皮質系から視覚皮質に神経系が切り替わり、外界に適するための末梢機能が発達する時期。
records.en:
A few months after birth, the central nervous
system switches over completely from the
mesocortical pathways to the visual cortex,
a period of time taken for the development of
peripheral functions suitable for the outside
world.
comments: And here begins the final scientific troll of Cross Channel... though not the last one. See book. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese describes a developmental period when neural processing switches from a midbrain-cortical system to the visual cortex and peripheral functions develop for adaptation to the outside world. The English changes the subject to the entire central nervous system, adds 'completely,' and makes the period itself something 'taken for' development.
records.remedy: the neural system shifts from the midbrain-cortical system to the visual cortex, while peripheral functions develop to adapt the infant to the outside world

highlights.text:
the central nervous
system switches over completely from the
mesocortical pathways to the visual cortex,
a period of time taken for the development of
peripheral functions suitable for the outside
world

records.jp: それは肉体の変化を招いた。
records.en: That beckoned a physical mutation.
records.assessment: 招いた means that the sustained effort caused a bodily change. 'Beckoned' suggests inviting something to approach, while 'mutation' adds a genetic sense absent from the general 肉体の変化.
records.remedy: caused a physical change

highlights.text: beckoned a physical mutation

records.jp: 母は若く恐怖の虜で、知識を持たなかった。
records.en:
Mom was a youthful prisoner of fear, so she
did not possess knowledge.
comments: And given how bullshit-filled his talks with her are throughout the story, it's not impossible she was the one to make this up. Maybe to explain the illness he was born with, as well, which she should've been well aware of, given it should be readily visible. Nothing but a mother playing with her son, in that sense -GHS
records.assessment: The source coordinates three conditions: she was young, captive to fear, and lacked knowledge. The English makes fear the cause of her ignorance and uses the abstract possession phrase 'possess knowledge.'
records.remedy: young, captive to fear, and without the knowledge to understand

highlights.text:
a youthful prisoner of fear, so she
did not possess knowledge

records.jp: 桿状体細胞が増加し、分布を決める。
records.en:
deciding to increase the amount of the rod-shaped
cells distributed.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that rod cells increased and established their distribution. The English makes the cells consciously decide to increase an 'amount' and collapses the two physiological developments into one modifier.
records.remedy: The rod cells increased and established their distribution.

highlights.text:
deciding to increase the amount of the rod-shaped
cells distributed

records.jp: 網膜周辺の未分化細胞が、擬似的な輝膜を形成した。
records.en:
The unspecialized cells around the retina
create a pseudo-tapetum lucidum.
comments: I love how 未分化細胞 keeps turning up around all sort of wonderful illnesses such as leukemia, see CCB2012; what if it is true? -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese describes a structure that formed during the past developmental change. The English shifts the formation into present tense.
records.remedy: formed a pseudo-tapetum lucidum

highlights.text: create a pseudo-tapetum lucidum

records.jp: エラーの重複か、硝子体と同化しようと透明度を失い損ねた細胞たちか。
records.en:
Overlapping errors, maybe, or the cellettes
failing to lose their transparency as they
merge into the glassy body, maybe.
comments: As described, this sounds like he would simply become blind, or at least have a severely impaired vision. -GHS
records.assessment: The source proposes cells that, while attempting to assimilate with the vitreous body, failed to lose their transparency. The English invents 'cellettes,' mistranslates the anatomical vitreous body as 'glassy body,' and states that merging actually occurred rather than was attempted.
records.remedy: cells that failed to lose their transparency while trying to assimilate with the vitreous body

highlights.text:
the cellettes
failing to lose their transparency as they
merge into the glassy body

records.jp: 結果として、瞳に入った光を、反射し細胞に二度重ねる構造を有した。
records.en:
The result being that I was endowed with
a structure where the light entering my
pupils would be twice overlapped on the
reflective cells.
records.assessment: The resulting structure reflects incoming light so that it passes over the receptor cells twice. The English instead makes the cells reflective and says the light is 'overlapped' on them twice.
records.remedy: light entering my pupils was reflected across the cells a second time

highlights.text:
the light entering my
pupils would be twice overlapped on the
reflective cells

records.jp: またこの目は、静止物より動くものに敏感だった。
records.en:
Also, these eyes had higher sensitivity
for things moving than ones still.
comments: See CCA0030 for the only thing he sees this way - Youko, who might not exist at all. Particularly odd considering that in Misato sendback, see CCD1001, he just uses a seeming sixth-sense that can't have anything whatsoever to do with sight. -GHS
records.assessment: The comparison requires sensitivity 'to' moving things and an idiomatic contrast with stationary ones.
records.remedy: more sensitive to moving things than to stationary ones

highlights.text:
higher sensitivity
for things moving than ones still

records.jp: 闇の中、母は俺に何度もキスをした。
records.en:
In the heart of the night, mom had kissed me
so many times.
records.assessment: 闇の中 is physical darkness in the recalled setting, not the temporal 'heart of the night.' The English also shifts the simple past into past perfect and adds the intensifier 'so.'
records.remedy: In the darkness, Mom kissed me again and again.

highlights.text:
In the heart of the night, mom had kissed me
so many times.

records.jp: 俺はどんな影響を受けたんだろう？
records.en:
What kind of influence could I have gotten
from that?
comments: Momcon, from the looks of it. Possibly his saliva fetishism. -GHS
records.assessment: English ordinarily asks what effect something had, not what kind of influence a person 'got.'
records.remedy: effect did that have on me

highlights.text: influence could I have gotten

records.jp: 潜在意識の黒い奔流から抽出できる記憶は、それだけだった。
records.en:
The memories that can be extracted from the dark
rushing torrent of the subconscious were those,
no more.
comments: That's the 7th ruby text word in this exposition dump. But no, there are more, waaay more. Start from CCA0003 and follow through. Nearly every time the two speak he's repeating, with tweaks, a memory or so. See CCC0045A/B: that's possibly why "she" forgets which Taichi it is. And of course, the very final memory, the one probably of her very moment of death: the one where she's far away and, crying, points at the hokora. If you want to fix this world where everyone's gone, and that includes her, -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that this was all the memory he could extract from the subconscious torrent. The English mismatches plural present 'can be' with past 'were,' uses an unexplained plural 'those,' and separates 'no more' from the quantity it limits.
records.remedy: That was all the memory I could extract from the black torrent of my subconscious.

highlights.text: The memories that can be extracted

were those,
no more

records.jp: あのあと、死んだんだろう。
records.en: She had died after that, I'm sure.
records.assessment: だろう marks inference, roughly 'probably' or 'I suppose.' 'I'm sure' makes the conclusion substantially more certain, and past perfect is unnecessary in the immediate sequence.
records.remedy: She probably died after that.

highlights.text: She had died after that, I'm sure.

records.jp: じゃあ……俺が見ていたあの七香は？
records.en: Well... what is the Nanaka that I have been seeing?
records.assessment: The Japanese asks who or what the Nanaka he had seen was. The English uses an article before a personal name, mixes present 'is' with present perfect progressive, and describes an apparent person as a thing without framing the question idiomatically.
records.remedy: Then... who was the Nanaka I'd been seeing?

highlights.text: what is the Nanaka that I have been seeing?

records.jp: きっといつも、記憶の底から見守っていてくれたんだ。
records.en: She has always been watching over me from the bottom of my recollections, definitely.
records.assessment: 記憶の底 is the depths of memory, not the bottom of plural recollections. きっと expresses hopeful conviction in context; sentence-final 'definitely' sounds like an external factual certification.
records.remedy: from the depths of my memory, I'm sure

highlights.text: from the bottom of my recollections, definitely

records.jp: 事実は、世界が知っていればいい。
records.en: The world can go know the truth.
comments: And that's all you get, readers! No clunky rainbow-colored truths or enough stupid to send me flying into a rage at the mere thought nearly two years after reading it. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese means that it is enough for the world itself to know the facts. The English combines 'can go' and bare 'know' into an ungrammatical imperative-like phrase.
records.remedy: It's enough for the world to know the truth.

highlights.text: The world can go know the truth.

records.jp: 愛していてくれただけで、俺には―――充分すぎる。
records.en: Merely having been loved, to me, it's--- more than plenty.
comments: See YMK/Aeka again. and particularly interesting given that Aeka's hair and her relationship with bullies... but that's another story. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that simply knowing she loved him is more than enough for him. The English uses a dangling passive gerund, then repeats the experiencer as both 'to me' and the unexplained pronoun 'it.'
records.remedy: Just knowing she loved me is more than enough.

highlights.text: Merely having been loved, to me, it's--- more than plenty.

records.jp: 涙を取り戻すと、次は認識が来た。
records.en: And with the regainment of tears, next came the recognition.
comments: See most Sendbacks, he couldn't cry... though he could cry just fine all throughout, so it's more troll anyway. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that once his tears returned, realization followed. 'Regainment' is an awkward nominalization and the article before abstract 'recognition' does not establish a specific prior referent.
records.remedy: once my tears returned, realization followed

highlights.text: with the regainment of tears, next came the recognition

records.jp: いてほしいんだ。
records.en: It's a want for them to be there.
records.assessment: The Japanese directly says 'I want them to be there.' The English converts the verb into a count noun governed by an expletive construction that is not idiomatic English.
records.remedy: I want them to be there.

highlights.text: It's a want for them to be there.

records.jp: 手を伸ばした先に、誰かがいるという安心。
records.en: To be reassured that someone will be there even before they extend their hands.
records.assessment: 手を伸ばした先 means at the point reached by an outstretched hand. The English reverses the timing, placing the person there before the hand is extended at all.
records.remedy: someone is there within reach when they stretch out a hand

highlights.text: someone will be there even before they extend their hands

records.jp: 電話で。言葉で。手紙で。態度で。
records.en: with telephone, with words, with letters, with behavior.
records.assessment: The Japanese lists means of reaching out. English requires 'by phone' and idiomatic parallel prepositional phrases rather than repeated instrument-like 'with' and bare singular 'telephone.'
records.remedy: by phone, through words, in letters, through actions

highlights.text: with telephone, with words, with letters, with behavior

records.jp: どこかで誰かが聞いてくれますように。
records.en: So that they can get someone somewhere to listen.
records.assessment: The Japanese voices the hope that someone somewhere will hear the call. The English makes callers causatively 'get' a listener to perform an action and turns the wish into a purpose clause.
records.remedy: Hoping that someone, somewhere, will hear.

highlights.text: So that they can get someone somewhere to listen.

records.jp: 逃避だけど正しかった。
records.en: She was running but she was right.
comments: Note the lack of anything that could sound even remotely SOS-like. After all, her SOS via the antenna was always intended to be her asking for help by putting that together, not talking to the world via it. The subtle implication is that the whole thing was never about looking for "certain" kinds of people - "friends", in ToF parlance - but for a want for people to be there. His flight was ignoring mankind all along, and her flight was not from the absence of people. -GHS
records.assessment: 逃避 means escape or escapism in the psychological sense. The English literalizes it as the physical act of running and adds a personal subject absent from the fragment.
records.remedy: It was escapism, but she was right.

highlights.text: She was running but she was right.

records.jp: 深い意識にかき乱され、無邪気に人を壊してしまう俺だ。
records.en: Disturbed by my deep consciousness, I've been innocent-mindedly destroying humans, that's what.
comments: Because he's been hurting them, we're supposed to understand... but now that he's admitted that he doesn't know, it's more hints that this is just how he's pretending they're not there. -GHS
records.assessment: The source says that his deep consciousness churns him up and that he innocently destroys people. 'Innocent-mindedly' is not idiomatic, 'humans' is clinical in this reflection, and the present perfect progressive plus trailing 'that's what' replaces the source's characterization of himself.
records.remedy: I am someone whose deepest consciousness churns him up until he innocently destroys people.

highlights.text: Disturbed by my deep consciousness, I've been innocent-mindedly destroying humans, that's what.

records.jp: 協調を衝動に阻害されるのだから、当然だ。
records.en: Seeing as my urge to cooperate was being obstructed by impulse, that'd be obvious.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that impulse obstructs his capacity for cooperation or harmony. The English instead invents a cooperative urge and makes a separate impulse obstruct that urge.
records.remedy: my ability to live in harmony is obstructed by my impulses

highlights.text: my urge to cooperate was being obstructed by impulse

records.jp: ゲートが消えて、世界は変わっていくかも知れない。
records.en: So the gate may disappear, and the world may change, perhaps.
comments: The world will go on ahead... -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the gate has disappeared and that the world may now change. The English makes the disappearance itself a future possibility.
records.remedy: the gate is gone

highlights.text: the gate may disappear

records.jp: 幻となって消えていく時が、来ているのだ。
records.en: The time will come when it will become an illusion and disappear.
comments: Eh, there'll be reprints, but the older version is easier to manipulate. And it doesn't have multiple screwups like changing the prompt for no good reason, missing some ruby text including the Tomoki is Food joke, a far worse pixelation effect, and changing the developer's name so it requires redoing the opening into something way way uglier, as well as ruining one of the jokes/major interpretations (FS Phenomenon). Nor a lack of every single change and improvement made in the console versions, though I guess given the scope of the job (which I know altogether too well), I could see why. -GHS
records.assessment: 時が来ている says that the time is already approaching or has come, not merely that it will arrive at some unspecified future point.
records.remedy: The time is coming

highlights.text: The time will come

records.jp: 俺が固有の寿命を終える前に、どうか。
records.en: I will wish that before my eigenlifespan ends, somehow,
comments: Not before his life ends... -GHS
records.assessment: 固有の寿命 means his own allotted or natural lifespan. The English invents the technical compound 'eigenlifespan,' which has no established meaning in English.
records.remedy: my own lifespan

highlights.text: my eigenlifespan

records.jp: この空が消えてなくなりますようにと。
records.en: for the sky itself to finally pass away.
comments: ...because he's wishing for him to be there after the world ends. Rev 6:9-11. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese wishes for the sky to disappear completely. 'Pass away' personifies it as dying and does not carry なくなる's complete disappearance, while 'finally' is added.
records.remedy: for this sky to disappear completely

highlights.text: the sky itself to finally pass away

records.jp: 残されたのは、世界でもっとも陳腐な部類の漢字一文字の単語と、生涯を通してありがちな人への渇望だった。
records.en: What she left me was a string of characters comprised of the world's most extreme cliche'-class words, and a craving to move throughout the course of my entire life towards being an ordinary person.
comments: My ass she ass! See CCA0004: like the Tasaki Store owner's parents left him more than an inheritance, Nanaka left him with way more. She's the one that leads him to the hokora, and the first words out of her back in CCA0003 were about God and religion. What she left him was also a big finger pointed at the hokora, which is about Christianity and religion. By Rule of Greek Chorus(?), the same was true of the Tasaki Store owner. That's why, in the Materials Book interview, Tanaka says the Tasaki Store owner has a pretty detailed personality for what should be less than a minor character. -GHS
records.assessment: The source says she left him one single-kanji word of the most commonplace kind and a lifelong, ordinary longing for other people. The English turns one character into a string made of multiple words, adds 'most extreme,' and changes longing for people into a project of becoming an ordinary person.
records.remedy: a single-kanji word among the most commonplace in the world, and the ordinary longing for other people that would remain with me throughout my life

highlights.text: a string of characters comprised of the world's most extreme cliche'-class words, and a craving to move throughout the course of my entire life towards being an ordinary person

records.jp: 満面の、祝福の笑みだった。
records.en: It was an ear-to-ear full face smile of blessing.
comments: See the Tasaki store owner's face, similarly described. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese describes a beaming smile of blessing across her whole face. The English stacks two competing descriptions of width, uses 'full face' without the required hyphenation or idiomatic construction, and makes blessing an awkward postmodifier.
records.remedy: a radiant, full-faced smile of blessing

highlights.text: an ear-to-ear full face smile of blessing

records.jp: そして七香を正しく認識すると同時に。
records.en: And then, simultaneously with my correct understanding of Nanaka,
records.assessment: 正しく認識する means to recognize or perceive Nanaka correctly in terms of what she is. 'Understanding of Nanaka' instead suggests a general intellectual or empathetic comprehension of her as a person.
records.remedy: recognizing Nanaka for what she was

highlights.text: my correct understanding of Nanaka

records.jp: 林の中、俺という存在が、ひとつっきり。
records.en: In the heart of that grove, the only one thing remaining was this being, this being called me.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that within the grove there was only one existence: Taichi himself. The English uses the ungrammatical quantifier sequence 'only one thing,' adds that he was 'remaining,' and repeats 'this being' in inflated explanatory prose.
records.remedy: there was only one existence: me

highlights.text: the only one thing remaining was this being, this being called me

records.jp: 静かすぎて体内の物音さえ聞き取れそうで。
records.en: It seemed so excessively quiet that even the sounds inside the body could be heard.
records.assessment: The Japanese refers specifically to sounds inside Taichi's own body. The English shifts to a detached generic body.
records.remedy: the sounds inside my own body

highlights.text: the sounds inside the body

records.jp: 今まで心象風景の暴君だった、強烈なエゴが感じられない。
records.en: I could no longer feel the violent ego that until now has been the tyrant of the imaginary landscape in my mind's eye.
comments: How odd he'd phrase it this way, isn't it. -GHS
records.assessment: The matrix verb is past while the relative clause uses present perfect with 'until now.' The surrounding realization requires a consistent current-perfect relation or a consistently narrated past one.
records.remedy: I could no longer feel the violent ego that until then had been

highlights.text: I could no longer feel the violent ego that until now has been

records.jp: 心細い。
records.en: Discouragement.
records.assessment: 心細い expresses feeling uneasy, insecure, or forlorn because support is absent. 'Discouragement' instead means a loss of confidence or enthusiasm after difficulty.
records.remedy: I feel uneasy.

highlights.text: Discouragement.

records.jp: 抱え込む。
records.en: take this upon myself.
comments: Going with lateral. Now he's gonna have to carry that heart with him 'till death. No tricks. -GHS
records.assessment: In sequence with placing a hand on his chest and squeezing, 抱え込む means that he holds or embraces the feeling within himself. 'Take this upon myself' means accepting a duty or burden.
records.remedy: hold it close

highlights.text: take this upon myself

records.jp: 何十週か、あるいは何万週か。
records.en: How many dozens, or perhaps how many thousands have there been?
comments: Notice the counter is technically fitting with 1771. -GHS
records.assessment: The source contrasts dozens of weeks with tens of thousands of weeks. The English omits 'weeks' from both alternatives and reduces 何万 from tens of thousands to mere thousands.
records.remedy: Dozens of weeks, perhaps, or tens of thousands.

highlights.text: How many dozens, or perhaps how many thousands have there been?

records.jp: こうして俺は、ついにヒトになったのである。
records.en: And like this, I finally had become one, single, individual person.
records.assessment: The Japanese gives a completed simple realization: he finally became human. The English uses an unlicensed past perfect and adds a redundant three-part countability gloss.
records.remedy: I finally became human.

highlights.text: I finally had become one, single, individual person.

records.jp: 両方まざると、もう形容する言葉はない。
records.en: The two sides mixed, that words to describe them I had no more.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that once the sadness and happiness mix, no words can describe the result. The English calls the emotions 'sides,' then joins them to an inverted clause with an ungrammatical 'that.'
records.remedy: When the two mixed, I had no words left to describe the feeling.

highlights.text: The two sides mixed, that words to describe them I had no more.

records.jp: 笑って、泣いた。
records.en: I cried, laughingly.
records.assessment: The Japanese coordinates two equally salient actions: he laughed and cried. The English subordinates laughter into the nonidiomatic manner adverb 'laughingly.'
records.remedy: I laughed and cried.

highlights.text: I cried, laughingly.

records.jp: 一日頑張れば、なんとかなるだろう。
records.en: If I give it all through this one day, I will make it somehow.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that if he works hard for one day, he should somehow manage to finish or fix it. 'Give it all through' is nonidiomatic, and 'make it' lacks the task-oriented result supplied by context.
records.remedy: If I work hard all day, I should be able to manage somehow.

highlights.text: If I give it all through this one day, I will make it somehow.

records.en: Taichi: "...right, Senpai?"
records.assessment: The conversational particle ね opens a soft address to Senpai here; it does not necessarily ask her to confirm a proposition. English 'right' invents an agreement-seeking question.
records.remedy: ...hey, Senpai.

highlights.text: ...right, Senpai?

records.jp: こういう他愛ない部活動、普通のガクセーらしい日常を。
records.en: About this kind of silly innocent club activities, about an ordinary life as if an ordinary student.
comments: CP CCA0030
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he had dreamed of harmless, trivial club activities and an ordinary student's everyday life. The English uses 'about' after 'dreaming' in the preceding unit, mismatches singular 'this kind' with plural 'activities,' and says ordinary life is only 'as if' he were an ordinary student.
records.remedy: Of harmless club activities like these, of the ordinary daily life of a regular student.

highlights.text: About this kind of silly innocent club activities, about an ordinary life as if an ordinary student.

records.jp: 思い出があれば、俺はそれでいい。
records.en: As long as there are memories, I will be fine with that.
comments: CP CCA0030
records.assessment: The Japanese says that memories of his own are enough for him. The English uses an impersonal existential construction, so any memories existing anywhere satisfy the condition.
records.remedy: As long as I have those memories

highlights.text: As long as there are memories

records.jp: 息を吸う。
records.en: Draw in a breath,
comments: CP CCA0030
records.assessment: The surrounding first-person narration requires an explicit subject. Without one, the English reads as an imperative.
records.remedy: I draw in a breath.

highlights.text: Draw in a breath,

records.jp: 夏の香りを含んだ夕風が、悪戯する手つきでそれをさらっていく。
records.en: An evening wind that still captured that scent of Summer kidnaps it with a mischievous sleight of hand.
comments: CP CCA0030
Uhm, but now that doesn't make sense. Oh, whatever. -GHS
records.assessment: The wind contains the scent of summer and playfully carries away the breath he drew. 'Captured' suggests imprisoning the scent, while 'kidnaps' and 'sleight of hand' add violent and stage-magician imagery to the simple personification.
records.remedy: The evening breeze, scented with summer, playfully snatches it away.

highlights.text: An evening wind that still captured that scent of Summer kidnaps it with a mischievous sleight of hand.

records.jp: さあ放送だ。
records.en: So, to broadcast.
comments: CP CCA0030
records.assessment: さあ放送だ announces that it is time to broadcast. The English leaves only a prepositional infinitive fragment without the idiomatic announcement.
records.remedy: All right. Time to broadcast.

highlights.text: So, to broadcast.

records.jp: 「こちら、群青学院放送部」
records.en: Taichi: "This is the Gunjou Institute Broadcast Club."
comments: CP CCA0030
records.assessment: The Japanese place name 群青 romanizes as Gunjō in standard Hepburn. 'Gunjou' is a keyboard-style long-vowel spelling rather than normalized Hepburn.
records.remedy: Gunjō

highlights.text: Gunjou

records.jp: 力強く言葉を押し出した。
records.en: I pushed out these forceful words:
comments: PCP CCA0030
records.assessment: 力強く modifies the act of pushing the words out: he speaks forcefully. The English instead makes the words themselves inherently forceful.
records.remedy: I forced the words out with conviction:

highlights.text: I pushed out these forceful words:

records.jp: 万感の思いをこめて。
records.en: and flood my words with thousands of feelings.
records.assessment: 万感 means the full weight or multitude of emotion, not literally thousands of countable feelings. The Japanese does not explicitly mention words in this fragment.
records.remedy: pouring all my feelings into it

highlights.text: flood my words with thousands of feelings

records.jp: 「こちら、群青学院放送部」
records.en: This is the Gunjou Institute Broadcast Club.
comments: PCP CCA0030
records.assessment: The Japanese place name 群青 romanizes as Gunjō in standard Hepburn. 'Gunjou' is a keyboard-style long-vowel spelling rather than normalized Hepburn.
records.remedy: Gunjō

highlights.text: Gunjou

records.jp: 立ち上がり、電源を落とす。
records.en: Stand up, switch off the power.
records.assessment: The Japanese continues first-person present narration. Without a subject, both English verbs read as commands.
records.remedy: I stand up and switch off the power.

highlights.text: Stand up, switch off the power.

records.jp: 片づけている時間はない。
records.en: Time to tidy up I haven't.
records.assessment: The English copies Japanese topic ordering into an inverted construction that is not grammatical English.
records.remedy: I don't have time to tidy up.

highlights.text: Time to tidy up I haven't.

records.jp: 祠に行かねばならない。
records.en: I must absolutely go to the hokora,
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he must go to the shrine. 'Absolutely' is added, the common noun 祠 is left as unexplained romanized Japanese, and the comma incorrectly binds the independent next sentence as part of the same clause.
records.remedy: I have to go to the shrine.

highlights.text: I must absolutely go to the hokora,

records.jp: 虚しい行為かも知れない。
records.en: This act may just be futile, I have no idea.
records.assessment: かも知れない already expresses that the act may be futile. The added 'I have no idea' restates uncertainty more broadly and changes the clipped reflection's register.
records.remedy: This act may be futile.

highlights.text: , I have no idea

records.jp: 一時の交差を胸に、瞬間の交差を求めて。
records.en: I will seek a moment of intersection, a temporary crossing in my heart,
comments: How would he do that if there were truly no one? -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he holds the temporary crossing in his heart while seeking another momentary intersection. The English's reordered apposition makes the crossing in his heart appear to be the object he is seeking.
records.remedy: Holding that temporary crossing in my heart, seeking another moment of intersection.

highlights.text: I will seek a moment of intersection, a temporary crossing in my heart,

records.jp: いくつもの週を越えて。
records.en: throughout a number of weeks that will transcend all count.
records.assessment: The Japanese says simply that he will continue across many weeks. The English adds that the weeks themselves will transcend counting and uses 'throughout' for the act of crossing successive intervals.
records.remedy: Across week after week.

highlights.text: throughout a number of weeks that will transcend all count

records.jp: また来週と告げるために。
records.en: For the sake of proclaiming "see you next week".
records.assessment: In the requested US English house style, the period belongs inside the closing quotation mark.
records.remedy: "see you next week."

highlights.text: "see you next week".

records.jp: 二本でもいまいち弱い。アンテナのゲージは、パワーを思わせる。
records.en: Two bars and it's still sorta weak. The gauge of the antenna reminds me of power.
comments: Although I can't find that word used to indicate that display, that's what he's obviously talking about. -GHS
records.assessment: The display is a signal-strength meter represented by antenna bars. 'Gauge of the antenna' sounds like a physical measurement of the antenna itself.
records.remedy: The antenna meter makes me think of power.

highlights.text: The gauge of the antenna reminds me of power.

records.jp: だが実際は、潰すまでもなかった。
records.en: But in truth, I didn't even reach the point of waste.
records.assessment: 暇を潰す means to kill or pass time. The source says that in reality there was no need even to kill time; the English instead describes failing to reach an undefined point of waste.
records.remedy: there was no need even to kill time

highlights.text: I didn't even reach the point of waste.

records.jp: 俺は目覚めた。
records.en: I was awake.
comments: In house in the grass, the insect. -GHS
records.assessment: 目覚めた is the event of waking up. 'Was awake' describes a state and removes the transition caused by the cold sensation.
records.remedy: I woke up.

highlights.text: I was awake.

records.jp: 近くに、少女がいた。こいつはみみみ。漢字で書くと美々美。義理の妹だ。
records.en: Next to me was a girl. This is Mimimi. Written in kanji it's beauty, kanji repetition, beauty. She's my Imouto-in-law.
comments: Some of the lines have been consolidated oddly to say the least, and so will my comments since they were mostly built on the fanmade edition's splitting. See CCD1001/B, especially the part where she wants to be a robot: the two are siblings in this way.

Tech term as this part is Taichi having VN delusions. Also see CCZDXC: "quantum theory", which is to say a pseudo-scientific troll that in actuality represents the author's idea of pre-chuuni denpa being still of use by Japanese young adults to escape in the Tolkenian sense from the prison that is the world fallen from the grace of the Christian God, permits it. -GHS
records.assessment: 美々美 is written with 美, the iteration mark 々, and 美; 々 is not itself 'kanji repetition.' 義理の妹 means a non-biological younger sister such as a stepsister, not the impossible English relation 'Imouto-in-law,' which also leaves a common Japanese noun untranslated.
records.remedy: Her name is written 美々美: 'beauty,' the repetition mark, then 'beauty' again. She's my stepsister.

highlights.text: Written in kanji it's beauty, kanji repetition, beauty. She's my Imouto-in-law.

records.jp: 毎朝起こしに来てくれる。
records.en: She comes every day to wake me up.
records.assessment: 毎朝 means every morning, specifically preserving the repeated wake-up routine's time of day. 'Every day' broadens it to any time during the day.
records.remedy: every morning

highlights.text: every day

records.jp: 「お兄ちゃんはみみみがいないと本当にダメなんだからー」
records.en: Mimimi: "When Mimimi isn't here, you really go all bad, Onii-chan!"
comments: Another VN/eroge cliche' that's never quite translated in a standard way, so the reference will have to stay like this until I translate every moege ever and finally have a standardized translation, as well as the undisputed dominion over the Universe that awaits anyone who does so. Seeing CCD1001 and CCD0002, however, this is also literally true. -GHS
records.assessment: 本当にダメ means that he is hopeless or cannot manage without her. 'Go all bad' suggests moral corruption, spoilage, or a change of state rather than dependence.
records.remedy: you're completely hopeless

highlights.text: you really go all bad

records.jp: 俺は苦笑した。
records.en: I made a bitter smile.
records.assessment: 苦笑した means that he gave a wry or rueful smile. English does not normally 'make' a bitter smile, and bitterness suggests resentment rather than awkward amusement.
records.remedy: smiled wryly

highlights.text: made a bitter smile

records.jp: 最近、少しおしゃまになってきたこいつの言動は、昔とは（略）―――
records.en: Lately she's been acting somewhat precocious, but some time ago she(snip)---
comments: Boring descriptions are boring, though the "time ago" usually means the Mansion. Remember Youko is technically also his older sister, besides childhood friend denpa super ninja with a sword she totally didn't steal from Touko. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that her recent, slightly precocious behavior differs from how she used to be before an explicit abridgment. The English changes 'formerly' into an isolated time phrase, leaves 'she' without a predicate, and loses the comparison's subject.
records.remedy: Lately, her words and actions have grown a little precocious; before, she was—(snip)—

highlights.text: Lately she's been acting somewhat precocious, but some time ago she(snip)---

records.jp: 学校に行かないと。自転車を引っ張り出す。
records.en: We have to go to school. I take out the bike.
records.assessment: The subjectless Japanese thought belongs to the first-person narrator: he has to get to school. The English changes this into a shared obligation for both characters.
records.remedy: I have to get to school.

highlights.text: We have to go to school.

records.jp: 「こうして乗せていってもらうの、久しぶりだね」
records.en: Mimimi: "It's been so long since the last time you gave me a ride like this, hasn't it."
records.assessment: The sentence is a tag question and must end with a question mark, not a period.
records.remedy: hasn't it?

highlights.text: hasn't it.

records.jp: 「さいで」
records.en: Taichi: "And all that."
comments: "Indeed" + "(snip)", further hints that this is thrown together in his mind to avoid the boring parts. -GHS
records.assessment: さいで is a clipped colloquial acknowledgment, effectively 'is that so' or 'right.' The English instead refers vaguely to additional omitted matters.
records.remedy: Right.

highlights.text: And all that.

records.jp: 「そうだよ。だいたいあんなヒステリー、俺の好みじゃないっての」
records.en: Taichi: "We are. The point is, I said, that hysteric isn't the kind of girl I like."
records.assessment: The preceding statement is that Taichi and Tōko are nothing to each other; そうだよ affirms that statement. 'We are' literally says the two of them are something, reversing the denial.
records.remedy: That's right.

highlights.text: We are.

records.jp: そんな話、聞いたことない。
records.en: That story, it's something I never heard before.
comments: Very very intentional. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says simply that he has never heard anything like that. The English duplicates the topic with 'that story' and 'it' and uses simple past with 'never' for an experience continuing to the present.
records.remedy: I've never heard anything about that.

highlights.text: That story, it's something I never heard before.

records.jp: 「だからぁ、牽制しあってるの！」
records.en: Mimimi: "I'm telling you, they're restraining themselves!"
comments: Misato's just looking for plausible deniability, Touko for Taichi to come talk to her, Kiri for him to settle things with Yutaka, Miki is just being unserious... even Yusa possibly wanted him. It's all literally true. -GHS
records.assessment: 牽制しあう means the interested parties keep one another in check. The English makes each independently restrain herself and omits the mutual competition.
records.remedy: they're all keeping one another in check

highlights.text: they're restraining themselves

records.jp: それっきり義理の妹は、黙り込んでしまう。
records.en: And after that, my Imouto-in-law sank into silence.
records.assessment: 義理の妹 is a non-biological younger sister, conventionally a stepsister or adoptive younger sister. 'Imouto-in-law' is neither natural English nor an accurate kinship category.
records.remedy: my stepsister

highlights.text: my Imouto-in-law

records.jp: 「あんまり妹とべたべたしてると、シスコンだって思われるわよ」
records.en: Touko: "If you keep staying all glued to that little sister of yours, you'll look like a siscon."
comments: If Tomoki were the protagonist, Misato'd totally be his non-blood-related imouto. -GHS
records.assessment: The English leaves the Japanese abbreviation シスコン untranslated. In ordinary English the accusation is that he is obsessed with or has a complex about his sister.
records.remedy: obsessed with your sister

highlights.text: a siscon

records.jp: 「うるさいわね、聞いたのよ！」
records.en: Touko: "Shut up, I just heard of it!"
records.assessment: 聞いた here means that someone told her about the bicycle ride. 'Heard of it' more often means learning that a thing exists.
records.remedy: heard about it

highlights.text: heard of it

records.jp: 「もきーーーーーーーーーーっ！！！」
records.en: Touko: "MokYYYYYYYYYY!!!"
comments: PCP CCC3004
This has 3 exclamation marks, CCC3004 has two. This is so in every version. -GHSoOCD
records.assessment: The source's stylized cry begins もき, which in standard Hepburn is 'moki.' The English changes the vowel to Y and capitalizes the entire tail rather than representing the prolonged i sound.
records.remedy: Mokiiiiiiiiii!!!

highlights.text: MokYYYYYYYYYY!!!

records.jp: 怒り出した。いつものことである。
records.en: And she fired into a rage. It's like always.
records.assessment: English says that someone 'flew into a rage,' not 'fired into' one, and いつものこと means that this is the usual pattern rather than that it is merely similar to always.
records.remedy: she flew into a rage. It happens all the time.

highlights.text: she fired into a rage. It's like always.

records.jp: 友貴と桜庭。食事をしている。
records.en: Tomoki and Sakuraba. They were eating in the cafeteria.
comments: Yes, hmmm, it needs to be subtly OFF to better BE this SCAMOTIGRIPHICATIONING of NORMALCY hum, yes, yes, yes, hum! -GHSoArtistic
records.assessment: The Japanese says only that Tomoki and Sakuraba are eating. The English invents a cafeteria location and shifts the snapshot into past progressive.
records.remedy: They're eating.

highlights.text: They were eating in the cafeteria.

records.jp: 俺は仲間に加わる。
records.en: I add myself to their Nakama.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi joins his companions. The English uses the reflexive object as though adding an item to a set, leaves 仲間 as untranslated Japanese, and capitalizes it as a proper name.
records.remedy: I join them.

highlights.text: I add myself to their Nakama.

records.jp: 物語には参加してこないが、同性の友人代表という役目を嫌な顔一つせずに担ってくれる、得難い友だった。
records.en: These are difficult friends to obtain, who don't participate to the story, but carry on their back the role of Male Friend Representatives without ever making one nasty face.
comments: This only applies to average VNs, of course, not here where Sakuraba is more important than anyone except probably Taichi, and even then it's only probably. -GHS
records.assessment: The source calls them rare, valuable friends who willingly fill the story's male-friend role despite not otherwise entering the plot. The English says the friends themselves are difficult to obtain, uses the ungrammatical 'participate to,' turns a generic role into a capitalized title, and literalizes burden-bearing and reluctance idioms.
records.remedy: They were rare friends: they never entered the story proper, yet willingly took on the role of representing his male friends.

highlights.text: These are difficult friends to obtain, who don't participate to the story, but carry on their back the role of Male Friend Representatives without ever making one nasty face.

records.jp: 呼びかけると、霧は笑顔で駆け寄ってきた。
records.en: Called out to, Kiri rushed over with a smile.
comments: The 360 version has below-the-knee dolls, like the earlier Deus Ex Chaos P-Mate trial, which work better to give a three-stage distance to character in 16:9 screen size, although they look sorta like crap in 4:3. Unfortunately, I don't have access to the data and can't correctly recreate the effect of Kiri actually coming in closer. -GHS
records.assessment: The narrator calls out, after which Kiri runs over. The English's dangling passive opener makes Kiri the one who is grammatically 'called out to' while suppressing Taichi's action.
records.remedy: When I called out, Kiri rushed over with a smile.

highlights.text: Called out to, Kiri rushed over with a smile.

records.jp: 「先輩は学食ですか？」
records.en: Kiri: "You ate in the cafeteria, Senpai?"
records.assessment: The Japanese asks whether the cafeteria is his usual or current lunch arrangement, not specifically whether he completed one past meal there.
records.remedy: Do you eat at the cafeteria

highlights.text: You ate in the cafeteria

records.jp: そう喜ばれると、こっちまで嬉しくなってくる。
records.en: She's so delighted that she'll make even me become happy.
comments: Still subtly off. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that seeing her delight is already making him happy too. The English turns this into her future causative action and uses the cumbersome phrase 'make me become happy.'
records.remedy: Seeing her so delighted makes me happy too.

highlights.text: She's so delighted that she'll make even me become happy.

records.jp: 「じゃあ今度、作ってきますから」
records.en: Kiri: "Then, next time I will be making some."
records.assessment: The speaker makes a straightforward future promise to prepare food. The future progressive is needlessly indirect and leaves the object as an unexplained 'some.'
records.remedy: I'll make some for you next time

highlights.text: next time I will be making some

records.jp: 「それもそうですね」
records.en: Kiri: "Yes, that is true, but still."
comments: uhmmm what's a hair troll -GHS
records.assessment: それもそうですね simply concedes that his point is true. The English adds 'but still,' implying an unstated counterargument continues.
records.remedy: Yes, that's true.

highlights.text: , but still

records.jp: 人形にほおずりする霧。
records.en: And Kiri goes to rub her cheek on the doll's.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Kiri rubs her cheek against the doll. The English uses the wrong preposition and leaves possessive 'the doll's' without a following noun.
records.remedy: rub her cheek against the doll

highlights.text: rub her cheek on the doll's

records.jp: 曜子姉がいる。彼女は俺の……姉みたいな人だ。
records.en: Youko-nee is there. She's a... big sister-like person to me.
comments: This scene, even in the "real" version, implies Youko is not a misanthrope. But more oddly, Taichi seems to see HER as a Big Sis, instead of Misato in the real (?) story. As said above, it's technically true. -GHS
records.assessment: 曜子 romanizes as Yōko in standard Hepburn. The explanatory phrase copies Japanese noun order into the unnatural 'big sister-like person to me' rather than expressing that she is like an older sister.
records.remedy: Yōko-nee is there. She's... like an older sister to me.

highlights.text: Youko-nee
a... big sister-like person to me

records.jp: 二年生の頃から、早々に部長の立場を引き継がれている。
records.en: She had promptly taken over the President's role from when she was in Second Year.
comments: Although it's not certain she was president back when Gunjou was first recruited, back in the earliest flashbacks in CCC1001/B, Misato has otherwise alway been the president. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that she was handed or assumed the club presidency early, while still a second-year student. The English uses past perfect without a later past anchor, makes 'from when' modify the takeover event, and capitalizes school-year and role common nouns.
records.remedy: She took over as president early, while she was still a second-year.

highlights.text: She had promptly taken over the President's role from when she was in Second Year.

records.jp: お気楽な三年生の人たちはさっさと引退したがっていたし。
records.en: Our carefree Third Years went to retire shortly afterwards.
comments: See CCB0001. Still no clue who these people would be. Perhaps that's the point. -GHS
records.assessment: The senior students wanted to retire as soon as possible, which explains the early handover. The English says they actually proceeded to retire shortly after some unstated event, losing desire and causality.
records.remedy: The easygoing third-years had wanted to retire as quickly as possible.

highlights.text: Our carefree Third Years went to retire shortly afterwards.

records.jp: 彼女は俺を見つけると、子犬みたいに駆け寄ってきた。
records.en: On spotting me, the girl rushed over like a little puppy.
comments: teh gurlz all fall to his feet and he's the sex god to them all. Same as Kiri above, the actual movement is missing due to missing doll. -GHS
records.assessment: The source uses the established pronoun 'she.' Reintroducing Yōko as 'the girl' creates detached narrator distance without source support.
records.remedy: she

highlights.text: the girl

records.jp: 「部活に来てくれたの？」
records.en: Youko: "Did you come for Club?"
records.assessment: 部活 is ordinary club activity, not a proper entity called 'Club.' English normally asks whether someone came for club practice or activities.
records.remedy: for club activities

highlights.text: for Club

records.jp: 「太一、部員なのにな……本当は毎日来ないといけないのにな」
records.en: Youko: "Taichi, but you're a club member... you just have to come by every day!"
records.assessment: Yōko plaintively notes that Taichi is a member and therefore is actually supposed to attend every day. The English's opening 'but' has no prior clause, while 'just have to come by' sounds like a casual instruction and loses the unfulfilled obligation.
records.remedy: Taichi, you're a club member... you're really supposed to come every day...

highlights.text: Taichi, but you're a club member... you just have to come by every day!

records.jp: 「だって、手伝ってくれるって言ってたのに……」
records.en: Youko: "After all... I did tell you to come help us..."
records.assessment: Yōko says that Taichi had promised to help her. The English reverses speaker and subject, making Yōko the one who gave him an instruction.
records.remedy: you said you'd help me

highlights.text: I did tell you to come help us

records.jp: 曜子姉の表情が凍る。
records.en: The expression on Youko-nee's face freezes.
records.assessment: The Japanese name 曜子 romanizes as Yōko in standard Hepburn; 'Youko' is a keyboard-style long-vowel spelling.
records.remedy: Yōko-nee

highlights.text: Youko-nee

records.jp: よくできた彼女。いつも弁当を作ってくれた。けど……
records.en: She was a very capable girl. She always made me a lunch box, hand made. And yet...
comments: Miki can only sort-of cook even after an unknown length of Unreset, see CCC0017. I have no idea why whoever did the script added that Miki voice line, it isn't in the text. This contradicts the Kiri scene above, but it's very likely intentional. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that she always made him boxed lunches. The English says she manufactured the container itself, then adds a stranded, punctuated 'hand made' as if labeling the box.
records.remedy: made me a boxed lunch every day

highlights.text: made me a lunch box, hand made

records.jp: あのときの記憶は、未だに俺を胸を突き刺すことがある。
records.en: My memories of that time still pierce at my heart from time to time.
comments: Well, he'll repay the debt later. -GHS
records.assessment: The source's remembered event sometimes still pierces his chest or heart. English 'pierce' is transitive and does not take 'at,' while plural 'memories' distributes the agency beyond the singular memory named.
records.remedy: The memory of that time still pierces my heart

highlights.text: My memories of that time still pierce at my heart

records.jp: 周囲を見渡して人がいないことを確かめる。
records.en: I make sure that there's no one looking over around us.
comments: See CCA0015B... when it was Youko, as confirmed in CCD1001. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he looks around and confirms nobody is nearby. The English combines incompatible phrasal constructions 'looking over' and 'around us.'
records.remedy: there's no one around us

highlights.text: there's no one looking over around us

records.jp: 曜子姉の顔がパッと輝く。
records.en: Bam, Youko-nee's face went glittering.
comments: Hasekura Youko version/nearly expressionless -GHS
records.assessment: パッと輝く means that Yōko's face suddenly lights up. 'Bam' adds impact-noise imagery, 'went glittering' is nonidiomatic, and the name is not normalized Hepburn.
records.remedy: Yōko-nee's face lit up at once.

highlights.text: Bam, Youko-nee's face went glittering.

records.jp: 「じゃあ……だっこしてくれる？」
records.en: Youko: "Then... could you carry me?"
comments: See CCD1001, told you someone was watching. -GHS
records.assessment: だっこして asks to be held in someone's arms. 'Carry me' focuses on transportation and does not preserve the requested physical affection.
records.remedy: will you hold me

highlights.text: could you carry me

records.jp: うちには両親はいない。
records.en: Neither of my parents are at home.
records.assessment: In formal edited US English, singular 'neither' takes 'is' here.
records.remedy: Neither of my parents is

highlights.text: Neither of my parents are

records.jp: なんだ？　この胸の痛みは？
records.en: The hell? What's this pain in the heart?
records.assessment: 胸の痛み is the pain in his own chest or heart. The English uses a generic definite phrase, which reads as a category rather than a bodily sensation he is experiencing.
records.remedy: What's this pain in my chest?

highlights.text: What's this pain in the heart?

records.jp: 俺……あいつのこと……？
records.en: You mean, I... she, I...?
records.assessment: The Japanese broken thought wonders whether his feeling concerns her. The English inserts 'You mean' without an interlocutor, then strands alternating pronouns without a grammatical relation.
records.remedy: Could it be... I feel that way about her...?

highlights.text: You mean, I... she, I...?

records.jp: 紆余曲折あって、俺たちは仲直りした。
records.en: With twists and with turns we had reconciled.
comments: "There was more but it's boring so let's just CTRL to the end." -GHS
records.assessment: 紆余曲折あって is the idiom 'after various twists and turns.' The English repeats 'with' and uses past perfect without a later past reference point.
records.remedy: After various twists and turns, we reconciled.

highlights.text: With twists and with turns we had reconciled.

records.jp: さあ、みんなの力で、やろう。
records.en: Well then, with all of your strengths, we can do this!
records.assessment: みんなの力 means by combining everyone's strength. English does not normally pluralize strength into each person's separate 'strengths' in this construction.
records.remedy: with everyone's strength

highlights.text: with all of your strengths

records.jp: 俺たちの部活の象徴である……タワー。
records.en: A tower... the symbol of our Club Activities.
comments: See CCC4009. Bet someone thought the tower wasn't a dick. -GHS
records.assessment: 部活 is the club or its activities, not a proper title. Capitalizing 'Club Activities' and making the tower symbolize activities rather than the club produces an artificial label.
records.remedy: the symbol of our club

highlights.text: the symbol of our Club Activities

records.jp: エイリアンは美希でもあった。量子力学的にそうだった。
records.en: The alien was also Miki. Quantum Mechanically so.
records.assessment: The adverbial phrase is not a proper name and should not be capitalized; as a sentence fragment it also needs idiomatic ordering.
records.remedy: So it was, quantum-mechanically.

highlights.text: Quantum Mechanically so.

records.jp: だけどエイリアンは敵だ。悲しいことだ。
records.en: However, aliens are Enemy. That's so sad.
comments: See CCB0018. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese identifies this singular alien as an enemy. The English generalizes to plural aliens, omits the article required before 'enemy,' and capitalizes the common noun.
records.remedy: the alien is an enemy

highlights.text: aliens are Enemy

records.jp: だから殺すか殺されるかなのだった。
records.en: Therefore, it was a thing of kill or be killed.
records.assessment: The Japanese concludes that the situation was kill or be killed. The English inserts the empty nominal frame 'a thing of,' which is not idiomatic with this fixed expression.
records.remedy: it was kill or be killed

highlights.text: it was a thing of kill or be killed

records.jp: さらに時は流れ、アンテナは成仏した。
records.en: With the further flowing of time, the antenna achieved its highest purpose.
comments: It's an odd "to attain" that's used in the sense of "entering Nirvana", as in, to attain the kind of peace that's wished to the dead. It's less odd when considering it's the Tower of Babel. -GHS
records.assessment: 成仏した literally says that the antenna passed on or attained Buddhahood, a comic personification of its end. The English replaces that joke with the unrelated claim that it fulfilled an ultimate purpose.
records.remedy: the antenna passed on

highlights.text: the antenna achieved its highest purpose

records.jp: 夢にまで見た、他愛ない部活動。
records.en: Until I have that dream, about silly innocent club activities,
comments: PCP CCA0030
records.assessment: The Japanese fragment names the harmless club activities he had dreamed of. The English changes the already dreamed-of object into a future condition 'until I have that dream' and leaves 'about' without a governing construction.
records.remedy: The harmless club activities I had dreamed of.

highlights.text: Until I have that dream, about silly innocent club activities,

records.jp: 普通のガクセーらしい日常。
records.en: about an ordinary life as if ordinary students.
comments: PCP CCA0030
Even in absolute madness he doesn't stop, as it's been said about the diaries. -GHS
records.assessment: The source names the everyday life typical of an ordinary student. The English leaves an 'about' fragment, mismatches singular life with plural students, and turns actual student life into an 'as if' resemblance.
records.remedy: An ordinary student's everyday life.

highlights.text: about an ordinary life as if ordinary students.

records.jp: 人としての思い出。
records.en: Memories of being as a person.
records.assessment: 人として means 'as a human being' or 'as a person.' Inserting 'being as' creates a malformed double copular construction.
records.remedy: Memories of living as a person.

highlights.text: Memories of being as a person.

records.jp: せっかくだから俺は二度寝するぜ。
records.en: Been so hard now, so I'm gonna go back to sleep!
records.assessment: せっかくだから means that since the opportunity or situation presents itself, he may as well go back to sleep. The English invents that something has 'been so hard' and omits a subject and finite auxiliary from that clause.
records.remedy: Since I'm here, I may as well go back to sleep.

highlights.text: Been so hard now, so I'm gonna go back to sleep!

records.jp: そして回想シーンに入ることにした。
records.en: And then I ended to dive into a Recollection Scene.
comments: Kaisou, precise exact term used for the sex scene review, you'll see it in scripts with sex scenes. His dreams are flashbacks, of course. But which is the truth and which is the fake... well in this case the answer is both, so it's not that complicated. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he decided to enter a flashback scene. English does not use 'ended to' for deciding, 'dive' changes neutral entry into a dramatic plunge, and 'Recollection Scene' is an invented proper label.
records.remedy: I decided to enter a flashback scene.

highlights.text: I ended to dive into a Recollection Scene.

records.jp: 見里先輩は『みみ』であり『みみみ』であり『美々美』である。
records.en: Misato-senpai was Mimi, Mimimi, and Beauty kanji repetition beauty.
comments: Due to Insaininess. -GHS
records.assessment: 美々美 is the name Mimimi written with 美, the iteration mark 々, and 美. The English treats 'kanji repetition' as an unmarked word inside the name and provides no grammatical explanation.
records.remedy: Mimimi written as 美々美: 'beauty,' the iteration mark, and 'beauty'

highlights.text: Beauty kanji repetition beauty

records.jp: これ以前の記憶は判然としない。
records.en: My memories of before this are indefinite.
comments: Those are memories of the Training Camp, see below. -GHS
records.assessment: 判然としない means that the memories are unclear or indistinct. 'Indefinite' means not fixed in extent or duration and does not describe blurred recall.
records.remedy: are indistinct

highlights.text: are indefinite

records.jp: すでにモードが違ってしまっている。
records.en: My Mode is already very much wrong,
comments: Specific term, which makes even more sense considering it originally was part of the Miki route: Taichi doesn't have a Murderous Maniac mode according to her. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that his operating mode has already changed. The English judges it 'wrong,' adds the intensifier 'very much,' and capitalizes mode as though it were a named system state.
records.remedy: My mode has already changed completely.

highlights.text: My Mode is already very much wrong,

records.jp: 今まで積み重ねてきた知識と経験で、俺は擬態している。
records.en: I am camouflaging, using the knowledge and the experience accumulated until now.
comments: He is camouflaging himself with the experience he's gathered from Japanese pop art, anime and VNs especially. Indeed, but the camouflage is his murderous self! What a spoiler. -GHS
records.assessment: 擬態している means that he is mimicking or presenting an adaptive outward form. English 'camouflage' is normally transitive or reflexive here and cannot stand as 'I am camouflaging' without an object.
records.remedy: I am disguising myself

highlights.text: I am camouflaging

records.jp: 息切れしている。それにひどく緊張しているようだ。
records.en: Panting, short breath. Furthermore, she seems to be horribly tense.
records.assessment: The source says that she is out of breath and also extremely tense. The English duplicates breathlessness in a comma fragment and uses the formal discourse connector 'Furthermore' for immediate physical observation.
records.remedy: She's out of breath. She also

highlights.text: Panting, short breath. Furthermore

records.jp: 鬼交替のチャンス。
records.en: A demon of a chance to change who is It.
comments: Although not the identical term, the one Taichi uses above is nearly the same double meaning for "playing tag" and "chase" he uses against Kiri in CCC0011C. The 鬼 demon here is the It in the game of tag; tag itself is most often found as 'onigokko', lit. "playing demon", which is where it comes from. Of course, this is also meant literally, so this works... or given it's typical of Taichi to hide the most innocuous of things in the most apparently hideous of monstrosities (and NOT viceversa), is it really? -GHS
records.assessment: 鬼交替 refers to switching who is 'it' in a chasing game. The English literalizes 鬼 as 'demon,' turning it into an intensifier, and uses the nonidiomatic phrase 'a chance to change who is It.'
records.remedy: A chance to switch who's it.

highlights.text: A demon of a chance to change who is It.

records.jp: 気がつくと俺はナイフを『そうび』していた。
records.en: And when I noticed, I had a knife 『equipped』.
comments: RPG terms. He just switched from VNs to RPGs, so blatant! See CCX0001. -GHS
records.assessment: The game-interface joke quotes the verb 'equipped,' but English requires either 'I had equipped a knife' or 'a knife equipped on me.' The translation retains Japanese object-plus-state ordering.
records.remedy: I had 『equipped』 a knife.

highlights.text: I had a knife 『equipped』.

records.jp: なんて魅力的なんだ先輩。
records.en: Why are you so demonically attractive, my Senpai.
comments: My my, is that another Higurashi reference I spot? 魅 is the first kanji in Mion's name, and the whole point of her name is that it has the kanji for Demon in it. It'd fit in the It/Demon pun above, as well as be further hints that the Mion/Shion confusion applies here. ToF is the Higurashi-est that Cross Channel gets, and as I'm fairly sure that Ryukishi got more than a few hints as to the meaning of Channel, I suspect Tanaka also had a hint or three about planned Higurashi event. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese simply exclaims how attractive Senpai is. 'Demonically' is invented, and possessive 'my Senpai' is not idiomatic direct address.
records.remedy: How incredibly attractive you are, Senpai.

highlights.text: demonically attractive, my Senpai

records.jp: あ、この場面、既視感。
records.en: Ah, this scene setting... it gives me paramnesia.
comments: See CCC3008. Told you it's his medical condition. Now begins him repeating the same stuff regardless of the situation, which is a typical behavior more or less of everyone in the cast. See CCC0045A for more, this may be inherited from his mother. How much repetition was there in those first days, maybe months, of his life? -GHS
records.assessment: 既視感 is the familiar feeling of déjà vu. 'Paramnesia' is a broad clinical category of memory distortion and does not naturally name this immediate recognition.
records.remedy: déjà vu

highlights.text: it gives me paramnesia

records.jp: そうだ、義理の妹との通学シーンだ。
records.en: Right, that scene where I go to school with my Imouto-in-law.
records.assessment: 義理の妹 means a non-biological younger sister, not an 'Imouto-in-law.' The English term is both untranslated and a nonexistent kinship category.
records.remedy: my stepsister

highlights.text: my Imouto-in-law

records.jp: 朝起こしに来て、軽口を叩いて、朝食を作ってくれて、ほれぼれするタイミングで自転車の後部座席に乗ってくるのだ、義理の妹というやつは。
records.en: That is, my Imouto-in-law that wakes me up in the morning, and cracks jokes at me, and makes me breakfast, and with charmful timing rides on the backseat of the bicycle.
comments: ...meaning she comes around too late? Maybe it's the boobs. Sorry: I mean to say, OF COURSE it's the boobs. -GHS
records.assessment: The source jokingly defines the stock stepsister who wakes him, trades banter, makes breakfast, and mounts the bicycle at an entrancingly perfect moment. The English uses a nonexistent kinship term, makes 'that' refer to a person, repeats conjunctions without parallel structure, invents 'charmful,' and uses 'rides on' for mounting the seat.
records.remedy: the classic stepsister: she wakes you in the morning, trades banter, makes breakfast, and climbs onto the bicycle's back seat with enchanting timing

highlights.text: my Imouto-in-law that wakes me up in the morning, and cracks jokes at me, and makes me breakfast, and with charmful timing rides on the backseat of the bicycle

records.jp: ノイズのないクリアな記憶。
records.en: Recollections that are Clear and devoid of Noise.
comments: Intentionally odd. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese gives one clear, noise-free memory. The English pluralizes it and capitalizes two ordinary descriptive nouns as unexplained technical categories.
records.remedy: A clear memory, free of noise.

highlights.text: Recollections that are Clear and devoid of Noise.

records.jp: 「なんか……結構弾力が……」
records.en: Taichi: "Really... so much elasticity, it's..."
comments: CP above
records.assessment: The broken observation concerns the pronounced springiness he feels. The English begins with an unsupported 'Really,' uses the technical mass noun 'elasticity' in casual speech, and strands 'it's' without a complement.
records.remedy: There's... quite a lot of spring to them...

highlights.text: Really... so much elasticity, it's...

records.jp: 脇に垂れた先輩の頭部が、電信柱を叩いた。
records.en: Senpai's head, hanging off the flank, smacked into a telephone pole.
comments: SYMBOLISM!!! Also what a coincidence... -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Senpai's head, dangling off to the side, strikes a utility pole. 'The flank' normally means the side of a body or formation and gives no idiomatic spatial relation to the bicycle.
records.remedy: dangling off to the side

highlights.text: hanging off the flank

records.jp: そのペインはダイレクトに俺に伝わってきた。
records.en: That Payn was transmitted to me in a Direct way.
comments: Still intentionally odd. -GHS
records.assessment: The source deliberately emphasizes the loanwords ペイン and ダイレクト, but standard transliteration would still yield 'pain' and 'direct.' The English invents 'Payn,' capitalizes both common words, and expands the adverb into the mechanical phrase 'in a Direct way.'
records.remedy: That pain was transmitted directly to me.

highlights.text: That Payn was transmitted to me in a Direct way.

records.jp: 「そうだよ」
records.en: Taichi: "We are."
comments: PCP above
records.assessment: The preceding claim is that Taichi and Tōko are nothing to one another, and そうだよ affirms that claim. 'We are' states the opposite: that they are something together.
records.remedy: That's right.

highlights.text: We are.

records.jp: 冬子。
records.en: Touko.
records.assessment: The Japanese name 冬子 romanizes as Tōko in standard Hepburn. 'Touko' is a keyboard-style long-vowel spelling.
records.remedy: Tōko

highlights.text: Touko

records.en: Touko: "Taichi...? What... is that... blood...?"
comments: See CCD0023. Is that error intentional? -GHS
