records.assessment: The speaker's name should be normalized to Tōko in Hepburn. Her shocked question asks about the blood she sees; English 'what is that blood' treats it as an unidentified type or object rather than asking what happened.
records.remedy: Tōko: "Taichi...? What's... that blood...?"

highlights.text: Touko: "Taichi...? What... is that... blood...?"

records.jp: 「何言ってるの？　その血……いったい……？」
records.en: Touko: "What are you talking about? That's blood... what the devil...?"
records.assessment: The speaker name should be Tōko under standard Hepburn. The source asks what he is saying and what the blood is, while 'what the devil' adds an archaic oath and still leaves the blood without a coherent question.
records.remedy: Tōko: "What are you saying? That blood... what happened...?"

highlights.text: Touko: "What are you talking about? That's blood... what the devil...?"

records.jp: 「ちょっと、嘘でしょ……しっかり、してよ」
records.en: Touko: "Come on, you're kidding me... steadfast now!"
comments: Dammit, it's Channelkakushi-hen scenario and I can't keep that "lie" literal. See CCD2002 for the point, CCX0001 for the first irony. -GHSob
records.assessment: しっかりして is an urgent appeal to pull oneself together or stay alert, not an instruction to become steadfast. The speaker name also requires Hepburn Tōko.
records.remedy: Tōko: "No... this can't be real... pull yourself together."

highlights.text: Touko: "Come on, you're kidding me... steadfast now!"

records.jp: ナイフを取り出す。
records.en: Take out a knife.
records.assessment: The first-person narration says that Taichi takes out a knife. Without a subject, the English reads as an imperative.
records.remedy: I take out a knife.

highlights.text: Take out a knife.

records.jp: 近寄る。
records.en: Approach.
records.assessment: The Japanese fragment continues Taichi's action. The bare English verb reads as a command rather than narration.
records.remedy: I approach.

highlights.text: Approach.

records.jp: 友貴と桜庭。俺は二人の背後から近づく。
records.en: Tomoki and Sakuraba. I approach from their back.
comments: In a crowded cafeteria? No, in a deserted cafeteria? When are these two ever eating together??? Metaphorically, he'll backstab them. Well, literally-metaphorically-uhm you either get it or it doesn't get clearer, that's it. -GHS
records.assessment: English says that someone approaches two people 'from behind,' not from the singular physical location 'their back.'
records.remedy: I approach them from behind.

highlights.text: I approach from their back.

records.jp: 「ははは、そうかそうか」
records.en: Taichi: "Hahahah, that's right, that's so right."
comments: CP above
records.assessment: そうかそうか acknowledges new information, roughly 'I see, I see.' 'That's right' twice instead makes Taichi affirm that the others' inaudible words are correct.
records.remedy: I see, I see

highlights.text: that's right, that's so right

records.jp: 友貴がうめき声を漏らす。
records.en: Tomoki let out a groaning voice.
records.assessment: English conventionally says that someone 'lets out a groan.' The source names the sound, not a distinct voice characterized as groaning.
records.remedy: let out a groan

highlights.text: let out a groaning voice

records.jp: 呼びかけると、霧は逃げた。
records.en: Called out to, Kiri ran away.
comments: PCP above
records.assessment: The narrator calls to Kiri, after which she flees. The dangling passive opener suppresses his action and grammatically makes Kiri merely the recipient of an unspecified call.
records.remedy: When I called out, Kiri ran away.

highlights.text: Called out to, Kiri ran away.

records.jp: 追いかける。
records.en: Chase.
comments: No 'tag' side meanings here. -GHS
records.assessment: The source continues first-person action. The English bare verb is an imperative rather than narration.
records.remedy: I chase her.

highlights.text: Chase.

records.jp: 走る。走る。
records.en: Run. Run.
records.assessment: The Japanese fragment narrates continued running. The English bare verbs read as two commands.
records.remedy: I run. I run.

highlights.text: Run. Run.

records.jp: 「だ、誰かっ！」
records.en: Kiri: "A-, anybody!"
records.assessment: Kiri is calling for help from an unspecified person. English uses 'somebody' or 'someone' as the standalone cry; 'anybody' normally requires a question or negative environment.
records.remedy: S-, somebody!

highlights.text: A-, anybody!

records.jp: 「殺されるっ、誰かっ！！」
records.en: Kiri: "I'll be killed, anybody!!!"
comments: But no one exists for her, that's one of her big plot points. It's telling she'd still call out. -GHS
records.assessment: The source is an immediate cry that someone is going to kill her, followed by another call for help. The English uses future passive as a prediction, joins it by comma to the unidiomatic cry 'anybody,' and omits the attacking agent implicit in the threat.
records.remedy: He's going to kill me! Somebody!!

highlights.text: I'll be killed, anybody!!!

records.jp: ナイフを取り出す。二本だ。
records.en: Take out knives. Two.
comments: Why does he have two now? Because two knives is ni-hon *badum-tish*? And how is this related with the now-two flashbangs? (Probably isn't.) -GHS
records.assessment: The narrator takes out two knives. The English reads as an instruction, omits the article, and strands the count as a separate verbless fragment without the Japanese's clear backward reference.
records.remedy: I take out two knives.

highlights.text: Take out knives. Two.

records.jp: 両手にぶらさげて走る。
records.en: Run while dangling them from both hands.
records.assessment: The narrator runs with the two knives dangling, one from each hand. The English reads as a command and 'from both hands' can mean that both hands jointly hold each knife.
records.remedy: I run with one dangling from each hand.

highlights.text: Run while dangling them from both hands.

records.jp: 追いかける。廊下を駆ける二人。
records.en: Chase. Two people running in the corridors.
comments: PCP above
records.assessment: The source uses clipped narration but still describes the narrator chasing and the pair racing down one corridor. English 'Chase' reads as an imperative, while the second fragment has neither a determiner nor finite verb and pluralizes the corridor.
records.remedy: I chase her. Two people race down the corridor.

highlights.text: Chase. Two people running in the corridors.

records.jp: 一気に距離が縮む。
records.en: I shrink the distance in a single gulp.
comments: PCP CCC0011C

And where's Nanaka/Youko/self restraint to keep him in check? Well, there's the Of This World thing, I guess, meaning this Taichi doesn't have a soul and is little more than a robot regardless. THIS is what it means for him not to be Taichi proper. -GHS
records.assessment: 一気に means all at once or in one burst. The English literalizes the energy of the idiom as swallowing 'in a single gulp,' creating an impossible physical image.
records.remedy: I close the distance in one burst.

highlights.text: I shrink the distance in a single gulp.

records.jp: 見下ろす。
records.en: Look down,
records.assessment: The fragment narrates Taichi looking down. The bare English verb reads as a command and is incorrectly linked by comma to the next independent fragment.
records.remedy: I look down.

highlights.text: Look down,

records.jp: これなら、ナイフを使わずに済む。
records.en: With this, I can end things without using the knives.
records.assessment: The source says only that the present situation means he can manage without using the knives. 'End things' adds a specific final outcome not expressed in the sentence itself.
records.remedy: I won't have to use the knives after all.

highlights.text: I can end things without using the knives.

records.jp: 俺はのしかかる。
records.en: I lean forwards.
records.assessment: のしかかる means to loom over, press down on, or climb on top of someone. Merely leaning forward removes the physical imposition central to the verb.
records.remedy: I climb on top of her.

highlights.text: I lean forwards.

records.jp: どこかでガラスの割れる音がした。
records.en: The sound of glass being cracked came from somewhere.
comments: PCP CCC0101
asdfcxpiovjdoaih symbolgasm!!! -GHS
records.assessment: ガラスの割れる音 is the sound of glass breaking or shattering. 'Being cracked' suggests a controlled fracture or single crack and weakens the audible break.
records.remedy: glass shattering

highlights.text: glass being cracked

records.jp: 床に頬をくっつける霧。
records.en: And Kiri goes to stick her cheek on the floor.
comments: PCP above
records.assessment: The Japanese snapshot says that Kiri presses or rests her cheek against the floor. 'Goes to stick' adds an attempted action and uses the adhesive-sounding verb 'stick' with the wrong preposition.
records.remedy: presses her cheek to the floor

highlights.text: goes to stick her cheek on the floor

records.jp: 曜子ちゃんがいる。

records.assessment: 曜子 requires Hepburn Yōko. The Japanese uses present scene-setting narration, while the English shifts to past tense.
records.remedy: Yōko-chan is there.

highlights.text: Youko-chan was there.

records.en: Youko: "Taichi..."
records.assessment: The Japanese name 曜子 romanizes as Yōko in standard Hepburn; 'Youko' is a keyboard-style long-vowel spelling.

records.en: Youko: "Yes... you can't come back anymore."
comments: Consider the new CCA0022A and this part becomes of fundamental importance: he's redoing here what he did there, but patterned over the failure of the camp. And he murders Youko as she, terrified of him, tells him he can't come back. Did she understand what she had done in those last few minutes? -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese name 曜子 romanizes as Yōko in standard Hepburn; 'Youko' is a keyboard-style long-vowel spelling.

records.jp: 「あなたも長くない……人として生きる力さえ失って……死に引き寄せられるか、偶然に殺されるか」
records.en: Youko: "You don't have long either... you lost even the strength to live as a person... will you be drawn to death, or will you be killed by coincidence?"
comments: This is a very Nanaka thing to say. Notice that Youko here never uses "Taichi" as pronoun for him as she usually does, always "anata", which is uncharacteristic. Attracted to death is maybe what he does in the Kiri route, when he refuses to follow Kiri and doesn't have the Youko scene; considering Youko is the first killed by coincidence in Miki's route, that's a very odd thing to say for her. If she's been dead all along, these may be her last words. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese describes an ongoing loss and two likely ends: being drawn toward death or dying through some chance event. The English shifts the loss to a completed past, asks a direct future question, and says an abstract coincidence itself will kill him.
records.remedy: you're losing even the strength to live as a person... you'll either be drawn toward death or die in some chance accident.

highlights.text: you lost even the strength to live as a person... will you be drawn to death, or will you be killed by coincidence?

records.assessment: The Japanese name 曜子 romanizes as Yōko in standard Hepburn; 'Youko' is a keyboard-style long-vowel spelling.

records.jp: 「なら……抱きしめて。優しくして」

comments: This still means to have sex & to hug. I don't remember if I've pointed it out, but since every third word in Japanese means something sexual, it's sort of a tired gag at this point. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese name 曜子 romanizes as Yōko in standard Hepburn; 'Youko' is a keyboard-style long-vowel spelling.
records.remedy: Yōko

highlights.text: Youko

records.jp: 曜子ちゃんは声もなく泣く。
records.en: Youko-chan cries while making no cry.
comments: Koe mo naku naku. See CCD5001, same behavior. -GHS
records.assessment: The name should be normalized to Yōko. 声もなく泣く is the idiom 'cry silently'; 'making no cry' is an unnatural double use of cry as both verb and count noun.
records.remedy: Yōko-chan cries silently.

highlights.text: Youko-chan cries while making no cry.

records.jp: 強く、首をかき抱いた。
records.en: I embraced her neck, with strength.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he wraps his arms tightly around her neck. English does not normally 'embrace a neck,' and the comma phrase 'with strength' is a calque rather than the adverbial force of the act.
records.remedy: I wrapped my arms tightly around her neck.

highlights.text: I embraced her neck, with strength.

records.jp: そうしたら……きっと寂しくない。
records.en: If I do... I'm sure it won't be lonely.
records.assessment: The implied experiencer of 寂しくない is Taichi: if he builds the tower and calls out, he surely will not feel lonely. The English makes an unspecified 'it' experience loneliness.
records.remedy: I won't feel lonely

highlights.text: it won't be lonely

records.jp: 一人でも、組み立ててみせる。
records.en: I shall try to build it, even if alone.
records.assessment: 組み立ててみせる expresses determination to complete the construction despite being alone. 'Shall try' weakens that resolve into an attempt and shifts the force into formal diction.
records.remedy: I'll build it, even if I have to do it alone.

highlights.text: I shall try to build it, even if alone.

records.jp: そして世界中に呼びかける。
records.en: And then, we shall be calling out to the whole Earth.
comments: Same as above, similar meaning but not quite the same terms as Gen 11 (全地). Still using NIV. -GHS
records.assessment: The source says that Taichi will call out across the whole world. The English changes the speaker from 'I' to 'we,' uses an unnecessary future progressive, and substitutes the planet as a physical object for people throughout the world.
records.remedy: I'll call out to the whole world.

highlights.text: we shall be calling out to the whole Earth

records.jp: 帰宅途中、田崎による。
records.en: En route back home, after visiting Tasaki.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that on the way home he stops by Tasaki. The English turns the stop into a completed event after which no main action follows, leaving a prepositional fragment.
records.remedy: On the way home, I stop by Tasaki.

highlights.text: En route back home, after visiting Tasaki.

records.jp: 作業ははかどった。
records.en: Work has progressed.
records.assessment: The Japanese reports that the work went well or made progress during the completed visit. The present perfect leaves the time frame open despite the preceding past event.
records.remedy: The work went well.

highlights.text: Work has progressed.

records.jp: だが世界が崩壊して久しいのに、ツケなんて無意味じゃないか？
records.en: Though it's been long since the world has had its downfall, so isn't credit meaningless?
comments: So everyone is gone. Except Sakakibara's still around. Sure! -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese asks whether running a tab is meaningless when the world has already been collapsed for so long. The English combines incompatible 'though' and 'so,' uses the nonidiomatic 'had its downfall,' and leaves the tag without a subject.
records.remedy: But if the world's been gone for so long, isn't running a tab meaningless?

highlights.text: Though it's been long since the world has had its downfall, so isn't credit meaningless?

records.jp: 「ね、曜子ちゃん？」
records.en: Taichi: "Isn't it, Youko-chan?"
records.assessment: The name requires Hepburn Yōko. The Japanese softly seeks agreement after the preceding proposition; English requires 'Right?' or a full tag such as 'isn't it?' rather than fronting the tag before the address.
records.remedy: Right, Yōko-chan?

highlights.text: Isn't it, Youko-chan?

records.jp: 彼女が微笑んでいる。あたたかい気持ちになる。
records.en: The girl is smiling. It makes me feel so warm.
comments: And right after killing her to produce the antenna, Youko is a literal ghost, no more real than Nanaka. No other character gets this treatment. -GHS
records.assessment: The source uses the established pronoun 'she.' Calling her 'the girl' reintroduces detached distance in a close first-person observation.
records.remedy: She is smiling.

highlights.text: The girl is smiling.

records.jp: 鬱陶しい。すぐ消す。
records.en: Gloom. It vanishes soon.
comments: Positive emotion -> negative emotion because of heavy sense of guilt. -GHSigmund
records.assessment: 鬱陶しい is Taichi's judgment that the warm feeling is annoying, after which he immediately erases or suppresses it. The English changes annoyance into gloom and makes the feeling vanish by itself at some future point.
records.remedy: Annoying. I erase it at once.

highlights.text: Gloom. It vanishes soon.

records.jp: その感情を判別することは、今の俺にはできない。
records.en: Distinguishing which emotion did that is impossible for the me as I am now.
comments: See CCX0001. Interesting. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that his present self cannot identify the emotion. The English inserts an unexplained causal action 'did that,' uses an awkward gerund subject with predicate inversion, and calques 今の俺 as 'the me as I am now.'
records.remedy: As I am now, I can't identify that emotion.

highlights.text: Distinguishing which emotion did that is impossible for the me as I am now.

records.jp: もうじき暗くなる。心もろともに。
records.en: Soon it shall be dark outside. To be one with the heart.
comments: Where is it crawling now? Huh? WHERE? IN YOUR SKIN, that's where it's crawling, BITCH. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that darkness will soon fall, taking his heart with it. The English creates an infinitive fragment about becoming one with an unspecified heart and uses elevated 'shall' for immediate narration.
records.remedy: Soon it will be dark—my heart along with it.

highlights.text: Soon it shall be dark outside. To be one with the heart.

records.jp: 熱による影響、あとで調べておこう。塔はとても天に近いのだから。
records.en: Will leave investigating if it's the influence of this heat later. The tower is getting pretty close to the heavens after all.
comments: Either the sun's... or his fever. That's the term used even in the Bible. ...wait, is this a tower, or is it Prometheus? A new Prometheus??? Well, the tower WAS frankensteined together. *badum dish* -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi resolves to investigate the effects of heat later and notes that the tower is very close to the sky. The English omits the first-person subject, turns the object into an indirect yes-or-no clause, and says the tower is progressively moving closer.
records.remedy: I'll investigate the effects of the heat later. The tower is very close to the heavens, after all.

highlights.text: Will leave investigating if it's the influence of this heat later. The tower is getting pretty close to the heavens after all.

records.jp: 電波代はいらない。青春に金なんて必要ないんだ。
records.en: This kind of "electromagnetic generation" needs no fees. No such thing as money needed for one's adolescence.
comments: This is where the confusion between EM waves and Denpa becomes a little hard to follow.
records.assessment: 電波代 means charges for radio transmission, not electromagnetic generation. The source then jokes that youth needs no money; the English converts it into the ungrammatical existential phrase 'no such thing as money needed' and abstracts youth into 'one's adolescence.'
records.remedy: There are no transmission fees. Youth doesn't need money.

highlights.text: This kind of "electromagnetic generation" needs no fees. No such thing as money needed for one's adolescence.

records.jp: 悪しき商業主義は滅びろ。このタワー型のが完成すれば！
records.en: Evil commercialism can go get annihilated. For once I have completed making this take a tower shape...!
comments: Evil Taichi, in his Typical Moege delusional state, speaks out against the Evils of Commerce. The contempt Tanaka has for this kind of writing is about as transparent as mine. Same word at times used for mankind in the main story. Second part is specific, since he's not constructing a "broadcast tower" in that sense. -GHS
records.assessment: The source curses commercialism and exclaims about completing the tower-shaped structure. 'Can go get annihilated' is an unidiomatic permission construction, while 'For once' begins a subordinate clause that never reaches a main clause and misreads completion as a temporal condition.
records.remedy: To hell with commercialism. Once this tower-shaped thing is complete...!

highlights.text: Evil commercialism can go get annihilated. For once I have completed making this take a tower shape...!

records.jp: 電話みたいに『みかか』することはない。
records.en: There's no Denpa equivalent of the Mikaka (NTT).
comments: www.ntt.co.jp - it's written Mikaka because that's what typing NTT comes out like on a Kana input keyboard. This is the reading key for Miki's text, more below when this bout of insanity is described. More importantly, this is the reading key for the damn 'yu', see CCX0001, and more. Laterally it's all about differences of language and Babel, still. ...though I guess that by requiring this halfway language in a translation, the very need for which can be blamed on Babel, we're now into enough meta that the threat to the perduring existence of the space-time continuum have surpassed the Nyan Combined With Meow level. -GHS
records.assessment: The source jokes that this system will not incur NTT-like charges, using みかか as keyboard-code slang for NTT. The English leaves both 'Denpa' and 'Mikaka' as unexplained pseudo-proper terms and turns a fee into an 'equivalent' organization.
records.remedy: There'll be no NTT-style charges.

highlights.text: There's no Denpa equivalent of the Mikaka (NTT).

records.jp: 無料配信だ。
records.en: Transmitting those is free of charge.
records.assessment: 無料配信だ declares the broadcast or distribution itself free. The English invents a plural object 'those' with no antecedent and uses a gerund action rather than the free service.
records.remedy: It's a free broadcast.

highlights.text: Transmitting those is free of charge.

records.jp: 美希のところに行くことにした。
records.en: I ended up going to Miki's place.
records.assessment: ことにした states a decision to go, not an unintended result that he 'ended up' doing. The English also shifts the immediate narration into past.
records.remedy: I decide to go to Miki.

highlights.text: I ended up going to Miki's place.

records.jp: 俺もそっと屋上に出た。
records.en: I also silently came out on the rooftop.
comments: This seems to be an expansion of what happens at the end of that first part similar to what the second was to the first. -GHS
records.assessment: English goes or steps out onto a rooftop, not 'out on' it in this motion construction.
records.remedy: stepped quietly out onto the rooftop

highlights.text: came out on the rooftop

records.jp: 美希は『塔』の前に立っている。
records.en: Miki was standing in front of the "tower".
records.assessment: The Japanese uses immediate present scene-setting and marks the tower with Japanese title brackets. The English shifts to past and uses straight quotation marks; the house style calls for typographic quotation marks when reproducing the scare-quote effect.
records.remedy: Miki is standing in front of the “tower.”

highlights.text: Miki was standing in front of the "tower".

records.jp: 「ぴいわいえふ？　なに？」
records.en: Taichi: "To imi sachi? What?
comments: What Miki says is the text that comes out if trying to write the Japanese text on a Kana keyboard, but outputting in Western characters.
P=se, Y=n, [F=pa E=i
where [ activates the Japanese accent that turns は ha into ぱ pa. GIS "kana keyboard" for a reference, though I guess it's useless if you can't read kana. -GHS
records.assessment: The source's heard syllables are ぴいわいえふ, approximately 'pī-wai-efu' under Hepburn; the English repeats a different prior string. It also opens but never closes the dialogue quotation mark.
records.remedy: Pī-wai-efu? What?"

highlights.text: To imi sachi? What?

records.jp: 人じゃない？確かにその可能性はある。
records.en: Is this not a person? The possibility exists, definitely.
records.assessment: The Japanese thought is 'Not human? That's certainly possible.' The English's 'this' treats a known individual as an object, while sentence-final 'definitely' awkwardly certifies only the existence of a possibility.
records.remedy: Not human? That's certainly possible.

highlights.text: Is this not a person? The possibility exists, definitely.

records.jp: 「さては……地球外生命体だな」
records.en: Taichi: "If so... that's an Extraterrestrial Life Form."
records.assessment: The phrase is a common noun, not a formal titled category, and should not be capitalized internally.
records.remedy: an extraterrestrial life-form

highlights.text: an Extraterrestrial Life Form

records.jp: エイリアンだ！
records.en: It's an Alien!
records.assessment: 'Alien' is a common noun in this exclamation and has no source-based reason for capitalization.
records.remedy: an alien

highlights.text: an Alien

records.jp: 俺が見抜いたのを見抜いたのか、美希の顔から笑みが消えた。
records.en: Perhaps having seen through me having seen through her, the smile vanished from Miki's face
comments: PCP above
Yeah, it doubled. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese plays on 見抜く twice but means that she may have realized he had seen through her. The English nests two progressive gerunds into an unreadable opener and omits final punctuation.
records.remedy: Perhaps she realized that I had seen through her; the smile vanished from Miki's face.

highlights.text: Perhaps having seen through me having seen through her, the smile vanished from Miki's face

records.jp: 「だが……おまえがもし改心し、部活に加わるというのなら……」
records.en: Taichi: "However... should you reform yourself, and come join into our Club..."
records.assessment: English says 'join our club,' not 'join into' it, and club is not a proper name requiring capitalization.
records.remedy: come join our club

highlights.text: come join into our Club

records.jp: シーツを取ると、未完成の『塔』が出てきた。
records.en: I take off the sheet and the incomplete "Tower" came into sight.
records.assessment: The English mixes present and past within one coordinated event. Removing the sheet reveals the structure; it does not independently come into sight, and tower is not a titled proper name.
records.remedy: I remove the sheet, revealing the unfinished “tower.”

highlights.text: I take off the sheet and the incomplete "Tower" came into sight.

records.jp: みんなの力が一つになった逸品だ。
records.en: This is the masterpiece that came from making the strengths of everybody into one.
comments: See CCC3002, same word he uses for his uhmmm dick. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese calls it a masterpiece created by combining everyone's strength. The English pluralizes strength and uses the cumbersome causative nominalization 'making ... into one.'
records.remedy: made by bringing everyone's strength together

highlights.text: came from making the strengths of everybody into one

records.jp: アンテナの形にするのは苦労した。みんなが硬直してくれたからこそ、はじめて実現できたと言える。
records.en: It was hard to work to make it take the shape of an antenna. It could be said it's the first time that we've managed to realize this not despite but because everybody had grown so very rigid.
comments: Same term used for Tomoki in CCD4025. Pun is because everyone's rigid in thinking and refuses to form into the whole demanded by Japanese culture, due to their human nature, culture which is with the ending of the VN as entirely rejected as the concept of the Harem Ending is in the metaVN reading in favor of the individualizing Christian (and Western) culture, at the cost of separating the Individual from the Group forever, but not in a manner so complete there's no communication. Also, the sky symbolizes sexual awakening. -GHS
records.assessment: The source says shaping it into an antenna was difficult and possible only because everyone had become rigid. The English adds 'the first time' as a temporal milestone, piles incompatible tense forms, and turns the exclusivity of the enabling condition into an editorial 'it could be said.'
records.remedy: Shaping it into an antenna was difficult. We could only make it work because everyone had gone rigid.

highlights.text: It was hard to work to make it take the shape of an antenna. It could be said it's the first time that we've managed to realize this not despite but because everybody had grown so very rigid.

records.jp: 理解が訪れることもなく、停止していた。
records.en: With understanding not coming to her, she had halted.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that she freezes without understanding ever arriving. The English calques that abstraction into a dangling 'with' phrase and uses past perfect without a later past anchor.
records.remedy: Unable to comprehend it, she froze.

highlights.text: With understanding not coming to her, she had halted.

records.jp: 無理もない、他の星の文化をいきなり理解しろというのは酷だ。
records.en: No wonder, just up and being told to understand the culture of another planet has to be rough.
comments: This is so meta it almost hurts. And that was before I translated it. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that it would be cruel to demand instant understanding of another planet's culture. The English's gerund phrase has no person who is being told, 'just up' is malformed, and 'has to be rough' weakens the ethical judgment into difficulty.
records.remedy: No wonder. It would be cruel to demand that she instantly understand another planet's culture.

highlights.text: No wonder, just up and being told to understand the culture of another planet has to be rough.

records.jp: 「完成したあかつきには、世界に向けて語りかけることができる」
records.en: Taichi: "And when the dawn will break on its completion, we shall be able to speak out towards the whole world."
comments: Literal because insane. ...except the languages are confused so that ain't happening. -GHS
records.assessment: 完成したあかつきには is an idiom meaning 'when it is completed,' not a literal dawn event. English time clauses also do not use future 'will' this way.
records.remedy: when it's complete

highlights.text: when the dawn will break on its completion

records.jp: 編曲／我
records.en: The Song of Friends
records.assessment: 編曲／我 is a credit reading 'arrangement: me.' The English invents a song title, omits the arrangement credit, and replaces the self-credit with 'Friends.'
records.remedy: Arrangement: me

highlights.text: The Song of Friends

records.jp: 「どうか」
records.en: Taichi: "Like that."
records.assessment: どうか is an appeal such as 'please' or 'somehow.' 'Like that' is a demonstrative manner phrase and supplies no appeal.
records.remedy: Please.

highlights.text: Like that.

records.jp: 言葉はわからないが、理解してくれたようだ。
records.en: There's no understanding of words, but there seems to still be comprehension.
comments: Shades of CCD0021, though the meaning is just literally the above: comprehension without words, i.e., a basic human nature that transcends culture. -GHS
records.assessment: The narrator says that he cannot understand her words, but she seems to have understood him. The English removes both people as subjects and makes 'understanding' and 'comprehension' abstract near-synonyms opposed without explanation.
records.remedy: I can't understand her words, but she seems to have understood me.

highlights.text: There's no understanding of words, but there seems to still be comprehension.

records.jp: これなら自慢のカラデを見せずに済みそうだ。
records.en: With this, it seems I can end this without making a show of the Karade of my Pride.
comments: See CCA0012. Looks like he gave up on "firearms", if you know what I mean, and you do because it's his dick. -GHS
records.assessment: The source says he apparently will not need to show off his prized 'karade,' preserving a deliberate source misspelling. The English invents an object to 'end,' capitalizes common words as pseudo-titles, and attaches pride through an unnatural of-phrase.
records.remedy: it looks like I won't have to show off my prized karade

highlights.text: I can end this without making a show of the Karade of my Pride.

records.jp: 平和万歳。平和を守るために軍隊を派遣してその費用は属国というか５２番目の州が持つのだ。
records.en: Peace Banzai. The expense of the deployment of troops for the sake of the protection of the peace is had by the dependent nations or should I say the 52 States.
comments: Evil Taichi is also sorta anti-American. Subtle. A rather obvious 7, plus a rather common error - google '52 states'. So very Taichi. -GHS
records.assessment: The political satire says 'long live peace,' then notes that troops are sent to defend it while the cost falls on a client state—rather, the fifty-second state. The English leaves 万歳 untranslated, says expense 'is had,' pluralizes both the client state and the numbered state, and changes ordinal 52nd into cardinal '52 States.'
records.remedy: Long live peace. Send in the troops to defend it, and make the client state—or rather, the fifty-second state—foot the bill.

highlights.text: Peace Banzai. The expense of the deployment of troops for the sake of the protection of the peace is had by the dependent nations or should I say the 52 States.

records.jp: なんとなく霧のことを問いただした気がする。
records.en: For some reason, it feels like she's asking about Kiri.
comments: He can totally hear her... -GHS
records.assessment: なんとなく means that he vaguely or somehow gets the sense she is pressing him about Kiri, not that she asks for an unspecified causal reason.
records.remedy: Somehow, I get the feeling she's pressing me

highlights.text: For some reason, it feels like she's asking

records.jp: 霧はそこにいた。美希からは見えない、背後の部分に。
records.en: Kiri was over there. She can't be seen from Miki, she's in a part in the rear.
comments: ...did even Taichi not have a correct image of the Tower as well? I can't imagine this making sense in other ways. See CCC3016. Kiri likes it back there(tm). -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says Kiri was there, incorporated into the part behind the structure that Miki could not see. The English mixes past and present, joins two finite clauses with a comma, and uses the opaque locative phrase 'in a part in the rear.'
records.remedy: Kiri was there, in the rear section hidden from Miki's view.

highlights.text: Kiri was over there. She can't be seen from Miki, she's in a part in the rear.

records.jp: 卍みたいな形に加工して組み込んである。
records.en: She has been inserted after being machined into the fylfot shape of a swastika.
comments: Since it's been used literally in CCB0002, here it goes again. -GHS
records.assessment: 卍みたいな形 means a shape like the manji or swastika symbol. 'Fylfot' and 'swastika' are two names for the form, so the English says the shape of one name is shaped like the other and adds an unnecessary archaic term.
records.remedy: a swastika-like shape

highlights.text: the fylfot shape of a swastika

records.jp: 「寒いのか地球外の友よ？」
records.en: Taichi: "You cold, perhaps, my friend from Outworld?"
records.assessment: 地球外の友 means 'extraterrestrial friend' or 'friend from beyond Earth.' 'Outworld' is an invented fantasy proper name that suggests a specific realm absent from the source.
records.remedy: my extraterrestrial friend

highlights.text: my friend from Outworld

records.jp: 美希が背を向けたとたん、かくん、としゃがみ込む。
records.en: The moment Miki turned her back on me, thump, she falls to a squat,
records.assessment: The Japanese says that as soon as she turns away, her knees buckle and she sinks down. 'Thump' is not the onomatopoeia's motion, 'falls to a squat' implies a stable crouching posture, and the tense shifts within the sentence.
records.remedy: her knees buckle and she sinks down

highlights.text: thump, she falls to a squat,

records.jp: 腰が抜けたように見える。
records.en: seemingly as if she had lost her hips.
comments: The limit on the Runaway From Monster timer is lowering. Global Decrese in Runaway Time is a phenomenon that NEEDS to be studied! I'm sure I'll get some $1.5bln on Startkicking to finance the research within a day! -GHS
records.assessment: 腰が抜ける is an idiom meaning that one's legs give way, often from fright. The English literalization suggests her hips are physically missing.
records.remedy: her legs had given out

highlights.text: she had lost her hips

records.jp: ぶつぶつと呟いている。危ないヤツだ。
records.en: She mutters something with muttering mutter. This one here's dangerous.
comments: 1) Given below... 2) Naturally ambiguous. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that she is muttering under her breath and judges her dangerous. The English tautologically makes a mutter by means of 'muttering mutter' and uses the demonstrative 'this one' as an unnatural personal reference.
records.remedy: She keeps muttering under her breath. She's dangerous.

highlights.text: She mutters something with muttering mutter. This one here's dangerous.

records.jp: 「なあ、ところで良いエイリアンは死んだエイリアンかエイドリアンだけだと思わないか？」
records.en: Taichi: "Ah, and by the way, don't you think the only good alien is either a dead alien or just an illegal one?"
comments: It's just a bad pun born from pronunciation difficulties, see CCX0001 for more, in which eiDOrian (Adrian) becomes almost like eirian (alien). Replaced with another bad one. See CC4015, similar to one there. -GHS
records.assessment: The source twists the slogan 'the only good X is a dead X' into a sound joke between alien and the name Adrian. The English replaces Adrian with 'illegal one,' discarding the actual name-pun and adding a legal-status joke absent from the Japanese.
records.remedy: either a dead alien or Adrian

highlights.text: either a dead alien or just an illegal one

records.jp: 「で、美希。おまえも部活に参加するだろ？」
records.en: Taichi: "Well, Miki. You're going to participate to Club as well, right?"
records.assessment: English participates 'in' an activity or joins a club; it does not 'participate to' one. Club is also an ordinary common noun here.
records.remedy: join the club

highlights.text: participate to Club

records.jp: 近寄って肩に手をかけようとすると、美希は弾かれたように立ち上がる。
records.en: As I approach and go to put a hand on her shoulder, Miki stands up with the force of an explosion,
records.assessment: 弾かれたように means that she springs up as though repelled or jolted away. The English invents explosive force and makes the comparison about sheer power rather than the recoil-like motion.
records.remedy: springs to her feet as if jolted away

highlights.text: stands up with the force of an explosion

records.jp: 俺は家に戻り、じゃがいもをかじり、水を飲み、寝台に横たわった。
records.en: I returned home, gnawed at some potatoes, drank some water, and laid down on the bed.
comments: Likely raw and to the bud. Now he got POISON!!! status, the moron. Interesting his home is still here, possibly to the west of town. -GHS
records.assessment: The intransitive past tense of 'lie down' is 'lay down'; 'laid' requires an object.
records.remedy: lay down on the bed

highlights.text: laid down on the bed

records.jp: この青い地球を。あの……キュートなエイリアンから。
records.en: ...this blue Earth of ours. From that... kyute Alien.
comments: Damn colorblind Japs, grumble grumble -GHS
records.assessment: キュート is the English loanword 'cute,' not the romanized pseudo-word 'kyute.' Alien is a common noun and does not require capitalization.
records.remedy: cute alien

highlights.text: kyute Alien

records.jp: 目が覚めた。
records.en: And then I was awake.
comments: Oh, this used to be a normal "I woke", which Taichi never uses. This change further stresses that this line is not quite intended to be read as it normally is. -GHS
records.assessment: 目が覚めた is the event of waking up. The English replaces it with the state of already being awake and adds a narrative transition not present in the source.
records.remedy: I woke up.

highlights.text: And then I was awake.

records.jp: これはもうダメだ。消火できるレベルじゃない。灰になってしまう。
records.en: This thing here's beyond help. This is not a fire at the level where it can still be extinguished. This had been cremated down to ash.
comments: Word means both "burned down" and "cremated". See CCC4011: interesting he decides to cremate Youko, but no one smells that; if this is a 1:1 replay, as close as it can be, then at the end of all that he might have put Youko on the tower, after which he burned it down. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese predicts that the burning structure will be reduced to ash. The English uses past perfect to say that this has already happened and 'cremated' to imply deliberate funerary burning.
records.remedy: It will burn to ash.

highlights.text: This had been cremated down to ash.

records.jp: 「まいったな」
records.en: Taichi: "Fine, I give up."
comments: CP CCC3023
records.assessment: まいったな expresses being troubled or at a loss about the situation, not a decision to surrender the project.
records.remedy: What a mess.

highlights.text: Fine, I give up.

records.jp: 頑張ればどんな夢だって叶う。信じれば力になる。
records.en: If I do my best, all dreams can become true. Belief shall become my strength.
comments: Full of madhouses, 'em self-believing. -GHS
records.assessment: English dreams 'come true,' not 'become true.' The source then says belief gives or becomes strength in direct contemporary prose; 'shall' introduces unsupported elevated diction.
records.remedy: any dream can come true. Belief gives me strength.

highlights.text: all dreams can become true. Belief shall become my strength.

records.jp: これら美しき『普通』が汚され、蹂躙されることなどありえない。
records.en: To let this beautiful Normalcy be filthied and then trampled is out of the question.
comments: Normalcy is his complex; filthied as in what Youko taught him. -GHS
records.assessment: The source declares it impossible for these beautiful forms of 'normality' to be defiled and trampled. The English invents an agent who might 'let' it happen, collapses the plural demonstrative into singular, capitalizes the abstract noun, and uses the nonexistent word 'filthied.'
records.remedy: These beautiful forms of “normality” cannot be defiled and trampled.

highlights.text: To let this beautiful Normalcy be filthied and then trampled is out of the question.

records.jp: 人として最高の決断であり、ありようなのだ。
records.en: It is the most supreme decision that can be taken for a person, and that has to be the truth.
records.assessment: The Japanese calls it the finest human decision and way of being. The English uses the redundant superlative 'most supreme,' adds passive 'can be taken,' and replaces way of being with an assertion that something is true.
records.remedy: the highest decision and way of life available to a human being

highlights.text: the most supreme decision that can be taken for a person, and that has to be the truth

records.jp: 自分の知覚力が神がかっているのがわかる。
records.en: I know now that my powers of perception are divinely inspired.
comments: PCP CCC4001
~troll~troll~troll~troll~troll~ (CP CCC4001) -GHS
records.assessment: 神がかっている says that his perceptive ability has become godlike or uncanny. 'Divinely inspired' instead attributes it to a deity communicating inspiration.
records.remedy: godlike

highlights.text: divinely inspired

records.jp: 校内に一人、外に向かっている。
records.en: Alone in this school building, I head outside.
records.assessment: Using his expanded perception, Taichi detects one person inside the school moving toward the outside. The English makes Taichi the lone person and narrates his own movement instead.
records.remedy: There's one person inside the school, heading outside.

highlights.text: Alone in this school building, I head outside.

records.jp: 都会の方は……さすがにわからない。
records.en: In the direction of the City... I have no idea, expectably.
comments: As it is Heaven. The Bible uses 町 machi for the 'city' that the Tower is to be built with, which isn't either term, though it's pronounced the same as 街 machi (which is used to identify the part of town between the mountains). -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that, as one would expect, even his heightened senses cannot reach the city. The English capitalizes city without a proper-name basis and uses the nonexistent adverb 'expectably.'
records.remedy: the city... as expected, I can't tell

highlights.text: the City... I have no idea, expectably

records.jp: まずは手近なところから頑張ろう。
records.en: First, let's begin doing our best from the places at hand.
comments: Because he wants to Make Friends. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi resolves to start with the nearest target or most accessible place. The English changes 'I' into collaborative 'let's,' pluralizes the target into places, and uses the nonidiomatic phrase 'doing our best from.'
records.remedy: I'll start with the closest target.

highlights.text: let's begin doing our best from the places at hand

records.jp: 編曲／我輩
records.en: The Song of Friends ~ Second
records.assessment: 編曲／我輩 is a credit reading 'arrangement: yours truly.' The English invents a sequel song title and omits both the arrangement role and self-credit.
records.remedy: Arrangement: yours truly

highlights.text: The Song of Friends ~ Second

records.jp: 棒読みのヒーロー口調で技の名を告げた。
records.en: I proclaimed the name of the technique in a flat monotone of a Heroic Voice.
comments: See CCC0016A, where he was replicating the diary content. This is something he's already done. -GHS
records.assessment: A monotone is already flat, and the Japanese says he announces the technique in a deadpan hero-style voice. 'Heroic Voice' is not a proper name and should not be capitalized.
records.remedy: a deadpan hero voice

highlights.text: a flat monotone of a Heroic Voice

records.jp: だけどとても痛そうな尻餅じゃないか。かわいそうに。
records.en: But still, don't that falling down on her butt look painful. So pitiful.
comments: He's worried about her falling down, not the tendons. Probably because he didn't cut her down at all. He's just playing with her like they always do, but he's particularly gloomy so he thinks he's murdering everyone. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese notes that the way she landed looks extremely painful and voices mock sympathy. The English has faulty subject-verb agreement, nominalizes the action as 'that falling down,' and uses an adjective fragment where a direct sympathetic address is needed.
records.remedy: doesn't that landing look terribly painful. Poor thing.

highlights.text: don't that falling down on her butt look painful. So pitiful.

records.jp: おそらくインプラントが原因だろう。間違いない。
records.en: I dare say that the origin of that is some sort of Implant. Make no mistake.
comments: Meaning she'd have some kind of Alien Implant that doesn't let her feel pain. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese speculates that an implant is probably the cause, then asserts that this is certain. 'Origin' is unnatural for an immediate physical cause, 'some sort of' adds vagueness, and implant is a common noun.
records.remedy: an implant is probably the cause. No doubt about it.

highlights.text: the origin of that is some sort of Implant. Make no mistake.

records.jp: 「らーららー」
records.en:
>                     Ooo       OOooo
Taichi: "Laaa lalaaa!"
comments: ら decrypts to the letter 'O'. 0, circle, loop, correct. Same as with how 'zero' is often kept in Western numeral. He's screaming "loop, loop" over and over and over and over and over. Furrygana'd for maximum weird. -GHS
records.assessment: The source contains only the sung syllables. The English adds an unexplained diagram-like line of vowel shapes before the dialogue.
records.remedy: Remove the added diagram line.

highlights.text: >                     Ooo       OOooo

records.jp: 動かない足を引きずって、離れようとする。
records.en: Limping on her unmoving feet, she works to gain distance.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that she drags her unusable leg or feet in an effort to get away. One cannot idiomatically limp 'on' feet described as unmoving, and 'works to gain distance' turns escape into abstract task prose.
records.remedy: Dragging her useless leg, she tries to get away.

highlights.text: Limping on her unmoving feet, she works to gain distance.

records.jp: 「らーらーららーらららー」
records.en:
>                     Ooo       Ooo       OOooo           OOOooo
Taichi: "Laaa laaa lalaaa lalalaaa!"
comments: Just one last time, either the reader 'gets' it or who am I kidding they can just read the damn notes. -GHS
records.assessment: The source contains only the sung syllables. The English adds an unexplained diagram-like line of vowel shapes before the dialogue.
records.remedy: Remove the added diagram line.

highlights.text: >                     Ooo       Ooo       OOooo           OOOooo

records.jp: 「トモダチだよキミィ」
records.en: Taichi: "You be a f-r-i-e-n-d!"
records.assessment: The Japanese tauntingly asserts 'You're my friend' or calls the listener 'friend.' The English uses an ungrammatical imperative-like 'You be' and invents letter-by-letter spelling.
records.remedy: You're my friend, you!

highlights.text: You be a f-r-i-e-n-d!

records.jp: トモダチはナイフで。
records.en: Friend by knife.
records.assessment: The Japanese fragment links making or defining friends with the knife. The English uses singular 'Friend,' omits any verb, and leaves 'by knife' without an article or intelligible relation.
records.remedy: Friends, made with a knife.

highlights.text: Friend by knife.

records.jp: 俺は美希にナイフをインストールする。太もものあたり。
records.en: I install a knife in Miki. Around the thigh.
comments: And Miki, who is God by virtue of destroying the Tower of Babel, now gets tortured in what is effectively a crucifixion. ...it does sound stupidly blunt when said like that. Except, this should be a replay of the very end of the new CCD0022A. Who was being tortured there? Not Yutaka, he survived. If Miki was Yutaka above, then who is she now? Outside of Youko, getting brutally and sadistically murdered (but not forgiven) for what she did to him, I have no idea. -GHS
records.assessment: The source extends the computer metaphor to inserting a knife into Miki near the thigh. The English's 'install in Miki' lacks the bodily location, then strands that location as an afterthought fragment.
records.remedy: I install a knife in Miki near the thigh.

highlights.text: I install a knife in Miki. Around the thigh.

records.jp: スロットがないので、新しく増設する必要があった。
records.en: There was no slot, so it necessitated installing a new one.
comments: You'll break your brand new PC, Misato! See CCD1001. -GHS
records.assessment: The lack of a slot makes it necessary for Taichi to add one. The English makes an unexplained 'it' perform the transitive verb 'necessitated' and hides the actor.
records.remedy: I had to add a new one

highlights.text: it necessitated installing a new one

records.jp: 抜くと果てしなくジューシーだった。
records.en: Juiciness without end on removal.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that when he pulls the knife out, the result is endlessly 'juicy.' The English nominalizes the quality, removes the actor from 'removal,' and leaves no finite verb.
records.remedy: When I pulled it out, it was endlessly juicy.

highlights.text: Juiciness without end on removal.

records.jp: 腱が切れているのにすごい。美希には才能がある。
records.en: When her tendon is severed, amazing! Miki has some genius in her.
comments: See CCD1001: more miracles? Or see CCD4022. Genius by fail. More likely, she's getting tired of this rough horseplay. There's no murdering, but he's passed the boundary. That's mass murder to him. Maybe. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese marvels that she can kick even with a severed tendon and concludes that she has talent. The English uses temporal 'when' instead of concessive 'even though,' leaves 'amazing' without a subject, and changes talent into an indwelling 'genius.'
records.remedy: Amazing, even with her tendon severed. Miki has real talent.

highlights.text: When her tendon is severed, amazing! Miki has some genius in her.

records.jp: だから俺は、足の裏を刃先で受け止めた。
records.en: Therefore, I had the edge of the blade stop the sole of her foot.
records.assessment: Taichi catches the sole with the tip of his blade. The English makes the blade edge the acting subject under a causative construction, substitutes an edge for the point, and shifts the immediate action into past perfect.
records.remedy: I catch the sole of her foot on the point of my blade.

highlights.text: I had the edge of the blade stop the sole of her foot.

records.jp: 貫かれた自分の足を、呆然と見つめる美希。
records.en: Miki goes to stare at her own pierced foot, dumbfounded.
records.assessment: The Japanese snapshot says that she stares, not that she moves or attempts to begin staring.
records.remedy: stares

highlights.text: goes to stare

records.jp: ナイフを抜くと、美希の足は完全に死んだのか、ぱたりと床に落ちた。
records.en: On removing the knife, Miki's foot fell down on the floor with a thump, as if it had perfectly died.
comments: Or, as if their game called for it. She's not that much in pain, is she. She probably whined more in her sex scenes! -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the foot drops limply to the floor, as though completely dead. 'Fell down on the floor' is redundant, and 'perfectly died' describes a completed death event rather than total lifelessness.
records.remedy: dropped limply to the floor, as though completely dead

highlights.text: fell down on the floor with a thump, as if it had perfectly died

records.jp: トモダチは簡単にできそうだ。
records.en: Seems making friends is simple.
records.assessment: The extraposition requires 'It seems,' or the clause must be recast with 'Making friends seems.'
records.remedy: Making friends seems easy.

highlights.text: Seems making friends is simple.

records.jp: 俺はゆっくり事を進めることにした。
records.en: I decided to slowly progress on the deed.
records.assessment: 事を進める means to proceed with the matter or action. English does not 'progress on the deed' in this transitive sense, and 'deed' adds formal moral coloring.
records.remedy: take things slowly

highlights.text: slowly progress on the deed

records.jp: 『コレ』がたいして恐ろしいものではないことはわかっている。
records.en: I understand that "this" is not something to be so afraid of.
records.assessment: The Japanese says the object is not particularly frightening. English 'something to be afraid of' ordinarily requires an experiencer or an idiomatic adjective construction.
records.remedy: not especially frightening

highlights.text: not something to be so afraid of

records.jp: 多少の才能はあるようだけど、一度だって恐怖を感じたことはない。
records.en: But it seems I have some measure of talent for it, I haven't felt terror not once.
comments: See CCD0022A: he broke himself first. -GHS
records.assessment: The source says the adversary seems to have some talent, but Taichi has never once felt fear. The English assigns the talent to Taichi, joins two independent clauses with a comma, and uses the double negative 'haven't ... not once.'
records.remedy: it seems to have a little talent, but I have never once felt afraid

highlights.text: it seems I have some measure of talent for it, I haven't felt terror not once

records.jp: 両手にそれぞれナイフを持つ。
records.en: I hold a knife in each respective hand,
comments: As with Kiri? -GHS
records.assessment: 'Each' already establishes separate distribution, so 'respective' is redundant and awkward in this simple bodily description.
records.remedy: each hand

highlights.text: each respective hand

records.jp: 血抜きをしないと。
records.en: I ought drain the blood.
records.assessment: The modal-like verb 'ought' requires an infinitive with 'to.'
records.remedy: I ought to drain

highlights.text: I ought drain

records.jp: まず衣服を剥ぐ。
records.en: First, tear off the clothes.
comments: "You're pretty, so off with the clothes". Hmmm. -GHS
records.assessment: The first-person narration says that Taichi strips away the clothing. Without a subject, the English reads as an instruction.
records.remedy: First, I tear off the clothes.

highlights.text: First, tear off the clothes.

records.jp: すでに抵抗はなくなっていた。
records.en: Opposition was already vanishing.
records.assessment: The Japanese states that resistance was already gone. The English changes the completed absence into an ongoing process and uses political or competitive 'opposition' instead of physical resistance.
records.remedy: The resistance was already gone.

highlights.text: Opposition was already vanishing.

records.jp: 虚をつかれた。
records.en: Attacked while off guard.
comments: 嘘をつかれた "I was lied to" looks so similar it may not be coincidental. -GHS
records.assessment: 虚をつかれた means that Taichi is caught off guard. The English omits him as subject and adds the narrower assertion that he was attacked during a preexisting off-guard state.
records.remedy: I'm caught off guard.

highlights.text: Attacked while off guard.

records.jp: 側頭部に重い衝撃。脳の中心まで抜けるほどの。
records.en: A heavy impact on the side of the head, enough that the center of the brain could come out.
comments: See CCX0001, as well as many parts of Week 1. That's where the Cover-Up Lobe(?) of his brain is. See CCD1001: that's where his automatism is. She's not attacking to kill him; she's attacking to make him regain his sense of reality. That's what the whole thing about universes changing and the Shimura Phenomenon means. -GHS
records.assessment: The impact feels as though it travels clear through to the center of his brain. The English instead suggests the brain's center could physically exit his skull.
records.remedy: enough to shoot through to the center of my brain

highlights.text: enough that the center of the brain could come out

records.jp: ぐらり、と傾く。視界が暗くなる。
records.en: I lean over with a violent shake. Vision grows dark.
records.assessment: Taichi reels or lists unsteadily as his vision darkens. 'Lean over' suggests deliberate bending, 'violent shake' invents a separate movement, and the English detaches vision from its experiencer.
records.remedy: I reel to one side. My vision darkens.

highlights.text: I lean over with a violent shake. Vision grows dark.

records.jp: 「痛いじゃないか……っ」
records.en: Taichi: "Well don't that hurt now...!"
records.assessment: The singular demonstrative subject requires 'doesn't,' and the source is a direct complaint that she hurt him rather than a dialectal tag observation.
records.remedy: That hurts

highlights.text: don't that hurt now

records.jp: 呼吸をすると、ズキッと痛みが走る。
records.en: I take a breath, and throb!, the pain runs.
comments: See CCA0027. And around it goes. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that breathing sends a sharp stab of pain through him. The English inserts onomatopoeia as an adverb with exclamation punctuation, then personifies generic pain as running without a destination.
records.remedy: When I breathe, a sharp pain shoots through me.

highlights.text: I take a breath, and throb!, the pain runs.

records.jp: 触れると、血が出ていた。
records.en: I touch, and blood is coming out.
records.assessment: He touches the injured spot and discovers that it is bleeding. The English omits what he touches and changes the discovered result into an ongoing progressive with blood itself as subject.
records.remedy: When I touch the spot, I find blood.

highlights.text: I touch, and blood is coming out.

records.jp: しかも疼痛がする。数時間後に嘔吐して死ぬ時間差トリックか。
records.en: But still there's pain. Is it this that time-delay trick where I have a bout of emesis and die several hours later?
comments: As in, the tip of the nightstick was poisoned? Perhaps he's rationalizing having eaten the potatoes raw to the bud (no I'm not letting that go, he started it!). -GHS
records.assessment: The source notes throbbing pain and jokes about a delayed trick in which he vomits and dies hours later. The English uses 'But still' without a contrast, replaces ordinary vomiting with clinical 'a bout of emesis,' and produces the ungrammatical question frame 'Is it this that ... trick where.'
records.remedy: It throbs, too. Is this some delayed-action trick where I vomit and die a few hours later?

highlights.text: But still there's pain. Is it this that time-delay trick where I have a bout of emesis and die several hours later?

records.jp: ま、それまでに見破れば死ぬことはないから平気だが。
records.en: Well, if I've managed managed to find out that much I won't die, so I'll be alright.
comments: Because he can cure the poison? -GHS
records.assessment: The source jokes that as long as he sees through the trick before then, he will not die. The English duplicates 'managed' and changes exposing the trick in time into learning an unspecified amount of information.
records.remedy: as long as I see through the trick before then

highlights.text: if I've managed managed to find out that much

records.jp: もういいや。
records.en: No more, now.
records.assessment: もういいや expresses giving up deliberation—'enough' or 'forget it.' 'No more, now' sounds like an order to stop a repeated external action.
records.remedy: Enough.

highlights.text: No more, now.

records.jp: どこまでも広がってすべてになる。まるで血袋。
records.en: Throughout everywhere it spreads and everything it becomes. She's like a blood bag.
comments: Women are convenient bloodbags for men. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says the blood spreads without limit until it becomes everything, then compares the result to a bag of blood. The English duplicates universal scope as 'throughout everywhere,' inverts object and verb, and introduces a female subject not explicit in the comparison.
records.remedy: It spreads everywhere, without end, until it becomes everything. Like a bag of blood.

highlights.text: Throughout everywhere it spreads and everything it becomes. She's like a blood bag.

records.jp: トモダチには血はいらない。信じるしかないだろう。
records.en: Friends don't need blood. Cannot do anything but believe, I guess.
comments: See CCD5001: perfect Youko doesn't need love, just like Alter Egos don't need anything but reciprocal assertion. That's exactly the same as people not needing blood to be friends. -GHS
records.assessment: The narrator says that he has no choice but to believe. The English omits the subject and turns the forceful rhetorical ending into a hedged afterthought.
records.remedy: I have no choice but to believe, do I?

highlights.text: Cannot do anything but believe, I guess.

records.jp: 深々と。美希は細く長いうめき声をあげた。
records.en: In the deepest depths. Miki released a narrow and long grunt.
records.assessment: 深々と means deeply, describing the preceding action, while 細く長いうめき声 is a thin, drawn-out moan. The English invents a spatial superlative, calls a sustained moan a grunt, and describes sound width as 'narrow.'
records.remedy: Deeply. Miki let out a thin, drawn-out moan.

highlights.text: In the deepest depths. Miki released a narrow and long grunt.

records.jp: 体が動かない。
records.en: Body doesn't move.
records.assessment: The Japanese refers to Taichi's own body. English requires a determiner or possessive before the singular count noun.
records.remedy: My body won't move.

highlights.text: Body doesn't move.

records.jp: 痺れているみたいに。
records.en: As if it had been numbed.
records.assessment: The source compares his current paralysis to numbness. Past perfect unnecessarily places the numbing before another past reference point.
records.remedy: As though it were numb.

highlights.text: As if it had been numbed.

records.jp: じょうずに使う。
records.en: I use nice and well.
records.assessment: じょうずに means skillfully. 'Nice' is an adjective and cannot coordinate with the adverb 'well' to modify use.
records.remedy: I use it skillfully.

highlights.text: I use nice and well.

records.jp: 使い終えた。
records.en: The use is finished.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi finished using the object or person. The English converts his completed action into a passive-like abstract state in which 'use' itself is finished.
records.remedy: I finish using it.

highlights.text: The use is finished.

records.jp: どれくらい佇んでいたのだろう。朝になっていた。
records.en: How long have I even stood there. It had become morning.
comments: Since time has little meaning... an hour? -GHS
records.assessment: The narrator wonders how long he had been standing there and observes that morning has arrived. The English uses present perfect for an interval completed by a past realization, punctuates the question as a statement, then shifts morning to past perfect.
records.remedy: How long had I been standing there? Morning had come.

highlights.text: How long have I even stood there. It had become morning.

records.jp: ひどく、気分が悪い。吐きそうだ。
records.en: I feel sick, horribly so. As if to throw up.
comments: PCP CCD2002
Hi, Touko. That's what the time-delay above means. -GHS
records.assessment: 吐きそうだ means that he feels about to vomit. The English infinitive fragment lacks a subject and treats the feeling as a comparison rather than imminent nausea.
records.remedy: I feel like I'm going to throw up.

highlights.text: As if to throw up.

records.jp: 陽光に焙られるのを忌避する虫のように、俺はその場を離れる。
records.en: Shirking from the scorching sunlight like an insect, I take distance from that spot.
records.assessment: The Japanese compares him to an insect avoiding being roasted by sunlight. 'Shirk' applies to duties, not physical light; 'scorching' makes an implied effect explicit; and English moves away or puts distance between itself and a place, not 'takes distance from.'
records.remedy: Like an insect recoiling from sunlight that would roast it, I leave the spot.

highlights.text: Shirking from the scorching sunlight like an insect, I take distance from that spot.

records.jp: 店で飢えを満たす。
records.en: I satisfy my starvation at a shop.
records.assessment: 飢え is hunger. 'Starvation' denotes a severe prolonged condition and is not idiomatically something one satisfies at a shop.
records.remedy: satisfy my hunger

highlights.text: satisfy my starvation

records.jp: メモを見る。
records.en: I look at the memos.
records.assessment: The Japanese refers to a single memo or note. The English pluralizes it without source support.
records.remedy: the memo

highlights.text: the memos

records.jp: そうだ、こうやってツケていた。
records.en: Right, that's how you go post up credit bills..
comments: I suspect that, in the simplest troll (that the Cross World is a physical place and ToF takes place in it, with a completely separate but overlapping cast), this is who posts up the memos. In various people's names. For no reason whatsoever. And he apparently mostly got vegetable juice. That, or time will mysteriously start looping from the previous Sunday when the parallel world people get here and then this Taichi puffs out of existence like everyone else for no explained reason. Or dies and falls into a ditch and doesn't get reset and somehow grows old for same. -GHS
records.assessment: Taichi remembers that this is how he had been recording purchases on credit. The English switches to generic second person, changes recording a tab into posting bills publicly, omits the infinitive marker after 'go,' and doubles the period.
records.remedy: Right. This was how I had been putting things on my tab.

highlights.text: that's how you go post up credit bills..

records.jp: 夏の熱気だけが、例年通りに降り注ぐ。
records.en: Nothing but the zealous hot hair of Summer pouring on, as every year.
comments: See CCA0015C
records.assessment: The source says only the summer heat pours down as it does every year. The English misspells 'air' as 'hair,' calls heat 'zealous,' capitalizes summer, and uses the incomplete phrasal verb 'pouring on' without an object.
records.remedy: the summer heat pours down, just as it does every year

highlights.text: the zealous hot hair of Summer pouring on

records.jp: 汗とともに、少し理性も戻ったのか、妙に冷静だった。
records.en: Perhaps a bit of rationality has returned, together with the sweating, as I was oddly composed.
records.assessment: The narrator infers that some reason may have returned along with his sweat because he is strangely calm. The English mixes present perfect with past 'was' and uses causal 'as' after already framing the result as uncertainty.
records.remedy: Perhaps a little of my reason returned along with the sweat; I was strangely calm.

highlights.text: Perhaps a bit of rationality has returned, together with the sweating, as I was oddly composed.

records.jp: 人類はあっという間に滅びてしまった。原因もわからないまま。
records.en: Humanity had fallen in the blink of an eye. Origin remains not understood.
comments: Pshaw, this is so obviously the Settei changing that it barely bears belaboring at this point. See CCC0006B, same trick as with Nanaka: although the term can imply either knowledge or understanding, Taichi knows, but doesn't necessarily understand. Plus, we had the Tower event, that comes AFTER the flood, not before! -GHS
records.assessment: The source says humanity perished almost instantly without anyone ever learning the cause. 'Had fallen' requires a later past anchor and can mean political defeat; the second sentence omits an article and uses unnatural inverted negation.
records.remedy: Humanity perished in the blink of an eye, with the cause still unknown.

highlights.text: Humanity had fallen in the blink of an eye. Origin remains not understood.

records.jp: 誰も生き残らないだろう。誰も。
records.en: No one's survived, I guess. No one.
records.assessment: The Japanese predicts that nobody will survive. The English instead makes a present-perfect claim that no one has survived up to now, while attaching speculation to an apparently completed fact.
records.remedy: No one will survive, I suppose.

highlights.text: No one's survived, I guess.

records.jp: その構図が見えた時、俺は―――
records.en: And the moment I saw that composition, I---
comments: The Ironic Composition of just these eight damaged people being left, perhaps, except there's at least Sakakibara left. But it's also further hints that he possibly didn't kill anyone at the Hasekura mansion, he just began 'ignoring' people. -GHS
records.assessment: 構図 here is the overall picture, pattern, or configuration he has grasped, not an artistic composition he literally sees.
records.remedy: the whole picture

highlights.text: that composition

records.jp: ぼんやりと、足を動かす。
records.en: My feet move absent-mindedly.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi vaguely or listlessly moves his feet. The English makes the feet autonomous and assigns a mental state to them.
records.remedy: I move my feet without thinking.

highlights.text: My feet move absent-mindedly.

records.jp: ら？
records.en:
>  O
La?
comments: Reminder that this sentence is extremely meaningful. -GHS
records.assessment: The source contains only the questioning syllable. The English adds an unexplained diagram-like line before it.
records.remedy: Remove the added diagram line.

highlights.text: >  O

records.jp: 橋を越えた町はずれで、俺は佇立する。
records.en: On the outskirts of town, passed the bridge, I stand still.
comments: West town, should be around where Kiri practices. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese locates him on the outskirts beyond the bridge. 'Passed' is a finite past verb or participle and cannot serve as the spatial preposition 'past' in this construction.
records.remedy: On the outskirts of town, past the bridge

highlights.text: On the outskirts of town, passed the bridge

records.jp: 唐突に搾り出されるイヤな気持ち。
records.en: All of a sudden a really ugly feeling squeezes out of me,
records.assessment: The Japanese uses a passive image: an unpleasant feeling is abruptly squeezed out from within him. The English makes the feeling itself perform the squeezing.
records.remedy: an ugly feeling is suddenly squeezed out of me

highlights.text: a really ugly feeling squeezes out of me

records.jp: 人間になど生まれなければ良かった―――
records.en: I wish I hadn't been born as anything remotely human---
comments: More suggestions that his is just pretending to be an insect pretending to be human. -GHS
records.assessment: The source wishes he had not been born human. 'Anything remotely human' adds both categorical distance and the possibility of near-human alternatives.
records.remedy: human

highlights.text: anything remotely human

records.jp: 気がつくと朝になっていた。原っぱに、俺は死んだみたいに転がっていた。頭痛によって叩き起こされたようなものだ。
records.en: And then I noticed it had become morning. I was sprawled down, as if dead, in an open field. It felt like being slapped awake up by a headache.
comments: See CCX0001 -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that when he came to, it was morning; he lay sprawled like a corpse and had effectively been jolted awake by pain. The English adds an object to 'noticed,' uses redundant 'sprawled down,' and combines incompatible particles in 'slapped awake up.'
records.remedy: When I came to, it was morning. I lay sprawled in an open field as though dead, effectively jolted awake by the headache.

highlights.text: And then I noticed it had become morning. I was sprawled down, as if dead, in an open field. It felt like being slapped awake up by a headache.

records.jp: 「曜子ちゃん……曜子ちゃん……」
records.en: Taichi: "Youko-chan... Youko-chan..."
comments: That's the very last person he should be calling for! This is still replaying the end of the Shinkawas. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese name 曜子 romanizes as Yōko in standard Hepburn; 'Youko' is a keyboard-style long-vowel spelling.
records.remedy: Yōko-chan... Yōko-chan

highlights.text: Youko-chan... Youko-chan

records.jp: 「どうしたの？」
records.en: Youko: "What is it?"
records.assessment: The Japanese name 曜子 romanizes as Yōko in standard Hepburn; 'Youko' is a keyboard-style long-vowel spelling.
records.remedy: Yōko

highlights.text: Youko

records.jp: 「また俺……壊れちゃう」
records.en: Taichi: "I got wrecked... again."
records.assessment: Taichi says that he is going to break down again. The English changes the feared imminent event into a completed past event and uses slang implying external damage.
records.remedy: I'm going to break again.

highlights.text: I got wrecked... again.

records.jp: もう曜子ちゃんはいなかった。
records.en: Youko-chan was already no more.
comments: He's killed her here, did he kill her there? -GHS
records.assessment: The name requires Hepburn Yōko. いなかった says she was no longer there; 'was no more' conventionally implies that she had died, adding a specific outcome.
records.remedy: Yōko-chan was already gone.

highlights.text: Youko-chan was already no more.

records.jp: なんだろう、このアルファベットは。
records.en: What's even up with that weird romaji.
comments: hee hee -GHS
records.assessment: アルファベット refers to these alphabetic characters, not specifically romanized Japanese. The English additionally judges them 'weird.'
records.remedy: these letters

highlights.text: that weird romaji

records.jp: しばらく俺は停止していた。
records.en: For a while I stood there, stopped.
records.assessment: 停止していた says that he remains frozen or motionless. The English redundantly describes standing and then adds 'stopped' as an awkward resultative adjective.
records.remedy: stood frozen there

highlights.text: stood there, stopped

records.jp: 気配を察することもできないほど、疲弊していた。
records.en: I was exhausted, to the point where I could no longer evaluate presences.
comments: He can no longer tell which is friend from which is not. This is where his game just breaks. -GHS
records.assessment: 気配を察する means to sense someone's presence. 'Evaluate presences' suggests analytically judging multiple manifestations rather than noticing anyone nearby.
records.remedy: sense anyone's presence

highlights.text: evaluate presences

records.jp: この声は……榊原先生。
records.en: This voice... it's Sakakibara-sensei's.
comments: See CCC4025. -GHS
records.assessment: The common Japanese title 先生 is left untranslated and attached to the surname. Natural English identifies the voice as belonging to his teacher, Sakakibara.
records.remedy: my teacher Sakakibara's

highlights.text: Sakakibara-sensei's

records.jp: そういえば生存者はまだいたんだ。
records.en: Well then, this means there's still survivors.
records.assessment: The plural count noun requires 'there are.'
records.remedy: there are still survivors

highlights.text: there's still survivors

records.jp: トモダチではないけれど。
records.en: He is not a Friend, however.
comments: That doesn't mean any weird thing; see CCC0011A. Teachers won't be Friends, especially someone as antisocial as Sakakibara is (or might be, it's not like "his" diary is all that credible). -GHS
records.assessment: トモダチ is emphasized in the source's stylized register but remains a common noun. Capitalization turns it into an unexplained formal category.
records.remedy: friend

highlights.text: Friend

records.jp: 先生は、屋上がどうの美希がどうのと言っていたように思う。
records.en: Sensei said something about the rooftop and something about Miki, I think.
comments: "Don't go to the rooftop, also, you spooked poor little Miki dammit". He may be looking for him as he left school. -GHS
records.assessment: The common Japanese title 先生 is left untranslated and used as though it were a personal name. Natural English identifies the person as his teacher.
records.remedy: My teacher said something

highlights.text: Sensei said something

records.jp: 俺は乾いた唇を上下に引きはがして、声を出した。
records.en: I parted my parched lower lip from the parched top lip and spoke to him.
comments: He just said he replenished his fluids! He must've stood there for hours! -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he tears his dry lips apart vertically and forces out his voice. The English repeats 'parched,' gives each lip a cumbersome positional label, and adds a male addressee rather than conveying the effort of speaking.
records.remedy: I pulled my parched lips apart and forced out my voice.

highlights.text: I parted my parched lower lip from the parched top lip and spoke to him.

records.jp: ずいぶんと待っていた。
records.en: I wait for quite a while,
records.assessment: The Japanese reports a completed interval of waiting before no answer came. The English shifts it into present tense.
records.remedy: I waited for quite a while

highlights.text: I wait for quite a while

records.jp: 「誰か」
records.en: Taichi: "Anyone."
comments: And still he seeks people. -GHS
records.assessment: 誰か as a standalone plea calls for 'someone' or 'somebody.' 'Anyone' usually belongs in a question, conditional, or negative environment.
records.remedy: Someone.

highlights.text: Anyone.

records.jp: もう無理だ。
records.en: It's all done now.
records.assessment: もう無理だ means that Taichi cannot endure or continue any longer. 'It's all done' instead says some external task or event has been completed.
records.remedy: I can't go on.

highlights.text: It's all done now.

records.jp: 気がつくと、山道に踏み込んでいた。
records.en: And then I noticed that I had treaded into the mountain path.
comments: Same "and then I noticed" as above. He instinctively goes to the hokora, following the hint of his dead mother, although she isn't personified quite yet. -GHS
records.assessment: The past participle of 'tread' is 'trodden,' not 'treaded,' but the Japanese more naturally says that he had wandered onto or entered the mountain path before noticing.
records.remedy: I had wandered onto a mountain path

highlights.text: I had treaded into the mountain path

records.jp: 誰かに叩かれた側頭部が、ズキズキと疼く。
records.en: The side of the head that a someone had smacked is now aching all throbby-throbby.
comments: See CCA0027, the SFX is the same Miki uses there. It may just be that the smacking of his head all along was nothing but an attempt at replicating what he misremembers to have 'caused' Miki's happy face at the end of that scene, which got conflated with this. That still works since this entire thing is still supposed to be around the Miki route. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the side of Taichi's head where someone struck him throbs. The English uses the impossible determiner sequence 'a someone,' detaches the head from him, and replaces the pain with childish reduplication unsupported by the neutral onomatopoeia.
records.remedy: The side of my head where someone struck me is throbbing.

highlights.text: The side of the head that a someone had smacked is now aching all throbby-throbby.

records.jp: 頭が破裂しそうだ。
records.en: Head feels like it would blow up.
records.assessment: The Japanese says his head feels about to burst. English requires a possessive before the count noun and uses immediate 'will' or 'is going to,' not hypothetical 'would.'
records.remedy: My head feels like it's going to burst.

highlights.text: Head feels like it would blow up.

records.jp: 歩くごとに、頭に響く。
records.en: Each step echoes in the head,
records.assessment: Each step sends a jolt through Taichi's head. The English turns his head into a generic acoustic chamber.
records.remedy: reverberates through my head

highlights.text: echoes in the head

records.jp: たぶん俺は、止まったら、止まる。
records.en: Maybe if I were to stop I would come to a halt.
comments: Laterally. See CCD5001: he moves onwards. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese repeats 'stop' to imply that if he stops walking, he himself will cease functioning altogether. The English reduces both halves to the same literal physical halt and loses the threatening second sense.
