records.remedy: if I stop walking, I'll stop for good

highlights.text: if I were to stop I would come to a halt

records.jp: 「祠だよ」
records.en: ???: "At the ho-ko-ra!"
comments: Tags were removed now that there's a visual guide. This Taichi here can't know who Nanaka is. -GHS
records.assessment: 祠 is the common noun 'shrine.' The English leaves it as emphatically syllabified Japanese, adds an exclamation mark, and fails to tell the reader where the speaker says they are.
records.remedy: At the shrine.

highlights.text: At the ho-ko-ra!

records.jp: 「知らなーい」
records.en: ???: "Something I don't know!"
comments: Dammit mom! -GHS
records.assessment: The speaker replies 知らなーい, meaning 'I don't know.' The English instead echoes Taichi's requested object as an excited fragment.
records.remedy: I dunno.

highlights.text: Something I don't know!

records.jp: いなくなっていた。
records.en: She vanished.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that when he looks or realizes, she is gone. 'Vanished' asserts a disappearance event he did not witness rather than the discovered absence.
records.remedy: She was gone.

highlights.text: She vanished.

records.jp: 場所もわからない道をふらふらと歩く。
records.en: I was walking unsteadily down a road, off someplace I don't know,
records.assessment: The source uses immediate narration as he staggers along a road without knowing where he is. The English shifts to past progressive, uses the malformed locative 'off someplace,' and ends with a comma that binds it incorrectly to the next unit.
records.remedy: I stagger along a road in a place I don't recognize.

highlights.text: I was walking unsteadily down a road, off someplace I don't know,

records.jp: 頭痛と喪失感だけの俺だ。
records.en: me with nothing but a headache and the memory of a sense of loss.
comments: As it's written with the kind of 'loss' usually seen in 'memory loss'. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese characterizes him as reduced to a headache and a sense of loss. The English adds a memory of the loss rather than the loss itself and leaves the entire unit as an appositive fragment.
records.remedy: I am nothing but a headache and a sense of loss.

highlights.text: me with nothing but a headache and the memory of a sense of loss

records.jp: それは人ではないのだろう、きっと。
records.en: That shouldn't be a person, definitely.
comments: Likely speaking about himself, but he might be speaking about the people he sees/doesn't see right about now. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese speculates with conviction that it probably is not a person. 'Shouldn't' can express obligation, and pairing it with sentence-final 'definitely' creates conflicting degrees of certainty.
records.remedy: That probably isn't a person.

highlights.text: That shouldn't be a person, definitely.

records.jp: 空虚な演出は、文字通り無意味になる。
records.en: It would be a play with no script nor stage, literally meaningless.
comments: Lateral... but not much. -GHS
records.assessment: 空虚な演出 is an empty performance or display. The English invents the more specific absence of both script and stage, neither of which is named by the source.
records.remedy: an empty performance

highlights.text: a play with no script nor stage

records.jp: 聞く者もない。
records.en: There'll be no one to listen, either.
comments: Though there's no guarantee for people to listen to the "radio", which in Week 1 (and most weeks) didn't literally have a script either. I would suspect Tanaka sort of wings it and hopes, but with the mess of cross-references, it sounds hard to believe. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that there is no listener now. The English shifts the absence into the future.
records.remedy: There's no one to listen

highlights.text: There'll be no one to listen

records.jp: 消してくれ。
records.en: Go and vanish.
records.assessment: 消してくれ asks for something to be erased or made to disappear. The English instead commands an addressee to perform the action of vanishing itself.
records.remedy: Make it disappear.

highlights.text: Go and vanish.

records.jp: 世界すべてを、俺の前から消してくれ。
records.en: for all in the world to just vanish from in front of me.
comments: With more than a little hint that, currently, it IS actually in front of his eyes. This is the end of the Training Camp. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese asks for the entire world to disappear from before him. 'All in the world' suggests all people or objects rather than the world itself, and 'from in front of' stacks incompatible locatives.
records.remedy: for the whole world to disappear from before me

highlights.text: for all in the world to just vanish from in front of me

records.jp: 途方もない苦痛が、頭の芯に響く。
records.en: Extraordinary pain reverberates throughout the center of my head.
records.assessment: 途方もない describes overwhelming or tremendous pain. 'Extraordinary' can sound positive or merely unusual, and something cannot reverberate 'throughout the center' as though a point were an extended region.
records.remedy: Tremendous pain reverberates through the core of my head.

highlights.text: Extraordinary pain reverberates throughout the center of my head.

records.jp: 構わず走る。
records.en: I don't care and run.
records.assessment: 構わず means that he runs on regardless of the pain. 'I don't care' instead asserts emotional indifference without identifying what he disregards.
records.remedy: I keep running regardless.

highlights.text: I don't care and run.

records.jp: 何者かが、あるいは偶然という神が、二枚の紙を重ねて画鋲で射止めた。
records.en: Someone, possibly the god called coincidence, overlapped two sheets of paper and shoots 'em dead with a thumbtack.
comments: AKA the Christian God. This is supposed to be the Worlds Crossing... but this doesn't actually explain why everyone was gone before the worlds crossed, or why so many things change in ways that are consistent with the 'other' world. Outside of this being in Taichi's mind, at least. Paper is read Kami, in fact, "two sheets of paper" is read "the God of Japan". The reason for this is Japan. See CCX0001, this part has been integrated there now.

That last term is seen at the end of CCA0013, when Taichi wins over Yusa's favor with a single handkerchief (which is usually found folded, dot dot dot). Though it does literally mean "to shoot dead", it is most often used in this meaning of "conquering/overcoming" or "winning [over]". -GHS
records.assessment: The figure says that someone—or the god of coincidence—laid two sheets together and pinned them through with a thumbtack. The English shifts from past to present and imports the idiom 'shoot them dead,' treating the paper as living targets.
records.remedy: laid two sheets of paper together and pinned them through with a thumbtack

highlights.text: overlapped two sheets of paper and shoots 'em dead with a thumbtack

records.jp: 気配を具現するなんて器用なことはできない。
records.en: I could never do something as skillful as incarnate a presence,
records.assessment: After 'as ... as,' English requires a gerund or full clause. 'Incarnate' is also an elevated theological verb for embodying a presence rather than making it perceptibly manifest.
records.remedy: as sophisticated as manifesting a presence

highlights.text: as skillful as incarnate a presence

records.jp: もう気配は探るまい。
records.en: I should probably not investigate presences anymore.
comments: Well how convenient now! -GHS
records.assessment: The volitional まい is a firm resolution not to probe for presences again. 'Should probably not' weakens it into tentative advice.
records.remedy: I won't search for presences again.

highlights.text: I should probably not investigate presences anymore.

records.jp: こわいんだ。
records.en: Because it's scary.
records.assessment: The emphatic こわいんだ reiterates 'I'm scared' with explanatory force. The English turns it into a subordinate cause clause and makes an unspecified 'it' scary.
records.remedy: I'm scared, that's why.

highlights.text: Because it's scary.

records.jp: 逃げ込むように学校に来ていた。
records.en: I came to school so that I could run away into it.
comments: Like Misato. The thing about the subdivision of duties probably happened long before. After all, there's no Fall of Mankind, is there. -GHS
records.assessment: 逃げ込むように says that he arrived at school as if fleeing into refuge. The English turns resemblance into deliberate purpose and uses the unnatural spatial phrase 'run away into it.'
records.remedy: I found myself at school, as though I had fled there for refuge.

highlights.text: I came to school so that I could run away into it.

records.jp: 美希と会うために廊下に行く。
records.en: I go to the corridor, so that I could meet Miki.
records.assessment: The Japanese gives his current purpose in going to the corridor. Past modal 'could' makes the meeting a past possibility rather than the intended present action.
records.remedy: to meet Miki

highlights.text: so that I could meet Miki

records.jp: 移動していないなら、まだそこにいてくれるはずだった。
records.en: If she did not move, then she should've still been there,
comments: That if... -GHS
records.assessment: The condition concerns whether she has moved since he left. The English simple past can describe a discrete past refusal to move rather than continued nonmovement.
records.remedy: If she hasn't moved, she should still be there

highlights.text: If she did not move, then she should've still been there

records.jp: 永遠になったからには死体はない。
records.en: When one becomes eternal, they have no cadaver.
comments: So she was crucified, and then got up and walked away. Oh and the gate of school, which would be her tomb, was open. It's unclear how much time has passed, but assuming the murder is on the night of Wednesday, and the resurrection on the dawn of Saturday, that's three days. 72 hours outside of the loop would be between 7 and 8 inside, so that sounds right. And so, she's been crucified, and after roughly three days the tomb is found empty. All of this rings a bell. -GHS
records.assessment: The source says that because Miki has become eternal, there is no corpse. The English generalizes to an abstract 'one,' switches pronouns, and uses clinical 'cadaver' for the absent body.
records.remedy: Now that she's eternal, there is no corpse.

highlights.text: When one becomes eternal, they have no cadaver.

records.jp: 永遠とはそうしたものだ。
records.en: For that is what eternity does.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that this absence is the nature of eternity—what eternity is like. The English instead personifies eternity as an agent that performs the preceding action.
records.remedy: that's what eternity is like

highlights.text: that is what eternity does

records.jp: 永遠化したなら、移動できないはずの美希がいないのも納得できる。
records.en: As she was Eternalized, Miki not being there when she shouldn't have been able to move is something I can accept.
comments: Troll is the World Switch, see CCD0022A and 23, when the same thing happens. The simple answer is that, if she ever was there, she just got up and left many hours before. This was nothing but a weird corridor play like many in the main scenario. -GHS
records.assessment: The source says that if she was made eternal, her absence despite being unable to move becomes explicable. The English capitalizes an invented passive technical verb, uses causal 'as' rather than the condition, and nests two negative gerund clauses into an opaque sentence.
records.remedy: If she was made eternal, I can understand why Miki is gone even though she shouldn't have been able to move.

highlights.text: As she was Eternalized, Miki not being there when she shouldn't have been able to move is something I can accept.

records.jp: だから良かったと思う。
records.en: And so, I thought, that's good.
records.assessment: The Japanese states his current conclusion that this was for the best. The English shifts 'thought' into past and interrupts the clause with two unnecessary commas.
records.remedy: So I think it was for the best.

highlights.text: And so, I thought, that's good.

records.jp: 正直、美希後の美希を見るのはつらい。
records.en: Honestly, it'd be tough to look at Miki's After-Miki.
records.assessment: The wordplay 美希後の美希 means Miki in her post-Miki state. The English makes 'After-Miki' a possessed object belonging to Miki instead of a temporal modifier of her.
records.remedy: post-Miki Miki

highlights.text: Miki's After-Miki

records.jp: 本当、そう思う。
records.en: Truly, I thought that.
records.assessment: The Japanese emphasizes that he truly thinks so now. The English shifts the conviction into past tense.
records.remedy: I think so.

highlights.text: I thought that.

records.jp: なぜあの子が犠牲にならなきゃいけなかった？
records.en: Why did that child just have to become a sacrifice?
comments: I suspect the impersonal here means he's switched subjects from Miki to whoever Miki is representing in the mansion massacre, likely Youko, possibly Yutaka. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese asks why she had to be sacrificed. The added 'just' gives the necessity a casual or arbitrary conversational flavor rather than preserving the direct protest.
records.remedy: have to be sacrificed

highlights.text: just have to become a sacrifice

records.jp: ら抜き言葉を気にしすぎる保守的な連中と同じくらい、許してはいけないのである。
records.en: This is las unforgivable las the grammar nazis would consider ladding "la" to lall the words that starts with l-a.
comments: Ranuki kotoba, see CCC4010. That's where all the 'ra's come from. This sounds only moderately less insane in Japanese. -GHS
records.assessment: The source compares the offense to conservative speakers obsessing over Japanese ra-dropping, setting up the decision to sing only 'ra.' The English invents adding 'la' to every English word, reverses omission into addition, corrupts multiple words, and ends with subject-verb disagreement.
records.remedy: as unforgivable as the conservative pedants who obsess over dropped ra syllables

highlights.text: las unforgivable las the grammar nazis would consider ladding "la" to lall the words that starts with l-a

records.jp: だから俺は高らかに『ら』だけを歌い続ける。
records.en: Therefore I shall keep singing out and loud my "LA".
records.assessment: 高らかに means proudly or resoundingly, and the source sings only the syllable ra as the payoff to the prior ra-dropping joke. 'Out and loud' is ungrammatical, 'my' is added, and 'LA' changes the Japanese syllable.
records.remedy: singing “ra” proudly and at full voice

highlights.text: singing out and loud my "LA"

records.jp: そのまま、屋上に足を向けた。
records.en: And as I was, my feet moved towards the rooftop.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that without changing course or state, Taichi headed for the rooftop. The English makes his feet act autonomously and calques そのまま as the incomplete 'as I was.'
records.remedy: Still as I was, I headed for the rooftop.

highlights.text: And as I was, my feet moved towards the rooftop.

records.jp: トモダチの塔はない。
records.en: There was no Tower of Friends.
records.assessment: The Japanese uses present scene-setting and the tower name does not require title capitalization throughout.
records.remedy: The tower of friends is gone.

highlights.text: There was no Tower of Friends.

records.jp: だけど、残骸さえもないのは？
records.en: But then, there's no wreckage either, how come?
comments: A word that turns up in pretty nice moments, that, in particular it's used to describe their friendship in CCA0030. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese asks why not even wreckage remains. The English joins two questions with a comma and attaches 'either' before an afterthought 'how come.'
records.remedy: But why isn't there even any wreckage?

highlights.text: But then, there's no wreckage either, how come?

records.jp: 怖くなってくる。
records.en: I became afraid.
records.assessment: The Japanese says fear is beginning to build in the current moment. The English shifts it to a completed past transition.
records.remedy: I'm starting to feel afraid.

highlights.text: I became afraid.

records.jp: 一度気づいたら、すべてが崩壊してしまう。
records.en: Once you notice it, all is Downfall.
comments: Meaning he was doing all that stuff to avoid accepting that his friends are no longer on good terms and that his 'eden' is lost. It's as upfront an admission as there are, here. This is why he doesn't want to go inside the house and meet Mutsumi, or why he must 'reset' if "shot" by Kiri, whatever that really means. Also, he has this possibly prophetic concept of them all coming back together to assemble the antenna, although the first version is less than healthy. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says everything collapses once the phenomenon is noticed. The English replaces the finite action with a malformed copular noun phrase and capitalizes an abstract common noun.
records.remedy: everything collapses

highlights.text: all is Downfall

records.jp: 濃密な夜が緋色さえも塗りつぶした頃、俺は自宅でもある町はずれの原っぱに横たわっていた。
records.en: In this hour when the dense night has painted out even the brilliant scarlet, I sprawl out in my home that is also the field in the outskirts.
comments: Scarlet = blood. Recreation of internal red via time aphasia to dodge the unmanageable real evening. -GHS
records.assessment: The source places him in the outskirts field that has become his home once dense night has covered even the scarlet sky. The English mixes present perfect and present, says he actively 'sprawl[s] out,' and makes one location both his house and a separately definite field.
records.remedy: By the time dense night had painted over even the scarlet sky, I lay in the field on the outskirts that had become my home.

highlights.text: In this hour when the dense night has painted out even the brilliant scarlet, I sprawl out in my home that is also the field in the outskirts.

records.jp: 力が出ない。頭痛も酷い。動けない。
records.en: I can't put strength into myself. Headache's terrible too. I can't move.
comments: This was what he was at the start, when he began the recollection scene. Sooo... has it ended? -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says he cannot summon any strength and that his own headache is severe. 'Put strength into myself' is a calque, while singular 'headache' needs a determiner or possessive.
records.remedy: I have no strength. My headache is terrible too.

highlights.text: I can't put strength into myself. Headache's terrible too.

records.jp: 記憶。ただそれだけが、救いではないか。
records.en: Memories. Those and only those may be my salvation.
comments: Term is also religious, of course. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese identifies memory, singular and abstract, as his sole salvation. The English pluralizes it into a set of discrete recollections and repeats the plural demonstrative.
records.remedy: Memory. That alone

highlights.text: Memories. Those and only those

records.jp: パッチワークのように貼り合わせた。ギャグを繰り出してセクハラをした。
records.en:
And I pasted together this Patchwork-like thing. And
that I unleashed gags and that I sexually harassed.
comments: This was added in CCX0001 as well. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says he stitched the imagined possibilities together like patchwork, cracked jokes, and committed sexual harassment. The English invents an object 'this ... thing,' capitalizes patchwork, then begins a sentence with 'And that I' without a governing verb.
records.remedy: I pasted them together like patchwork. I cracked jokes and committed sexual harassment.

highlights.text:
And I pasted together this Patchwork-like thing. And
that I unleashed gags and that I sexually harassed.

records.jp: 完全ではないとしても、楽しい可能性であることに違いはない。
records.en: Even if it wasn't perfect, there was no mistaking how these were fun possibilities.
comments: A simple Trollsplanation is that he killed everyone and all that's happening in the main VN is him hallucinating from this point before he dies. But if he finds peace in his last moment before death, not much changes, philosophically speaking, making it a double troll regardless. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese refers to the constructed scenario as one enjoyable possibility despite its imperfection. The English shifts it to a plural set without an antecedent in the translated unit.
records.remedy: it was an enjoyable possibility

highlights.text: these were fun possibilities

records.jp: あれから、どれだけの時間が経過したのか。
records.en: And from then, how many hours did even elapse.
comments: This may be where he wakes up from the dream waaay above. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese asks how much time passed, without specifying hours. The English narrows the duration and uses emphatic 'even' in an ungrammatical indirect-question order.
records.remedy: how much time had passed

highlights.text: how many hours did even elapse

records.jp: 今日は何日だったっけ？
records.en: What day was even today...?
records.assessment: 何日 asks for the calendar date; the next unit separately states that he lacks a sense of the day of the week. 'What day' blurs those distinct questions, and 'even' is awkwardly placed.
records.remedy: What was today's date again?

highlights.text: What day was even today...?

records.jp: 曜日感覚がない。
records.en: I lost my sense of weekday.
comments: Long ago, given everything. Term still relates to Youko. Maybe she was just named after that, back at the Mansion. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he currently has no sense of what day of the week it is. The English asserts a completed past loss and uses singular 'weekday' without a determiner.
records.remedy: I have no sense of what day of the week it is.

highlights.text: I lost my sense of weekday.

records.jp: 自分が人間ではなくなってしまったかのような感覚さえある。
records.en: This sensation like I've become something no longer human is all there is.
records.assessment: The source says that he even feels as if he has ceased to be human. The English adds that this sensation is the only thing that exists and uses the malformed noun-plus-clause sequence 'sensation like.'
records.remedy: I even feel as though I've ceased to be human.

highlights.text: This sensation like I've become something no longer human is all there is.

records.jp: そんな陳腐なことを、誰が言えるのだ。
records.en: Who'd ever say that kind of stale hackneyed line.
comments: Of course, he's no god; that'd be still Nietzscheianism. He's the representative of the technical equivalent, doing like said equivalent his best to follow the Real one. -GHS
records.assessment: 陳腐 means hackneyed or stale, making the pair redundant, while こと is an idea or claim rather than specifically a line of dialogue.
records.remedy: such a hackneyed idea

highlights.text: that kind of stale hackneyed line

records.jp: 神とは現象だ。
records.en: God is a Phenomenon,
comments: See CCD0009 now. This is simply assertion based on nothing. -GHS
records.assessment: 現象 is a common noun and has no source-based reason for capitalization.
records.remedy: phenomenon

highlights.text: Phenomenon

records.jp: だから俺は現象なのかも知れない。
records.en: therefore, I might just be Phenomenon myself.
comments: However, he's agreeing that he's a god with this. In other words, he's trolling himself. -GHS
records.assessment: The sentence begins a new independent thought and requires capitalization. 'Phenomenon' is a singular count noun requiring an article and is not a proper category requiring a capital.
records.remedy: Therefore, I might be a phenomenon myself.

highlights.text: therefore, I might just be Phenomenon myself.

records.jp: その解釈は、美味だった。
records.en: That explanation was a tasty delicacy.
comments: Try empty calories. -GHS
records.assessment: 解釈 is an interpretation, not an explanation supplied by someone else, and 美味 metaphorically says the interpretation is delicious or appealing. Calling the interpretation 'a delicacy' and then modifying it with 'tasty' is redundant and concretizes the metaphor into food.
records.remedy: That interpretation was delicious.

highlights.text: That explanation was a tasty delicacy.

records.jp: 俺は、焼かれる。
records.en: I am burning.
records.assessment: The passive 焼かれる says that the sunlight is burning or roasting Taichi. The English active-progressive construction means that he himself is on fire.
records.remedy: I am being burned.

highlights.text: I am burning.

records.jp: そう。俺は、ちゃんと聞いていたはずなのだ。
records.en: Right. Because I should've heard those correctly.
records.assessment: The Japanese affirms that he must have properly heard the phrase. The English begins with causal 'Because' despite having no governing result and uses 'correctly' for the completeness or fidelity of hearing.
records.remedy: Right. I must have heard the words properly.

highlights.text: Right. Because I should've heard those correctly.

records.jp: 『好きだったのに―――』
records.en: 『When I loved you---』
comments: PCP above
records.assessment: 好きだったのに means 'even though I loved you' or 'I loved you, and yet,' with のに carrying an essential frustrated contrast. The English changes it into a neutral temporal clause and omits the concessive relation.
records.remedy: Even though I loved you—

highlights.text: When I loved you---

records.jp: 「俺を……好き？」
records.en: Taichi: "You loved... me?"
records.assessment: The recalled fragment prompts the immediate question 俺を好き, literally whether she likes him. The English past tense makes the affection definitively over rather than asking about its object.
records.remedy: You... like me?

highlights.text: You loved... me?

records.jp: 声がひりつく。
records.en: Speaking smarts.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that his voice feels raw, stinging, or rasping as he speaks. The English makes the abstract act of speaking the body part that hurts.
records.remedy: My voice stings.

highlights.text: Speaking smarts.

records.jp: 「こんな……俺を？」
records.en: Taichi: "This... me here?"
records.assessment: こんな俺 means 'someone like me' with self-deprecating force. The English treats himself as a demonstrative object located 'here' and never forms a natural question.
records.remedy: Someone... like me?

highlights.text: This... me here?

records.jp: 世界はこんなに嬉しいのだから。
records.en: Because the world's making me this much happy.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that the world feels or is this joyful, which motivates wanting to wake into it. The English makes the world a causal agent acting on him and uses the nonidiomatic degree phrase 'this much happy.'
records.remedy: the world is this full of joy

highlights.text: the world's making me this much happy

records.jp: また何でもない毎日を、続ける喜びがあるのだから。
records.en: Because I now have the joy to persevere in this daily life of perfect normality again.
records.assessment: The source celebrates continuing ordinary, uneventful days again. 'Persevere' adds arduous endurance, 'perfect normality' overstates 何でもない, and English takes joy 'in' continuing rather than 'to' persevere.
records.remedy: the joy of continuing ordinary, uneventful days again

highlights.text: the joy to persevere in this daily life of perfect normality again

records.jp: 次はもうちょっとうまくやれると思うから。
records.en: As I think I should be able to make things go well next,
comments: See CCD0022A. He's not healed, not by far. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese says that next time he thinks he can handle things a little better. The English omits 'time' after 'next' and uses the causative phrase 'make things go well' instead of his own performance.
records.remedy: do a little better next time

highlights.text: make things go well next

records.jp: 転生するなら次は『たにし』になって何も考えずに暮らそうと考えもしたが、また人間になってもいいかなあと思う。
records.en: And so even if I had this idea of wanting to reincarnate into a pond snail and live my life without having anything to think about at all, maybe it would just be nice if I were to be a human again, I think.
comments: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viviparidae Pond snail = Tanishi, written with the same 'ta' as in Tanaka. -GHS
records.assessment: The Japanese contrasts a thought he had entertained—becoming a pond snail and living thoughtlessly—with his current sense that being human again might be acceptable. The English uses concessive 'even if' for a real past thought, stacks 'maybe,' 'would,' 'if,' and 'I think,' and turns 'having nothing to think about' into lacking any ability or object for thought.
records.remedy: I had considered being reincarnated as a pond snail and living without a thought in my head, but now I think becoming human again might not be so bad.

highlights.text: And so even if I had this idea of wanting to reincarnate into a pond snail and live my life without having anything to think about at all, maybe it would just be nice if I were to be a human again, I think.

records.jp: 自覚できないうわごとを発した。
records.en: I fired off into ramblings, incapable of self-awareness.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that he uttered delirious words without being aware of them. 'Fired off into ramblings' combines incompatible phrasal constructions, while the trailing adjective says Taichi generally lacks self-awareness rather than that the speech is unconscious.
records.remedy: I babbled deliriously without even realizing it.

highlights.text: I fired off into ramblings, incapable of self-awareness.

records.jp: 脳がとける。
records.en: The brain melts.
records.assessment: The Japanese refers to Taichi's own brain. English requires a possessive rather than the generic definite article.
records.remedy: My brain melts.

highlights.text: The brain melts.

records.jp: だけど最後に俺は少しだけ―――
records.en: But at last, I will, just a little---
records.assessment: The source begins a final, immediate fragment about what Taichi does or experiences a little at the end. The English shifts it into future tense and isolates the verb from its absent complement with two commas.
records.remedy: But at the very end, I, just a little—

highlights.text: But at last, I will, just a little---

records.jp: 最古の記憶は。
records.en:
These are the recollections
of that which is so far gone.
comments: 最古 saiko, oldest, is also readable as Psychopath. Oldest memories, a psychopath's memories: first line of the story spoils one of the two plot twists of the simplest interpretative layer. See CCA0030 for one of the clearest tells of this. -GHS
records.assessment: 最古 marks the earliest or oldest memory. The rendering replaces the superlative with mere remoteness, changes a singular fragment into plural recollections, and supplies an object not present in the Japanese.
records.remedy: Retain the singular earliest-memory fragment and its superlative force.

highlights.text:
These are the recollections
of that which is so far gone.

records.jp: 日付さえおぼろげな、遠い霞のなか。
records.en:
The date alone vague and indistinct,
laying at the heart of a dim distant haze.
comments: See CCD0023. The day of the week is also difficult to tell. -GHS
records.assessment: さえ is scalar and additive: even the date is hazy. 'The date alone' instead suggests that only the date is vague. 'At the heart of' is added, and 'laying' is ungrammatical in this intransitive construction.
records.remedy: Express that even the date is vague within a distant haze, without the added center metaphor.

highlights.text: The date alone
laying at the heart of

records.jp: 枠に切り取られた散在する瞬きに目を奪われる。
records.en:
a scattering of twinkles cut off by
the frame that absconds with my sight.
records.assessment: The scattered glints, cut out by the frame, capture the observer's gaze. The English instead makes the frame the agent that 'absconds' with sight, changing the source's attachment and using an inapplicable English verb.
records.remedy: Make the framed, scattered glints the object that captures the gaze.

highlights.text: the frame that absconds with my sight

records.jp: 一言で形容してしまうのが惜しいほど優美で。
records.en: so gracefully elegant that to describe it in a few words is to disappoint it.
records.assessment: The source says the sight is so elegant that reducing it to a single description would feel regrettable or wasteful. The English instead says that description disappoints the object, adding an unsupported interpersonal relation and weakening 一言's compression to 'a few words.'
records.remedy: Describe an elegance too rich to reduce to a single phrase.

highlights.text: to disappoint it

records.jp: 真新しく清潔、かつ閑静な地方都市……のはずれ。
records.en:
A brand new, pure, immaculate, and quiet suburban
city... 's rear end.
records.assessment: The Japanese describes the outskirts of a brand-new, clean, quiet regional city. The English turns 地方都市 into 'suburban city,' renders はずれ as the anatomically comic and grammatically detached 'rear end,' and redundantly splits 清潔 into 'pure, immaculate.'
records.remedy: Identify the location as the outskirts of a new, clean, quiet regional city.

highlights.text:
A brand new, pure, immaculate, and quiet suburban
city... 's rear end.

records.jp: つまりはしっこだ。
records.en: In short, this is just the appendix.
comments: see what I did there -GHS
records.assessment: はしっこ means an edge, end, or fringe. 'Appendix' names an attached supplement or organ and is not an English equivalent in this locative context.
records.remedy: Call it the edge or outskirts.

highlights.text: appendix

records.jp: ちなみに向こう側にはデパートもあり、時間さえかければ都心にも出られる路線がそのつま先を置き、レンタルショップはおろかゲーセン・本屋・飲み屋・出張（ヘルス）まである。
records.en: Speaking of this other side, there's department stores, and if one takes the time, the routes that lead to the city center will lay at one's feet rental shops of course, and game centers, and book stores, and even "health services" shops.
comments: They're "massage parlors". Those are not scare quotes; they are an actual part of the name. And they will play a part, however weird, in the VN. Most famous ones are PeachLand and MateBook. -GHS
records.assessment: The source lists amenities on the far side and says a rail line reaches toward the city center if one is willing to spend the time. The English attaches the rental shop to what the route 'will lay at one's feet,' omits the drinking establishment, pluralizes and redistributes items, and converts an outcall adult service into ordinary 'health services' shops. The resulting syntax also obscures the list's structure.
records.remedy: Keep the rail-line clause separate and reproduce the full amenity list, including the drinking establishment and outcall adult service.

highlights.text: Speaking of this other side, there's department stores, and if one takes the time, the routes that lead to the city center will lay at one's feet rental shops of course, and game centers, and book stores, and even "health services" shops.

records.jp: 飽食の極みを迎えた文明の、爛熟した果実がここにある。
records.en: There it lies, the over-ripened fruit of a civilization that welcomes the heights of appetite.
comments: Appetite, see CCA0021 -GHS
records.assessment: 飽食 is satiation or overabundant consumption, not appetite. The source characterizes a civilization that has reached the extreme of surfeit; the English reverses this into welcoming appetite.
records.remedy: Refer to a civilization at the height of overconsumption or surfeit.

highlights.text: welcomes the heights of appetite

records.jp: 要するにベッドタウンだ。
records.en: In other words, it's more of a dormitory than a proper town,
comments: I'll try to only tweak terms if they don't google to something relevant. This is particularly interesting for one reason: somehow Mutsumi lives in a dormitory, leaving Taichi unattended for days at an end... but the town itself is all but a dormitory. Very odd. -GHS
records.assessment: ベッドタウン is the established Japanese borrowing for a bedroom community or commuter town. The English instead calls the place a dormitory and adds the contrast 'than a proper town,' which the source does not state.
records.remedy: Identify it as a bedroom community or commuter town.

highlights.text: In other words, it's more of a dormitory than a proper town,

records.jp: なお地図上では、二つの地を分断するこの雄峰、『丘』ということにされている。
records.en: According to the map, the majestic mountain ridges that cleave this territory in two are labeled hills.
comments: The mountains are religion, specifically Christianity, and the politicians (AKA those Of The World) call religion a small trifling little thing; a hill. And then Christianity is curry and therefore the message of Cross Channel is that politicians think mountains are curry. That doesn't seem too unlikely, by the way. -GHS
records.assessment: The source points to this singular majestic peak, which separates two places and is designated a 'hill' on the map. The English pluralizes the peak into ridges, changes two places into one territory split in two, and pluralizes the map label.
records.remedy: Keep the singular peak, the two separated places, and the singular cartographic label.

highlights.text: According to the map, the majestic mountain ridges that cleave this territory in two are labeled hills.

records.jp: が、調子に乗って隣町の相原市（超遠い）へあと五キロという地点にまで到達したところで故障。
records.en: But, getting carried out in the moment, he had a breakdown after getting to a point about five kilometers from the neighboring town of Aihara City (hyper far away).
comments: Keeping 超 consistent as it seems a bit of a running gag. The bike will take you far, but not everywhere on its own. A "Aihara" seems to exist, dunno the point of it. -GHS
records.assessment: The source says that after getting carried away and reaching a point five kilometers short of the distant neighboring city, the bicycle broke down. 'He had a breakdown' instead predicates a personal or psychological breakdown of the rider; the preceding 'getting carried out' also fails to express 調子に乗って.
records.remedy: Make the bicycle the thing that breaks down after he gets carried away and rides that far.

highlights.text: he had a breakdown

records.jp: 桜庭一族は正反対におっとりとした一族で、父親は盲腸の痛みに気づかず死の一歩手前まで旅だったという武勲の持ち主だ。
records.en: But the Sakuraba family was the complete opposite, a household of placid gentleness. His father had even accomplished the Feat of Arms of having voyaged to the brink of death by ignoring the pain of his appendicitis.
records.assessment: 気づかず says the father failed to notice the pain, consistent with the family's oblivious placidity. 'Ignoring' instead implies conscious awareness followed by deliberate disregard and therefore changes the comic causal premise.
records.remedy: Say that he never noticed the appendicitis pain until he was near death.

highlights.text: ignoring the pain of his appendicitis

records.jp: 夜中になっても帰宅しない息子を案じて『誘拐されたんです！』と警察に駆け込むあたり、桜庭一族のまろやかな天然さが垣間見えて面白い。
records.en: It was funny to see a chink in the Sakurabas' naturally mellow nature when, in the dead of night, said son still had not returned and they anxiously stampeded off to the police shouting "he has been kidnapped!".
records.assessment: The family's panicked report provides an amusing glimpse of their mellow, guileless obliviousness. Calling it a 'chink in' that nature makes the behavior an exception or breach in the trait rather than an instance that reveals it.
records.remedy: Present the police report as an amusing glimpse of the family's mellow cluelessness.

highlights.text: a chink in the Sakurabas' naturally mellow nature

records.jp: 要するに奴は、帰宅の途中、道を外れて山に入ったわけだ。
records.en: In short, this idiot, while coming back home, drifted into a mountain that's not connected with the road.
comments: Map seems to fit, he just walked home on the south side and overshot the area of his mansion, ending towards the power plant. -GHS
records.assessment: 道を外れて says that he left or strayed from the road and entered the mountain. The English instead describes the mountain itself as unconnected to the road, relocating the relation and adding a geographic claim absent from the source.
records.remedy: Say that he strayed off the road and into the mountain on his way home.

highlights.text: drifted into a mountain that's not connected with the road

records.jp: 『秘密基地が』
records.en: Sakuraba: "In the hidden base..."
records.assessment: The quoted fragment marks 'the secret base' with が as its grammatical subject. The English converts it into a location introduced by 'in,' and replaces the compound's conventional 'secret base' sense with 'hidden base.'
records.remedy: Keep 'the secret base' as the suspended subject of the quoted fragment.

highlights.text: In the hidden base...

records.jp: 桜庭は報道の残酷さを思い知った。
records.en: Sakuraba understood with his flesh the cruelty of the press.
records.assessment: 思い知った means that he learned or came to understand the cruelty of the press, generally through harsh experience. The source has no body or flesh expression; adding one turns the idiom into an unsupported physical image.
records.remedy: Say that he learned the cruelty of the press the hard way.

highlights.text: with his flesh

records.jp: 二束三文の土地が、みるみるうちに札束に変わった。
records.en: In the strike of the blink of an eye, this three pennies for two acres of a land was transformed into rolls of banknotes.
comments: There's a two and there's a three... grrr, where's the other two? Maybe that miru-miru. -GHS
records.assessment: 二束三文 is an idiom meaning virtually worthless or dirt-cheap, not a literal price-to-acre conversion. The English invents pennies and acreage, while みるみるうち means visibly or rapidly rather than 'in the strike of the blink.'
records.remedy: Say that dirt-cheap land rapidly turned into bundles of cash.

highlights.text: this three pennies for two acres of a land

records.jp: 富豪が何人も誕生し、ビルが建ち、人が増えた。
records.en: With everybody reborn a millionaire, buildings were constructed, and people increased.
comments: I don't get it, shouldn't it be "tents were erected, and people were constructed"? -GHS
records.assessment: 何人も says that a number of wealthy people or tycoons emerged. The English changes this limited group into everybody and adds literal rebirth, substantially exaggerating the distribution of wealth.
records.remedy: Say that several fortunes or wealthy magnates emerged as buildings and population increased.

highlights.text: everybody reborn a millionaire

records.jp: だからといって、ベンチにライトを仕込むことはないだろうに。
records.en: Nevertheless, they didn't 'rearn' to build the benches 'light', didn't they.
comments: grrrrroooooaaaaannnnn ライト = light + right, 仕込む = build into + teach/learn. I suppose it's harder to spot in Japanese. Perhaps a warning that even the Japanese better know enough English to spot this stuff if they want to understand some of the jokes and themes. Works backwards still: better know just a pinch of Japanese, or you'll be losing some of this stuff regardless. -GHS
records.assessment: The source says that even so, there is surely no need to install lights in benches. The English introduces an undefined 'rearn,' turns installed lights into the adjective 'light,' reverses the construction into something they did not learn to build, and fails to convey the complaint.
records.remedy: State that free electricity still does not justify installing lights in the benches.

highlights.text: Nevertheless, they didn't 'rearn' to build the benches 'light', didn't they.

records.jp: 「もしかしてアレ？　生理っぽいやつ？」
records.en: Taichi: "Could it be that thing? That biological-ish thing?"
records.assessment: 生理 in this teasing context specifically refers to menstruation or a period. 'Biological-ish thing' removes the referent almost entirely and turns a pointedly intrusive question into a vague abstraction.
records.remedy: Retain the euphemistic but unmistakable reference to a period.

highlights.text: biological-ish thing

records.jp: 実際には『こんのぉっ！』と言ってる。
records.en: In truth, she's saying "reallyyy!",
records.assessment: こんのぉっ is an angry, drawn-out この, roughly an incomplete 'you...!' or 'you little...!' It does not mean 'really.' The reconstruction therefore substitutes a different word and breaks the explanation of the clipped preceding cry.
records.remedy: Reconstruct the cry as a lisped or clipped angry 'you...!' expression.

highlights.text: reallyyy!

records.jp: 俺は戦士か。
records.en: What am I, a soldier?
comments: See CCA0027. -GHS
records.assessment: 戦士 means a warrior or fighter, whereas 'soldier' corresponds to a distinct military role. The substitution loses the explicit combatant term and weakens any lexical callback built on it.
records.remedy: Use 'warrior' or 'fighter.'

highlights.text: soldier

records.jp: これでも今日は滅茶苦茶話している方だ。
records.en: And for all this, today's the day to speak out nonsense wantonly.
records.assessment: The Japanese says that even this counts as talking an extraordinary amount today, relative to their norm. The English instead makes today an occasion for speaking nonsense recklessly, misreading 滅茶苦茶 as the content or manner of speech and losing the comparative 話している方だ construction.
records.remedy: Say that, even so, they have talked an extraordinary amount today by their usual standard.

highlights.text: today's the day to speak out nonsense wantonly.

records.jp: 盛大にため息をつかれると、こちらも萎える。
records.en: With a lengthy, exasperated sigh, this also withers.
records.assessment: こちらも refers back to the narrator: being met with such an extravagant sigh makes him lose heart or wilt as well. 'This also withers' replaces the person with an unanchored demonstrative and fails to identify whose spirits fall.
records.remedy: Say that the grand sigh makes the narrator wilt or lose heart too.

highlights.text: this

records.jp: 割れてる。
records.en: It was split.
comments: It was split + it was made to split. This could mean it's broken; this could mean it's split as in a personality. -GHS
records.assessment: 割れてる states a present resulting condition: it is split or cracked. 'Was split' changes that acknowledgment into a completed past passive event and weakens the immediate joke.
records.remedy: Use 'It is' or 'It is cracked.'

highlights.text: was split

records.jp: 憮然とした顔つきがデフォルト設定の冬子だ。
records.en: A disappointed face is in Touko's default settings.
comments: The computer terminology begins! -GHS
records.assessment: 憮然とした here describes a sullen, displeased, or indignant expression, not disappointment. The English assigns a different emotional state to the character's default face.
records.remedy: Use 'sullen,' 'displeased,' or an equivalent default scowl.

highlights.text: disappointed

records.jp: だってテント張って機材並べて。
records.en: After all, with all the tents spread and the machine parts set up,
comments: 機材 is the term used for the generic "machinery" that is brought up from the Club Room to the Antenna on the rooftop. The Training Camp looks more mysterious by the minute. They had survival games from the sound of it, but what anything else involved is never seen. If only because the idea they'd actually train with equipment and everything sounds so off for people who can't even look at each other. But they did stay there for a time, didn't they. -GHS
records.assessment: 機材 means equipment or gear. 'Machine parts' narrows it to components of machinery, which the source does not say, and changes the image of equipment being laid out.
records.remedy: Use 'equipment' or 'gear.'

highlights.text: machine parts

records.jp: 林道を抜けて、広場に出る。
records.en: Out of the forest path we come out to a wide grove.
records.assessment: 広場 is an open area, clearing, plaza, or field. A grove is a cluster of trees, so the English reverses the spatial transition from leaving the forest road and emerging into open ground.
records.remedy: Use 'clearing' or 'open area.'

highlights.text: wide grove

records.jp: 光が満ちる。
records.en: The light is in the rise,
records.assessment: 光が満ちる means that light fills or floods the space. 'Is in the rise' is not an English rendering of that image and instead suggests an unrelated act of rising.
records.remedy: Use 'Light floods in' or 'The clearing fills with light.'

highlights.text: The light is in the rise,

records.jp: 「こ、この匹夫……」
records.en: Touko: "Y-, you sphincter..."
comments: Curiously, all versions have a variation on this line. -GHS
records.assessment: 匹夫 is a contemptuous term for a lowly, common, ignorant, or boorish man. It has no anatomical meaning; 'sphincter' substitutes an unrelated body part and destroys the insult's register.
records.remedy: Use 'wretch,' 'boor,' 'base man,' or another contemptuous personal insult.

highlights.text: sphincter

records.jp: 二人で、みんなのもとに。
records.en: In a duo in front of everyone.
comments: It's ambiguous whether this is Taichi and Misato or Touko and Taichi. In the first case, Youko is not here; in the latter, she is. Supposing intentionality. -GHS
records.assessment: みんなのもとに marks movement toward or joining everyone. 'In front of everyone' replaces the destination with a static public position and changes the fragment's spatial relation.
records.remedy: Use 'Together, we headed over to everyone.'

highlights.text: in front of everyone

records.jp: 広場で機材の後かたづけをしていた五つの顔が、一斉にこちらを向いた。
records.en: The faces of the five who were tidying up the equipment in the grove turned my way in unison.
records.assessment: 広場 is the clearing or open area established immediately before, not a grove of trees. The repeated substitution reverses the setting while the five people turning together remains accurate.
records.remedy: Use 'clearing' or 'open area.'

highlights.text: grove

records.jp: 五組の視線を感じる。ますます気が高ぶる。
records.en: I feel the sights of a group of five on me. More and more my excitement grows.
records.assessment: 五組の視線 means five sets or pairs of eyes. 'A group of five' instead denotes five people or five undifferentiated looks and loses the counted paired gaze established by the preceding five faces.
records.remedy: Use 'five pairs of eyes' or 'five sets of eyes.'

highlights.text: a group of five

records.jp: 連携ピッタリの超上級放置プレイ。
records.en: Perfectly Coordinated Hyper Pro-Level Leave-It-To-Chance Sketch.
comments: Reading some sarcasm here... -GHS
records.assessment: 放置プレイ is the comic idea of coordinated, expert-level neglect or ignoring someone, with プレイ carrying a play/scenario nuance. 'Leave-it-to-chance sketch' introduces randomness and a comedy skit, neither of which is present.
records.remedy: Use an image such as 'perfectly coordinated, expert-level neglect play.'

highlights.text: Leave-It-To-Chance Sketch

records.jp: 鬱陶しい。
records.en: How gloomy.
records.assessment: In the immediate context of bothersome bangs, 鬱陶しい means annoying, bothersome, or irritating. 'Gloomy' instead describes mood or atmosphere and breaks the stated causal link to his hair.
records.remedy: Use 'Annoying' or 'What a nuisance.'

highlights.text: gloomy

records.jp: 徒歩の速度でよくこけないもの。
records.en: That's not something that falls easily to walking speeds.
records.assessment: The Japanese marvels that she manages not to topple over while riding at walking speed. The English instead describes an unspecified thing failing to reduce or 'fall' to walking speeds, reversing the physical event and losing the rider as subject.
records.remedy: Use 'I'm amazed she doesn't fall over at walking speed.'

highlights.text: falls easily to walking speeds

records.jp: 「ねえ、たいっちゃん裏山って行ったことある？」
records.en: Girl: "Say, Taicchan, you ever been to the forest heart of the mountain?"
comments: Despite being written with "rear" and "mountain", "urayama" is not the other side of the mountain, it's the part of the mountain less exposed to light. (Or the mountain behind one's house, but Taichi's house is nowhere near the hokora, despite how in CCZAS... but never mind.) Adapting a bit because "darker parts of the mountain" sounds kinda silly. -GHS
records.assessment: 裏山 is the hill or mountain behind a place, conventionally the nearby back hill. The English invents a forest and relocates the destination to a mountain's interior or heart, neither of which is stated.
records.remedy: Use 'the hill out back' or 'the mountain behind here,' according to the established geography.

highlights.text: forest heart of the mountain

records.jp: 「もんのすごい御利益があるわけさ」
records.en: Girl: "He's got this amazing graciousness, y'know."
comments: This should be where the "Tender Grace" music takes its name, but it doesn't quite work here. I'll put it later. -GHS
records.assessment: 御利益 is a divine or religious benefit, blessing, or efficacy granted by a deity or sacred site. 'Graciousness' instead describes a person's courteous or merciful character and loses the promised benefit.
records.remedy: Say that the deity brings extraordinary blessings or benefits.

highlights.text: amazing graciousness

records.jp: 「いや、笑いたくなるのはごもっともですよ。あたしだって人からンなこと真顔で言われたら笑うわ」
records.en: Girl: "Naaah, wanting to ridicule it is totally natural. If some guy saidd'at to me with a really straight face I'd laugh too."
comments: Said + that. The actress sounds like she's stumbling on that one. -GHS
records.assessment: 笑いたくなる means feeling the urge to laugh. 'Wanting to ridicule it' adds an intention to mock or belittle something, changing an involuntary comic reaction into directed scorn.
records.remedy: Use 'Of course you'd want to laugh' or equivalent.

highlights.text: wanting to ridicule it

records.jp: 「知ってる」
records.en: Nanaka: "Knew it."
comments: More like a "whatevs", but will become literal in CCB0002, and furthering the confusion on that 'know' above. And it won't be the first time. -GHS
records.assessment: 知ってる is the blunt present-state reply 'I know' or 'I already know.' 'Knew it' instead means a prior suspicion has just been confirmed, changing the response's temporal and pragmatic force.
records.remedy: Use 'I know.'

highlights.text: Knew it

records.jp: 「林道の脇にある？」
records.en: Taichi: "Is it on the side of the mountain trail?"
records.assessment: 林道 is a forest or logging road, normally a road through managed woodland rather than a mountain footpath. 'Mountain trail' changes both the terrain and the kind of route.
records.remedy: Use 'Is it beside the forest road?'

highlights.text: mountain trail

records.jp: ここだけの話、ちょっと惚れた。
records.en: Just between you and me, that's quite charming.
records.assessment: ちょっと惚れた says the narrator fell for her a little or was briefly smitten. 'That's quite charming' transfers the state from his attraction to a judgment about an unspecified act and substantially weakens the confession.
records.remedy: Use 'Between you and me, I fell for her a little.'

highlights.text: that's quite charming

records.jp: 「核戦争がおこっても守ってくれちゃうくらい御利益があるって話だ」
records.en: Nanaka: "They say even if we have a nuclear war, his tender grace is so great that it will totally protect you."
records.assessment: 御利益 again denotes the shrine or deity's protective efficacy or blessings, not a male figure's tender graciousness. The possessive pronoun also fixes a gender absent from the Japanese.
records.remedy: Say that its blessings are supposedly powerful enough to protect someone even in a nuclear war.

highlights.text: his tender grace

records.jp: 「どんなガン保険も本気を出したガンには無力なもんだよ」
records.en: Taichi: "Even if a cancer insurance gave all it had, it's still powerless in front of cancer!"
comments: See CCD5001. -GHS
records.assessment: 本気を出した modifies the cancer: any insurance is powerless once cancer becomes serious or shows its full force. The English makes the insurance exert itself instead, reversing which side of the comparison intensifies.
records.remedy: Use 'Any cancer insurance is powerless once the cancer gets serious.'

highlights.text: Even if a cancer insurance gave all it had

records.jp: 「それ肯定できちゃうくらい権利意識が細分化してる社会ってのも、末期的だよね」
records.en: Nanaka: "A society with a sense of entitlement so refined that it can assert to something so specific has to be on its death throes."
comments: See CCC3025 -GHS
records.assessment: 肯定できちゃう means being able to approve, endorse, or accept that proposal. 'Assert to something' has no corresponding English relation and loses the claim that atomized rights-consciousness could make such a service socially affirmable.
records.remedy: Say that a society whose sense of rights is fragmented enough to endorse something so specific is already terminal.

highlights.text: can assert to something so specific

records.jp: 「しかも転んで傷つけて戻ってきてさ」
records.en: Nanaka: "And then he came back all hurt after a fall."
records.assessment: 傷つけて has the father damage the bicycle after falling and then return with it. 'He came back all hurt' instead assigns the damage to the father himself and omits the damaged object.
records.remedy: Say that he fell, damaged it, and brought it back.

highlights.text: all hurt

records.jp: 「……パパも大変なんだよ」
records.en: Taichi: "...papa's a big fuss as well."
comments: See CCX0001, that's what he uses for his father there too. -GHS
records.assessment: パパも大変 says that Dad has it hard too or that being Dad is difficult. Calling him 'a big fuss' instead characterizes him as a nuisance and changes the predicate.
records.remedy: Use 'Dad has it rough too.'

highlights.text: papa's a big fuss

records.jp: 「母に言いつけたさ」
records.en: Nanaka: "That's what mom always says."
comments: Can be read as "he told mother", but also "mother told him", keeping the ambiguity between who is this 'mom'. Since the term also means "used to say", splitting the difference and going with this. -GHS
records.assessment: 母に marks Mother as the recipient of 言いつけた: the speaker told or tattled to Mother. The English invents a habitual statement made by Mother and reverses the direction of speech.
records.remedy: Use 'So I told Mom on him.'

highlights.text: That's what mom always says

records.jp: アホだこいつの親。
records.en: And these idiots had a child.
comments: Lit. "this guy's parents are idiots", but it's ambiguous whose parents it would be naturally. -GHS
records.assessment: こいつの親 is this person's parent, syntactically the subject being called an idiot. The English instead invents plural idiots who produced a child, changing the referent, number, and proposition.
records.remedy: Use 'This girl's parent is an idiot.' or the contextually appropriate singular equivalent.

highlights.text: these idiots had a child

records.jp: 再見！
records.en: Rediscovery!
records.assessment: 再見 here is a compact joke on seeing the same sight again. 'Rediscovery' means finding or recognizing something anew rather than seeing it again and loses the immediate visual repetition.
records.remedy: Use a compact visual reprise such as 'Behold, again!' or 'Another sighting!'

highlights.text: Rediscovery

records.jp: 「サドルってときに気持ちよかったりする方？」
records.en: Taichi: "Doesn't it at times feel good when you're saddling with a sad'O?"
comments: サドル saddle +サドる be sadistic, particularly appropriate considering that Taichi is (supposedly) an M, see Yutaka. -GHS
records.assessment: The source asks whether the bicycle saddle sometimes feels good, exploiting the immediate eroticized bicycle context. The English invents an incoherent construction involving 'saddling' and a 'sad'O,' importing a sadism pun that is not grammatically present and obscuring the actual question.
records.remedy: Ask whether the saddle ever feels good, preserving the suggestive ambiguity without adding a sadist figure.

highlights.text: when you're saddling with a sad'O

records.jp: 「腰が痛いんだ」
records.en: Nanaka: "Your groin hurts, is that it."
records.assessment: 腰 refers here to the waist, hips, or lower back, not the groin. The substitution makes the supposedly innocent diagnosis explicitly sexual and materially changes the exchange.
records.remedy: Use 'Your lower back hurts, is that it.'

highlights.text: groin

records.jp: 「腰が痛くてね」
records.en: Taichi: "My groin hurts, that's it."
comments: Callback. -GHS
records.assessment: The repeated 腰 again means the waist or lower back. Rendering it as 'groin' repeats the anatomical error and undermines the speaker's attempt to pass off his posture as an ordinary back complaint.
records.remedy: Use 'My lower back hurts, that's all.'

highlights.text: groin

records.jp: 「気をつけなよー。子孫繁栄がやばいぞ」
records.en: Nanaka: "Take some care theeere! The safety of the offspring seems at risk!"
comments: "Your balls are getting chafed in your pants" + "my son's in pain", where "son" is also an euphemism for dick, ergo Nanaka is futanari?????? -GHS
records.assessment: 子孫繁栄 concerns the future continuation or flourishing of one's descendants: his reproductive prospects are in danger. 'The safety of the offspring' instead implies danger to already existing children and changes the causal joke.
records.remedy: Warn that his future family line or ability to have children is at risk.

highlights.text: The safety of the offspring seems at risk

records.jp: 「子孫作りてぇー」
records.en: Taichi: "Let's make some offspriiiing!"
records.assessment: 作りてぇ is the speaker's rough contraction of 'I want to make/have,' expressing his own desire. 'Let's make' turns that desire into an inclusive proposal to the listener and adds a target absent from the Japanese.
records.remedy: Use 'I wanna make some babies!' or an equivalent first-person desire.

highlights.text: Let's make some offspriiiing

records.jp: 「あ、でも普段はブルースネークで安全なんですよ？」
records.en: Taichi: "Ah, but usually it's the green snake, so you're safe, OK?"
comments: Switched because in Japan blue = green -GHS
records.assessment: ブルー is explicitly blue, not green. Changing the snake's color breaks the stated red-blue-yellow sequence that structures the surrounding joke.
records.remedy: Use 'blue snake.'

highlights.text: green

records.jp: 「とうに気づいてるんじゃねぇかこのアマ……」
records.en: Taichi: "You noticed that from the start, dinn'cha, you nun..."
comments: Also "bitch", yes, but Taichi is more of a wannabe motherfucker than a son of a bitch. Plus it's funnier that he keeps calling his mother a virgin. Also, technically nun fits closer given everything. -GHS
records.assessment: アマ in this colloquial katakana use is a derogatory term for a woman, roughly 'bitch' or 'damn woman,' not the religious noun 'nun.' The literal homophone erases the insult and produces an unrelated characterization.
records.remedy: Use an appropriately harsh insult directed at a woman.

highlights.text: nun

records.jp: 早いで済まされる現象ではないのだが。
records.en: Not a Phenomenon that's going to be settled quickly.
comments: See CCC3017, CCD0021, CCX0001... this is all but a warning that we're in for the long haul. -GHS
records.assessment: 早いで済まされる means the event cannot be explained away merely by saying she was fast. The English instead says the phenomenon will not be resolved quickly, changing speed as an insufficient explanation into the time needed to settle a problem.
records.remedy: Use 'That was beyond anything you could explain by saying she was fast.'

highlights.text: Not a Phenomenon that's going to be settled quickly

records.en: Taichi: "......mother of...?"
comments: "Oya" is an absolutely normal exclamation of surprise, except it also means 'parent'. -GHS
records.assessment: The small-kana ぉゃ represents a subdued, puzzled おや—roughly 'huh?' or 'well?' It is not the noun 親 or a fragment meaning 'mother of,' so the English invents an unrelated phrase.
records.remedy: Use a quiet puzzled reaction such as '...Huh?'

highlights.text: mother of...?

records.jp: 身を起こす。
records.en: I got off the bed,
records.assessment: 身を起こす means raising one's body or sitting up. 'Got off the bed' carries the action through to leaving the bed, adding a different endpoint not stated by the source.
records.remedy: Use 'I sat up.'

highlights.text: got off the bed

records.jp: 夏休みが開けて、９月の頭。
records.en: It's the beginning of September, as opened by Summer vacation.
comments: A hideously pretentious way of saying "the first week of September was vacation". Although September is the ninth month, http://www.etymonline.com/index.php?term=September etymoloy of the English/Western words for it make it a 7. Translingualism continues. -GHS
records.assessment: The source places the scene at the start of September after summer vacation has ended. 'Opened by Summer vacation' instead makes the vacation inaugurate the period and reverses the temporal relation.
records.remedy: Use 'Summer vacation was over, and it was the beginning of September.'

highlights.text: as opened by Summer vacation

records.jp: 室内には夏の熱気がじわじわと満ちつつある。
records.en: The Summer heat slowly leaks out from inside the room.
comments: Because Summer is ending, or because of Heat Death of Parallel World - not necessarily because his window is open. -GHS
records.assessment: 満ちつつある says the summer heat is gradually filling the room. The English has it leaking out of the room, reversing the direction and changing accumulation into dispersal.
records.remedy: Use 'The room was gradually filling with the summer heat.'

highlights.text: leaks out from inside the room

records.jp: 坂のてっぺんで、商店街に繋がる交差点に合流する。
records.en: The shopping street that leads from downtown connects into a crossing at the summit of the hill.
comments: See map. Connect, crossing are returning terms because SYMBOLISM but also troll. 'Shopping street' will be used to indicate the Tasaki store area here, at the edge of downtown, but not actual downtown, so I indicate both anyway. -GHS
records.assessment: The source has the traveler or route join an intersection at the top of the hill, with that intersection leading to the shopping district. The English makes the shopping street itself connect into the crossing and adds an unsupported downtown origin.
records.remedy: Use 'At the top of the hill, I join the intersection leading to the shopping district.'

highlights.text: The shopping street that leads from downtown connects into a crossing

records.jp: 小娘の分際で語彙も豊富なので、話していて飽きない。
records.en: Her social class is rich in young femaleness, and her vocabulary is similarly rich, so one never grows tired of talking to her.
comments: Sexual implication that she's fun to talk to because she's hot + contrast with her being poor in money (not yet stated). Also they can fight with words and so she's his waifu forever and also ever. Social standing will sort of return. Love how of all OMFG HARD KANJI's here, "vocabulary" is furry'd. The reason is that 彙 wasn't joyo until 2010, so there's nothing deep about it, but it's funny in retrospect. -GHS
records.assessment: 小娘の分際で is a disparaging concessive, roughly 'for a little girl like her,' not a statement that her social class is rich in femininity. The English replaces the contrast between youth and vocabulary with a nonsensical social classification.
records.remedy: Use 'For a little girl, she has a rich vocabulary, so talking to her never gets boring.'

highlights.text: Her social class is rich in young femaleness

records.jp: 美希はもう一人の一年生部員・佐倉霧とよくつるんでいる。
records.en: Miki is often found mate-ing with one other first year member of the club, the one with the Japanese word for fog for a name, Sakura Kiri.
comments: "Mate-ing" will recur, plus vague lesbian subtext. There's several fog puns 'round her route especially, so here's your warning. -GHS
records.assessment: つるんでいる says that Miki often hangs out or associates with Kiri. 'Mate-ing' adds an animal or sexual implication, while the explanatory gloss of Kiri's name is absent from the source.
records.remedy: Use 'Miki often hangs out with the club's other first-year member, Sakura Kiri.'

highlights.text: mate-ing with
the one with the Japanese word for fog for a name,

records.jp: よくふらりと店をあけ、遠方の土地にローカル線の写真を撮りに行く。
records.en: He must've casually opened the store, then trundled off to some faraway place to take pictures of their local train line.
records.assessment: In context 店をあけ means leaving or vacating the shop while wandering off, not opening it for business. The English reverses that action before correctly describing the trip to photograph a distant local railway.
records.remedy: Use 'He often wanders away from the shop to photograph local railway lines in far-off places.'

highlights.text: opened the store

records.jp: ３０代の頃は泣く子を殺すと言われるほどに悪顔だった氏だが、ご両親の死後しばらくを経て、険の取れた豊かな顔つきへと変わっていった。
records.en: When he was in his thirties, he had the kind of nastiness in his face that is often used to scare crybabies to sleep ("kids who sleep grow up well, kids who cry die"), but sometime after the death of his parents, his face changed into one of abundance, its harshness lost.
comments: I worked in the referenced proverb because Bible Game'ses are only about edutainment, sort of how you learned the totally correct furrygana's up there and how your about to learn how to correctly use 'your' in a sentence. There's another 豊, hope that's clear enough that this is a reference to a major subtext in CC. -GHS
records.assessment: The source hyperbolically says his face was so villainous that people said it could kill a crying child. The English changes killing into frightening children to sleep and inserts an unrelated explanatory proverb, materially rewriting the image.
records.remedy: Use 'In his thirties, he looked so menacing people said his face could kill a crying child.'

highlights.text: he had the kind of nastiness in his face that is often used to scare crybabies to sleep ("kids who sleep grow up well, kids who cry die")

records.jp: 遺産以外の何が、元暴走族の粗暴な鉄オタを善人に変えうるというのか。
records.en: Something outside the inheritance has changed someone who's more of a member of a biker gang than a railway fanatic into a nice guy, perhaps.
comments: See CCX0001. This guy's the Greek chorus: what happened to him is religious conversion. I suspect the hospital, too. -GHS
records.assessment: The source asks rhetorically what other than an inheritance could have turned a rough former biker-gang member and railway obsessive into a good person. The English instead asserts that something outside the inheritance did so, loses 'former,' and converts two traits into a comparison between them.
records.remedy: Use 'What besides an inheritance could turn a rough former biker and train fanatic into a good man?'

highlights.text: Something outside the inheritance has changed someone who's more of a member of a biker gang than a railway fanatic into a nice guy, perhaps.

records.jp: 『９／７、緑茶王、１３０円……黒須太一』
records.en:
9/7
Green King Tea
130￥
Kurosu Taichi
comments: HACK massive reformatting for slightly above average justice. This may be relevant, may be not: http://dic.nicovideo.jp/a/%E7%B7%91%E8%8C%B6%E7%8E%8B -GHS
records.assessment: 緑茶王 is the compound 'Green Tea King.' 'Green King Tea' changes which words form the product name and no longer represents the source's title-like 王 construction.
records.remedy: Use 'Green Tea King.'

highlights.text: Green King Tea

records.jp: 「お早いご通学で」
records.en: Taichi: "You're quick on your school commute."
comments: Her house is technically closer than Taichi's. Joking formality that could easily be read as scornful. The possibility she spends day and night at school is far from remote, given how it's possibly around 1AM. -GHS
records.assessment: お早い comments with mock politeness on her being at school early. 'Quick on your school commute' instead describes speed or efficiency during the journey and misses the early-arrival point.
records.remedy: Use 'You're at school early.' with an appropriately teasing formal tone.

highlights.text: quick on your school commute

records.jp: 「よくそんな暑そうな格好ができるな」
records.en: Taichi: "You really manage to wear that hot-looking thing often, can't you."
comments: Since she's always in that dress, and how she has multiple of them at home will become a joke later on, emphasis on 'often'. I actually wonder if that "hot" is meant English style as well. Taichi may not know English, but that doesn't stop him from affecting himself American or at least non-Japanese, especially 'round this first route. -GHS
records.assessment: Here よく expresses amazement at how she can bear such warm-looking clothing, not frequency. The English inserts 'often' and leaves 'hot-looking' open to a different sense instead of describing an outfit that looks stifling.
records.remedy: Use 'How can you stand wearing something that looks so hot?'

highlights.text: wear that hot-looking thing often

records.jp: 「へいへい」
records.en: Taichi: "Hey hey."
records.assessment: へいへい is a resigned or dismissive 'yeah, yeah' or 'all right, all right.' Rendering it as the attention-getting greeting 'hey hey' changes the speech act.
records.remedy: Use 'Yeah, yeah.'

highlights.text: Hey hey.

records.jp: 最近は、針に磨きがかかっている。
records.en: And lately, taken to polishing those needles.
records.assessment: 針に磨きがかかっている says the figurative quills have lately become even sharper or more formidable. The English invents an omitted subject actively taking up the habit of polishing them.
records.remedy: Use 'Lately, her quills have grown sharper still.'

highlights.text: taken to polishing those needles

records.jp: 異形の舌先が、ちろりと地表を薙いだ。
records.en: The tip of its heteromorphic tongue is scythed down in a flash, and lays calm on the surface of the earth.
comments: Oddly, that 'scythe down' seems to also mean that, which is the only thing that seems to make sense. Used both as this returns in a highly metaphorical scene in CCD4002. "Chirori" is an illegal and evil SFX as there'll be lots in this accursed moege and they're the #1 reason why Cross Channel is so damn hard to translate. -GHS
records.assessment: The source makes the tip of the grotesque tongue briefly flick or sweep across the surface. The English instead makes the tongue the passive object of being scythed down and adds that it comes to rest calmly, reversing agency and inventing a result.
records.remedy: Use 'The tip of its misshapen tongue flicked across the surface.'

highlights.text: The tip of its heteromorphic tongue is scythed down in a flash, and lays calm on the surface of the earth.

records.jp: 「なんつったりして」
records.en: Taichi: "Awww what a dumb thing I said."
comments: Giko neko/2chan meme. Seems to date to 1999, however, and can't date the meme to 2003 or earlier either. The meme seems to have overtaken all other references. No 'official' English translation that I found, but a literal works anyway. -GHS
records.assessment: なんつったりして is a playful retraction equivalent to 'just kidding' or 'or so I say.' The English turns it into remorseful self-criticism and fails to reveal the preceding claim as a prank.
records.remedy: Use 'Just kidding.'

highlights.text: Awww what a dumb thing I said.

records.jp: スリップダウン。
records.en: Bail into slipdown.
comments: Lit. sliding as one bails off a racing motorbike. That one doesn't seem to have a single English term tho. -GHS
records.assessment: The source consists only of the stylized loan expression 'slip down.' Adding 'bail into' imports an unsupported racing or motorcycle maneuver rather than simply describing the fall.
records.remedy: Use 'Slip down.' or a functional 'Down I went.'

highlights.text: Bail into

records.jp: でも意外と、心の隙は多い。
records.en: But hearts, surprisingly, have many openings.
records.assessment: The source remains about this particular person: despite her aloofness, she has surprisingly many openings in her emotional guard. The plural 'hearts' turns the observation into a generic claim and removes its subject.
records.remedy: Use 'But surprisingly, she leaves plenty of openings in her guard.'

highlights.text: hearts

records.jp: 相手の価値を減じるため、歯牙にもかけずに空気のごとく素知らぬ顔で居続けるべきなのだ。
records.en: to remove value from the interlocutor one ought stand firm on a feigning of ignorance that fields no fangs, as if confronted by empty air.
comments: "She's not tsun enough". That's his complaint with Touko, his interpretative error, and his error in general: thinking people can be perfectly alone and independent. -GHS
records.assessment: 歯牙にもかけず is an idiom meaning not to consider someone worth one's notice. The English renders its component image as the nonsensical 'fields no fangs,' obscuring the required disdain even though the surrounding comparison to empty air survives.
records.remedy: Use 'To diminish the other person's worth, you should refuse even to acknowledge them and keep acting as if they were air.'

highlights.text: that fields no fangs

records.jp: 心組みに攻撃性が足りない。２５てん。
records.en: The heart-felt intentionality of this aggression is inadequate. 25 points.
records.assessment: The source says that her attitude or mental preparation lacks aggression. The English instead makes an already-existing aggression the object whose heartfelt intentionality is inadequate, reversing the relation between mindset and aggression.
records.remedy: Use 'Not enough aggression in her attitude. Twenty-five points.'

highlights.text: The heart-felt intentionality of this aggression is inadequate.

records.jp: 引いては、彼女の俺に対する立場を示唆してしまっている。
records.en: And when it happens, it ends up implying her position in my regards.
records.assessment: 引いては marks an extension or consequence—'by extension' or 'ultimately'—not a temporal event. 'When it happens' invents a time relation and weakens the point that her behavior reveals her stance toward him.
records.remedy: Use 'By extension, it ends up revealing her stance toward me.'

highlights.text: And when it happens

records.jp: 目線の先、広々とした給水塔が階段とは別にあって、その土台を共有して、大きなアンテナが立っていた。
records.en: Ahead in my line of sight, standing apart from the large water tower on the staircase with which it shares the foundation, stood a large antenna.
comments: This line is odd. The water tower described as "spacious" seems just not appropriate. I'm sort of forcing this reading, because it does sound like it's being described as separate from the staircase, which contradicts the BG of the outside of the school: the water tower is clearly on top of the staircase.

And the antenna is clearly on a different level from the staircase, so how it can share foundation I simply don't know. Plus there's those three steps before the antenna, so, dunno. Anyway, there are Two Towers in this place close to God and the outside world: it's a Tolkien reference. -GHS
records.assessment: The source places the water tower apart from the stairwell and says the antenna shares the tower's foundation. The English instead places the water tower 'on the staircase' and makes the antenna stand apart from the tower, reversing the spatial relations in the sentence.
records.remedy: Use 'Ahead, apart from the stairwell, stood a broad water tower, and a large antenna rose from the same foundation.'

highlights.text: Ahead in my line of sight, standing apart from the large water tower on the staircase with which it shares the foundation, stood a large antenna.

records.jp: 早くも強みを増しつつある陽光のもと、惚けた表情が張りつく。
records.en: An expression of engrossment clings to her face, under the sunlight already growing in strength.
comments: As in, she's lost in her flight. -GHS
records.assessment: 惚けた表情 is a blank, dazed, or absent expression, not one of engrossment or deep absorption. The substitution changes the visible emotional state even though the strengthening sunlight and expression clinging to her face are retained.
records.remedy: Use 'A dazed expression clung to her face beneath the sunlight already gathering strength.'

highlights.text: engrossment

records.jp: 夏日のうすらいとなって。
records.en: The date of Summer's lease is coming to an end,
comments: Usurai is a really pretentious way of saying "the season is ending": http://nihongohaomosiroi.seesaa.net/article/159092872.html (Japanese) so have some Shakespeare instead. -GHS
records.assessment: うすらい is the poetic word for thin ice, and the next sentence explicitly continues the image by saying it will melt in an instant. The English replaces that local simile with an imported Shakespearean phrase about summer's lease and invents the season's ending.
records.remedy: Use 'Like thin ice on a summer day.'

highlights.text: The date of Summer's lease is coming to an end,

records.jp: なんてことを言ってみたり。
records.en: Why do I keep saying this stuff...
records.assessment: The source is a light narrative aside equivalent to 'or so I tried saying' after the preceding line. The English turns it into a self-directed question and invents repeated habitual behavior with 'keep,' changing both function and tone.
records.remedy: Use 'Or so I tried saying.'

highlights.text: Why do I keep saying this stuff...

records.jp: ※男心を鷲掴む抗えない逆三角の情熱……太一語。女性用下着（ショーツ）の意。
records.en:
* "Passion of the reverse triangle that like
an eagle unopposably ensnares the male heart"
comments: See CCZAS. We're in a Post-Babel world too, it seems, that humans have their own languages. Eagles because Tolkien (actually Bible, but let's not go into the advanced stuff). -GHS
