records.assessment: The discharge happens suddenly or unexpectedly after he loses consciousness. 'Unconsciously' changes the adverb into a claim about the manner or agency of the discharge.
records.remedy: Use 'suddenly discharged' or 'unexpectedly went off.'

highlights.text: unconsciously

records.jp: 射精したのかと思ったら、桜庭の荷電粒子砲（自称）の先端からは、手品さながらに花束が突きだしていた。
records.en: While I thought whether he'd ejaculate, from the pointed tip of Sakuraba's Charged Particle Cannon (self-named) out blows a bundle of flowers, as in a magician's trick.
comments: Yutaka's fallen down the stairs, he thought he was dead, but whoops, he just hurt his leg and lost his memories. And here's die Zubkonshous cenZoring it. -GHSigmund
records.assessment: The narrator first thinks he has ejaculated, only for flowers to emerge. The English makes this a simultaneous question about a future ejaculation and loses the reveal structure.
records.remedy: Use 'Just when I thought he'd ejaculated...'

highlights.text: While I thought whether he'd ejaculate

records.jp: 気弱なお坊ちゃんなのだ。
records.en: He's a fainthearted obou-chan.
comments: His molestations towards the ojou-san would get punished by her male counterpart, even if it's in a double-nested dream. -GHS
records.assessment: The honorific noun characterizes him as a sheltered or pampered young master. Leaving it as an unexplained romanization with an English suffix untranslated withholds that characterization.
records.remedy: Use 'a fainthearted, sheltered young master' or an equivalent characterization.

highlights.text: obou-chan

records.jp: 頭が下がる。
records.en: I bow my head to that.
records.assessment: The idiom expresses admiration, respect, or feeling humbled by her effort. The English literalizes it as a physical bow and loses the evaluative meaning.
records.remedy: Use 'I have to admire her' or 'I'm humbled.'

highlights.text: I bow my head to that.

records.jp: 得心した。
records.en: I was satisfied.
comments: The puzzle solved, he loses interest. -GHS
records.assessment: The verb means that he understood or was convinced by what he inferred. 'Satisfied' substitutes contentment for comprehension.
records.remedy: Use 'I understood' or 'That convinced me.'

highlights.text: satisfied

records.jp: 近所に住む美少女の遊紗ちゃん。
records.en: This is Yusa-chan, the beautiful young girl that leaves near me.
comments: She lives on the other side of the road from him, technically. For the curious, she dropped the second 'u' because when she transferred from Upper Misaka she decided to eliminate all 'u'gly things (sorry, but the Higurashi joke is irresistible). -GHS
records.assessment: The line identifies a beautiful girl who lives nearby. The English uses 'leaves' instead of 'lives,' reversing the residence verb through a mechanical word error.
records.remedy: Replace 'leaves' with 'lives.'

highlights.text: leaves

records.jp: ちょっと重くていらっしゃる。
records.en: She's sort on the heavy side,
comments: Suuuper important. -GHS
records.assessment: The intended euphemism that she is sort of on the heavy side is clear, but the missing 'of' creates a mechanical grammar error.
records.remedy: Use 'sort of on the heavy side.'

highlights.text: sort on

records.jp: が、毎日楽しそうに生きておられるから、よしとしよう。
records.en: but it's all fine, since she lets me have something enjoyable every day.
comments: Same as above, the food, not just Yusa. -GHS
records.assessment: The mother herself appears to live happily every day, which the narrator takes as sufficient. The English instead claims she provides him with daily enjoyment, changing the subject and inventing a benefit to him.
records.remedy: Say that she seems to enjoy life every day, so he will call it fine.

highlights.text: she lets me have something enjoyable every day

records.jp: ただ一つ難点があるとすれば、世間を知らなすぎること。
records.en: If I had to find a just one blemish in her, it'd be that she is completely clueless of all things worldly.
records.assessment: The duplicated determiner and adverb make a mechanical grammar error in an otherwise accurate statement that her one flaw is excessive naivety.
records.remedy: Use 'just one blemish' or 'a single blemish.'

highlights.text: a just one

records.jp: 両手を幽霊みたいに掲げて、誇示するかのように進む。
records.en: As if being cradled by a ghost, the sway nothing but a manifestation of its existence.
comments: Still about the sway of the bread AND his thoughts. The ghost is Nanaka, the Holy Spirit, who is hinting that his delusions are uhm, no, wait, Nanaka IS in his delusions so the two sway the same, though if there's a sway you gotta bring in Youko, because the sway gotta be between two points right?, so it's between Youko and Nanaka (Eve and Mary in Christian symbolism), whether Youko exists or not, which is another loaf of bread. Uhm, horrid sex joke that implies overfamiliarity with rape nukige here. -GHS
records.assessment: She walks with both hands raised like a ghost, as if displaying the item. The English invents a ghost cradling something, changes the subject to the sway, and omits her pose and forward motion.
records.remedy: Say that she walks on with both hands raised like a ghost, as though showing it off.

highlights.text: As if being cradled by a ghost, the sway nothing but a manifestation of its existence.

records.jp: 「うん、いたね」
records.en: Taichi: "Yep, was is the word."
records.assessment: The answer confirms that he was there, but the English retains two competing copulas and is mechanically ungrammatical.
records.remedy: Use 'Yep, he was.'

highlights.text: was is

records.jp: 「コンバットは一般のひとは攻撃しませんよ」
records.en: Yusa: "But Combat doesn't normally attack people!"
records.assessment: The dog does not attack ordinary members of the public. The English instead says it does not normally attack people, changing a restriction on targets into a frequency claim.
records.remedy: Use 'Combat doesn't attack ordinary people.'

highlights.text: normally attack people

records.jp: 「今は恰幅が良くなってしまったが、奴には軍人の血が流れてるからな」
records.en: Taichi: "Today his physique has improved, but the blood of soldiers flows inside that guy."
comments: Because he ate soldiers and his owner is Adolph Hitler. Waitasec oh crap I can't find the name of Marmaduke's owners in Japanese... whoa I just realized what I was trying to do, NVM. -GHS
records.assessment: The dog has now grown stout or portly, not improved its physique. The English reverses the bodily change into a positive fitness claim.
records.remedy: Use 'He's grown stout now, but...'

highlights.text: physique has improved

records.jp: 「一個ずつ食べようか？」
records.en: Taichi: "Wanna eat half each?"
comments: And his sandwich...? -GHS
records.assessment: He suggests eating one item each. The English instead divides a single item into halves, changing the quantity and action.
records.remedy: Use 'Want to eat one each?'

highlights.text: half each

records.jp: 「全然ないんです！　よかったですー！」
records.en: Yusa: "None there is none! I'm so lucky!"
comments: Conversely, an oddly direct straightforward answer. She might be lying through her teeth. -GHS
records.assessment: The first clause correctly intends that there is none at all, but duplicates incompatible constructions and is mechanically ungrammatical.
records.remedy: Use 'There's none at all!'

highlights.text: None there is none

records.jp: 「だろうねぇ」
records.en: Taichi: "Ain't that nice."
records.assessment: The reply conveys 'I thought so' or 'I figured,' confirming an expectation. The English changes this into a positive evaluation that the situation is nice.
records.remedy: Use 'Thought so' or 'I figured.'

highlights.text: Ain't that nice

records.jp: 「もし何かあったら、あたしには高等コースに知り合いがいっぱいいるんですますー、とか言って牽制してやりたまえ」
records.en: Taichi: "If anything bad happens, gladden me by feinting with something like, 'I know a looot of people in classes above that will payback you!'."
comments: ...odd he'd give this suggestion otherwise, since according to CCC3007, there's no bullying. I'm sure what the Newspaper Club did to Sakuraba in CCA0002 wasn't bullying either, nor is what Taichi does bullying at all, and not just according to Kiri, although I would suspect shooting upperclassmen with crossbows is sort of a bullying, in a sense. IOW, it's a load. -GHS
records.assessment: He advises her to deter trouble by saying she knows many people in the upper course, with a joking imitation of her speech. The English invents pleasing him and a promise of retaliation, while 'feinting' does not express warning others off.
records.remedy: Tell her to hold them in check by saying she knows lots of people in the upper course, retaining the playful speech imitation.

highlights.text: gladden me by feinting with something like, 'I know a looot of people in classes above that will payback you!'

records.jp: 「もう、ですます、とか言いませんけど……」
records.en: Yusa: "But really, I don't say things like 'will payback you'..."
comments: "De sumasu" means sort of what I adapted above, while "-desumasu" tossed at the end of the sentence sounds like a really bad moe affectation. See CCC4022 when it returns, copied off by Miki, so it's gotta be visible. Given below and how she phrases it, I suspect this was got her bullied. Also see CCD0008D, when he teases Touko on her own affectations, which she never come up either. Although not visible here, he also used 'atashi' in the sentence above, which isn't the pronoun Yusa uses. -GHS
records.assessment: She says she no longer uses the childish hybrid polite ending being teased. The English instead repeats an invented threat from the prior mistranslation and entirely omits the speech-habit correction.
records.remedy: Say that she does not say 'desu-masu' like that anymore, with enough context to preserve the teased speech habit.

highlights.text: will payback you

records.jp: 昔ちょっとからかったのを根に持ってるな。
records.en: There's this resentfulness due to having been bullied some time ago.
comments: That "long ago" will soon mean "the Hasekura incident", meaning this is Taichi equally as Yusa. It's half the explanation for his grudge against Yutaka. Culprit vague even if it wasn't, as Yusa may well have been bullied (and likely still is) by others, at the very least back when she had taken the test, as Kiri and Touko were. -GHS
records.assessment: She still holds a grudge because the narrator teased her a little in the past. The English makes her the passive victim of unspecified bullying and intensifies the action.
records.remedy: Say that she still resents him for teasing her a little before.

highlights.text: having been bullied

records.jp: 趣味は美少女フィギュアとちょっと終わりかけだが。
records.en: Hobby's Bishoujo Figurines so he's sorta near the end, tho.
comments: And maybe that's why he chuunis in the diary (that's not grammatically incorrect, chuuni is a verb I've decided now). -GHS
records.assessment: The narrator jokes that the teacher is a little far gone or hopeless because his hobby is beautiful-girl figures. 'Near the end' literalizes the idiom without conveying that judgment.
records.remedy: Use 'though his bishoujo-figure hobby means he's a little far gone.'

highlights.text: near the end

records.jp: 「……クラスのみんなも一生懸命生きてて、わたし楽しいです」
records.en: Yusa: "...everybody in my class gives it all they have, so they can have fun with me!"
comments: "everybody in class is living to their hardest, so I enjoy myself" + "everybody in class is doing their damnest to make fun of me". -GHS
records.assessment: She says that everyone in class is living or trying their hardest and that she herself is having fun. The English makes their effort serve the purpose of letting them have fun with her.
records.remedy: Use 'Everyone in class is trying their best, and I'm having fun.'

highlights.text: so they can have fun with me

records.jp: 「いざとなったらあの人が出張るか。いや遊紗ちゃん、きみの生活安泰だ」
records.en: Taichi: Ah, but when things get tough that woman truly stands out. Well, Yusa-chan, yours is a life of peace!"
comments: fat joke^2, that hides how her mom is not exactly a subtle presence at Gunjou. -GHS
records.assessment: He says that in a crisis her mother will step in or take the field. 'Stands out' describes prominence rather than intervention and loses the protective contingency.
records.remedy: Use 'when things get tough, that woman will step in.'

highlights.text: truly stands out

records.jp: 「そんな授業あったなあ、昔」
records.en: Taichi: "I had that too class too, long ago."
comments: Definitely why he keeps the diary. Odd 'long ago' now. -GHS
records.assessment: The line recalls having that class long ago, but two competing placements of 'too' remain in the sentence and create a mechanical grammar error.
records.remedy: Use 'I had that class too, long ago.'

highlights.text: too class too

records.jp: 「ああ……じゃ先生と？」
records.en: Taichi: "Ahhh... so, how about the teacher?"
records.assessment: He infers that she therefore paired with the teacher. The English makes the teacher a new suggestion rather than a question about what already happened.
records.remedy: Use 'Ah... so, with the teacher?'

highlights.text: how about the teacher

records.jp: 「無論だ」
records.en: Taichi: "Unnecessary."
records.assessment: He answers 'Of course,' affirming his decision. 'Unnecessary' instead rejects an unstated necessity and does not answer her question.
records.remedy: Use 'Of course.'

highlights.text: Unnecessary

records.jp: 名付けて理性背水の陣である。
records.en: The name I give to it is, The Waterloo of Rationality.
records.assessment: The coinage invokes a last-stand formation with one's back to the water. 'Waterloo' substitutes a different historical defeat and loses the source metaphor.
records.remedy: Use a coinage such as 'Rationality's Last Stand.'

highlights.text: Waterloo

records.jp: 少女のまなざしがじっと我が白髪に注がれる。
records.en: The maiden's gaping pours fixed on Our snowy mane.
comments: Hideously purple. Remember CCA0012; purple = nukige. This is NOT going to make him look cooler if she gets him, and she does! -GHS
records.assessment: The girl's gaze is fixed steadily on his white hair. 'Gaping pours' neither supplies the noun 'gaze' nor forms a grammatical description of her looking.
records.remedy: Use 'The girl's gaze rested steadily on my white hair.'

highlights.text: gaping pours

records.jp: そういえば以前、コ○ルトな小説に出てくる王子様が確か白髪の美形だったとか。
records.en: Now that I think of it, there was once a prince that appeared in a Co**lt novel that I'm sure was handsome despite his snow-white hair.
comments: Want to 'censor' it as C****t, but it obviously reads cunt. I know it's three and a half letters too many, but most people can't count. Hum, a certain Yoshida Midori is published under them... -GHS
records.assessment: The remembered prince is a handsome white-haired man; the hair is part of the description. 'Despite' invents a concession that treats the white hair as an obstacle to his beauty.
records.remedy: Say that the prince was a handsome man with white hair.

highlights.text: despite

records.jp: 熱く語っていた。
records.en: So much passion around that one.
comments: "She told me all excited" (she reads the novels, see CCA0020) + "he spoke passionately" + "the tale was passionate". Besides -GHS
records.assessment: The source says that she had spoken passionately about the prince. The nominal English mentions ambient passion but omits both the speaker and the act of telling him.
records.remedy: Use 'She'd talked passionately about him.'

highlights.text: So much passion around that one.

records.jp: してみると俺は、王子様とイメージしているのだろうか。
records.en: Well then, I should have that same princely image myself, right?
comments: Depression as he knows his facade won't work. But what could Yusa be thinking of this? -GHS
records.assessment: He wonders whether she therefore imagines him as a prince. The English makes the princely image something he himself should possess and removes her as the perceiving subject.
records.remedy: Use 'Does that mean she imagines me as a prince?'

highlights.text: I should have that same princely image myself

records.jp: 「それ、受け取ってもいいかい、フロイライン？」
records.en: Taichi: "Then is it fine if I take this, fr{a}ulein?"
comments: More formal than his average, but not purple. -GHS
records.assessment: The German address is emitted with literal brace markup in the middle of the word, producing a visible typography defect rather than the intended form.
records.remedy: Render the address as 'Fräulein' or a consistent plain-ASCII equivalent.

highlights.text: fr{a}ulein

records.jp: 少女の涙を優しくぬぐう。
records.en: Gently the girl's tears get wiped off.
comments: Intentionally ambiguous. -GHS
records.assessment: The narrator gently wipes the girl's tears. The passive English removes him as the acting subject and presents the wiping as an agentless event.
records.remedy: Use 'I gently wipe away the girl's tears.'

highlights.text: Gently the girl's tears get wiped off.

records.jp: 平然と仕切り直す俺。
records.en: I calmly restore our boundaries.
comments: He knows he went too far. -GHS
records.assessment: He calmly resets the exchange and starts over after the failed line. 'Restore our boundaries' invents a statement about interpersonal limits rather than restarting.
records.remedy: Use 'I calmly start over' or 'I calmly reset the conversation.'

highlights.text: restore our boundaries

records.jp: くしゃみをした拍子に、打ち出された鼻汁弾は新幹線よりも速い初速で（本当）こちらの制服に打ち込まれた。
records.en: On the very downbeat of the sneeze, the launched glob of mucus fired onto to my uniform with a nuzzle velocity superior to even that of the Shinkansen (no, seriously).
comments: Only laterally a musical reference, but it's close enough to keep. Sneezes aren't anywhere near the order of magnitude of that speed, see Mythbusters. -GHS
records.assessment: The English contains both a duplicated preposition and 'nuzzle' in place of the projectile term 'muzzle,' creating two mechanical defects in the otherwise preserved ballistic comparison.
records.remedy: Use 'fired onto my uniform with a muzzle velocity...'

highlights.text: fired onto to
nuzzle velocity

records.jp: 今度こそ、親指の腹で涙をぬぐいつつ。
records.en: This time I can indeed wipe her tears with the belly of my thumbs.
comments: But was it accidental, or did her own Internal Demon set this up? -GHS
records.assessment: He wipes the tears with the pad of one thumb. The English changes the singular body part to both thumbs.
records.remedy: Use 'the pad of my thumb.'

highlights.text: thumbs

records.jp: 「可愛い後輩を、困らせたままにしておくようなハンカチじゃないんだよ」
records.en: Taichi: "Leaving a cute Kouhai in trouble is not worth a handkerchief."
records.assessment: He says this is not a handkerchief that would leave a cute junior in distress, valuing her welfare above the cloth. The English reverses the relation and says leaving her in trouble is not worth a handkerchief.
records.remedy: Use 'This isn't a handkerchief worth leaving a cute junior in trouble over.'

highlights.text: Taichi: "Leaving a cute Kouhai in trouble is not worth a handkerchief."

records.jp: 「弁償はいいけど、風邪には気をつけた方がいいな、遊紗君」
records.en: Taichi: "Reimburse is no problem, but you'd better watch out for colds, Yusa-kun."
comments: Intentional mis-honorific. He normally doesn't use -kun period, and it tends to come out when he's in sort of a panic. IOW, he's not all quite there right now. -GHS
records.assessment: He says compensation is unnecessary, then warns her about catching cold. The English instead suggests reimbursement is acceptable or unproblematic and is also grammatically malformed.
records.remedy: Use 'Don't worry about replacing it, but...'

highlights.text: Reimburse is no problem

records.jp: ぽん、と頭を軽く叩いて、歩き出す。
records.en: Tok, I gently give her a light poke on the face, and resume walking.
records.assessment: He gives her head a light pat or tap before walking on. The English moves the contact to her face and changes it into a poke.
records.remedy: Use 'I lightly pat her on the head.'

highlights.text: poke on the face

records.jp: ハンカチ一枚で射止められた少女の好意を、べつだん安いとは思わなかった。
records.en: I didn't think the the goodwill of this girl that I made all mine with a single handkerchief to be particularly cheap,
comments: See CCZAS, this is the "shoot dead" used there for the Cross World. -GHS
records.assessment: The duplicated article is a mechanical grammar error in an otherwise recoverable judgment about the girl's goodwill.
records.remedy: Remove one occurrence of 'the.'

highlights.text: the the

records.jp: だが同時に彼女におもいっきり子供生ませたいと思ってしまった俺は脳が腐っていること間違いなかった。死ね、死んでしまえ。
records.en: but simultaneously wanting for this girl to birth me a baby with all her heart meant my brain was rotten, and no mistake. Die, just die.
comments: As usual, he is not kidding. -GHS
records.assessment: The narrator intensely wants to make the girl bear his children. The English attaches the intensity to how wholeheartedly she would bear a baby, changing whose desire is being described.
records.remedy: Attach the intensity to his desire rather than to her imagined action.

highlights.text: with all her heart

records.jp: 「あんまん」
records.en: Taichi: "Anman."
records.assessment: The source names a common sweet bean bun. Leaving the food name as unexplained romanized Japanese withholds ordinary lexical content from the English reader.
records.remedy: Render the food as a sweet bean bun or otherwise supply its ordinary English sense.

highlights.text: Anman

records.jp: 「んなわけないでしょ！！　サンドイッチでしょ！」
records.en: Touko: "'s not that at all you know!!! It's a sandwich you know!"
comments: lisp -GHS
records.assessment: The clipped Japanese opening is colloquial but grammatical in context. The English begins with a stranded contraction and adds a repeated tag, producing malformed dialogue rather than equivalent conversational compression.
records.remedy: Use a grammatical emphatic denial before identifying it as a sandwich.

highlights.text: 's not that at all you know

records.jp: 手を払われる。
records.en: a swat of her hands,
records.assessment: The passive source says the narrator has his hand brushed or knocked aside. The English instead describes an indeterminate swat involving her hands and loses the affected hand and action direction.
records.remedy: State that she bats or brushes his hand away.

highlights.text: a swat of her hands

records.jp: 拾う。
records.en: recovered.
records.assessment: The source is the concrete action of picking the fallen item up. The English substitutes an abstract result and omits the visible retrieval action.
records.remedy: Render the action directly as picking it up.

highlights.text: recovered

records.jp: 「あんたに、関係ない」
records.en: Touko: "That's... none of yer business."
records.assessment: The source is blunt and casual but carries no marked regional dialect. The English adds conspicuous dialect spelling that changes the character's voice.
records.remedy: Keep the curt refusal without invented dialect.

highlights.text: yer

records.jp: そっぽを向く。
records.en: Uncooperative.
comments: Ohhh man it begins. -GHS
records.assessment: The source narrates the physical action of turning her face away. The English replaces that action with the narrator's evaluative label.
records.remedy: State that she turns away.

highlights.text: Uncooperative

records.jp: 「自分しか、自分の心配をしてくれる人間がいないのは、つらいだろ？」
records.en: Taichi: "Having no human alive, none outside of you, that worry about you... it's painful, right?"
comments: Hyperliteral as this is either her refusal to see mankind or, well, meant hyperliterally. See CCC0000: this is The Sentence. -GHS
records.assessment: The source says it is painful when nobody but oneself will worry about oneself. The English adds the absolute claim that no human is alive, then damages the relation with a subject-verb agreement error.
records.remedy: Express that being the only person who worries about oneself is painful.

highlights.text: Having no human alive, none outside of you, that worry about you

records.jp: 「何言ってるのかわからない」
records.en: Touko: "What's that even mean I don't know."
records.assessment: The source is a direct statement that she does not understand what he is saying. The English splices a question and declaration without the syntax needed to connect them.
records.remedy: Use a grammatical equivalent such as 'I don't know what you're talking about.'

highlights.text: What's that even mean I don't know

records.jp: 「顔色悪いな。生理か？」
records.en: Taichi: "Your face looks off-color. Menses?"
comments: It sounds like he's ridiculing her, and that definitely is what she thinks, but he may be seriously worried. He does the same in CCD0020B. -GHS
records.assessment: The source bluntly asks whether her poor complexion is due to her period. 'Off-color' is semantically distracting in English and the isolated clinical noun 'Menses?' does not function as the same direct question.
records.remedy: Use a plain question about looking pale and being on her period.

highlights.text: off-color. Menses

records.jp: 「馬鹿じゃないの！」
records.en: Touko: "Aren't you stupid!"
records.assessment: The source is an angry exclamatory insult, not an information-seeking negative question. The English question form conflicts with its exclamation punctuation and weakens the speech act.
records.remedy: Use a direct exclamation such as 'You idiot!'

highlights.text: Aren't you stupid

records.jp: 呪詛を吐いて、出て行く。
records.en: That curse spat out, she leaves.
comments: She does not make HIM leave... -GHS
records.assessment: The source says she spits out a curse and leaves. The English absolute construction is malformed and obscures who performs the spitting.
records.remedy: Make her the agent of both actions in a grammatical sentence.

highlights.text: That curse spat out, she leaves

records.jp: 「……あんまいい死に方できないぞ」
records.en: Taichi: "...that ain't a really good way to die ya know."
comments: It's like he knows that she's starving herself, despite never figuring it out in most routes until he sees her pass out in front of him. Suspecting it's another thing he knows - it's certainly not the first summer he's known her - and its origin is simply going to become detached as the Game starts.

There's also some stuff about 'anma'/'anman' that strike me as a pun, given how 'anma' also means blind person (who traditionally gave the 'anma' massages), especially given that Touko goes blind. But that may be overthinking things.
Finally, see CCD0020B, where this line refers to himself. May be just an older revision, though. -GHS
records.assessment: The source warns that she will not come to a good end or die well. The English recasts the conduct itself as a method of dying and adds marked dialect.
records.remedy: Render the warning as not coming to a good end.

highlights.text: that ain't a really good way to die ya know

records.jp: 変なまま固定されてしまっている。
records.en: And the strangeness is becoming fixed.
comments: Well lookie there. Wonder if this means "she has been seeing people when my Settei says there aren't any". -GHS
records.assessment: The source says her strange state has become fixed or persistent. The English turns the adjective into an abstract entity that is itself 'becoming fixed,' producing an unidiomatic calque.
records.remedy: Say that she seems stuck in this strange state.

highlights.text: the strangeness is becoming fixed

records.jp: こういう時は、先輩とお話でもして心を濯ぐのだ。
records.en: At times like these, I should go talk with Senpai and rinse out the heart.
comments: ...or possibly, "I'm starting not to stand her in really bad ways". -GHS
records.assessment: The source figuratively proposes cleansing or refreshing his heart by talking with his senior. The literal 'rinse out the heart' is not an intelligible English expression for that function.
records.remedy: Use an English image of cleansing or refreshing his spirits.

highlights.text: rinse out the heart

records.jp: 壁に寄りかかって所在なげにしている美希と遭遇。
records.en: A random encounter with Miki leaning against the wall, idling.
comments: Yes, it's a formal version of the RPG term. -GHS
records.assessment: The source describes her as looking at a loss or ill at ease while leaning against the wall. 'Idling' only says she is inactive and drops that visible unease.
records.remedy: Describe her as looking at a loss or restless.

highlights.text: idling

records.jp: 「……もしかして、部活ですか？」
records.en: Miki: "...don't tell me, to club?"
records.assessment: The source asks whether he is perhaps going to club activities. The English prepositional fragment is not grammatical and does not name the activity.
records.remedy: Ask whether he is going to club activities.

highlights.text: to club

records.jp: 「もしかしなくともそうだ」
records.en: Taichi: "I'm not going to tell you, but that's it."
records.assessment: The reply plays on 'perhaps' and means there is no perhaps about it: that is exactly where he is going. The English misreads the preceding idiom as a request not to be told and invents a refusal to answer.
records.remedy: Preserve the repartee by saying there is no 'perhaps' about it.

highlights.text: I'm not going to tell you

records.jp: 「ただの顔見せだけどね」
records.en: Taichi: "But I'm only showing face, OK."
records.assessment: The source uses the ordinary idiom of merely putting in an appearance. The articleless literal calque 'showing face' is not standard English.
records.remedy: Say that he is only putting in an appearance.

highlights.text: showing face

records.jp: 「お　は　よ　う」
records.en: Taichi: "H E L L O."
records.assessment: The source spaces out 'good morning' for exaggeratedly clear enunciation. The English changes the greeting itself to 'hello,' losing the time-specific wording while preserving only the spacing.
records.remedy: Space out an English 'good morning' instead.

highlights.text: H E L L O

records.jp: 滑舌全開で挨拶した。霧に。
records.en: A greeting with full throttle eloquence. To Kiri.
records.assessment: The source describes maximum clarity of articulation, not eloquence. The English substitutes a different speaking quality and makes the physical delivery obscure.
records.remedy: Describe him enunciating with exaggerated clarity.

highlights.text: full throttle eloquence

records.jp: だけど嫌われるほどに、相手が気になってたまらない。
records.en: However, the more he is hated, the more irresistibly attracted the target will become.
comments: Paraphrasis: "I'm an M". Analysis: Kiri doesn't understand how Taichi works. -GHS
records.assessment: The source says that the more she hates the narrator, the more he cannot help being interested in her. The English changes the narrator into a generic male and then makes the target become attracted, reversing who feels the attraction.
records.remedy: Keep the narrator as the person increasingly drawn to the person who hates him.

highlights.text: the more he is hated, the more irresistibly attracted the target will become

records.jp: 両手をおきゃん（死語の世界）に広げながら、二人に並んで歩く。
records.en: With both arms spread towards the urchin (nice etymology), I line up to walk with them.
comments: Originally "okyan (from the Land of the Dead Words)" (AKA "old word"). It's a tomboyish girl. Adapted with the urchin, similar meaning, and it comes from hedgehog, seemed appropriate. -GHS
records.assessment: The source uses an intentionally obsolete expression and explicitly jokes that it belongs to the world of dead words. The English invents a spatial 'urchin' and replaces the parenthetical joke with praise for an etymology.
records.remedy: Preserve both the deliberately obsolete manner and the aside identifying it as a dead word.

highlights.text: towards the urchin (nice etymology)

records.jp: 立ち止まる。
records.en: She stops.
records.assessment: In sequence, the first-person narrator stops when addressed. The English assigns the action to the girl who has just called to him.
records.remedy: Make the narrator the subject: 'I stop.'

highlights.text: She stops

records.jp: 「からかうのはやめてください。これ以上は無視しますから」
records.en: Kiri: "Please stop with the jokes. If they continue, they will be ignored."
comments: If she DID, then she'd be relatively fine. -GHS
records.assessment: The source warns that she will ignore him if he continues teasing her. The English passive makes the jokes the apparent thing ignored and removes the speaker's agency and addressee.
records.remedy: State that she will ignore him if he keeps it up.

highlights.text: they will be ignored

records.jp: このくらいにしておくか。今日は。
records.en: Should I leave it at this then? At least for today.
records.assessment: The source is the narrator's decision to stop at this point for today. The English splits it into an unresolved question and a sentence fragment.
records.remedy: Use a complete decision such as 'I guess I'll leave it at that for today.'

highlights.text: Should I leave it at this then? At least for today.

records.jp: いっぺんに食べてしまっては興ざめだ。
records.en: Eating them in a single gulp is the way of the killjoy.
records.assessment: The source says eating everything at once spoils the pleasure. The English instead labels that behavior 'the way of the killjoy,' changing the result into a characterization of the eater.
records.remedy: State that eating it all at once spoils the fun.

highlights.text: the way of the killjoy

records.jp: 自分の側頭部を殴る。
records.en: I strike at my temporal lobe.
comments: See CCX0001, CCZAS -GHS
records.assessment: The source says he hits the side of his own head or temple. The temporal lobe is an internal brain region and cannot name the external place he visibly strikes.
records.remedy: Say that he strikes the side of his head or his temple.

highlights.text: temporal lobe

records.jp: 「あ、ハモハモした……」
records.en: Miki: "Ah, harmonics..."
comments: Specific, again see CCA0027 -GHS
records.assessment: The source says their voices overlapped or harmonized when they spoke at once. The isolated technical noun 'harmonics' neither states that event nor forms a natural reaction.
records.remedy: Say that they spoke in unison or their voices harmonized.

highlights.text: harmonics

records.jp: 霧に睨まれる。
records.en: I'm glared by Kiri.
records.assessment: English 'glare' requires 'at' for its target; this passive construction is ungrammatical even though the underlying action is recoverable.
records.remedy: Use 'Kiri glares at me' or 'I'm glared at by Kiri.'

highlights.text: I'm glared by Kiri

records.jp: ……なんでやねん。
records.en: ...I'm a-lovin' it.
comments: http://www.osaka-info.jp/ja/model/osakaben/html/0048.html -GHS
records.assessment: The source is a comic Kansai-style retort meaning roughly 'Why the hell?' or 'What was that for?' The English substitutes an unrelated advertising-slogan-like declaration of enjoyment.
records.remedy: Use a comic incredulous retort rather than a declaration of pleasure.

highlights.text: I'm a-lovin' it

records.jp: 「わたしが死んでも……ふたりとも、喧嘩したらだめだよ……うっ……」
records.en: Miki: "I might die but... you two, you can't be fighting anymore... ngh..."
records.assessment: The source sets up a hypothetical concession, 'Even if I die,' before the plea not to fight. The English changes that relation into a claim that she may actually die.
records.remedy: Preserve the concessive hypothetical: 'Even if I die...'

highlights.text: I might die but

records.jp: 霧に詰め寄る。
records.en: I press the question onto Kiri.
comments: Also get near her, but, well, he just asked a question and everything. -GHS
records.assessment: The source narrates the speaker closing in on or confronting Kiri. The English invents a question as an object and loses the physical or confrontational action.
records.remedy: Say that he presses Kiri or closes in on her.

highlights.text: press the question onto Kiri

records.jp: 「いやん、本気で怒ってる？」
records.en: Miki: "Meown, you seriously mad?"
comments: Catlike -GHS
records.assessment: The source is a coy squeal like 'Oh no' before asking whether she is seriously angry. The English invents a catlike vocalization absent from the source.
records.remedy: Use a coy interjection without adding a cat voice.

highlights.text: Meown

records.jp: 「それだけはーっ！！」
records.en: Miki: "But that's insaaane!!!"
comments: She's so poor she likely doesn't have side dishes... -GHS
records.assessment: The source protests 'Anything but that!' at the threatened loss of lunch-side-dish trading. The English calls the threat insane instead of pleading against that specific consequence.
records.remedy: Use an emphatic 'Anything but that!'

highlights.text: But that's insaaane

records.jp: さすがに３Ｐとは言えなかった。
records.en: All the same, it can't be said to be a proper 3P of a threesome.
comments: See below -GHS
records.assessment: The source says the narrator could not bring himself to call the situation a threesome. The English turns his reluctance into an impersonal claim about classification and redundantly defines the term with itself.
records.remedy: Keep the narrator's agency and say that even he could not bring himself to call it a threesome.

highlights.text: it can't be said to be a proper 3P of a threesome

records.jp: 鼻血出そう。
records.en: That's to nosebleed!
records.assessment: The source says the narrator feels as though he is about to get a nosebleed. The English construction is ungrammatical and does not express that impending bodily reaction.
records.remedy: Say that he feels a nosebleed coming on.

highlights.text: That's to nosebleed

records.jp: 「うん、俺もちょっと顔出してこないと」
records.en: Taichi: "Yeah, me too, I gotta show face a little."
records.assessment: The source uses the ordinary idiom of briefly putting in an appearance. The articleless literal phrase 'show face' is not idiomatic English.
records.remedy: Use 'put in an appearance' or 'show my face for a bit.'

highlights.text: show face

records.jp: 「霧、今はまだ美希を預けておくが……いずれは小生がいただくカラナ」
records.en: Taichi: "Kiri, for now I leave Miki in your care still... but there will come a day when her humble servant takes her for himself!"
comments: Adventure hero style, not too purple. -GHS
records.assessment: The pompous first-person self-reference belongs to the speaker. The English makes him sound like the girl's servant while simultaneously referring to himself in the third person, obscuring both voice and agency.
records.remedy: Keep the mock-pompous first person: he will eventually claim her himself.

highlights.text: her humble servant takes her for himself

records.jp: 美希が居残って、そっと俺に耳打ちを残す。
records.en: Miki stays behind, and with a whisper in my ear she left the words,
records.assessment: The source says she stays behind and leaves him a quiet aside or whisper. The English calque 'left the words' and its surrounding word order are not natural English narration.
records.remedy: Say that she stays behind to whisper in his ear.

highlights.text: with a whisper in my ear she left the words

records.jp: 「その分、美希は先輩のこと好きですから」
records.en: Miki: "And that is why Miki really likes you, Senpai."
comments: Sudden third person affectation. -GHS
records.assessment: The source means that, to make up for the other girl's hostility, Miki likes him that much more. The English changes this compensatory relation into direct causation.
records.remedy: Preserve the compensatory link, such as 'To make up for that, Miki likes you.'

highlights.text: And that is why

records.jp: 「いつか霧ちんと和解してセクハラできる日が来るといいです―――」
records.en: Miki: "I'd be nice if someday you would succeed in properly reconciling with Kiri-chin and be able to sexually harass---"
records.assessment: The source says it would be nice if he could reconcile and reach that joking outcome. The English typo makes Miki herself the thing that would be nice and leaves the sentence without a coherent grammatical subject.
records.remedy: Begin with 'It'd be nice if someday...' and retain the addressed person's action.

highlights.text: I'd be nice

records.jp: 「ばいばい」
records.en: Taichi: "Bai bai."
records.assessment: The source is the English loan farewell 'bye-bye.' Re-romanizing it as Japanese syllables in English dialogue needlessly obscures an ordinary English phrase.
records.remedy: Write 'Bye-bye.'

highlights.text: Bai bai

records.jp: 小走りに霧と合流し、遠ざかっていく二人。
records.en: At a half-run she flows in with Kiri, and the two fade into the distance.
records.assessment: The source says she trots over and joins Kiri. 'Flows in with' is a lexical calque that does not express joining up with someone in English.
records.remedy: Say that she trots over to join Kiri.

highlights.text: flows in with Kiri

records.jp: 両名の背中に呼びかける。
records.en: I call out towards the backs of both.
records.assessment: The source simply says he calls out to both girls from behind as they leave. The literal direction toward their backs is an unnatural English construction.
records.remedy: Say that he calls out to both of them.

highlights.text: towards the backs of both

records.jp: 立ち止まり、振り向いたのは美希だけだったが。
records.en: Stops in her tracks and turns around, however, Miki alone.
records.assessment: The source states that only Miki stopped and looked back. The English strands the verbs before their subject and appends 'Miki alone' after multiple commas, leaving no grammatical sentence.
records.remedy: Use a direct sentence: 'Only Miki stopped and turned around, though.'

highlights.text: Stops in her tracks and turns around, however, Miki alone

records.jp: 「くれぐれも体調には気をつけるんだぞ」
records.en: Taichi: "Be thoroughly careful with your physical conditions!"
records.assessment: The source warns them to take particular care of their health. The plural 'physical conditions' sounds like multiple medical states and is not the natural object of 'be careful with.'
records.remedy: Tell them to take good care of their health.

highlights.text: physical conditions

records.jp: 美希が元気良く挙手し、霧がちらりと目線を流した。
records.en: Miki gave a vigorous salute, Kiri shed but a peeking glance.
records.assessment: The source says Kiri casts a brief sidelong glance. 'Shed' cannot govern a glance this way, and 'peeking glance' is a malformed calque.
records.remedy: Say that Kiri cast a brief sidelong glance.

highlights.text: Kiri shed but a peeking glance

records.jp: 鞄から原稿用紙を取り出す。
records.en: I take out the manuscript's paper from my bag.
records.assessment: The source names manuscript paper as a type of paper. The possessive makes the paper belong to a manuscript rather than identify the stationery he takes from his bag.
records.remedy: Use 'manuscript paper.'

highlights.text: manuscript's paper

records.jp: 「でしょうねえ」
records.en: Taichi: "Do you now."
records.assessment: The source agrees that she naturally would not remember, roughly 'I figured as much.' The English instead asks a skeptical question and reverses the reply's speech function.
records.remedy: Use an agreeing response such as 'I thought so.'

highlights.text: Do you now

records.jp: うつむいて、懊悩している。
records.en: She hangs her head in shame and, oh no!, grows anguished.
comments: Term for anguish odd enough it needs ruby text, and it's "ou nou". The furries's'ses' will return, see CCB2002, which is nearly unheard of for furigana, plus there's CCB0006 when "nou" is used literally as 'no'. I'm taking this as totally intentional. -GHS
records.assessment: The source says she hangs her head and agonizes. The English adds shame as a specific cause and inserts a jaunty 'oh no!' that undercuts the described anguish.
records.remedy: Describe her hanging her head in anguish without the added aside.

highlights.text: in shame and, oh no!, grows anguished

records.jp: 叫んで焦る先輩。
records.en: Flustered shouts Senpai.
records.assessment: The source says the flustered senior cries out. The English places the adjective and verb before the subject without a grammatical inversion structure.
records.remedy: Use 'Senpai cries out in a panic.'

highlights.text: Flustered shouts Senpai

records.jp: 「スケープゴートは、いやです」
records.en: Misato: "It is scapegoat, that is bad!"
comments: Makes sense if you replace "seethrough" with it, which is the point of the joke. -GHS
records.assessment: The source says she does not want to be made a scapegoat. The English labels an unspecified thing 'scapegoat' and calls it bad, losing the first-person refusal.
records.remedy: Say 'I don't want to be a scapegoat.'

highlights.text: It is scapegoat, that is bad

records.jp: 「俺だっていやですよ」
records.en: Taichi: "I do not like them myself."
comments: Well, they are more of a Jewish thing; Jesus sorta replaced the lot of 'em. -GHS
records.assessment: The source replies that he would not want that either. The plural pronoun has no antecedent and changes shared aversion to the situation into disliking people or things.
records.remedy: Use 'I wouldn't want that either.'

highlights.text: I do not like them myself

records.jp: 「でも俺、先輩をスケープゴートにしたかったわけじゃなくて、日陰に移動したかっただけなんすけど」
records.en: Taichi: "But me, I was not trying to make scapegoat of you, Senpai, I just wanted us to move to the shade."
comments: Because he's daaaaaark and needs to be in the shadoooooows -GHS
records.assessment: The source says he was not trying to make her a scapegoat. The English drops the required article before the predicate noun.
records.remedy: Use 'make a scapegoat of you.'

highlights.text: make scapegoat of you

records.jp: 「あっ、そうですね、じゃあそうしましょう」
records.en: Misato: "Ah, I see now, well then let us."
records.assessment: The source accepts the suggestion and says they should move. The English ends after the auxiliary 'let us' without naming or substituting for the action.
records.remedy: Complete the response, such as 'Then let's do that.'

highlights.text: well then let us

records.jp: 「ところで先輩、昨日はお酒飲んでましたね」
records.en: Taichi: "Anyway, Senpai, yesterday you were drinking alcohol, were you."
records.assessment: The source matter-of-factly reminds her that she drank yesterday. The English appends a positive tag to a positive statement, producing a malformed confirmation question.
records.remedy: Use a statement or a correctly formed tag question.

highlights.text: were drinking alcohol, were you

records.jp: 「まさかわたし……酔って……たいへんなことを？」
records.en: Taichi: "Could it be that... drunk... I did something really bad?"
records.assessment: The source line is the senior's alarmed first-person question about what she may have done while drunk. The English speaker label assigns her words to the narrator.
records.remedy: Attribute the line to the senior.

highlights.text: Taichi

records.jp: 「ええ、それはもう口にはできないような破廉恥プレイを」
records.en: Taichi: "Yes, that was the kind of shameless playact one should simply never again describe."
comments: Similar term used to describe the 'download panties' part of the Kiri sex scene in the Recollections. FWIW. -GHS
records.assessment: The source claims she engaged in unspeakably shameless play. 'Playact' makes it mere pretending, while 'never again describe' adds prior description and future prohibition not present in the line.
records.remedy: Call it shameless conduct too indecent to put into words.

highlights.text: playact one should simply never again describe

records.jp: 「でもご安心を。僕がうまく処理して、人目につかないよう片づけておきました」
records.en: Taichi: "But be at ease! This harmless young boy skillfully dealt with it, it has been cleaned up so that the public eye will never notice!"
records.assessment: The source uses an ordinary first-person pronoun while claiming he handled the matter discreetly. The English adds a self-exonerating description of him as a harmless young boy.
records.remedy: Keep the first person without the invented self-description.

highlights.text: This harmless young boy

records.jp: 釈然としないものを残しつつも、先輩は頭を下げた。
records.en: Something she is unsatisfied about still remained, and Senpai hung her head.
comments: Curiously, same term as CCA0011A. -GHS
records.assessment: The source says she bows her head in thanks despite lingering uncertainty. 'Hung her head' conventionally signals shame or dejection and changes the gesture's function.
records.remedy: Say that she bowed her head.

highlights.text: hung her head

records.jp: 「聞きます？」
records.en: Taichi: "Are you asking?"
records.assessment: The source asks whether she wants to hear the details. The English asks whether she herself is asking, reversing the direction of the offered information.
records.remedy: Use 'Want to hear?'

highlights.text: Are you asking

records.jp: 「なんでしたら責任取りましょうか？」
records.en: Taichi: "Will you take responsibility, whatever it is?"
comments: I don't even know if he's being a bastard if he just understands her at a deep level. See CCD1001B: I suspect the latter while thinking he's the former. -GHS
records.assessment: The source has the narrator offer to take responsibility if she wishes. The English demands that she take responsibility, reversing the subject and intent.
records.remedy: Have the narrator ask whether he should take responsibility.

highlights.text: Will you take responsibility

records.jp: 「いや、聞いちゃったら、そういう気分になるかなって」
records.en: Taichi: "Nah, if you're asking, then who knows if you really will..."
records.assessment: The source explains that hearing the story might put her in the mood to want him to take responsibility. The English changes hearing into asking and leaves the prospective feeling unstated.
records.remedy: Say that he wondered whether hearing it would put her in that mood.

highlights.text: if you're asking, then who knows if you really will

records.jp: 「聞きます？」
records.en: Taichi: "Are you asking?"
comments: CP above
records.assessment: The repeated source question again offers to tell her the details. The English again reverses the exchange into asking whether she is requesting something.
records.remedy: Use 'Do you want to hear?'

highlights.text: Are you asking

records.jp: 「本当にたいしたことでは」
records.en: Taichi: "That was really a big mess."
comments: Mirrors above. -GHS
records.assessment: The source begins reassuring her that it really was not a serious matter. The English removes the negation and tells her it was a major mess, reversing polarity just before the fabricated story.
records.remedy: Preserve the negative reassurance: 'It really wasn't anything serious.'

highlights.text: That was really a big mess

records.jp: 「拝啓、春眠の候、その後いかがお過ごしでしょうか……」
records.en: Misato: "Dear sir, I hope that things have been well since the month with those sweet small clumsy feet..."
comments: April. Means her father's been in jail for at least five months. More stuff of this kind (Japanese only): http://jikou-aisatu.seesaa.net/ Adapted reference is E.E. Cummings, seems appropriate although it's not exactly a (semi)standard reference, like the original. -GHS
records.assessment: The source parodies a formal seasonal letter greeting about spring drowsiness. The English invents a month characterized by small clumsy feet and loses the seasonal phrase.
records.remedy: Use a mock-formal springtime greeting appropriate to a letter.

highlights.text: month with those sweet small clumsy feet

records.jp: 「先輩、しっかり」
records.en: Taichi: "Senpai, steadfast!"
records.assessment: The source urges her to pull herself together. The isolated adjective 'steadfast' describes a trait rather than functioning as the intended encouragement.
records.remedy: Use 'Pull yourself together, Senpai.'

highlights.text: steadfast

records.jp: 早起きしてれば遭遇できたのだろうか。
records.en: If I were an early riser, I could have that sort of random encounter, likely.
comments: Player should've picked "go straight to school" instead of "stay in bed some more". That's why he never meets anyone on the road in the morning (provided it IS morning at all). -GHS
records.assessment: The source wonders whether waking early on this occasion would have let him encounter the scene. The English uses a general present condition with a mismatched past result and appends a dangling probability adverb.
records.remedy: Use a coherent past counterfactual question.

highlights.text: If I were an early riser, I could have that sort of random encounter, likely

records.jp: そういうところが駄目なんだよ。エーロー失格なんだよ。
records.en:
That kind of things is just a waste. It's a disqualifier for an Eror!
* "Eror" (spanish pronunciation) = Taichian for an
heroic being with a strong perverted side.
comments: See CCC3025. The perverted hero is liked more than a thousand molesters? -GHS
records.assessment: The source says that missing such opportunities is exactly what is wrong with the narrator. The English changes the judgment into those things being a waste and also mismatches singular and plural.
records.remedy: Say 'That's exactly what's wrong with me.'

highlights.text: That kind of things is just a waste

records.jp: 「サラシってあるでしょう？　あんな感じにすれば、透けないと思いますよ」
records.en: Taichi: "It is bleached cotton, right? From the feeling of it, I do not think it will become transparent."
records.assessment: The source proposes wrapping the towel like a sarashi so the shirt will not show through. The English defines a material, omits the wrapping action, and treats the cloth itself as the thing becoming transparent.
records.remedy: Explain that wrapping it like a sarashi should prevent show-through.

highlights.text: It is bleached cotton, right? From the feeling of it, I do not think it will become transparent

records.jp: 「ちょっと待っててくださいね。動いたらめっですよ」
records.en: Misato: "Wait just a little while now. If you move you get a nai-nai!"
comments: Now addressing Poko-chin the doggy. Original term "meh!" is used to scold small children or animals. Made something just as childish. -GHS
records.assessment: The source uses a baby-talk scolding equivalent to 'no-no' if he moves. Leaving an invented romanization in English obscures both the warning and its teasing register.
records.remedy: Use a recognizable baby-talk scolding such as 'no-no.'

highlights.text: nai-nai

records.jp: めっ、されたい気分もあるが、我慢した。
records.en: I did feel I wanted to have this 'nai-nai', but I endured.
comments: See CCD0021. Is this an omen of things to come? -GHS
records.assessment: The narrator repeats the same baby-talk scolding term. The unexplained romanization again withholds its meaning and comic register.
records.remedy: Repeat the same intelligible English baby-talk term.

highlights.text: nai-nai

records.jp: 寄せた乳房の先端、二粒の野いちごでもって先走る竿の先端を「めっ」と……。
records.en: Udder cusps squeezed together, and with their two wild strawberries on top they approach the tip of an impertinent flagpole, and as a salute, 'nai-nai'...
comments: Adapted because Taichi's not sick, but not well either. -GHS
records.assessment: The source's fantasy uses human-body metaphors for breasts and an aroused, pre-ejaculating penis. The English dehumanizes the breasts as udders and mistakes the physiological modifier for a personality judgment about a flagpole.
records.remedy: Preserve the human erotic metaphors and the physiological meaning without inventing animal anatomy or insolence.

highlights.text: Udder cusps
impertinent flagpole

records.jp: 「ああああ、ばかばかばか！　俺のばかっ！」
records.en: Taichi: "AAAAAH, stupidstupidstupid! You are so stupid!"
comments: 4xA + 3xBaka, and then... idiot added one baka too many. -GHS
records.assessment: The source ends the outburst by calling the narrator himself an idiot. The English redirects that final accusation to another person.
records.remedy: Keep the self-reproach: 'I'm such an idiot!'

highlights.text: You are so stupid

records.jp: 「ま、まったくですな」
records.en: Taichi: "Da-, damn if it does."
records.assessment: The source is a stammered, polite agreement, roughly 'W-well, quite.' The English idiom instead emphatically denies the proposition and adds profanity, reversing polarity and register.
records.remedy: Use a stammered formal agreement such as 'W-well, quite.'

highlights.text: damn if it does

records.jp: 「それで、今朝はどうしました？」
records.en: Misato: "Well then, what are you here for on this morning?"
records.assessment: The time phrase is ungrammatical in English. The source simply asks what brought him there that morning.
records.remedy: Use 'this morning' without 'on.'

highlights.text: on this morning

records.jp: 「昨日依頼された原稿をお届けに参りました」
records.en: Taichi: "I impose to deliver the hand-written script requested of me yesterday."
comments: Hyperformal. -GHS
records.assessment: The verb phrase is not idiomatic English and makes the delivery action difficult to parse. The source formally says he has come to deliver the manuscript requested the previous day.
records.remedy: Use 'I've come to deliver the manuscript you requested yesterday.'

highlights.text: I impose to deliver

records.jp: 「ぺけくん、すごいです。見違えました」
records.en: Misato: "Peke-kun, that is amazing! That is beyond recognition!"
comments: That's way not meant flatteringly, see CCC4019 for more. -GHS
records.assessment: The source praises the addressee with an idiom meaning she can hardly recognize how much he has improved. The English demonstrative instead appears to describe the manuscript as unrecognizable.
records.remedy: Make the addressee explicit, for example 'I hardly recognize you.'

highlights.text: That is beyond recognition

records.jp: 「いやあ～」
records.en: Taichi: "Naaa～h!"
records.assessment: The source is a bashful, self-effacing reaction akin to 'Aw, shucks.' The English reads as a drawn-out refusal or denial.
records.remedy: Use a bashful interjection such as 'Aw, shucks.'

highlights.text: Naaa～h

records.jp: 「これにございます」
records.en: Taichi: "I would be most glad."
comments: Still formal. -GHS
records.assessment: The source formally presents the manuscript: 'Here it is.' The English instead expresses willingness or pleasure and omits the presentation action.
records.remedy: Use a formal presentation such as 'Here it is.'

highlights.text: I would be most glad

records.jp: 先輩の瞳が、きっと厳しさを増す。
records.en: Senpai's very pupils sternly grow in severity.
records.assessment: The English construction is unidiomatic and redundantly literal. The source says the senior's gaze or eyes grow distinctly sterner as she reads.
records.remedy: Use 'Senpai's gaze steadily grew sterner.'

highlights.text: pupils sternly grow in severity

records.jp: 用紙の上を軽やかに視線は走った。
records.en: Her gaze ran light over the script paper.
records.assessment: The adverb is malformed in English. The source depicts her gaze moving lightly or briskly across the manuscript.
records.remedy: Use 'Her gaze ran lightly over the manuscript.'

highlights.text: ran light

records.jp: 先輩は顔を上げた。
records.en: Senpai's face lifted.
records.assessment: The source makes Senpai the agent who raises her face or looks up. The English makes her face act independently.
records.remedy: Use 'Senpai looked up.'

highlights.text: Senpai's face lifted

records.jp: 後光を背負って、彼女は言った。
records.en: Her areolar halo a burden, this is what she said:
comments: I wonder if that's a pun with nipples. Sorry, I meant, I WONDER IF THAT'S A PUN WITH NIPPLES. THAT WORD ALSO MEANS 'AREOLA' AFTER ALL. I'd leave it just "areolar", but then it's not obvious enough it's intended to also be a halo. -GHS
records.assessment: The source says she spoke with a halo or radiance behind her. The English introduces an anatomical sense of 'areolar' and an unsupported burden, corrupting the image.
records.remedy: Use 'With a halo shining behind her, she said:'

highlights.text: areolar halo a burden

records.jp: 「期待してます」
records.en: Misato: "I am expecting it."
comments: Suuubtle insult. -GHS
records.assessment: The source is an encouraging 'I'm looking forward to it' or 'I'm counting on you.' The English is an unnatural calque that can imply mere prediction.
records.remedy: Use 'I'm looking forward to it.'

highlights.text: I am expecting it

records.jp: すごすごと校舎に戻る。
records.en: Dejected I return to inside the building.
records.assessment: The directional phrase is ungrammatical. The source says he trudges dejectedly back into the school building.
records.remedy: Use 'I trudged dejectedly back into the school building.'

highlights.text: return to inside

records.jp: と、先輩が小首をかしげた瞬間。
records.en: And, the very instant that Senpai tilted her neck,
records.assessment: The literal body-part choice is unnatural and changes the conventional gesture. The source says she cocked or tilted her head.
records.remedy: Use 'cocked her head.'

highlights.text: tilted her neck

records.jp: 先輩が起きた。
records.en: Senpai had woken.
records.assessment: The source narrates the immediate event in simple past: Senpai woke up. The English past perfect incorrectly subordinates it to a later past reference point.
records.remedy: Use 'Senpai woke up.'

highlights.text: had woken

records.jp: 「わたし確か」
records.en: Misato: "I have been..."
records.assessment: The source is an interrupted recollection, 'I think I...' or 'I was sure...' The English substitutes a bare perfect-progressive auxiliary and loses the act of remembering.
records.remedy: Use an incomplete recollection such as 'I think I...'

highlights.text: I have been

records.jp: 素に戻り言う。
records.en: She returns to the topic and says,
records.assessment: The source says she returns to her normal, unaffected self before speaking. The English instead claims she returns to the subject of conversation.
records.remedy: Use 'Returning to her usual self, she says,'

highlights.text: returns to the topic

records.jp: 「手当してもらってここに」
records.en: Taichi: "You then received medical services here."
records.assessment: The source says she was treated and then brought here. The English relocates the treatment to the present location and omits the transfer.
records.remedy: Use 'You were treated and brought here.'

highlights.text: received medical services here

records.jp: 「怪我したんですか、わたし？」
records.en: Misato: "So I was injured, was I?
records.assessment: The English dialogue lacks its closing quotation mark, leaving the presentation structurally incomplete.
records.remedy: Add the closing quotation mark after the question mark.

highlights.text: was I?

records.jp: あちこちに張られた絆創膏。
records.en: the bandages affixed in a spread all over.
records.assessment: The phrase is not idiomatic English. The source describes adhesive bandages stuck here and there over her body.
records.remedy: Use 'adhesive bandages stuck here and there.'

highlights.text: affixed in a spread all over

records.jp: 「全身に軽い打撲とか、あるんで」
records.en: Taichi: "You got light bruises all over, that is why."
records.assessment: The causal phrase has no stated result and leaves the sentence dangling. The source is a fragment explaining that she has light bruises and similar injuries all over.
records.remedy: Use 'You've got light bruises and such all over.'

highlights.text: that is why

records.jp: むちむちした大腿部が露出した。むちむち。
records.en: A femoral region plump and voluptuous got exposed. Plump and voluptuous.
comments: Uh-oh x2 -GHS
records.assessment: The source plainly and insistently describes a plump thigh. The clinical anatomical phrase is a large, unsupported register shift that suppresses the comic repetition.
records.remedy: Use 'A plump, fleshy thigh was exposed. Plump and fleshy.'

highlights.text: femoral region

records.jp: 「ほら、このむちむちした太股のとこ、ちょっとささったとですよ。だから今日は部活の方も休んでご自愛いただいてですね……」
records.en: Taichi: "Look at this plump and voluptuous thigh, it got all pockmarked! So, today you are taking a break from club activities and taking care of yourself..."
records.assessment: The source says the thigh was pierced or pricked a little. 'All pockmarked' invents numerous pits and exaggerates the injury.
records.remedy: Use 'it got pricked a little.'

highlights.text: all pockmarked

records.jp: ぱくぱくと口を開閉させる。
records.en: Pak-pak, she makes her mouth open and close.
comments: IT'S PACMAN VS. SINISTAR BITCHES! ALL! BETS! ARE! OFF!!! See CCA3004 -GHSeriousNoReally
records.assessment: The Japanese mimetic is copied into English without an intelligible equivalent. The source depicts her opening and closing her mouth soundlessly.
records.remedy: Use an English description such as 'Her mouth opens and closes like a fish's.'

highlights.text: Pak-pak

records.jp: 「包帯、かえときます？」
records.en: Taichi. "Should I refresh the dressing?"
records.assessment: The speaker label ends with a period rather than the established dialogue delimiter, creating a visible presentation error.
records.remedy: Change 'Taichi.' to 'Taichi:'

highlights.text: Taichi.

records.jp: カクカク頷く。
records.en: Two sharp nods.
comments: She seems frightened and she's not talking anymore. Whatever went wrong, it already went wrong. -GHS
records.assessment: The source depicts repeated jerky nodding but does not specify exactly two nods. The English adds a precise count without support.
records.remedy: Use 'She nods jerkily.'

highlights.text: Two sharp nods

records.jp: 包帯を持ってきて、取り替える。
records.en: I bring some gauze and go to refresh.
records.assessment: The English leaves 'refresh' without an object and does not clearly state that the bandage is replaced. The source explicitly says he brings a bandage and changes it.
records.remedy: Use 'I bring a fresh bandage and replace the old one.'

highlights.text: go to refresh

records.jp: 「色っぽいおみ足で」
records.en: Taichi: "Aren't your legs so sexy."
records.assessment: The English uses interrogative syntax with declarative punctuation and sounds malformed. The source is an admiring comment on her alluring legs.
records.remedy: Use 'What sexy legs you have.'

highlights.text: Aren't your legs so sexy.

records.jp: 流れ出てしまうなんて。
records.en: is leaking out without end.
records.assessment: The source expresses dismay that such beautiful blood is flowing out; it does not say the flow is endless. The English adds unsupported duration.
records.remedy: Use 'to think it's flowing out like this.'

highlights.text: without end

records.jp: 目眩を感じて、目を閉じた。
records.en: Feeling dizzy, I close the eyes.
comments: Dizzy's written with eye, dazzle. Interesting considering he claims he has eyeshine. -GHS
records.assessment: English requires a possessive here because the narrator closes his own eyes. The source makes that subject clear.
records.remedy: Use 'I close my eyes.'

highlights.text: close the eyes

records.jp: 蠢くものたちは、触れるだけで赤くなる。
records.en: All these squirming little thingies turn red with just a touch.
comments: Humans. Or genitals. -GHS
records.assessment: The diminutive, flippant noun is unsupported by the neutral source phrase for writhing or moving things and weakens the altered-state register.
records.remedy: Use 'The writhing things turn red at a touch.'

highlights.text: little thingies

records.jp: 全ての感覚が強化され、不可視のものが見えるようになる。
records.en: All the senses strengthen, so that what is invisible becomes as visible.
comments: Being able to see what's not there is not a superpower; it's hallucinating. -GHS
records.assessment: The comparative particle has no complement and makes the result clause ungrammatical. The source says invisible things become visible.
records.remedy: Use 'what is invisible becomes visible.'

highlights.text: becomes as visible

records.jp: 意識が切り替わる感覚。
records.en: and I feel my awareness being completely replaced.
comments: See CCC3012A on this. -GHS
records.assessment: The source describes the sensation of consciousness switching modes. The English intensifies this into complete replacement, asserting a stronger ontological change than the text supports.
records.remedy: Use 'the sensation of my consciousness switching over.'

highlights.text: completely replaced

records.jp: 動く。
records.en: Motion.
records.assessment: The source is a verb, 'Move' or 'I move.' The English turns the action into an isolated abstract noun.
records.remedy: Use 'I move.'

highlights.text: Motion

records.jp: どこからが自分で、そうでないかがわからない。
records.en: A sense of self off from somewhere doesn't understand whether it isn't.
comments: Oddly ambiguous. I suspect this ties to CCX0001. -GHS
records.assessment: The English is syntactically incoherent and does not convey the source distinction between self and non-self. The source says he cannot tell where he ends and what is not him begins.
records.remedy: Use 'I can't tell where I end and what isn't me begins.'

highlights.text: A sense of self off from somewhere doesn't understand whether it isn't

records.jp: ノイズ。
records.en: Interference. Noise. White noise.
comments: Describing this a little because it is VERY specific in Japanese, not so in English. Makes slightly more sense with the edit at the end of CCC3025. This is what he uses to censor the bad stuff; and yet, he's currently in Wrong Mode, isn't he? Even odder at the end of the character vignettes at the end of every Sendback route, where this is his disconnection with the character. -GHS
records.assessment: The source contains only the single word 'Noise.' The English expands it into three distinct technical descriptions, two of which are unsupported interpretations.
records.remedy: Use the single word 'Noise.'

highlights.text: Interference. Noise. White noise.

records.jp: 何か現象があったらしい。
records.en: There's a phenomenon of sort, it seems.
records.assessment: The source says some phenomenon apparently occurred. The English uses present existence instead of a past event and contains an ungrammatical singular phrase.
records.remedy: Use 'Apparently, some phenomenon occurred.'

highlights.text: There's a phenomenon of sort

records.jp: 詳細はわからない。
records.en: The details I don't understand.
records.assessment: The topical inversion is unnatural in English. The source simply says the narrator does not know the details.
records.remedy: Use 'I don't know the details.'

highlights.text: The details I don't understand

records.jp: 体感できない。
records.en: Cannot feel my own body.
records.assessment: In context, the source says the phenomenon cannot be experienced or perceived directly. The English instead asserts that the narrator cannot feel his own body, supplying a different object.
records.remedy: Use 'I can't feel it directly.'

highlights.text: feel my own body

records.jp: 世界と一体化した、その全能感だけがすべてだ。
records.en: It has integrated with the world, and that sole feeling of omnipotence is now everything.
comments: See CCX0001. -GHS
records.assessment: The source describes the narrator's sense of omnipotence from becoming one with the world. The English assigns the integration to an unexplained 'it' and loses the narrator as experiencer.
records.remedy: Use 'That sense of omnipotence from becoming one with the world is everything.'

highlights.text: It has integrated with the world

records.jp: その矛盾が、視野の狭窄と改変をもたらす。
records.en: That contradiction brings a stricture and a change of the field of view.
comments: He's going back to focusing, maybe. -GHS
records.assessment: The source uses the ordinary visual term 'narrowing' or 'constriction.' 'Stricture' is a specialized anatomical or regulatory noun and is miscollocated with a field of view.
records.remedy: Use 'narrowing and alteration of the field of vision.'

highlights.text: stricture

records.jp: 現世とは異なる法則・衝動・配列に従って本能を構築した獣だ。
records.en:
It's a beast constructed of instincts, abiding by
laws - urges - priorities in contrast with the present age.
comments: Ah, it's '98 game beginning? -GHS
records.assessment: The source contrasts the beast's laws with those of this world or the mortal world, not with a historical present age. The English changes the axis from ontological difference to time period.
records.remedy: Use 'different from those of this world.'

highlights.text: in contrast with the present age

records.jp: 意識をこらせ。
records.en: Apply awareness.
records.assessment: The imperative is not idiomatic English. The source commands the self to concentrate or focus its consciousness.
records.remedy: Use 'Focus your awareness.'

highlights.text: Apply awareness

records.jp: 聞き取れ。
records.en: Listen.
records.assessment: The source commands the self to make out or catch the sound, not merely to listen. The English drops the successful-perception component in the command sequence.
records.remedy: Use 'Make it out.'

highlights.text: Listen

records.jp: 解読しろ。
records.en: Decypher.
records.assessment: The English word is misspelled.
records.remedy: Use 'Decipher.'

highlights.text: Decypher

records.jp: 宮澄見里。
records.en:
Miya - palace
Sumi - clarity
Mi   - looking
Sato - village
Miyasumi Misato.
comments: Astonishing, I know, in fact, functionally impossible, but... this doesn't work with furries. -GHS
records.assessment: The source unit states only the character's name, with a pronunciation note in the source apparatus. The English inserts an unmarked four-line semantic decomposition of the written name.
records.remedy: Retain the name without the unmarked kanji-gloss expansion.

highlights.text:
Miya - palace
Sumi - clarity
Mi   - looking
Sato - village

records.jp: 『いつもお一人なんですね』
records.en: 『You are always alone, are you.』
comments: Removed the speaker tag, centred. -GHS
records.assessment: The English tag question is malformed and punctuated as a statement. The source observes that the addressee is always alone and seeks confirmation.
records.remedy: Use 'You're always alone, aren't you?'

highlights.text: are you.

records.jp: 『一緒に、部活しませんか？』
records.en: 『Will you not have club together with me?』
records.assessment: The phrase is not idiomatic English and obscures the invitation. The source asks whether he would like to do club activities together or join her club.
records.remedy: Use 'Would you like to do club activities together?'

highlights.text: have club together

records.jp: 視界がクリアに。
records.en: The sight line implements clearness.
comments: Intentionally off. Don't blink now, or you'll miss like a third of the VN. See CCZAS. -GHS
records.assessment: The English is syntactically and semantically incoherent. The source simply says the narrator's vision clears.
records.remedy: Use 'My vision clears.'

highlights.text: The sight line implements clearness

records.jp: 頭痛がする。
records.en: Headache ensues.
records.assessment: The source states that the narrator has a headache. The English removes the experiencer and recasts it as an impersonal event in an unsupported formal register.
records.remedy: Use 'My head hurts.'

highlights.text: Headache ensues

records.jp: 「まったくもー……」
records.en: Taichi: "Dammit, really..."
records.assessment: The source is an exasperated 'Honestly' or 'Good grief.' The English adds profanity and sharpens the irritation.
records.remedy: Use 'Honestly...' or 'Good grief...'

highlights.text: Dammit

records.jp: このタイミングで。
records.en: This timing it has to have.
records.assessment: The English is incoherent. The source laments that the episode is happening at this particular moment, roughly 'Of all times.'
records.remedy: Use 'Of all times...'

highlights.text: This timing it has to have

records.jp: 血と夕日の組み合わせは、本当に良くない。
records.en: Blood and sunset assembled are truly not a good thing.
comments: Same word for putting together the antenna. -GHS
records.assessment: The source refers to the combination of blood and sunset. 'Assembled' incorrectly describes objects deliberately put together and produces an unnatural predicate.
records.remedy: Use 'The combination of blood and sunset is really bad.'

highlights.text: assembled

records.jp: 泣きそう。
records.en: It's to cry.
records.assessment: The English is ungrammatical and removes the narrator as experiencer. The source says he feels as though he might cry.
records.remedy: Use 'I feel like crying.'

highlights.text: It's to cry

records.jp: 「いやー、困ったもんですね。わはは」
records.en: Taichi: "Well, looks like I troubled you. Wahahah!"
records.assessment: The source calls the situation troublesome or a problem. The English instead says the narrator caused the addressee trouble, changing the subject and relation.
records.remedy: Use 'Well, this is a problem, isn't it? Ha ha.'

highlights.text: looks like I troubled you

records.jp: マイヴィーナス、先輩が泣いていた。
records.en: Mai Venus, Senpai, was crying.
comments: Still off. -GHS
records.assessment: The source uses the English possessive loan 'my' as a comic epithet. Rendering it as 'Mai' makes it look like a personal name and loses the possessive meaning.
records.remedy: Use 'My Venus, Senpai, was crying.'

highlights.text: Mai Venus

records.jp: 徒手空拳の構え。
records.en: I take a posture of empty-handedness.
comments: This very explicitly does NOT contain "karate". -GHS
records.assessment: The source is an established expression for assuming an unarmed fighting stance. The literal abstraction does not convey that he squares up to fight.
records.remedy: Use 'I assume an unarmed fighting stance.'

highlights.text: posture of empty-handedness

records.jp: 「自分に打ち克つのは克己って書くくらいで難しいナァー！！」
records.en: Taichi: "To surmount the self is nearly as difficult as pronouncing the words 'self control'!!!"
comments: 克 vs 支 (from Hasekura), hmmm. About the same difficulty, though "sorry" would prolly be more appropriate. See CCD5001 for where this goes. Given that this scene is the reading key for Taichi's other weirdness, in more ways than one. -GHS
records.assessment: The source jokes that overcoming oneself is so difficult the written word for self-control literally contains the characters for conquering oneself. The English replaces the orthographic joke with pronunciation and changes the comparison.
records.remedy: Preserve the writing-based wordplay, with a concise note if needed.

highlights.text: nearly as difficult as pronouncing

records.jp: 「あ、いつものぺけくんに戻ってる……」
records.en: Misato: "Ah, the Peke-kun of always has returned..."
comments: I wish I could say they're sort of arc words, but "the xxx of always" will barely return after this. -GHS
records.assessment: The noun phrase is an ungrammatical calque. The source says he has returned to his usual self.
records.remedy: Use 'Ah, the usual Peke-kun is back...'

highlights.text: the Peke-kun of always has returned

records.jp: 跪く。
records.en: On a bent knee.
comments: Lit. just to kneel, but look at the lavish of furries and that purple up there! He's still gone. And he's totally hiding his erection. -GHS
records.assessment: The source narrates the action 'I kneel.' The English gives only a prepositional fragment and does not state the action.
records.remedy: Use 'I kneel.'

highlights.text: On a bent knee

records.jp: 「ワタクシメのカラデがご入り用ですか？」
records.en: Taichi: "Dost ye have need of your worthless servant's Karade?"
comments: Shakespearian-ish stuff should be correct. If it isn't, it's Taichi's fault, not mine (hey, if the author can say it...) -GHS
records.assessment: The deliberately grandiose register can be preserved, but this auxiliary-pronoun combination is ungrammatical: 'dost' takes 'thou,' while 'ye' takes 'do.'
records.remedy: Use 'Dost thou...' or 'Do ye...'

highlights.text: Dost ye

records.jp: 「カラデとかいうわけのわからない格闘技はどうでもいいのですが……」
records.en: Misato: "That martial art of meaning incomprehensible you call Karade is quite beside the point, however..."
comments: See CCC0016A. A little off, IMO, but it's more important the two characters say the same thing. -GHS
records.assessment: The modifier is ungrammatical English. The source calls Karade an incomprehensible martial art.
records.remedy: Use 'That incomprehensible martial art you call Karade...'

highlights.text: of meaning incomprehensible

records.jp: 「そんな感じです」
records.en: Misato: "That is what it felt."
records.assessment: The complement requires 'like' in English. The source means 'Something like that.'
records.remedy: Use 'Something like that.'

highlights.text: what it felt

records.jp: 「……もう平気ですか？」
records.en: Taichi: "...are you alright now?"
records.assessment: The canonical source assigns this question to the other speaker. The English speaker label attributes it to Taichi and reverses who checks on whom.
records.remedy: Assign the line to Misato.

highlights.text: Taichi:

records.jp: 先輩の下肢を（今度は下心なく）白日にさらした時。
records.en: Time to bring Senpai's lower extremities to the light (this time without ulterior motives).
records.assessment: The source is a temporal subordinate clause: 'When I exposed Senpai's lower limbs to the light...' The English turns it into a malformed declaration that it is time to act.
records.remedy: Use 'When I exposed Senpai's lower legs to the light...'

highlights.text: Time to bring

records.jp: 何者かが、傷口を食いちぎろうとしたようにも見える。
records.en: It looks as if someone or something wanted to bite off the mouth of that wound.
comments: The 'a someone' of CCA0016 -GHS
